--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page serves as the preface to the French edition of the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili. The translator, Jacques Gohory, introduces the work and discusses the mystery of its true author, Francesco Colonna, and the complex nature of the book's symbolism.</meta>

->Jacques Gohory of Paris sends greetings to the Reader.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'O' at the start of the text, featuring classical foliage, scrolled vines, and floral motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

This marvelous work, Reader, is by Francesco Colonna, who assumed the name of "Poliphilo" <note>original: "Poliphili nomen ementiti". Poliphilo translates to "lover of many things" or "lover of Polia".</note>. I believe he did this either so that, by remaining hidden during his life, he might hear the honest judgments of men regarding himself—just as the painter Apelles used to do—or because, following the example of the architect from Cnidus, he placed his hope for praise and glory in the opinion of posterity rather than in his own age. For, just as that architect had inscribed his own name, "Sostratus of Cnidus, son of Dexiphanes," into a notable stone of the Pharos lighthouse at Alexandria, and then covered it with a thin, crumbling layer of plaster bearing the name of the Egyptian King; so too has this author left his name silently noted in the first letters of each chapter. <note>These initial letters form an acrostic: **POLIAM FRATER FRANCISCVS COLVMNA PERAMAVIT**, which translates to: "Brother Francesco Colonna passionately loved Polia."</note>

His language clearly proves he is Italian by birth. By his surname, he seems to assert that he belongs to the family of the Colonna <note>original: "Columniū". The Colonna were a powerful Roman noble family.</note>, from that illustrious house (I believe) which carries on an eternal enmity with the bears <note>A reference to the Orsini family, the long-standing rivals of the Colonna; "Orsini" is derived from "ursa," meaning bear.</note>. His style is entirely new, perhaps devised by him in this manner and forged from a certain mixture of the Greek, Latin, and Tuscan tongues. He did this so that his divine wisdom might reach the understanding of many peoples, and also for the sake of his own memory, as if consecrating himself to immortality through various enduring monuments. 

Some say it is in the interest of the state that the secrets hidden beneath these coverings of architecture and ceremony should not be known by the common people. Instead, they should be reserved only for those initiated into the sacred mysteries of a higher philosophy, who have hidden themselves away in the contemplation of obscure things. Indeed, a dream of this kind—with its forest, its fountain, its monster, the darkness and difficulty of the path, the series of labors, the <term>hieroglyphic characters</term> <note>At this time, "hieroglyphics" referred to symbolic pictures believed to contain hidden wisdom, rather than the literal Egyptian writing system.</note>, and finally the delay in attaining Polia—all claim this book for a certain great and recondite art.

A Knight of Malta, a man of ready and cultivated talent, had first drafted an outline of this work and had strongly requested that I read it carefully. But when the fortune of each of us soon led us away from here, my friend Jean Martin <note>original: "Ianus Martinus"</note> took up the task of polishing the work, at the request of the noble printer Jacques Kerver. It is indeed filled with such a wealth and variety of excellent things that even the most learned cannot regret how much they may profit from reading it.

FAREWELL.

<summary>Jacques Gohory introduces Francesco Colonna as the hidden author of the work, revealed via a secret acrostic, and explains the book's complex blend of languages and architectural allegories.</summary>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page follows the preface by Jacques Gohory. While Gohory introduced the mystery of the author Francesco Colonna, this page contains the formal dedication by Jean Martin, the influential French Renaissance translator and editor who saw this edition through to publication.</meta>

# TO THE LORD, MY LORD THE

->*Count of Nanteuil-le-Haudouin, Sir Henry de Lenoncourt,*<-
->*Knight of the Order, Governor of Valois, and Captain of*<-
->*fifty men-at-arms.*<-

---

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop-cap 'M' set within a rectangular frame. The letter is decorated with Renaissance-style strapwork and foliage motifs.</image-desc>
My Lord, although I know your lordship is continually occupied with the great affairs in which it pleases the King's Majesty to employ you, so much so that there remains for you little or no time to devote to matters of pleasure, I shall not fear to dedicate to you this *Poliphilo*. This work was composed in Italy in the year one thousand four hundred and sixty-seven by a learned gentleman of an illustrious house, and was recently translated into French by another virtuous gentleman of good knowledge. His translation was given to me by a friend of mine so that I might revise it and lend a hand in bringing it to light—a task which I believe I have performed as faithfully as I would wish someone to do for me, should I happen to leave any of my own undertakings unfinished. 

The reasons (My Lord) that move me to dedicate it to you are, in the first place, that in many of its passages it treats so naturally <note>original: "nayvement". In this context, it means with lifelike accuracy or vividness.</note> of architecture or the art of building well, that it is hardly possible to do better. Therefore, I am of the opinion that it is due to you, considering that you take as much pleasure in it as a lord of your quality could, as you have effectively shown in your beautiful building at Nanteuil. You yourself designed the arrangements <note>original: "ordonnances". Martin is referring to the architectural plans and the classical "Orders" (columns and proportions).</note> for it, which are so convenient and so well-conceived that there is no architect in this Kingdom today who would not consider it a masterpiece if such or similar inventions had come from his own mind. 

The second cause is that this book is so abundant in singular and diverse things that we have no author in our language who can currently be compared to it; and you take marvelous delight in hearing such readings when your convenience allows it. Then the third and principal reason is so that this *Poliphilo* does not go wandering through the world like an orphan <note>original: "pupille". This term refers to a minor under the care of a guardian; Martin is seeking a patron to protect the book from critics.</note> destitute of a protector, but rather that, under your endorsement and safeguard, he may be received into the houses of great lords and gentlemen who bear you friendship, with as welcoming a face as one is accustomed to receive things that come from friends. 

Be then favorable to him, My Lord, and take him (if you please) as humanely from me who presents him to you, as this gift is made to you with very humble and entire affection. With which I pray the Creator to give you, My Lord, in perfect health, a very long and very happy life. From Paris, this 14th day of August, 1546.

->Your very humble and very obedient<-
->servant Jean Martin.<-

<summary>Jean Martin dedicates the French edition of Poliphilo's story to Henry de Lenoncourt, praising the nobleman's own architectural skill shown at Nanteuil as the reason for the gift.</summary>
<keywords>Jean Martin, Henry de Lenoncourt, Nanteuil-le-Haudouin, architecture, Renaissance patronage, book dedication, 1546</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory material for the 1546 French edition of the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*. Having previously dedicated the work to the Count of Nanteuil, Jean Martin now addresses the general readership, providing a concise summary of the fantastical plot and the architectural wonders described in the book.</meta>

# JEAN MARTIN, SECRETARY TO MY
## LORD the Most Reverend Cardinal of Lenoncourt.
### TO THE READERS.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting classical Renaissance foliate scrolls and architectural motifs.</image-desc>If you desire (My Lords) to understand in few words what is contained in this work, know that Poliphilo <note>The name Poliphilo is derived from Greek, meaning "lover of many things" or "lover of Polia."</note> says he saw admirable things in a dream, among which he describes several antiquities worthy of memory, such as Pyramides, Obelisks, great ruins of buildings, the variety of columns, their measurements, pedestals, bases, and capitals with which they are adorned. Then the architraves, friezes, cornices, and frontispieces with their craftsmanship. A great horse, an Elephant of marvelous size, a Colossus, and a magnificent gate, with its plan, arrangement, moldings, and stonework. Afterwards, how five beautiful Nymphs led him to the baths: and meanwhile he does not forget to make mention of an excellent fountain. Further, he describes the Palace of Queen Eleutherilide <note>Her name is derived from the Greek "Eleutheria," meaning Liberty.</note>: who for love of him had a solemn feast prepared, in which one can learn many things beneficial to human health. After this, he specifies the diversity of precious stones, with their natural virtues: the pastime of a dance: and consequently illustrates three gardens, of which one is made of glass, the other of silk, and the third made as a Labyrinth surrounded by a Peristyle <term>Peristyle: a continuous porch formed by a row of columns surrounding a courtyard or garden.</term> or environment of columns made of terracotta. In the middle of this peristyle is situated a pyramid engraved with Egyptian characters, which are called Hieroglyphic letters <note>In the Renaissance, "hieroglyphics" were viewed as mystical symbols of universal wisdom rather than a phonetic language.</note>. Departing from there, he goes to the three gates, and enters through the middle one, where he finds his beloved Polia, whose beauty, grace, and the fashion of her clothing he expresses. This Polia shows him four triumphs of the great Jupiter: then shows him the mortal ladies with whom the gods were in love: together with the beloveds of the Poets: and there one recognizes the affections and various effects of love. After follows the triumph of Vertumnus and Pomona <note>Roman deities of the changing seasons and fruit trees.</note>, together with the great god of the gardens <note>Referring to Priapus, the god of fertility and gardens.</note> with his sacrifices: and that said, the author comes to describe a temple made of rich materials, and constructed with great skill, where several other sacrifices are performed following the order of ancient religion and ceremonies. These being completed, Polia leads her Poliphilo to the seashore to await the coming of the god Cupid: and meanwhile she persuades him to go see the antiquities which are in a destroyed temple: which he does: and finds there a great number of Epitaphs, at which he stops for a long time, until he happens to encounter an Underworld <note>original: "vn Enfer". Martin uses the word for Hell to describe a pagan subterranean realm or catacomb.</note> painted in Mosaic work: looking at which, a sudden terror comes over him, which makes him depart from there, and return to his Polia: to whom he has no sooner arrived, than Cupid appears in a Boat furnished with many exquisite things, and steered by six damsels trained in the office of rowing. Into this Poliphilo and his beloved enter: wherefore Love suddenly sets sail, spreading his golden wings embellished with all colors. During the voyage the sea gods and goddesses, nymphs, Tritons and other monsters do honor and reverence to Cupid, recognizing him as their lord. Finally this god descends on the island of Cythera, which the author describes...

<summary>Jean Martin provides a comprehensive overview of the book's narrative, outlining Poliphilo's journey through architectural marvels, symbolic gardens, and mythological encounters as he seeks his beloved Polia.</summary>
<keywords>Jean Martin, Poliphilo, Polia, architectural theory, Renaissance allegory, Cupid, Hieroglyphics, Cythera</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues Jean Martin’s summary of the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*. Having described the initial architectural wonders and gardens, the text now focuses on the island of Cythera and the narrative transition into the second book, while also commenting on the quality of the translation and its hidden meanings.</meta>

[Poliphilo] describes and distinguishes the island into small thickets, meadows, gardens, rivers, and fountains, in such a way that he has made it more beautiful than the Elysian Fields <note>The paradise of the afterlife in Greek mythology.</note> of which the Greek and Latin poets have made such great mention. There, the amorous Nymphs make several beautiful presents to Cupid, which he receives and accepts: then he proceeds upon a triumphal Chariot to a marvelous Theater situated in the middle of the island, at the center of which is the fountain of Venus, surrounded by seven columns of precious stones. There the author recounts all the mysteries that were performed nearby, then how, for the coming of the god Mars, he and his lady-love were constrained to retire with the Nymphs, who led them to another fountain, near which was the tomb of Adonis, in commemoration of whom the goddess Venus every year has a funeral procession made, and she herself assists, performing the office of Prioress <note>original: "Prieuſe". Martin uses a contemporary religious title for the goddess's role in the pagan rite.</note>. The Nymphs being seated around the foot of this fountain, they request Polia that it be her pleasure to tell them of what race she is descended, and how she became amorous, together with the discourse of her loves, and there ends the first book. In the second, this same Polia, to satisfy the request of the Nymphs, details her kinship entirely to them, and does not fail to say how the city of Treviso <note>original: "Treuiz"</note> was first built. Then she pursues the difficulty there was before she could condescend to become amorous, and then the happy success she has of her loves. Upon which the history finishes with several notable accessories, and Poliphilo awakens at the song of the Nightingale.

You may believe, My Lords, that beneath this fiction there are many good things hidden, which it is not lawful to reveal, and also you would have no pleasure if they were specified to you particularly: for you would never taste the favor of the fruit which can be gathered in this reading: wherefore I will say no other thing to you, but will refer everything to the exercise of your studies. Nonetheless, to make known to you the name of the author, I will indeed say this word in passing, that one must follow from the beginning until the end the capital letters enriched with Arabesque leaves, and those will instruct you of what you desire <note>Martin is referring to the book’s famous acrostic: the first letter of each chapter spells out *POLIAM FRATER FRANCISCVS COLVMNA PERAMAVIT* (Brother Francesco Colonna loved Polia intensely).</note>. Regarding the name of Polia, she herself explains it at the beginning of the second book, where she says she bears the name of the Roman lady who killed herself for having been violated by the son of a proud King <note>A reference to Lucretia, whose suicide after being raped by Sextus Tarquinius led to the founding of the Roman Republic.</note>: and in order to give an understanding of her surname with the ancient nobility of her race, she details the history of one Lelius who was the founder of Treviso in the domain of the Venetians: wishing thereby to infer that she is descended from him. There, My Lords, is all I wish to say of it, except that this book has not had as good a destiny as its subject deserved, because it did not fall at the first stroke into the hands of the true French Cicero, who is Nicolas de Herberay, Lord of Les Essarts, who has made an *Amadis* of Castile <note>Herberay des Essarts was famous for his translation of the chivalric romance *Amadis de Gaule*.</note> recently come into our hands speak so properly, that I do not know if those of our posterity will be able to follow him, much less surpass him. Truly, if this book had at first sight fallen into his hands, and he had wished to employ his style to make it speak our natural tongue, I am of the opinion that it would now be the pearl of all those which for twenty years have been communicated to us in this language: for as for those from before, I do not think one should make much account of them. Nevertheless, I still wish to testify that whoever the gentleman might be who first translated it into our common speech, he is wor[thy]...

<summary>Jean Martin summarizes the plot of the island of Cythera and the second book, while revealing the hidden acrostic that names the author. He also praises the translator Nicolas de Herberay, suggesting the work would be even more perfect had Herberay handled it.</summary>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues Jean Martin’s preface to the French edition of the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili. While the previous page summarized the plot of the second book, Martin here shifts to discussing the technical challenges of the translation and his own role in editing the manuscript provided by an anonymous "gentleman."</meta>

...deserves that one be grateful to him, especially since he extracted it from an Italian language mixed with Greek and Latin, so confusedly put together that the Italians themselves, unless they are more than moderately learned, cannot make sense of it; and furthermore, he has done so much that from a prolixity more than Asiatic <note>In classical rhetoric, "Asiatic" refers to a style that is excessively ornate, wordy, and florid, as opposed to the more restrained "Attic" style.</note>, he has reduced it to a French brevity, which will satisfy many people. But if there are some who are annoyed that I have not entirely restored it according to the Italian: so that they do not blame me, I wish to beg them to understand how I was induced to set my hand to this work.

Immediately after I published <note>original: "mis en lumiere," literally "brought to light."</note> my *Arcadia* by Sannazaro <note>Jacopo Sannazaro (1458–1530) was an Italian poet; Jean Martin published his French translation of Sannazaro's pastoral masterpiece in 1544.</note>, a friend of mine who had the copy of this book brought it to me to share it; and after much discussion, he begged me that for love of him I would be willing to take the charge of revising it. This I granted him, as to one for whom I would wish to do much greater things; and indeed, finding myself at the time with a little leisure, I began in his presence to change not only some spellings <note>original: "ortógraphes"</note> that are no longer in use for us, but furthermore to transpose some words that still retained the Italian phrasing <note>original: "fraze"</note>, so corrupted that truly I am amazed at how this gentleman had been able to manage it so well. Certainly, this made me so scrupulous <note>original: "religieux," here meaning conscientious or devoted to the previous translator's work.</note> toward him that I never wished to amplify or diminish anything in the sentences <note>original: "clauſes"</note> he had fashioned, except occasionally to change their order to make them easier to read. This, my Lords, is how we proceeded with the translation <note>original: "interpretatiõ"</note> and printing of this book, which you will receive, if it pleases you, with as much good affection as that with which it is presented to you.

<meta>catchword: This book</meta>

<summary>Jean Martin explains that he edited an existing rough translation of the work, streamlining its complex "Asiatic" style into clear French while modernizing the spelling and phrasing.</summary>
<keywords>Jean Martin, translation process, Sannazaro, Arcadia, editing, Italian language, Greek and Latin influences, French brevity</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the preliminary matter of the 1546 French edition of the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*. Having explained in the previous prose section how he came to revise the manuscript for a friend, Jean Martin now presents a laudatory poem—likely a "liminary poem"—praising the work’s dual "birth" in Italian and French, and its moral value.</meta>

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'C' at the top left of the poem. The letter is white on a dark rectangular background filled with ornate floral and foliate scrollwork. A small grotesque face is subtly integrated into the design within the curves of the letter.</image-desc>

This book, excellent and new,
Comparable to the works of the ancients,
Tells of all that is beautiful
Upon this fertile and arable earth.
But it would have been a wretched thing,
If its loving second father <note>The "second father" refers to the translator or editor (Jean Martin or his anonymous friend) who "rebirths" the book in French.</note>
Had not, by his helping hand,
Restored it to the world and made it happy.

Poliphile <note>The protagonist and narrator of the story; his name means "lover of Polia" or "lover of many things."</note> first
Gave it what we call its essence:
And the other [editor] secondly
Kept it from death by his power—
Death, which was taking its pleasure
By plunging the book into the river of forgetfulness <note>A reference to Lethe, the river in the Underworld that caused souls to forget their past lives.</note>.
But now he brings it to public knowledge
So that it may be ennobled by praise.

The French will now read it,
They who did not even know it existed in the world:
And they shall speak many praises
Of a friendship chaste, pure, and clean:
When a good heart is founded upon such things,
Only good can come to it;
Whereas he who abounds in lechery
Can never attain honor.

Bacchus <note>In Greek mythology, Bacchus (Dionysus) was "twice-born"—first from his mother Semele and then from the thigh of his father Jupiter.</note> was fathered twice,
As the poets tell us,
And this book speaks with two voices,
At least to those who read it.

Now, since foreigners prize
These two <note>Referring to the original author and the translator.</note>, I would be quite mistaken—
And would say the very stars are against us—
If this discourse were not well received.

<note>original: "Poliphile" — the lover/protagonist; "Bacchus" — the god of wine/rebirth; "congnoissance" — knowledge/recognition; "louenges" — praises; "loz ennobly" — ennobled by fame/praise; "munde" — pure/clean (from Latin *mundus*).</note>

<summary>This page contains a commendatory poem celebrating the French translation of the Hypnerotomachia, comparing its rebirth in a new language to the double-birth of the god Bacchus. It frames the book as a moral work that promotes chaste friendship over lasciviousness.</summary>
<keywords>Jean Martin, Poliphile, Bacchus, rebirth, translation, French Renaissance, virtue vs. vice, liminary verse</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface of the 1546 French edition of the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*. The previous page concluded a poem praising the work’s restoration into French. Here, Jean Martin—the book's editor and polisher—explains the linguistic challenges of the original text and how he came to work on the manuscript provided by a friend. The catchword "Ce liure" (This book) from the previous page connects to the beginning of the poem, while this prose section continues the formal address to the readers and patrons.</meta>

[He] deserves that one be grateful to him, especially since he extracted it from an Italian language mixed with Greek and Latin, so confusedly put together that even the Italians themselves, unless they are more than moderately learned, cannot derive any meaning from it; and furthermore, he has done so much that from a verbosity more than Asiatic <note>Jean Martin refers to "Asiatic" style, a rhetorical term used since antiquity to describe a prose style that is overly ornate, wordy, and florid. He contrasts this with "French brevity," reflecting the Renaissance desire to make the French language appear clearer and more refined.</note>, he has reduced it to a French brevity that will satisfy many people. But if there are some who are annoyed that I have not entirely restored it according to the Italian, so that they do not blame me for it, I wish to beg them to understand how I was induced to set my hand to this work.

-><-

Immediately after I had published my *Arcadia* <note>Jacopo Sannazaro's *Arcadia* (1504) was a highly influential pastoral work. Jean Martin’s French translation was published in 1544, helping establish his reputation as a translator of Italian literature.</note> by Sannazaro, a friend of mine who had the copy of this book <note>The book in question is the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*, which had been circulating in an anonymous French draft before Martin took it over.</note> brought it to me to share it with me, and after much discussion, prayed that for the love of him I would take the charge of revising it. This I granted him, as to one for whom I would wish to do much greater things; and in fact, finding myself for the hour with a little leisure, I began in his presence to change not only some spellings that are no longer in use for us, but moreover to transpose some words that still retained the Italian phrasing—so corrupted <note>The original Italian text of the *Poliphilo* is famously written in a "macaronic" or "Polyglot" style, mixing Latin and Greek syntax with Italian, which Martin found awkward for a French audience.</note> that truly I am amazed how this gentleman had been able to manage it so well. And certainly, this made me so scrupulous <note>Martin uses the word "religieux" (religious) here in the sense of being meticulous or duty-bound to respect the original translator's effort.</note> toward him that I never wanted to amplify or diminish anything in the clauses he had made, except occasionally to change their order to make them easier to read. This, my Lords, is how the interpretation and printing of this book proceeded; which you will receive, if it please you, with as much good affection as it is presented to you.

<summary>Jean Martin explains that he edited an anonymous gentleman's draft of the book to smooth out its "corrupted" Italianate phrasing and excessive wordiness, aiming for a clearer French style. He clarifies that he was motivated by a friend's request and a desire to make the difficult, multilingual original text accessible to French readers.</summary>
<keywords>Jean Martin, translation theory, Italian influence, Jacopo Sannazaro, Arcadia, Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, linguistics, Renaissance French, editing</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory material for the 1546 French edition of the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*. The previous page described Jean Martin's role in editing and "polishing" the text from its original, complex mix of languages into refined French. This page features a poem—likely written by Jean Martin or a contemporary admirer—praising the work’s "rebirth" in the French tongue and comparing its dual authorship (original creator and French translator) to the mythological double-birth of Bacchus.</meta>

<sig>a iiii</sig>

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'C' decorated with foliate scrolls and intertwined ribbons.</image-desc>

This excellent and new book,
Comparable to those of the ancients,
Tells of everything that is beautiful
Upon this fertile and arable earth.
But it would have been in a wretched state,
If its loving second father <note>The "second father" refers to Jean Martin, the translator and editor who "rebirthed" the text into French after it was left in a rough state by an anonymous translator.</note>
Had not, by his helping hand,
Restored it to the world and made it happy.

Poliphile <note>The protagonist and titular character of the book, often associated here with the original author (widely believed to be Francesco Colonna).</note> first
Gave it what is called its essence:
And the other [the translator], secondly,
Guarded it from death by his power;
For death was taking its pleasure
By plunging the book into the river of forgetfulness <note>A reference to the Lethe, the river in the underworld that caused souls to forget their past lives.</note>.
But he brings it back into knowledge
So that it may be ennobled by praise.

Frenchmen will now read it,
Who did not think it existed in the world:
And many praises will be said
Of chaste, pure, and clean friendship:
On which, when a good heart is founded,
Only good can come to it;
Whereas he who abounds in lewdness
Cannot attain any honor.

Bacchus <note>In Greek and Roman mythology, Bacchus (Dionysus) was "twice-born"—first from his mother Semele and later from the thigh of his father, Jupiter. The poem uses this as a metaphor for the book's original Italian creation and its French translation.</note> was sired twice,
As the poets tell us,
And this book speaks with two voices,
At least to those who read it.

Now, since foreigners prize
These two, I would be quite deceived—
And would say the stars are ill-aligned—
If its discourse is not well-received.

<summary>This page contains a celebratory poem honoring the French publication of the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*, crediting the translator as a "second father" who saved the work from oblivion. It uses the myth of Bacchus's double birth to justify the translator's heavy hand in reshaping the original text for a French audience.</summary>

<meta>This page follows the introductory poems from the 1546 French edition of the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*. Having previously established the role of Jean Martin in translating and "polishing" the text, the book now presents a tribute to the original author, Francesco Colonna, through a sonnet provided in both Italian and French. This framing emphasizes the book’s transition from its Italian roots to its new life as a masterpiece of French literature.</meta>

# SONNET.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring the letter amidst ornate floral and foliate patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

Behold the tall Column <note>The word *Colonna* is a pun on the name of the presumed author, Francesco Colonna. The poem treats him as the pillar supporting the weight of ancient knowledge.</note> that supported
That beautiful model of ancient memory—
Every figure, every structure, and building:
And contained various forms of signs <note>original: "segni." This refers to the mysterious hieroglyphs and symbolic ornaments found throughout the book.</note>.

What a thousand eyes, and thousands upon thousands of pens
Have seen and written with great toil,
Is all explained here in a brief dream—
A dream, I mean, that happened to the author.

O crude minds, who are only men in part:
And you who are intent on base profit,
These pages are heavy burdens to you <note>The poem warns that the book is intellectually demanding and will not appeal to those interested only in money or shallow pursuits.</note>.

O pure spirits, and noble Frenchmen:
By God, see in these learned pages
How much genius and art are worth and can achieve.

->Heaven, not just earth.<- <note>original: "Cœlum, non solum." A Latin motto suggesting that the work's themes are divine or celestial, rather than merely worldly.</note>

## EXPLANATION OF THIS SONNET.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' with intricate scrolling acanthus leaves and floral motifs in a square frame.</image-desc>

See here the most lofty column,
Where the most ancient knowledge is recorded.
Every line, every plan, every work beautiful and good,
And many a fragment is well applied there.

What a thousand eyes and hands have practiced
With great labor, is given in this book
Easily, explained through discourse
Under a brief dream, which the author ordains.

O coarse spirits whom reason abandons,
And you intent on miserable gain,
This book is such that its value <note>original: "prix." This word carries the double meaning of the financial cost of the book and its intrinsic worth.</note> astonishes you.

But O Frenchmen, fair and prudent spirits,
See how much can be achieved in a person
By art and spirit when they are in harmony.

### Of the sleep that took Poliphilo, and how

->IT SEEMED TO HIM WHILE SLEEPING THAT HE<-
->*was in a desert land, then in a dark forest.*<-

---

<margin>Agrypnia is the wakefulness caused by illness or fantasy.</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorative historiated initial 'P' featuring intricate leaf and vine scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>
ON an April morning around the break of day, I, Poliphilo <note>His name translates from Greek as "Lover of Many Things" or "Lover of Polia"</note>, was in my bed, with no other company than my loyal guardian Agrypnia, who had kept me through the whole night in various conversations and taken pains to comfort me: for I had declared to her the cause of my sighs. At last, as the only remedy, she advised me to forget all these troubles and cease my grieving: then, knowing that it was the hour when I ought to rest, she took her leave and left me alone. Therefore, I remained fantasizing, consuming the rest of the night in thinking to myself. If love is never equal, how is it possible to love that which does not love? And in what manner can a poor, doubtful soul resist, being struck by so many assaults? Especially considering that the war is internal, and the enemies are familiar and domestic, along with being continually occupied by very fickle opinions. After this, there came to my memory the miserable condition of lovers, who, to please others, desire to die sweetly; and to satisfy themselves, are content to live in discomfort, not sating their famished desire except with vain, dangerous, and painful imaginations. I worked so much at this discourse that my spirits, weary of this frivolous thinking—fed by a false and feigned pleasure, and by the divine object of my lady Polia (whose image is engraved in the depths of my heart)—sought from then on nothing but natural rest, so as not to remain any longer between such a hard life and so sweet a death: whereby I found myself all seized by sleep and fell asleep. O Jupiter, sovereign God, shall I call this vision happy, marvelous, or terrible, which is such that in me there is no part so small that it does not tremble and burn when thinking of it? It seemed to me (certainly) that I was in a spacious plain, sown with flowers and greenery: the weather was serene and temperate, the sun bright, and softened by a gracious wind: therefore everything there was marvelously peaceful and in silence, which seized me with a fearful admiration <note>In the 16th century, "admiration" meant a sense of wonder or astonishment</note>: for I perceived no sign of human habitation there, nor even a haunt of beasts: which made me hasten my steps, looking here and there. However, I could see nothing but leaves and branches that did not move at all.

<summary>After a night of insomnia caused by his unrequited love for Polia, Poliphilo falls into a deep sleep and begins a dream-vision where he finds himself alone in a silent, abandoned landscape.</summary>

But at last I walked so much that I found myself in a large and dark forest: and I cannot recall nor remember in what manner I might have gone astray: nevertheless, however it happened, I was seized by a grievous and sudden fear, so much that my pulse began to beat beyond the usual: and my face paled severely. The trees there were so close together, and the foliage so thick, that the rays of the sun could not penetrate through: which makes me fear that I have arrived in the Black Forest <margin>The Hercynian Forest <note>original: "Hercinia sylua." A vast, ancient forest mentioned by Roman writers like Caesar, often used to signify a place of wild, primordial danger.</note></margin>, in which nothing dwells but wild and dangerous beasts: for fear of which I strove as much as possible to find a quick exit: and indeed I set myself to running without keeping to path or trail, nor knowing which direction I should take, often stumbling among the trunks and stumps of trees that were there level with the ground. I went sometimes forward, then suddenly turned back, now to one side, now to the other, my hands and face torn by brambles, thistles, and thorns. And what made it worse than anything was that at every step I was held back by my robe, which caught on the bushes and thickets. The toil I had from it was so great and so excessive that I was beyond all counsel <note>Meaning he was at his wits' end and did not know what to do.</note>: and I did not know what to do except to complain in a loud voice: but all that was in vain, for I was heard by no one, except for the beautiful Echo <note>In mythology, Echo was a nymph who could only repeat the last words spoken to her.</note>, who answered me from the depths of the forest: which made me cry out for the help of the compassionate Ariadne, and long for the thread <note>Ariadne provided Theseus with a ball of thread to help him find his way out of the Labyrinth after killing the Minotaur.</note> she gave to the disloyal Theseus to guide him through the Labyrinth.

## Poliphilo, fearing the danger of the forest, offers his
# PRAYER TO JUPITER: THEN FIND-
*ing the way out, parched with thirst. And just as he wished to refresh himself at a fountain, he heard a melodious song, to follow which he abandoned the water that was ready for him, whereby he found himself afterwards in greater anguish than before.*

---

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a central grotesque mask at the top, surrounded by symmetrical floral scrolls and leaf patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

My understanding being clouded, without being able to know what course I should take—whether to die in this straying forest or to hope for an uncertain salvation—I made every effort to get out. But the further I went, the deeper I entered into great darkness, feeling very weak and trembling from the fear I felt; for I expected nothing else but that some beast would come to confront and devour me, or that, stumbling with my foot against a trunk or root, I might fall into some abyss and be swallowed by the earth, just as Amphiaraus was <note>Amphiaraus was a legendary Greek seer and hero who was swallowed by the earth during the war of the Seven Against Thebes to save him from a dishonorable death.</note>. In this manner, my mind was troubled, without hope and without reason, wandering without a path or trail. Therefore, seeing that there was no other remedy for my situation, I went to recommend myself to divine mercy, saying:

> O Father of Light <note>original: "Diespiter." An archaic Latin title for Jupiter, literally meaning "Father of Day" or "Sky Father."</note>, most great, most good, most powerful, and most helpful, if through humble and devout prayers humanity can merit the help of divine favor and ought to be heard by you, I, now repentant and sorrowful for all my past frailties and offenses, supplicate and invoke you, sovereign eternal father, ruler of heaven and earth: may it please your incomprehensible deity to deliver me from these perils, so that I may finish the course of my life by some other, better end.

Hardly had I finished my prayer, most devoutly uttered and with a completely humbled heart, my eyes full of tears—believing firmly that the
<margin>T</margin>
gods succor and save those who invoke them with a pure will—than I found myself out of the forest. Whereupon, just as if I had come from a cold and damp night into a clear and serene day, my eyes emerging from such darkness could not (for some time) well endure the brightness of the sun. I remained sunburnt, sad, and distressed, so much so that it truly seemed as if I had emerged from a dungeon <term>basse fosse<note>Literally a "low pit," this refers to an underground dungeon or oubliette where prisoners were kept in total darkness.</note></term>, almost entirely broken and shattered by chains and irons, with a weakened face and a slowed heart, such that I no longer valued anything that was before me. Furthermore, I had such a thirst that the fresh and delicate air could not in any way refresh me, nor satisfy the dryness of my mouth. But after having regained a little courage, I resolved by all means to appease this thirst; therefore, I went searching through that country until I found a thick vein of fresh water, springing and bubbling in a beautiful fountain, which flowed through a small brook. This brook became a noisy river as it crossed the stones and trunks of trees fallen and overturned in its channel, against which the water surged as if angry and grieved that they sought to delay her—she who was augmented by several other rivulets, along with certain torrents born from the snows...

But at last I journeyed so far that I found myself in a forest, vast and dark: and I cannot recall nor remember in what manner I might have gone astray: nevertheless, however it happened, I was seized by a heavy and sudden fear, so great that my pulse began to beat beyond its usual measure, and my face turned deathly pale. The trees there were so crowded, and the foliage so dense, that the rays of the sun could not penetrate through: which made me fear I had arrived in the Black Forest <note>The "foreſt noire" here refers to the legendary and frightening wildernesses of the north.</note>,
<margin>The Hercynian Forest <note>original: "Hercinia sylva." A vast ancient forest in Germany described by Roman authors like Julius Caesar as being so large it took nine days to cross.</note></margin>
where none dwell but wild and dangerous beasts. Out of fear of these, I strove with all my might to find a quick exit, and indeed began to run without following any path or trail, nor knowing which way I should turn, often stumbling among the trunks and stumps of trees that lay level with the ground. I went sometimes forward, then suddenly turned back, now to one side, then to the other, my hands and face torn by briars, thistles, and thorns. And what distressed me more than anything else was that at every step I was held back by my robe, which caught upon the bushes and thickets. The toil I endured from this was so great and so excessive that I was left without counsel; I knew not what to do, save to complain in a loud voice. But all this was in vain, for I was heard by no one, except for the beautiful Echo <note>In Greek mythology, the nymph Echo was cursed to only repeat the sounds she heard.</note>, who answered me from the depths of the forest. This made me call for the aid of the compassionate Ariadne, and long for the thread she gave to the treacherous Theseus to guide him through the Labyrinth <note>Ariadne helped Theseus escape the Minotaur's maze by giving him a ball of thread to retrace his steps.</note>.

<header>POLIPHILE.</header>

# ❧ Poliphile, fearing the peril of the forest, offers his
## PRAYER TO JUPITER: THEN HE FINDS
*the way out, parched with thirst. And just as he wished to refresh himself at a fountain, he heard a melodious song, which he followed, abandoning the water at hand, whereby he later found himself in greater anguish than before.*

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'O' decorated with intricate scrolling foliage and vine patterns.</image-desc>
With my understanding clouded, unable to know what path I ought to take—whether to die in that lost forest or to hope for an uncertain salvation—I made every effort to escape it. But the further I went, the deeper I entered into great darkness, feeling weak and trembling from the fear I felt; for I expected nothing less than some beast coming to confront and devour me, or that, striking my foot against a trunk or root, I might fall into some abyss and be swallowed by the earth, as was Amphiaraus <note>In Greek mythology, the seer Amphiaraus was swallowed up by a gap in the earth opened by Jupiter's thunderbolt to save him from being stabbed in the back.</note>. In this manner my mind was troubled, without hope and without reason, wandering without a way or path. Therefore, seeing that in my situation there was no other remedy, I went to recommend myself to divine mercy, saying:

> O Father of Heaven <note>original: "Diespiter." An archaic Latin name for Jupiter, literally meaning "Day-Father."</note>, most great, most good, most powerful, and most helpful, if by humble and devout prayers humanity may merit the help of divine favor and ought to be heard by you, I, now repentant and sorrowful for all my past frailties and offenses, beseech and invoke you, sovereign eternal father, ruler of heaven and earth, that it may please your incomprehensible deity to deliver me from these perils, so that I might finish the course of my life by some other, better end.

Scarcely had I finished my prayer, uttered very devoutly and with a humbled heart and eyes full of tears—believing firmly that the gods help and save those who invoke them with a pure will—than I found myself outside the forest. It was just as if I had emerged from a cold and damp night into a clear and serene day; my eyes, coming out of such darkness, could not for a time endure the brightness of the sun. I was sunburnt, sad, and distressed, so much so that it truly seemed I was emerging from a deep dungeon, almost entirely broken and shattered by chains and irons, with a weakened face and a slowed heart, such that I no longer valued anything that was before me. Furthermore, I had such a thirst that the cool and delicate air could in no way refresh me, nor satisfy the dryness of my mouth. But after having regained a little courage, I resolved by every means to quench this thirst; therefore, I went searching through that country until I found a great vein of fresh water, springing and bubbling in a beautiful fountain <note>In this context, a "fountain" refers to a natural spring or source.</note>, which flowed through a small brook. This brook became a noisy river as it crossed the stones and trunks of trees fallen and overturned in its channel, against which the water surged as if angry and vexed that they thought to delay it—a river that was further increased by several other small streams along with some torrents born of the snows.

## Poliphilo, fearing the peril of the forest, made his PRAYER TO JUPITER: THEN HE FOUND

*the exit, parched with thirst. And as he wished to refresh himself at a fountain, he heard a melodious song, which he followed, abandoning the water at hand, whereby he later found himself in greater anguish than before.*

My understanding being clouded, without being able to know what path I should take, whether to die in this lost forest or hope for an uncertain salvation, I made every effort to escape: but the further I went, the more I entered into great darkness, very weak and trembling with the fear I felt: for I expected nothing but that some beast would come to confront and devour me: or that striking my foot against a trunk or root, I might fall into some abyss and be swallowed by the earth, as was Amphiaraus <note>In Greek mythology, Amphiaraus was a seer and king who was swallowed by the earth during the war of the Seven against Thebes.</note>. In this manner my mind was troubled, without hope and without reason, wandering without way or path. Therefore, seeing that there was no other remedy for my plight, I went to recommend myself to divine mercy, saying:

> O Diespiter <note>original: "Diespiter." An archaic Latin name for Jupiter, meaning "Sky Father."</note>, most great, most good, most powerful, and most helpful, if by humble and devout prayers humanity can merit the help of divine favor and ought to be heard by you, I, now repentant and grieving for all my frailties and past offenses, beseech and invoke you, sovereign eternal father, ruler of heaven and earth, that it may please your incomprehensible deity to deliver me from these perils, so that I may finish the course of my life by some other better end.

Scarcely had I finished my prayer, most devoutly uttered and with a completely humbled heart, my eyes full of tears—firmly believing that the gods succor and save those who invoke them with pure will—than I found myself outside the forest. Whereupon, just as if I had come from a cold and damp night into a clear and serene day, my eyes emerging from such darkness could not (for a time) well endure the brightness of the sun. I was parched, sad, and distressed, so much so that it truly seemed as if I were coming out of a deep pit, almost entirely broken and shattered by chains and irons, with a weakened face and a slowed heart, such that I no longer valued anything present before me. Furthermore, I had such a thirst that the cool and delicate air could in no way refresh me, nor satisfy the dryness of my mouth. But after having regained a little courage, I resolved by every means to appease this thirst: therefore I went searching through that country, until I found a large vein of fresh water, springing and bubbling in a beautiful fountain, which flowed through a small brook; this became a noisy river across the stones and trunks of trees fallen and overturned in its channel, against which the water surged as if angry and vexed that they thought to delay it—water which was increased by several other rivulets, along with some torrents born of the snows.

On the side where this edifice stood, the hills rose a little higher and seemed to join the building, which was situated between two mountains and served as a barrier to a valley. Because I judged it to be a thing worthy of being seen, I directed my path that way; but the closer I approached, the more this magnificent work revealed itself, and my desire to look upon it grew. For it no longer resembled a tower, but rather a marvelous obelisk founded upon a great mound of stones, the height of which beyond all comparison exceeded the mountains on either side. When I had come quite close, I stopped to contemplate at more leisure such a great insolence <note>In this context, "insolence" refers to the daring, prideful, or overwhelming scale of the architecture.</note> of architecture, which was half demolished and composed of blocks of white marble joined without cement—and so well-fitted that where it was still intact, the point of a needle could not have entered between two stones. There were all sorts of columns, some fallen and broken, some whole and in their places, with their capitals, architraves, friezes, cornices, and bases <note>These are the standard components of a classical "Order" (like Doric or Ionic). The architrave, frieze, and cornice make up the horizontal section supported by the columns.</note> of singular invention and workmanship, along with many other pieces of noble sculpture. These were totally unrecognizable as to what their carving had once been, and were almost reduced to their original raw form, tumbled and scattered here and there across the fields.

### THE STRIFE OF LOVE IN A DREAM

...among which, and between these fragments, many wild plants, herbs, and shrubs of many kinds had sprouted, such as myrtles, mastic trees (<term>lentisques</term>), wild olives (<term>oliuastres</term>), centaury, verbena, gooseberry bushes, and capers. Then, against the ruined walls grew houseleek (<term>ioubarbe</term>), polypody fern, hart’s-tongue fern (<term>scolopendre</term>), hay, savin (<term>sauine</term>), and pellitory (<term>parietaire</term>). There, many small lizards scurried about, and every tiny sound they made in this deserted place caused me a marvelous sense of dread <note>Poliphilo uses "horreur merueilleuse," a Renaissance concept of the "sublime"—a mix of awe and fear when facing the vastness of antiquity.</note>, considering that I was already in a state of suspense and doubt. There was a marvelous abundance of porphyry, jasper, and serpentine stone of all colors, very beautiful and rich. Together with these were a great quantity of pieces from various stories in high relief (<term>bosse</term>) and low relief (<term>demytaille</term>), showing the excellence of their own time and blaming and accusing our own, in which the perfection of this art is almost entirely annihilated. 

Approaching then the main front of this great edifice, I looked upon an exquisite portal, well-proportioned to all the rest of the structure. The stretch of its wall continued from one of the mountains to the other, and was six stades <note>A "stade" or stadium is an ancient Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet or 185 meters.</note> and twenty paces in length, as far as I could guess. The alignment of the mountains was plumb from the top to the bottom of the foundation. Because of this, I remained quite pensive and astonished as to how, with what iron tools, with what labor, and by which hands of men such a building had been constructed, at such great expense and consumption of time that it was almost beyond belief. This wall was (in my judgment) the fifth part of a stade in height from the final cornice down to the foot, level with the pavement. It was made (as I have said) to enclose this valley, which one could not enter or leave except by this gate, upon which was founded the great pyramid. This was so marvelous that I estimated the expense to be inestimable, the length of time to make it incredible, and the multitude of men who worked on it innumerable and infinite. For if merely looking at it confounded my understanding and dazzled my sight, what could it do to one's intelligence regarding the construction itself? 

Now, so that I do not fail to describe what I have seen, I will describe its form in very few words. Each face or side of the square of the plinth <note>The "plinthe" is the heavy square base supporting a structure.</note> where the alignment of the steps that made the pyramid began, was six stades in length. These, multiplied by four for the circuit and circumference of the four squares which were equal, make twenty-four stades. The height was made in this manner: drawing the sloping lines A-B and A-C along the four corners from the plinth to the very top of the steps where they met to form the pyramid. The cathetus <note>The "cathet" or cathetus is the vertical line dropped from the apex to the center of the base.</note> or perpendicular line A-D, being in the middle of them and falling straight onto the center of the plinth at point D (where the diagonal lines crossed), was five parts in height, of which the sloping and side lines had six.

# FIRST BOOK OF

The pyramid was composed in the form of a tiered platform, containing one thousand four hundred and ten steps, the last ten of which were converted into a marvelous cube or massive square stone, forming the tapering and narrowing of the pyramid. This was so great and impressive that it was impossible to believe human hands could have seated it so high. It was made of that same marble stone as the steps, and was placed there as a base and foundation for the obelisk, of which I shall speak hereafter. It measured four paces in diameter across each of its square faces. At the four upper corners, along the diagonal lines, were fixed and leaded four feet of <term>Harpies<note>Mythological creatures, usually depicted as birds with the faces of women; here, their talons serve as decorative bronze supports.</note></term>, hairy and clawed, made of cast metal, ending toward the top in an interlaced antique foliage that embraced the foot of the obelisk. The obelisk was supported on these four feet or paws of Harpies, which were two paces in height; the diameter of the obelisk at the bottom was of the same measure. Its length was seven times as much, tapering little by little toward its point, made entirely of a single stone of <term>Thebaic Pyropecile<note>original: "Pyropecile Thebaïque." A Renaissance term for red Egyptian granite or porphyry, prized for its fiery, speckled appearance and sourced from Thebes.</note></term>, inscribed with Egyptian hieroglyphic letters on its four faces and sides, polished and shining like a well-burnished mirror. Upon the point was fashioned a nymph of gilded copper, set upon a vase turning like a pivot—a work surely made to strike wonder into all who beheld it. For the nymph was fashioned in such proportion that, being placed so high in the air, she appeared perfectly to be of ordinary stature. And beyond her size, it was a strange thing to consider how she had been raised and carried so high. Her garment flew around her as if lifted by the wind, so much so that part of her thigh was seen uncovered; she had two wings extended and open, as if she were ready to fly, toward which her gaze was turned. Her hair flew over her forehead in great abundance, but the back of her head was bald and without hair <note>This is a classic depiction of "Occasio" or Opportunity—she has hair in front to be seized as she approaches, but is bald behind so she cannot be caught once she has passed.</note>. In her right hand, toward which she looked, she held a <term>cornucopia<note>original: "corne d'abondance." A "horn of plenty," a symbol of abundance and nourishment.</note></term> full of all good things, turned toward the earth; her other hand rested upon her breast, which was bare. This statue was easily turned by every wind, with such a noise from the friction against the base (which was of bronze and hollow) that the like was never heard. I do not think there has ever been such an obelisk; certainly that of the Vatican in Rome is not its equal, nor that of Alexandria, nor even those of Babylon. It possessed such a height of wonder that I was ravished with amazement while contemplating it, and even more so for its inestimable size, for I could not think nor comprehend by what invention, or with what engines, cranes, and goats <note>A "cabre" or "goat" is a type of tripod lifting shear used in construction.</note>, such a great weight and burden had been raised so high. But to return to the pyramid: it was founded upon a great <term>plinth<note>The heavy square base of a column or monument.</note></term>, massive as I have said, which was fourteen paces high and six <term>stades<note>original: "stades." An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note></term> in length, forming the substructure of the first and lowest step. This plinth had not (in my judgment) been brought there from elsewhere, but was carved from the same rock in this form, and adapted in its natural place for this great structure. The remainder of the steps were made of marble blocks, assembled and arranged in order. The plinth did not touch the mountains, but was distant from them on each side by a length of ten paces. On its right face, at the place where I approached, and in the middle of its square, there was carved...

# POLIPHILO VII

...carved in relief, the terrifying head of Medusa, screaming (as it seemed) with a furious expression, grimacing, with sunken eyes, drooping eyebrows, a wrinkled and scowling forehead, and her mouth open, which was hollowed out and pierced by a small vaulted path, passing through to a perpendicular line from the center of the edifice. At this mouth-opening (which served as a door to enter this path) one climbed by the interlacing of her hair, which was formed with such regularity and compass-precision that it served as steps. And instead of braids, there were twisted long coils of serpents that enveloped and bit one another, extending around the head and the face down to beneath the chin. They were so skillfully and lifelike-ly fashioned by the workmanship that they gave me great fright: for their eyes were made of shining stones: so much so that if I had not been quite certain that the material was marble, I would not have dared approach so easily. The path carved inside the mouth led straight to a <term>viz<note>original: "viz." A spiral or winding staircase, named for its resemblance to the threads of a screw.</note></term> and round ascent located in the middle of the work, by which one climbed, turning, up to the top of the pyramid, as far as the level of the cube upon which the obelisk was seated. But what I esteemed most excellent is that this ascent was bright throughout, because the ingenious architect had, by singular invention, made in several places of the building certain secret <term>conduits<note>Light-wells or shafts designed to channel sunlight into the interior of the masonry.</note></term> that corresponded directly to the aspect of the sun as it made its course against the three parts: the upper, lower, and middle of the structure. The lower part was lit by the conduits from above, and the upper by those from below, which illuminated it sufficiently by reflection and reverberation of light, because the layout of the building was so well calculated according to the three faces—eastern, southern, and western—that at all hours of the day the staircase was lit by the sun, inasmuch as its conduits were made in the form of <term>vent-holes<note>original: "souspiraux." Small openings or breathing-holes that admit both air and light.</note></term> and distributed in their places all around the pyramid, from the cube down to the <term>plinth<note>The heavy square base supporting the structure.</note></term>, where I climbed by a straight and massive step, hollowed and carved in the form of a square vault in the same rock. On the right side at the bottom of the edifice, where it was joined to the mountain and came to an end above, the plinth was set back by ten paces. When I had come before the head of Medusa, I climbed by her hair which served as steps (as I have said above) and entered into her mouth, following that path until I finally came out at the very top upon the cube. Then, having arrived there, my eyes could not bear to look down: for everything below me seemed <note>original: "imperfaict." In this context, it suggests the landscape appeared blurred, diminished, or dizzying due to the immense height.</note>: and I did not dare leave the middle of this stone to approach the edge. Around the exit of this spiral staircase at the top were several copper posts made in the form of balusters or flat spindles fixed into the stone, one foot of distance between each; and they were half a pace in height, linked and continued to one another toward the top by a crown of the same material, made in a wavy pattern, serving as a hedge and enclosure for the opening of the spiral stair, which they surrounded on all sides except for the side where one exited onto the platform; this was done (as I presume) so that no one might fall headlong recklessly into that great hollow: for climbing so high, and turning through so many steps, caused a staggering with wondrous dizziness. ->Lichas the Libyan, stonemason, erected me.<-

Upon the first face of the <term>plinth<note>The heavy square base supporting the pyramid.</note></term> on which the pyramid was founded, there was carved a cruel battle of Giants, who lacked nothing but life itself; for they were so excellently depicted with the movement and great quickness of their enormous bodies that it is impossible to describe it. Nature was so well followed and imitated there, and its effects so aptly expressed, that it seemed their feet struggled along with their eyes, and that they ran here and there. There were horses overturned while trying to kick others, dead and wounded; several, wishing to set their feet upon those who had fallen, stumbled in great numbers. There were others, unbridled and furious, breaking through the press and the fray. Some of these Giants had cast away their weapons and were embracing in the manner of wrestling; many had fallen and were being dragged by their feet; others were trampled and overwhelmed, lying among the dead beneath the horses, from where some tried to raise themselves, placing their <term>targes<note>Small, round shields.</note></term> before the blows of swords, or otherwise ancient <term>cimeters<note>Scimitars or curved blades, depicted in an antique style.</note></term>, quite artistically fashioned. The majority fought on foot, in confusion and in troops. Many were armed with <term>hauberks, cuirasses, and cabassets<note>Types of armor: chainmail tunics, breastplates, and light open-faced helmets.</note></term>, enriched with various crests, plumes, and devices; others were entirely naked, appearing to assault their enemies with an inflamed courage. Many were portrayed with a fearsome countenance as if crying out; others with an obstinate and furious face—some ready to die, others entirely dead—revealing their robust limbs, such that one could see the raised muscles, the joints of the bones, and the hard tension of the stretched sinews. The combat seemed so terrifying and horrible that one would have thought Mars had joined in battle against <note>Porphyrion and Alcyoneus were the most powerful of the Giants who waged war against the Olympian gods.</note>Porphyrion and Alcyoneus. The figures were in <term>half-relief<note>Sculptural figures that project halfway from the background.</note></term> of white marble, and the background was of very black <term>touchstone<note>A smooth, dark stone (often basanite) used here to provide a sharp color contrast with the white marble figures.</note></term>, to give grace and luster to the images and to make the workmanship stand out. There, one could see strange bodies, extreme efforts, passionate acts, diverse deaths, and uncertain victory. Alas, my tired and weary spirits, my understanding confused by such continual diversity, and my senses troubled by such marvelous things, are not sufficient—I do not say to declare the whole—but even to well express the smallest part of this so noble sculpture. God! From whence proceeded such great audacity and presumption, along with the disordered will to assemble stones in such a great heap? With what rollers, with what chariots, and other <term>traction machines<note>Hoisting engines or cranes used for lifting heavy loads.</note></term> were these blocks of incredible size raised so high to erect such a marvelous pyramid? Certainly, <note>An ancient Greek architect who proposed carving Mount Athos into a colossal statue of Alexander the Great holding a city.</note>Dinocrates never proposed more superbly to the great King Alexander the form of his concept and design for the structure of Mount Athos. In truth, this work exceeds the extravagance of the Egyptians, the miracle of the Labyrinth of Crete, and the fame of the Mausoleum; also, without any doubt...

## ing CHAPTER *other great and marvelous works, namely a Horse, a reclining Colossus, an Elephant, and especially a beautiful Gateway.*

<image-desc>A large, ornate decorative initial letter 'I' housed within a rectangular border. The letter is depicted as an architectural column or pillar, surrounded by flourishing Renaissance-style acanthus leaves and vine motifs.</image-desc>

It is only right that I be allowed to say that in the entire universal world, such magnificent works were never made, nor contemplated by mortal eye—nor even (what is more) imagined by any human understanding. I would almost dare frankly to affirm that it is not within the knowledge or power of man to raise, invent, understand, nor define so great an excellence of building. I was truly so overtaken by wonder, and so occupied in looking at it, that nothing else (however comforting and pleasant it might be) could enter my imagination—except for when, considering all the parts of this beautiful and harmonious composition, I saw the statues made in the forms of young maidens. Then I sighed so loudly that my sighs echoed through this desert and solitary place, clouded by a thick and heavy air, because of the memory I held of Polia, my best beloved, whose image is imprinted upon my heart; upon her, my soul has made its nest, and rests as if in a secure sanctuary. Alas, she had not abandoned me in this so lost a journey. Having thus arrived at the place where the sight made me forget all other thoughts, I went to observe a beautiful portal of excellent craftsmanship, and in all its composition consummate and perfect—indeed, such that I do not feel within myself enough knowledge to sufficiently describe it, considering that in our time, the common terms proper and familiar to architecture are buried and extinguished along with the works themselves. O sacrilegious and execrable Barbarism, you have assaulted the noblest part of the Latin treasure, accompanied by insatiable greed; and you have covered with cursed ignorance the art so worthy, which once made Rome flourish and triumph.

Most of these columns are still seen standing and whole, with <term>Doric capitals<note>The simplest of the classical column toppings, characterized by a plain, circular cushion-like stone.</note></term>, measuring in height half the diameter of their base. In this plaza, about ten paces or so from the gate, there was a <term>copper horse<note>Likely representing Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek mythology.</note></term>, marvelously large, with two extended wings: its hoof measured five feet in circumference upon the surface of its base. The length of the leg from the tip of the hoof to beneath the chest was nine feet. The head was high and raised, as if it were wild, without bit or bridle, with two small ears, one pointing forward, the other backward; the mane was long, falling in waves and hanging on the right side. Upon this horse, and around it, were fashioned several small children who were struggling to ride it, but not a single one of them could keep his seat because of its great agility and swift movement; therefore, some fell, others were ready to fall; many had already tumbled and were trying to climb back up. You would have seen some who were clutching the mane; and others had fallen beneath its belly, appearing as if they wished to get back up.

I was greatly astonished considering this large machine of a horse, so very well made that all its members corresponded in measure to the proportion of the body. And it certainly put me in mind of that horse of **Seius** <note>Poliphilo refers to the *Equus Sejanus*, a legendary horse in Roman history said to be of great beauty but cursed, bringing ruin to every one of its owners.</note>. After I had looked at it for a long while, I went to observe from afar the figure of an **Elephant**, which was in no way inferior in size or craftsmanship. And just as I wished to go see it, I heard something like the groaning of a sick person, which made the hair on my head stand up; and without thinking further on it, I drew toward the place where I had heard the voice, climbing upon a great mound of ruins. 

When I had passed beyond, I found a marvelous **Colossus**, having feet without soles, legs hollow and empty, and likewise all the rest of the body up to the head, which could not be looked upon without horror. Then I conjectured that the wind, entering through the opening of the feet, had caused this sound in the form of a groan, and that the craftsman had thus made it quite intentionally. This colossus was lying on its back, made of bronze or cast metal, and cast with excellent skill. It seemed to be of a man of middle age, lying with his head a bit high, and resting on a cushion <note>original: "quarreau," a square pillow or block.</note> in the manner of a sick man. He had a mouth open six paces wide, as if he had wanted to complain. By the hair of his head one could climb onto his chest, and from there enter into his mouth by the hair of his beard. 

When I had come that far, I emboldened myself to enter inside; then, descending by a small step, I went down into the throat, then into the stomach, and from there through all the other parts of the body, even into the bowels and entrails. O marvelous concept of human understanding, an undertaking more than admirable! I saw all the internal parts of the natural body open and passable, the name of each written in three languages, namely **Chaldean** <note>In the Renaissance, "Chaldean" typically referred to Aramaic or Syriac, often used to suggest ancient, mystical knowledge.</note>, **Greek**, and **Latin**, along with the diseases that can be engen- <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("engendrées"), meaning "engendered" or "produced."</note>

### FIRST BOOK OF

...[to discov]er, and by the same means, the cause and the remedy <note>The Colossus serves as a massive anatomical model designed to show how the body functions and how it fails.</note>. Everywhere there was a passage, so that one could clearly see bones, arteries, nerves, veins, muscles, and intestines: for it was provided with several small secret windows which gave sufficient light; and there was not a single vein missing, no more than in that of a perfect man. When I was at the level of the heart, I perceived the place where love forges its sighs, and the spot where it most grievously offends. Then I let out a great cry, calling Polia so loudly that I felt the whole machine resound, which gave me a fright. Then I began to weigh the excellence of such an invention, by which, without dissection <term>anatomy: here used in the archaic sense of a physical dissection of a cadaver</term>, a man could make himself excellent and singular. O noble ancient spirits! O truly golden age, when virtue was equal with fortune; you have left only ignorance and avarice as an inheritance to this unhappy century.

After I had left this colossus, I saw the forehead and the top of the head of another: but it was in a feminine form, of which all the rest was buried beneath these ruins, so that I could see no further. For this reason, I returned to the first place, where I contemplated a great Elephant of black stone, sparked with flakes of gold and silver, like powder sown over it <note>The author likely describes obsidian or a dark touchstone with mineral inclusions.</note>. The stone was so polished and so clear that it reflected everything around it as if it were a mirror of fine glass; however, there were some spots where the metal had tarnished it with its green rust. This Elephant had upon the top of its back a sort of pack-saddle or covering of copper, tied with two wide straps tightened underneath and surrounding the whole belly. Between these was made a square pillar in the form of a pedestal, of a measure corresponding to the thickness of the obelisk raised upon the back of the beast, because nothing of great weight should be seated in vain, for it could not be durable. Three faces of this pedestal were carved with Egyptian letters <note>Hieroglyphs; during the Renaissance, these were often interpreted as mystical allegories rather than a phonetic language.</note>, and on the fourth was the door to enter it. 

The elephant (in truth) showed itself expressed so perfectly that nothing was lacking in its craftsmanship. Its pack-saddle or covering was adorned with small figures and stories in half-relief: and right in its middle could be seen erected an obelisk of green Lacedaemonian stone <term>Lacedaemonian stone: also known as *porfido verde antico*, a prized green volcanic stone from Sparta</term>, which had equal faces one pace wide by the diameter of its base, and seven other geometric paces in height; it diminished to a point, and at the summit was fixed a ball of clear and transparent material. This great animal was supported by a base or counter-base of Porphyry <term>Porphyry: a hard purple-red igneous rock used in antiquity for imperial monuments</term>. The two great tusks that protruded from its mouth were made of white stone, shining like ivory. To its covering was attached with rich gilded buckles a breastplate of the same copper, in the middle of which was written in Latin letters: **CEREBRVM EST IN CAPITE.** <note>original Latin: "CEREBRVM EST IN CAPITE"</note>—that is to say: **The brain is in the head.** And similarly, the end where the neck joins the head was surrounded by a beautiful band, from which hung an ornament in the form of a chamfron <note>A piece of armor used to protect a horse's head, here used decoratively for the elephant.</note> cast over the beast's forehead, composed of two entire squares and bordered with antique foliage, also made of copper.
