# THE FIRST BOOK OF

...to understand, and by the same means the cause and the remedy. Everywhere there was a passage, such that one could clearly see bones, arteries, nerves, veins, muscles, and intestines; for it was furnished with several small secret windows which gave sufficient light. Not a single vein was missing, any more than in the body of a perfect man. When I was level with the heart, I perceived the place where Love forges his sighs, and the spot where he causes the most grievous injury. Then I let out a great lament, calling "Polia!" so loudly that I felt the whole machine resound, which frightened me. Then I began to weigh the excellence of such an invention, by which, without <term>anatomy</term><note>The practice of dissecting bodies to study their structure, which was gaining renewed scientific interest during the Renaissance.</note>, a man could make himself excellent and singular. Oh, noble spirits of antiquity! Oh, truly golden age, when virtue was equal to fortune! You have left to this unhappy century only ignorance and avarice as an inheritance. After I had exited this colossus, I saw the brow and the top of the head of another, but it was in a feminine form; all the rest was buried under these ruins, so that I could see no further. For this reason, I returned to the first place, where I contemplated a large elephant of black stone, sparked with flakes of gold and silver, like powder scattered over it. The stone was so polished and clear that it reflected everything around it as if it were a mirror of fine glass; however, it lacked this in a few places where the metal had tarnished it with its green rust. This elephant had upon its back a sort of pack-saddle or covering of copper, fastened by two wide straps tightened underneath and encircling the whole belly. Between these was made a square pillar in the form of a pedestal, of a size corresponding to the thickness of the <term>obelisk</term><note>A tall, four-sided, tapering monument which ends in a pyramid-like shape at the top.</note> erected on the back of the beast; for nothing of great weight should be seated in vain, as it could not be durable. The three faces of this pedestal were carved with Egyptian letters <note>meaning hieroglyphs, which Renaissance scholars viewed as sacred, symbolic riddles</note>, and on the fourth was the door to enter it. The elephant (in truth) was shown expressed so perfectly that nothing was lacking in its craftsmanship. Its pack-saddle or covering was adorned with small figures and stories in <term>half-relief</term><note>Sculptural elements that project halfway from the background, also known as mezzo-rilievo.</note>. And right in its center could be seen erected an obelisk of green <term>Lacedaemonian stone</term><note>A rare green volcanic stone (Verde Antico) sourced from Laconia, near Sparta.</note>, which had on its equal faces a width of one pace at the diameter of its foot, and seven other geometric paces in height. It diminished to a point, and at the summit was fixed a ball of clear and transparent material. This great animal was supported by a base or counter-base of <term>Porphyry</term><note>A very hard, purple-red rock prized by the Romans for imperial monuments.</note>. The two large tusks that issued from its mouth were made of white stone, shining like ivory. To its covering was attached, with rich gilded buckles, a breast-plate of the same copper, in the middle of which was written in Latin letters: **THE BRAIN IS IN THE HEAD.** <note>original: "CEREBRVM EST IN CAPITE."</note> Similarly, the end where the neck joins the head was encircled by a beautiful band, from which hung an enrichment in the form of a <term>champron</term><note>Decorative armor worn on the head of a horse or, in this case, the elephant.</note> cast over the brow of the beast, composed of two nested squares and bordered with antique foliage, also made of copper.

The proboscis <note>the elephant's trunk</note> or snout did not touch the pedestal, but was slightly raised and turned back toward the forehead. It had hanging ears, wide and wrinkled in a strange fashion, showing by their size that they exceeded the natural scale. The pedestal was oblong and oval, carved with Egyptian hieroglyphic characters and adorned with moldings. The length was twelve paces, the width five, and the height three. On one of the sides, I found a small door and a staircase of seven steps, by which I reached the platform of the pedestal; there I saw that in the square block placed beneath the belly, another small door had been hollowed out. Within the concavity of this Elephant were metal pegs, fixed to the two sides in the form of rungs, by which one could easily climb and move through this hollow machine. This made me feel a great desire to see it, so I entered through this door; then I climbed by the pegs into this marvelous, hollowed-out body, which was built such that enough mass had been left on the inside (just as it had on the outside below) to support its obelisk—yet there was enough space on each side of the Elephant’s flanks that a man could pass through with ease. From the vault of the back, toward the rear, hung a burning lamp attached by chains of brass <note>original: "arain"</note>, which was never extinguished and illuminated all this great empty space. In this place, I saw the figure of a naked man, as large as the ordinary natural size, having a crown upon his head; the whole was made of black stone, but the eyes, the teeth, and the nails were of silver. This figure was set upright upon the lid of a semi-circular sepulcher <note>a tomb</note>, carved with scales and the necessary moldings. He had his right arm extended forward, holding a scepter, and his left hand rested upon a shield, curved in the shape of a boat's keel and carved around the edge in the likeness of a horse’s jawbone; upon it was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters:

# POLIPHILE. VII

I found myself completely astonished and somewhat seized by fear. Therefore, without stopping further, I set off to leave; and passing along the front side toward the head, I perceived another lit lamp and another sepulcher <term>sepulcher: a small room or monument, cut in rock or built of stone, in which a dead person is laid or buried</term> similar in every way to the first, except that the figure was of a woman who had her right arm raised, pointing with the index finger of her hand to the part that was behind her. With the other hand, she held a tablet touching the lid of the sepulcher, upon which was written in three languages.

Whoever you are, take from this treasure as much as your soul desires; but I warn you, remove the head and do not touch the body. <note>original Hebrew: "חיה מי שתיה תח קח מן האוצר הזה כאוה נפשך אבל אזהיר אותך הסר הראש ואל תוגע בגופו׃"</note>

Whoever you are, take from this treasure as much as you please; but I advise that when you take the head, do not touch the body. <note>original Greek: "ΟΣΤΙΣΕΙ, ΛΑΒΕ ΕΚΤΟΥΔΕ ΤΟΥ ΘΗΣΑΥΡΟΥ ΟΣΟΝ ΑΝ ΑΡΕΣΚΟΙ· ΠΑΡΑΙΝΩ ΔΕ ΩΣ ΛΑΒΗΣ ΤΗΝ ΚΕΦΑΛΗΝ, ΜΗ ΑΠΤΟΥ ΣΩΜΑΤΟΣ."</note>

Whoever you are, take as much as you please of this treasure: but I warn you, take away the head, do not touch the body. <note>original Latin: "Quisquis es, quantumcunque libuerit, huius thesauri sume: at moneo, aufer caput, corpus ne tangito."</note>

->That is to say:<-

Whoever you are, take of this treasure as much as you please: but I admonish you to take the head, and touch not the body.

These things were quite new to me, especially the riddles <term>enigme: a mysterious or paradoxical statement; a riddle</term>, which I read and reread several times, hoping to understand them; but their meaning seemed very ambiguous to me, and such that I did not know how to interpret them. Furthermore, I dared not undertake anything, for I was overcome by a devout horror <note>Poliphilo uses "horreur deuote" to describe a feeling of religious awe or sacred dread</note> in this dark place, having no light but from two lamps. Moreover, the great desire I had to contemplate the beautiful gate at my ease was the reason I did not stop there further, and I left, intending nonetheless to return to consider it more at leisure. Thus I descended by the place where I had entered, and looked at this great beast from the outside, thinking what human boldness had been so reckless as to undertake such a high work, what chisels, what tools and ironworks had been able to penetrate a matter so hard and so resistant, especially as all the internal carvings <note>original: "touches de dedãs"</note> corresponded exactly to those on the outside. After I had descended to the very bottom onto the pavement, I noticed the base which supported it, around which were attached such hieroglyphics.

These things were quite new to me, especially the riddles, which I read and reread several times, hoping to understand them; but their meaning seemed very ambiguous to me, and such that I did not know how to interpret it. Furthermore, I did not dare to undertake anything, for I was overcome by a devout dread <note>Poliphilo often describes his fear as "devout" or "religious," suggesting a mix of awe and terror in the face of the ancient and sacred.</note> in this dark place, having no light except for two lamps. <header>POLIPHILO.</header>

...did you carry away with you into the grave the bounty of our wealth?

When I came before the door—which well deserved to be carefully studied for the excellence of its workmanship—I felt a desire to understand the **proportion and measurement** that the craftsman had observed there. To find it, I promptly made use of this practical method: I measured one of the square bases that supported the double columns on each side, and by that, I easily understood its logic.

First, he had made a square figure **A B C D**, divided by three straight lines and three crossing lines, equally distant from one another, composing sixteen squares. Then, he added half of its size on top of the square figure; this section, divided by the same measurements, made twenty-four squares in total, including the sixteen from the first square figure. After drawing two diagonals in the first figure **A B C D**, which were marked by two lines crossing through the middle, they formed four squares, each having its own diagonal or transverse line. Furthermore, he made a **Rhombus** <note>original: "Rhombe"; a diamond or lozenge shape</note> or lozenge above the large square, by tracing four lines within its space over the four principal points that equally divide the four sides of the void. After I had conceived this figure in my mind, I thought:

What can modern architects do, who think themselves wise, yet are without scholarship and without doctrine? They remain without rule or measure; therefore, they corrupt and deform all manner of buildings, both private and public, despising Nature—who teaches them to do well, if only they would imitate her. Nevertheless, they may enrich their work and add or diminish to satisfy the eye, provided that the **mass** <note>original: "massif"; the core structural volume of the building</note> remains whole, to which all parts must agree. By this "mass," I mean the body of the edifice, which even without ornaments reveals the knowledge and spirit of the master; for it is easy to enrich a thing after it has been invented. However, above all, one must value the distribution, partition, and arrangement of the members. From this, one must conclude that it is a common thing for any worker—even down to the apprentices—to know how to ornament a work; but **invention**, certainly, lies within the minds of the learned. 

To return then to our subject: taking away the rhombus and the diagonal lines from the large square and its half, and leaving the three perpendiculars and the three crossing lines (except for the one in the middle which ends at the center of the perpendiculars, cut into four parts and portions), by this rule you will find two perfect squares—one at the top and the other at the bottom—each containing four small squares which form the door. Now, if you take the diagonal of the bottom square, it will teach you what thickness must be given to the **arch** <note>original: "sintre"; the structural curve or centering of the portal</note> of the portal, if you set it upright toward the line **A B**, which will serve as the architrave. And the midpoint of the upper square will show you the arc and curvature that must be given to the door by turning one point of the compass in a semi-circle, resting on the crossing line that cuts the square-and-a-half into two equal parts. But if it be made by any other way, I do not consider it perfect.

# POLIPHILO.

This measurement was invented by the ancient builders, who were highly expert in masonry, and it was observed in their arches and vaults to give them both grace and resistance. The pedestal, or counter-base of the columns, began at the level of the pavement with a plinth; and the whole structure was one foot high, furnished with its moldings and their bead-like astragals <note>original: "astragales ou fuzees"; small, rounded moldings, often shaped like a string of beads or spindles</note>, following the alignment of the building and serving as a base for the side-posts or jambs of the door.

The space contained between lines A, B, E, and F was divided into three parts: one for the architrave <term>architrave</term><note>the lowest part of an entablature, resting directly on the column capitals</note>, another for the frieze, and the third for the crown or cornice, which had one part more than the other two. That is to say, if the architrave has five parts, and the frieze as many, the cornice must have six. In this work, the cornice exceeded that measure because the skilled craftsman had created a half-foot overhang on the cymatium <term>cymatium (cymaise)</term><note>the uppermost molding of a cornice, usually with an S-shaped profile</note> of the cornice. This was done so that the projection of its moldings would not obstruct the view of the sculptures located above, although one could also enlarge the architrave and the frieze with their ornaments, as the work requires.

Beneath the cornice, there was a square on each side, as wide as its projection. The frieze situated below was as wide as half of this square, or a third of one of the twenty-four squares. The space between the two squares was divided into seven parts: the middle one, which aligned perfectly with the opening of the door, was used for a niche <note>original: "vn nid"; literally a "nest," here referring to a decorative alcove</note> to hold the figure of a nymph. On each side, three parts remained for other sculptures.

The projection of the highest crown or cornice can be easily found by making a square from the line of its thickness; the diagonal of this square will be its projection. Now, considering the entire figure of the twenty-four squares together, you will find that it contains a perfect square and a half. Divide the half that is above the square into six parts, using five horizontal lines and five perpendicular lines, and draw a line from the middle of the fifth crossing line to the corner of the large perfect square A, where the architrave begins. Then, raise it perpendicularly above the keystone of the curved architrave or vault of the door; it will show you the regular height of the pediment <term>pediment (frontispice)</term><note>the triangular gable or decorative piece forming the top of the portal</note> or peak above, the extremities of which must join and correspond to the overhang or projection of the final cornice or cymatium, and with similar moldings.

This gate was constructed from squared stones, so perfectly joined that it seemed to be made of a single piece. The semi-diameter of the column's foot formed the height of the base, which consisted of a <term>torus</term> <note>original: "bozel," a large convex molding</note>, a <term>scotia</term> <note>original: "contrebozel," a concave molding</note>, and a <term>plinth</term> <note>the flat slab at the bottom of the base</note>, formed in this manner: dividing the height of the base into three parts, one was given to the plinth, which had a width of one and a half times the diameter of the column's foot. This gate was constructed of ashlar blocks <note>large, square-cut stones used for fine masonry</note>, joined so precisely that it appeared to be carved from a single piece of stone. On either side of it, at a distance of two paces, lay two great columns, almost entirely buried in the ruins; I uncovered them somewhat and saw that their bases and capitals were made of copper. I measured the height of one base, and by doubling it, I found the diameter of the foot of the column; by this same proportion, I determined its length, which exceeded twenty-eight cubits. The two columns nearest the gate were made, one of <term>Porphyry</term> <note>a hard, purple-red volcanic stone associated with imperial power</note>, and the other of <term>Ophite</term> <note>also known as serpentine; a green-mottled stone resembling snakeskin</note>; the other two were fluted <term>Caryatids</term> <note>columns carved in the shape of female figures</note>. On both sides, there were several others: some arranged in pairs, others placed at equal intervals, all made of very sturdy <term>Laconian</term> <note>a deep green marble from Laconia, Greece</note> stone.

The half-diameter of the column’s foot determined the height of the base, which consisted of a <term>bozel</term> <note>a torus, or large rounded molding</note>, a <term>contrebozel</term> <note>likely a scotia or a smaller secondary molding</note>, and a <term>plinth</term> <note>the square slab at the very bottom of a column base</note>, formed in this manner: dividing the height of the base into three parts, one was given to the plinth, which had a width of one and a half diameters of the column’s foot. The remaining two parts were divided into four: one was for the upper torus, and the other three were divided into two—one for the lower torus and the other for the scotia. The fillets <note>thin, flat decorative bands</note> each measured one-seventh of the total. Such measurements were observed by the ancient <term>Architects</term>, as they seemed to them both pleasing and regular.

Upon the capitals of these columns was placed a beautiful <term>architrave</term> or <term>epistyle</term> <note>the horizontal beam resting directly on the columns</note>, made with three faces: the first at the bottom was adorned with a molding of beads in the shape of a rosary; the second had the same work, except that after every two round beads there was a long one shaped like a spindle; the third was made with pierced "ears" <note>likely decorative volutes or scrolled brackets</note> carved in the manner of foliage. Above this was the frieze or <term>zophore</term> <note>a horizontal band often featuring continuous relief sculpture</note>, carved with ancient branches and flowers, interlaced with vine branches and various herbs, interspersed with many kinds of birds. 

After this came a row of <term>mutules</term> or <term>modillions</term> <note>ornamental brackets under a cornice</note> resembling the heads of olive trees, projecting from the wall at equal intervals, upon which began the moldings of a great cornice. The rest of the building from there upward was demolished and fallen, but there were signs of large double windows, stripped of their ornaments, which gave some indication of what the building had been in its entirety. 

Beneath this architrave met the point of the gate's frontispiece <note>a pediment or decorative header</note>; on its two sides, which had the form of <term>dipleure</term> <note>original: "dipleures," from the Greek for "double-sided," meaning isosceles</note> triangles (that is to say, having two equal sides), were carved two rounds enclosed by moldings and surrounded by triumphal wreaths made of oak leaves tied with silk ribbons. Within these were two figures in high relief, emerging from the flat background or concave of the rounds from the waist up. Their chests were covered with cloaks knotted on the left shoulder in the ancient fashion; one had a mixed beard, and both were crowned with laurel, presenting great majesty in their gaze. Upon the projections of the frieze resting above the columns, certain eagles were carved with open wings, perched upon festoons of greenery interspersed with fruit, hanging slightly toward the middle; the ends of these festoons seemed to be attached on both sides by ribbons in semi-relief, with many pierced folds like real ribbons. Opposite this gate was situated a great colonnade. And because I have previously...

It remains now to describe its enrichments: for the Architect must first conceive and arrange in his understanding the **massif** <note>the solid core or main structural body of a building</note> of the whole work, and afterwards think of the ornaments, which are but the accessories to the principal part, considering that in the first is known the knowledge and experience of the craftsman, but the second is very easy, and common almost to apprentices.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap initial letter 'A' containing an architectural scene with two classical columns supporting a pediment, with drafting tools such as a compass and square integrated into the ornate design.</image-desc>
BEFORE passing further, I wish to pray the lovers, who (perhaps) expect to hear from me things that would be more pleasing to them, and such as are the thoughts with which they entertain their hearts, that they would be willing to excuse me if I dwell a little long in this description: for I hope hereafter to satisfy them in what they desire. To bring then to an end my enterprise, I have said above that the principal part of the Architect is the invention of the **massif** body of the whole edifice: for he can afterwards easily reduce it into small divisions, no more nor less than a musician having invented the tone upon a beat, by a long or a *maxima* <note>the longest note value in medieval and Renaissance music</note>, he proportions it afterwards into chromatic minims—that is to say, temporal notes—which he relates back to the fixed and solid note. Thus in the invention of the Architect, the principal and most necessary rule is the **square**, which, after it is distributed and divided into several other small squares, provides the accord and suitable proportion or **harmony** of the entire edifice, so that all the accessories return and respond to their principal: and thus was that gate made. Firstly, on the right side was a pedestal furnished with its moldings, higher than it was wide; that is to say, of **diagonal proportion** <note>original: "proportion diagonée"; a rectangle where the height is equal to the diagonal of its square base</note>. Certainly it behoves me to use terms known among the men of the art, notwithstanding that they are not common: for we are degenerate and diminished from that treasure which could properly express and declare all the particularities of this work, and we must speak of it with the coarse and improper words that remain to us.

Now within the square of this pedestal was carved in **alabaster** stone, diaphanous or transparent, a man somewhat exceeding middle and virile age, of a robust and rustic face, his beard hard, strong, and bristly, the hairs straight, coarse, and stinging, so that his chin resembled the back of a wild boar. He was seated upon a stone, wrapped in a goat skin, of which the hind legs were knotted at his sides, the neck hanging between his legs, and the hair turned toward his flesh. it was dedicated to both sexes of the gods, namely to a god and a goddess, as to a mother and son, father and daughter, husband and wife, or other similar pairings; the fluting was attributed to the female sex, and the filling <note>This refers to "cabling" or "rudenture," where the lower part of a column's flutes are filled with a convex molding.</note> to the male sex.

These fluted columns were first made for the temple of a goddess, the architects wishing to represent the folds of women's garments through the fluting; and upon them they placed capitals with their volutes or scrolls to signify their hair, worn in the Greek fashion—that is to say, tucked up above the ears.

The **Caryatid** columns, which have for a capital the head of a woman adorned in her finery, were first made to the shame of the rebellious people of **Caryae**, a city in the **Morea** <note>Morea was the medieval name for the Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note>, who allied themselves with the **Persians** against the other **Greeks** of their own nation. This was done so that it might serve as a perpetual memory to condemn the more than feminine inconstancy of the people of Caryae.

The bases of these four columns were made of copper, enriched with carvings of oak leaves and decorated with acorns. The capitals were of the same material, covered with abaci <term>abacus: the flat slab forming the top of a column's capital</term> or notched tiles, and in the middle of each notch was a beautiful fleur-de-lis. The body of the capital was draped with two rows of **Acanthus** leaves, each row containing eight leaves, in the **Roman** and **Corinthian** style. From these leaves emerged small volutes, which met in the middle of the vessel and composed the lily placed among the notches or arcs of the abacus. The remainder curled back in the manner of scrolls at the four corners of this work.

**Marcus Agrippa** <note>A Roman general and architect, son-in-law to Augustus, responsible for building the original Pantheon.</note> had such columns placed at the portal of the great **Pantheon** temple in **Rome**.

To each capital was attributed a height of one entire diameter of the column's base, observing the proportion and measure of all its parts and accessories.

The threshold of the door was made of a large green stone <note>Likely green porphyry or "serpentino."</note>, speckled with white, black, yellow, and other diverse and imperfect spots, upon which were placed and seated the doorposts or jambs. These were as wide as the threshold and one pace more in height, where, as with the lintels <note>original: "cótresors"</note>, there was no sign that there had ever been hinges or bolts.

Above the vaulting of the door was the architrave with its moldings and ornaments, such as beads or paternosters, moldings <note>original: "oreilles de forys," architectural "ears" or crossettes that extend from the top of a door frame.</note>, and others. The keystone or wedge of the arch or vault was made of a very black agate stone, carved in the shape of an eagle, almost entirely detached from the block, having its wings spread and holding a child between its talons, directly by the navel. It was so discreetly fashioned that it seemed the bird feared to wound him. You would have said, seeing his little face, that he was afraid of falling, for which reason he had extended his arms and grasped the wings of the eagle at the thick bones near the shoulder, pulling his little legs upward over the tail, which seemed to pass beneath the vaulting. It was certainly so perfectly imitated from the white vein of the agate, or onyx, and the eagle from the sardonyx <note>The author marvels at "lithoglyphic" art—using the natural layers of a multicolored gemstone (like a cameo) to depict different subjects in different colors.</note>, which is the other vein near it in the same stone, that I remained quite astonished, wondering in what manner the ingenious craftsman had imagined applying that stone to such a beautiful invention. Seeing the feathers that the bird had ruffled around its neck, its beak open, and its tongue panting, you could have known that it was smitten with the love of this child <note>This is a depiction of the myth of Ganymede, a beautiful youth abducted by Jupiter in the form of an eagle to serve as cupbearer to the gods.</note>. <note>Original Greek: ΑΦΡΟΔΙΤΗΙ ΚΑΙ ΤΩΙ ΥΙΩΙ ΕΡΩΤΙ ΔΙΟΝΥΣΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΔΗΜΗΤΡΑ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΜΗΤΡΙ ΣΥΜΠΑΘΕΣΤΑΤΗΙ. Original Latin: Diis veneri & filio Amori Bacchus & Ceres de suis (s. substantiis) matri pientissime.</note>

This means: To the most compassionate mother Venus, and to her son Love, Bacchus and Ceres have given this from their own property. 
On either side of the tablet were two small flying children, completely naked and made of the same metal, their hands placed on the edges as if they were supporting it. On the faces of the frieze that projected above the columns were carved various ancient spoils, such as small hauberks, cuirasses, coats of mail, shields, helmets, burning torches, bundles of rods with axes <note>The "fasces," a Roman symbol of authority.</note>, bows, quivers of arrows, and other similar machines useful and convenient for war, both on land and at sea. These signified (without a doubt) the triumphs, victories, and power which once caused Jupiter to change his own form <note>A reference to Jupiter's many transformations, such as into a bull or swan, to pursue his loves.</note>, and which ordinarily cause men to die in sweetness and pleasure. Above this was placed the great cornice with its required moldings and lines, which corresponded to the rest of the building. For just as in the human body, if one quality is discordant with another, a sickness follows because the occurrence and the composition are in conflict; similarly, if the members of a body are not set in their proper and fitting place, a deformity of the person follows. In the same way, a building is discordant and "sick" if order and due composition are not maintained within it. This order is corrupted and debased by modern idiots who are ignorant of the true placement of the areas and parts of a building; for the wise and expert master compares it to a well-proportioned and properly clothed human body. After the frieze, there was a molding, and above it four squares—namely, two on the two projections of the frieze above the columns, and two directly above the middle of the door. Nevertheless, because time—the destroyer of all things—had still left it whole, I could do no less than to say this little bit about it, by way of a summary or notice. The remainder of the enclosure on one side and the other showed in appearance that it had been an excellent edifice, which could be easily understood by several works that remained whole in many places, even the lower parts, such as the <term>telamones: columns carved in the shape of men, also called atlantes</term> <note>original: "colonnes nayues"</note> figured in the form of stooped men, sustaining the heaviest burden. Their measurement could not be known, for they were made as required by the proportion sufficient for the weight, the ornament, and the reason understood and drawn from the human likeness; because just as a man sustaining a heavy burden holds his feet bent under his legs, in this manner the telamones applied beneath the greatest loads were shortened. But the <term>Corinthian</term> and <term>Ionic</term> columns, which are slender, were placed there for decoration and beauty; wherefore the composition of this building was accomplished with all the required perfections, as much in the diversity of different colored marbles—such as white, black, <term>porphyry: a hard igneous rock with a deep purplish-red color</term>, <term>serpentine: a dark green stone with snake-like patterns</term>, and <term>alabaster</term>, diversified with mixed and confused veins—as in many praiseworthy ornaments. I saw there (certainly) a form of <term>pulvinated bases: cushion-shaped or rounded bases</term> <note>original: "bases puluinées"</note>, which upon the <term>plinth: the heavy square slab serving as the base of a column</term> or lift, had two <term>tori: convex, rounded moldings</term> <note>original: "contrebofelz"</note> and <term>scotiae: concave, hollow moldings</term> <note>original: "trochiles"</note>, or "little boats," separated by the interposition of two fillets to distinguish the moldings. Most of the ruins were covered in Ivy and Periwinkle, which spread over them and occupied many parts of the edifice. Similarly, many shrubs grew between the cracks of the stones, such as Houseleek, Erogene <note>possibly Erigeron or fleabane</note>, Pellitory, Celandine, Mouse-ear chickweed <note>original: "Alsine ou oreille de soryz"</note>, Polypody, Maidenhair <note>original: "Adianthe, ou perruque de Venus"</note>, and Rusty-back fern <note>original: "Ceterac"</note> rusted on one side, along with the great Moonwort <note>original: "Lunaire"</note>, and others always living, loving and haunting old walls; together with the Maidenhair spleenwort <note>original: "Polytric"</note>, the greening wild olive, and Capers dwelling in the rocks and ruins, by which almost all the marbles and works were covered and reclothed. There was so great a number of columns overturned one upon the other that they seemed like great heaps of trees fallen within a thick forest. And likewise a great quantity of statues and figures in all forms, naked and clothed, some planted on the right foot, others on the left, having their heads

Many statues stood upright upon their platforms, while others sat upon chairs and seats of honor in various manners, accompanied by innumerable trophies, spoils, and infinite ornaments of horse and ox heads. From the horns of these heads hung bundles of greenery with festoons of fruit and foliage—slender and thin at the ends but thickening toward the middle—with small children mounted upon them and playing about. All was so ingeniously perfect that one could rightly judge and recognize that the spirit and industry of the Architect had been most excellent. For, to the pleasure and contentment of the onlookers, he had so properly expressed the concept and intention of his imagination, both in the proportions and measurements of the edifice and in the perfection of the art of sculpture. Had the material been not marble, but soft wax or clay, it could not have been better guided or put into work. 

This is the true art, which reveals and challenges our presumptuous ignorance—or our detestable presumption, which is a public and harmful error. It is the clear light that sweetly ravishes us in its contemplation to illuminate our darkness; for no one remains blind with their eyes open, except those who flee and refuse it. It is this art that accuses cursed avarice <note>Greed or extreme desire for wealth</note>, the destroyer of all virtue, which indeed incessantly gnaws at the heart of the one it possesses and holds captive. This is because it is entirely contrary to noble spirits and is the mortal enemy of noble and worthy Architecture—even though, in this present age, everyone holds it as their idol, offering it honors and sacrifices, which is an unworthy, evil, and greatly pernicious thing. O dangerous and mortal poison, you make miserable the one who is afflicted by you! How many magnificent works have perished and been suppressed because of you? 

In this manner, I was ravished and overcome by a sovereign pleasure, contemplating the relics of holy, venerable antiquity, so worthy of esteem. I found myself uncertain, inconsistent, and insatiable, looking here and there, accompanied by a continual affection and admiration, wondering to myself what might be the significance of these histories <note>Here referring to the narrative scenes or symbols carved into the stone</note>, which I found quite obscure. It would be a very great and praiseworthy thing to be able easily to describe the unparalleled work and singular composition of this so exquisite building, along with the grandeur of the edifice and the excellence of the gate, full of all admiration; for the pleasure I took in looking at it exceeded my astonishment. And without any doubt, I truly thought in my heart that no manufacture is foreign or difficult for the gods; and I almost suspected that such an incomprehensible work could not have been composed by human hands, nor such concepts so well expressed, nor such magnificent novelty invented by any mortal understanding, and yet at the same time so perfectly defined. For I have no doubt that if the natural historian <note>A reference to Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose *Natural History* served as the primary Roman encyclopedia of art and science</note> could have seen it, he would have made little account of Egypt, nor of its craftsmen, who, separated from one another and assigned to different places, each having taken a limb to carve according to the measure given to them, and coming afterwards to bring back each finished piece, it was found that they all agreed in the composition of a great colossus as perfectly as if they had been carved by a single craftsman. 

He would also have held in little esteem the great industry of Satyrus the Architect, along with the work of the great Memnon, who fashioned three figures of Jupiter from a single massive stone, one of which, being seated, had a sole of the foot seven <term>cubits: an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches</term> long. Likewise, he would have made little of the marvelous figure of Queen Semiramis, fashioned at Mount Bagistan <note>Now known as Behistun in modern-day Iran</note>, which was seventeen <term>stadia: an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</term> in size. For the pyramids of Egypt, the theaters, amphitheaters, baths, temples, aqueducts, and so famous colossi—neither the great figure of Apollo, transported to Rome by Lucullus, nor the Jupiter dedicated to Claudius Caesar, nor even that of Lysippus at Tarentum, nor the masterpiece of Chares of Lindos at Rhodes <note>The Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note>, nor that of Xenodorus made both in Gaul and in Rome; nor likewise the Colossus of Serapis, being nine cubits long and made entirely of emerald stone; nor the Labyrinth of Egypt, nor the image of the brave Hercules at Tyre—almost none of these were anything compared to this beautiful work. Wherefore, he would easily have passed those over in silence, and employed his style and great eloquence to describe and highly praise this single work, exceeding without compari—

LIVRE PREMIER DE

...surpassed all others that were ever made. I could not (in truth) satisfy myself with seeing things so marvelous, and I said to myself: "If the fragments of sacred antiquity, if the ruins and broken pieces—indeed, almost the very dust of it—give me such great contentment and admiration, what would it be like if they were whole?" Then I thought without delay: "Perhaps in there, within these deep and hollow places, is the altar of sacrifices and the holy flames of the goddess Venus, or her statue of Aphrodite <note>original: "Aphrodise"</note>, together with Cupid her son." 

While in this state of thought, I placed my right foot upon the threshold of the door, and suddenly a white mouse crossed my path; nonetheless, I passed further in without thinking more of it. I found that the inside was no less rich than the outside, for the side walls were of white marble, and exactly in the middle of each side was set a large roundel of Jet <term>Jet: A hard, polished black gemstone formed from fossilized wood, prized in antiquity for its deep luster</term>, surrounded by a triumphal wreath made of green Jasper. This roundel was so black and so highly polished that one could see oneself in it as if in a crystalline mirror. I would have passed on without noticing it, but when I was between the two, I perceived my own figure on one side and the other; at this I became somewhat terrified, thinking they were two men. 

Beneath these roundels, along the side walls, were made marble seats two feet high, set upon a pavement of mother-of-pearl, clean and without any stain. Likewise, in the vault above, one could not have seen a single spiderweb, because a fresh wind was always blowing through it. The vault was joined to the side walls by a belt <note>A decorative cornice or molding</note> that began at the capitals of the pilasters <note>original: "arrierecorps"</note> of the door and continued to the back of the entrance, containing in length (as I could judge by the rules of perspective) twelve paces or thereabouts. 

In this belt were carved in bas-relief <note>original: "demybofte"; a style of sculpture where the figures project only slightly from the background</note> several small sea monsters, swimming in water, fashioned in the form of men from the navel upward, while the rest finished in twisted fish tails, upon which sat several naked women of the same nature and figure, embracing the monsters and being similarly embraced by them. Some blew into trumpets <note>original: "buccines"</note> made of snail shells; others held strange and wonderfully fantastic instruments. Many there were crowned with the flower and herb of the water-nymph, called by the French "white or yellow water-lily" <note>original: "blanc ou iaunet d'eau"</note> and by the Arabs "Nenuphar" <term>Nenuphar: A historical term for the water lily, derived from Persian and Arabic</term>, seated in chariots made of great sea shells and drawn by dolphins. Some were laden with baskets full of fruit, and others carried horns of plenty <note>Cornucopias</note>. You would have seen some who fought one another with handfuls of rushes and reeds; others girded with thistles and mounted on sea-horses, making shields of turtle shells—all differing in their actions and forms, and indeed making efforts so vividly expressed that one could almost see them move. 

The vault was divided into two squares, separated by a frieze two feet in width, which served as a border running all around, passing along the belt and following the arch of the vault. It was entirely constructed of mosaic <note>original: "mufaïque"</note> made of small tiles of colored glass, so skillfully done that it seemed to have been made in that very hour. It was a foliage of greenery as vivid as emerald, the underside of which (where it happened to fold back) was of a vermilion color like ruby, and the flowers azure...

...azure <note>The text begins mid-word, likely "azurées" (azure-colored).</note> resembling Sapphires, scattered so appropriately throughout the work that you would have said they were born there. In one of the squares was depicted the beautiful Europa crossing the sea upon the enchanted Bull, and King Agenor her father, commanding his sons, Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix, to go and search for their sister; and how, while searching for her, they valiantly killed the scaly Dragon which they found near the fountain; then, by the counsel of Apollo, they built a city where the ox stopped, and gave the country the name Boeotia, from the lowing of the oxen. Afterward, how Cadmus built Athens <note>In classical mythology, Cadmus is the legendary founder of Thebes; the author here attributes the founding of Athens to him.</note>, Phoenix built Phoenicia, and Cilix built Cilicia. In the other square was carved the unruly Pasiphaë, enclosed within the artificial cow with the bull mounted upon her; then the great monster, the Minotaur, shut within the Labyrinth; and the ingenious Daedalus, who fled from the prison and flew through the air by means of the wings he had fashioned for himself and his son Icarus: who, for refusing to believe his father’s counsel, tumbled and was drowned in the sea, to which in dying he left his name. Also, how the father, having reached safety, hung up his wings in the temple of Apollo and devotedly fulfilled his vow.

These histories were so complete that not a single tile had been displaced, so firm was the cement with which they were assembled.

I went step by step, contemplating the excellence of the work and the great knowledge of the craftsman, who had so perfectly observed all the rules of portraiture, painting, sculpture, and perspective: for he had drawn the lines of the masonry to their vanishing point <note>original: "au poinct de leur obiect"</note>, so that in some places they were lost to sight; whereby he reduced, little by little, imperfect things to their true perfection; and on the contrary, he brought distant things close and moved the nearest things further away, with a pleasant placement of landscapes composed of plains, mountains, valleys, country houses, groves, rivulets, and fountains, enriched with cattle and small figures <note>original: "mannequins"</note>, darkening the colors according to the distances and the appropriate light.

He had, moreover, made the drapery of the garments so close to nature that one could almost have grasped it: for in everything and in every part he had so well followed nature that, if one had not looked closely, one would have judged it real and not feigned. This left me so Ravished with wonder and transported by amazement that I hardly thought myself to be present there, but was entirely outside of myself.

Thus walking one step after another, I reached the end of the entry where the painting finished; and further on it was so dark that I did not dare to venture into it; wherefore I resolved to turn back.

Hardly had I turned my face when I felt, through these ruins, something like a rattling of bones, or a clashing of great branches, by which I was very greatly terrified.

Soon after, I heard more clearly something like the dragging of some large dead beast, like an ox or a horse; and this noise always approached the door.

Then it was not long before I heard the hissing of a serpent: and then I lost both heart and voice; and even the hair stood up on my head, and I gave myself up for dead and undone.

Seeing then that the poisonous and detestable smoke that this Dragon spewed reached nearly to where I was, I threw myself at random into those thick shadows, holding my life as lost, piteously calling upon the immortal Gods, and fleeing by winding paths, where I entirely lost the light, so that I did not know how to judge whether I was inside the Labyrinth of **Daedalus** <note>The legendary craftsman of Greek myth who built the complex maze for King Minos to house the Minotaur.</note> the ingenious: so many were the twisting paths, trails, alleys, crossroads, doors, and passages, designed to make one fail and forget the exit, only to return always to the first error, and wander in even deeper obscurity.

I truly feared having arrived in the hollow rock of **Polyphemus** <note>The one-eyed Cyclops from the *Odyssey* who trapped Odysseus and his men in his cave.</note> the cruel Cyclops: or in the cavern of the malicious thief **Cacus** <note>A fire-breathing giant from Roman mythology who stole cattle from Hercules and was killed in his cave on the Aventine Hill.</note>: therefore I immediately threw my arms before my eyes, for fear of the pillars that supported the pyramid: and I went groping, turning back many times to look behind me, to see if I could still see the place through which I had entered, or even if the devouring Dragon was coming after me. But I found that the light had utterly failed me. And to increase my great fear, these dark caves were full of **Bats** <note>original: "Chauuesouyrz."</note>, which fluttered around my ears: so that I, who was already terrified, thought everything I heard, felt, or touched was the cruel Dragon. And although my eyes found themselves somewhat accustomed to these shadows, nonetheless I could see nothing: therefore my arms had to perform the office of my eyes, just like the **Snail** <note>original: "Lymaçon."</note>, which goes feeling the path with its horns, and if it finds an obstacle, suddenly pulls them back to itself. In such a manner I went groping across these blinded turnings, and through these devious paths, in greater toil and perplexity than **Mercury** when he became a **Stork** <note>Likely a reference to the myth where the gods fled from the monster Typhon and transformed into animals; Mercury is often said to have become an ibis, which early translators sometimes rendered as a stork.</note>: indeed, than the God **Apollo** when he was constrained to guard the Sheep in Thrace: or than the beautiful **Diana** when she was changed into a little bird: even in more extreme anguish than **Psyche**, after having lost **Cupid** her husband: and in more laborious peril than **Lucius Apuleius** when he was transformed into an **Ass** <note>A reference to *The Golden Ass*, the only ancient Roman novel in Latin to survive in its entirety, in which the protagonist is accidentally turned into a donkey.</note>, and heard the counsel and deliberation of the thieves regarding his imminent death. My fear was more than doubled by the wild flying and beating of the air of these bats: for when I heard them whistling so close to me, I thought I was already between the Dragon's teeth.

And though this fear was excessive, and almost extreme, yet it was more vehement when it came back to my memory that I had perceived the **Wolf** <note>An encounter earlier in the book; in Renaissance folklore, being seen by a wolf before you see it was considered a sign of losing one's voice or a general omen of doom.</note>, which made me presume that it was a very bad omen, indeed a manifest sign of my sad and sorrowful end. Therefore I ran here and there, my ears open and my eyes closed, reduced to such necessity that death was much dearer and more desired by me than life. Nonetheless, I had a marvelous regret to die without having obtained the long-desired effect of my loves. Alas, if only I had at least seen my lady **Polia**: no death (truly) would be grievous or tiresome to me. Shall I then lose by a single misfortune two things so very precious as life and my beloved? Never (alas) will you see her again. Here is the end of your pleasures, along with your amorous thoughts. Alas, what misfortune, or what malignant **Star** <note>Poliphile often blames astrological influence for his trials, reflecting the Renaissance belief in the power of the heavens over human fate.</note> has así cast you into such mortal languor: and destined you to serve as fodder for a beast as vile as this **Dragon**, in whose belly you must be entombed? Alas, at least let me be swallowed whole, so that I may rot in this state within its poisonous entrails. O miserable end, O lamentable death. Where are the eyes so dried out and deprived of natural moisture, that they should not distill and melt into tears? But here it is, I feel it at my shoulders. Who ever saw a greater cruelty of fortune? Here is spiteful death, and the final hour of the cursed moment when this poor human flesh will be meat for a serpent. What calamity is more strange and rigorous than to live after one's death, and remain without burial? O how much more grievous is the misfortune of abandoning his lady so loyal! Farewell, farewell then Polia, my heartfelt and singular friend.

Thus to myself I lamented, so weary and troubled in every way, that I had nothing left but my spirit wandering through these shadows: with which I took as a last refuge to invoke the all-powerful Gods of heaven, and my **good Angel** <note>Poliphile's guardian spirit.</note>, with a pure and affectionate conscience, believing that they would have pity on this my sinister accident. Then, as I was in this state of perplexity, I perceived from afar a small light: therefore there is no need to ask if I ran toward it with great joy: but certainly it was short-lived: for when I had arrived near, I saw that it was a lamp, forever burning, which hung before an altar: which (as I could understand) was five feet high, and twice as wide: and upon it were placed three statues of gold. Then I found myself frustrated in my intention, and overtaken by a devout horror. This light was hardly clear, but rather all murky because of the thick air. Nevertheless, I saw somewhat the layout of these underground places, namely the great openings, the dark and deep ways, with the vaults supported by thick pillars of four, six, and eight sides <note>Referring to square, hexagonal, and octagonal columns, showing the author's obsession with geometric architecture.</note>, which one could not clearly discern, owing to the weakness of the light: nonetheless they seemed well-made and of suitable proportion to sustain the excessive weight of the great and marvelous pyramid that was above. For this reason, after having made a brief prayer before this altar, I set myself again to seek the exit: and I had not walked much, when there appeared to me another small splendor shining through a narrow hole, almost like the neck of a funnel. O what a celebration I made for it, and with what heart I followed it!

I had not (certainly) sooner perceived it, than I renounced all the desires to die to which I had shortly before resigned myself: and I recommenced my amorous thoughts, persuading myself by a feigned and flattering hope, that I could still in time easily acquire what I lately held for lost. When then I had reached this light, which from afar had seemed so small, I found that it was a large opening: through which I exited in great haste, and set myself to run, without looking back at where I had come from. Finally, after I had escaped those dark caverns, which truly resembled a chamber of hell (for my life had been in great danger there, even though it was the most holy Aphrodisian <note>original: "treffainct Aphrodife"—referring to the sacred precinct of Aphrodite, the goddess of love</note>), and I had arrived in that graceful country, I turned my head to see where I had come from. I looked upon a mountain that was not very steep, but moderately declining in a descent, covered with beautiful green trees, such as **Oaks**, **Maples**, **Limes**, **Ashes**, and others like them. Along the plain, it was bordered with **Medlars**, **Hazels**, **Sorb-apples**, and **Service-trees**, wrapped in **Honeysuckle**, **Privet**, **Hops**, and **Bindweed**. Below grew **Polypody**, **Hart’s-tongue fern**, both types of **Hellebore**, **Clover**, **Plantain**, **Bugle**, **Sanicle**, and many other herbs that thrive in the shade. The opening through which I had exited was somewhat high, and the mountain was all covered in brambles and bushes; and from what I could guess, it was opposite the beautiful gate through which I had entered. Therefore, it is to be believed that there used to be a similar entrance on this side as on the other, and that time and old age had reduced it to a heap of ruins, and converted it into a large mound completely stripped of any recognizable features. For among the stones many shrubs had grown, so that I could hardly discern with my eye the hole through which I had emerged. I think that one could not have gone back in because of the branches, trunks, and roots that occupied it; nor (what is more) even find it without difficulty. At least for my part, I do not think I could have returned there, so secluded and wild was the place. 

Descending, I first came along the hillside to a grove of **Chestnut trees**, which I presumed to be the habitation of the god **Pan**, or of **Sylvanus** <note>Pan and Sylvanus were ancient deities of the wild, woods, and shepherds</note>, because of the beautiful pastures and fresh shadows that were there. Then, passing further on, I found an antique bridge made of **white marble**, which had only a single arch, but it was quite large and built with good proportions. At the top of this bridge, all along the armrests or parapets on both sides, there were seats of the same stone, upon which I did not dare to sit, even though I had great need of it, for I was very tired and weary. The flowerbed was sown with all manner of flowers and fragrant herbs suitable for **medicine**, bedewed by those small streams, which rendered the place so pleasant that I thought myself then to be in the **Fortunate Isles** <note>The Fortunate Isles, or Isles of the Blessed, were a semi-mythical paradise in Greek mythology, often identified with the Canary Islands.</note>: and I could not believe that it was without inhabitant. Being then in this thought, I raised my gaze a little, and perceived above the tops of the trees the roof of an edifice: for which I was greatly rejoiced, and drew in great haste toward that part. Then, arrived quite near, I found that this dwelling was **octagonal**, that is to say, of eight sides or faces, and that in one of them there was a beautiful fountain, which came very opportunely for the thirst I had endured. The roof at the summit of the building was also of eight squares, just like the rest of the body: and it seemed to me from afar to be covered in lead, because it finished in a point. 

In one of the faces of the structure there was a stone of white marble, polished as well as possible, having a height of one and a half times its width: the width of which square (as I could estimate) was six feet in measure. At the two sides of this stone there were two **fluted columns** with <term>rudentures</term> <note>Also known as "cabling," these are convex moldings that fill the lower third of the grooves in a fluted column.</note> or moldings, furnished with their bases and capitals, and above them the **architrave**, **frieze**, and **cornice**, upon which sat the **pediment**, having for its height the fourth part of the square: in the <term>tympanum</term> <note>The triangular or semi-circular decorative wall surface over an entrance, bounded by a pediment.</note> or flat surface of which there was a triumphal wreath: and within it two doves drinking from a small vessel, all of one solid stone. 

Between the two columns within the square was carved a beautiful **sleeping Nymph**, stretched out upon a cloth, part of which seemed bunched beneath her head, as if it had served her as a pillow. The other part she had drawn to cover that which modesty requires one to hide. And she lay upon her right side, holding her hand beneath her cheek, as if to support her head. The other arm was extended along the left hip, down to the middle of the thigh. From the nipples of her breasts (which seemed to be those of a maiden) there issued from the right a stream of cold water, and from the left one of hot water: which fell into a large stone of **porphyry** <note>A very hard, purple-red igneous rock highly prized in antiquity for imperial monuments.</note>, made in the form of two basins, distant from the Nymph about six feet in distance. 

In front of the fountain upon a rich pavement between the two basins, there was a small channel, in which these two waters joined together, exiting the basins one opposite the other: and thus mixed they made a small stream of tempered heat suitable for procreating all greenery. The hot water sprang so very high that it could not hinder those who put their mouths to the right breast to suckle it, and there drink the cold water. This figure was so excellently expressed, that the image of the goddess **Venus** formerly made by **Praxiteles** <note>One of the most famous Greek sculptors of the 4th century BCE; his Aphrodite of Cnidus was legendary for its beauty.</note>, was never so perfectly carved, even though to purchase it **Nicomedes**, King of the **Cnidians**, spent all the wealth of his people. Yet it is true that this good craftsman made her so beautiful, that there were afterwards some men who fell in love with her: so that I cannot persuade myself that this Nymph had been made by the hand of an artist, but rather that from a natural and living creature, she had been transformed into this stone. She had her lips half-open, as if she had wished to catch her breath: so that one could see all the inside of her mouth almost to the knot of the throat. The stream that flowed from this fountain ran between two hedges of rosebushes, which were quite low, and watered a field full of sugarcane. Along its course grew artichokes, beloved by the beautiful Venus, asparagus, **satyrion** <note>A type of orchid (likely *Orchis mascula*) which in the Renaissance was believed to be a powerful aphrodisiac, named after the lustful satyrs.</note>, melilot, and wild chicory. On both sides were orange and lemon trees, planted in a straight line and laden with their fruit, their branches hanging within a pace of the ground, so that they were round and wide toward the bottom, the top rising to a point in the manner of a pyramid, and smelling so very sweet that my spirits were entirely refreshed. I would have considered myself too happy and content if I had found some dwelling there. The desire urged me to go further, and I did not know where to turn. Along with this, I was weary, troubled, doubtful, and in fear of falling into some unfortunate accident, because I recalled to memory the **hieroglyphs** <note>In this context, Poliphilo refers to the symbolic picture-writing he encountered earlier on the bridge, which served as architectural warnings or mottos.</note> that were on the left side of the bridge; and thinking that such a warning had not been written there in vain and without good cause, which is to say: *Always make haste slowly.* <note>original Latin: "Semper festina tardè." This was the famous motto of the printer Aldus Manutius (who published the original 1499 edition of this book), symbolized by a dolphin and an anchor.</note> Just then, I heard a marvelous noise behind me, which sounded like the beating of a **dragon's** wings; and before me another sound like that of a trumpet. At this, I turned suddenly, quite lost, and saw beside me several carob trees, with their ripe fruit long and hanging, which, shaken by the wind, had knocked against each other; therefore I came back to myself and began to laugh at what had happened to me. Then I invoked the good gods, **Jugatinus**, **Collatinus**, and **Vallonia** <note>Minor Roman deities: Jugatinus presided over the joining of couples; Collatinus over hills; and Vallonia over valleys. Poliphilo prays to them as he navigates the varying terrain.</note> (the first of whom is named from "joining," the second from "hill," and the third from "valley"), praying to them that as I walked through their holy places, they might be favorable and propitious to me; for I almost feared meeting an army because of the trumpet. However, I presumed it was some shepherd’s horn made of bark, and I reassured myself as best I could. A short time later, I heard a company of people coming toward me singing; and it seemed to me by the voices that they were young maidens, accompanied by the sound of some lyre. Therefore, I ducked beneath the branches to see what it might be, so that I perceived five young ladies, who walked with good grace, their hair tied with ribbons of gold thread, wearing wreaths of **myrtle** <note>A plant sacred to Venus, symbolizing love and immortality.</note> upon their heads, along with other divine flowers...

### POLIPHILO

...gracefully arranged, dressed in silk attire in the fashion of the **Island of Cos** <note>original: "l’isle de Cos." When they had spotted me, they immediately stopped and ceased their singing, looking at one another without saying a word, so that it seemed they were astonished to see me, as if it were a strange and new thing to them. This land is more blessed and greater than Mount Taurus on its northern slopes, even though it is said that the grapes it produces are two cubits <note>original: "deux coudées"; a cubit is roughly 18 inches, making these grapes three feet long</note> long, and that a single fig tree there bears seventy <term>muids<gloss>an ancient French measure of capacity, often exceeding 250 liters</gloss></term> of fruit each year. It truly exceeds the fertility of the Hyperborean isle in the Indian Sea. It surpasses Portugal, and even the isle of Talge in the Caspian Sea. And although Egypt is called the common granary of the whole world, its abundance is less than nothing compared to that of this province. We have no swamps or marshes that might breed foul air. Our mountains are not too rugged, but are merely small hills and beautiful valleys, enclosed on the outside by high, sheer, inaccessible rocks, so that we have no reason to fear anything. In this place are all things that can bring pleasure. It is the promenade of the great gods, the desired rest and the reassurance of the spirit. We serve a Queen of great excellence and liberality, named <term>Eleutherilide<gloss>a name derived from the Greek word for "freedom" or "liberty," representing Free Will</gloss></term>, who is most benign and of a cordial nature; she, through her great knowledge, virtue, and more than human felicity, governs and rules all this beautiful country. It will be a most agreeable thing to her that you are conducted by us before her supreme majesty. And if our companions, her other servants and household, knew you were here, they would run here in flocks to see what so rarely happens to us. Therefore, cast out all fear and sadness, for you are in a place of peace, tranquility, and friendship.

## How, after Poliphile was reassured by THE FIVE MAIDENS, HE WENT TO THE baths with them: and how there was great laughter because of the fountain and the distance; then, how he was led by them before Queen Eleutherilide, in whose palace he saw another beautiful fountain and many marvelous things.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'R' at the beginning of the paragraph. The letter is ornate, set against a background of scrolling vines and architectural motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

Received by the five maidens as courteously as has been said, and reassured by their words, which were as sweet and benign as possible, I dedicated myself to doing them entirely whatever service might be in my power and that I thought would be pleasing to them. And because they carried in their hands certain vases of gold and precious stones, full of musk soap and other scents, mirrors, combs, kerchiefs, shifts, and linens for bathing, I offered to carry them for them. This they would not permit, but said to me: "We are going to the baths, and we want you to come with us, for it is not far from here, and we think you have already seen the fountain." To which I promptly replied: "Most beautiful and exquisite Nymphs, if I had a thousand tongues, I could not sufficiently thank you for such courtesy and benignity as you show toward me; for you have, in a happy hour, raised me from death to life. Therefore, not to accept such a gracious invitation should be imputed to me as cowardice and too great a folly. Certainly, I would consider myself more fortunate to be your perpetual slave than to rule elsewhere with authority, seeing as (as far as I can tell) you are the treasure of all good and all worldly joy. Know that I have seen at my leisure the fountain..."

We are five companions, as you can see. As for me, I am called **Aphaé** <note>original: "Aphaé," from the Greek *aphē*, meaning touch</note> (that is to say, **Touch**). She who carries the boxes and the linen is **Osphrasie** <note>original: "Osphrasie," from the Greek *osphrēsis*, meaning smell</note> (**Smell**). Therefore, since your good fortune has brought you here, you shall come with us; and after we have enjoyed ourselves a little, we shall return to the palace of the Queen. You will find her full of all clemency and liberality; be certain that by reciting to her the story of your loves and your high pretensions, you will easily induce her to help you." With these words and conversation, they led me to the place, and I was very happy with all that had happened to me—so much so that nothing was left to desire except my lady Polia, to complete the perfect number and give achievement to my supreme happiness. However, I found myself wonderfully ashamed that my clothing was not suitable for such a noble assembly; but after becoming somewhat accustomed to them, I began to frolic with the nymphs, which made them laugh, and me as well.

During these events, we arrived at the baths, which were (certainly) a marvelous edifice. It was an **octagonal** place—that is to say, of eight angles or sides—on the outside of which were two pillars set upon a single pedestal, which began at the level of the pavement and surrounded the entire enclosure. These pillars emerged from the wall by a third of their width and were enriched with beautiful capitals, above which ran the architrave, frieze, and cornice. In the frieze were carved little nude children holding belts or cords from which hung beautiful festoons, otherwise known as bundles of greenery. Upon the cornice was placed the <term>retube<gloss>a dome or vaulted ceiling</gloss></term>, which is a round <term>semi-dome vault<gloss>original: "cul de four," a masonry term for a vault shaped like the back of an oven</gloss></term> but made in an octagonal form to correspond with the rest of the building. Its faces were pierced through with foliage of various designs; the openings were closed with glass or perhaps plates of fine crystal, which from a distance had looked like lead to me. The <term>pteryge<gloss>a pinnacle or small turret</gloss></term> (that is to say, the pinnacle or lantern) was a similarly octagonal point upon which there was a round globe; and upon the center of this globe was a pivot with a vane turning to all winds. The pavement of the floor beneath the water was of mosaic assembled from small fine stones, by which were expressed all sorts and manners of fish. The water was attractively warm, not by artificial heat, but only by nature: and what is more, so neat and clear that looking into it, you would have judged those fish to be moving and rubbing all along the seats where they were portrayed to the life, namely: carp, pike, eels, tench, lampreys, shad, perch, turbot, soles, rays, trout, salmon, mullet, plaice, crayfish, and infinite others, which seemed to stir with the movement of the water: so closely did the work approach nature.

Thus I endured this ardor with marvelous patience, and my suffering was accompanied by a modest shame, knowing that I was unworthy to be in this divine company. Because of this (though I often refused while making excuses), I was forced to enter the bath, like a **crow among the doves** <note>original: "Corneille entre les Colombes" – a classic metaphor for someone plain or out of place among the beautiful and elite.</note>. Therefore, I kept myself apart, full of shame, my eyes wandering and restless, not daring to look upon such excellent and singular objects.

Then **Osphrasie** <note>Osphrasie represents the sense of Smell.</note> said to me, "My friend, what is your name?" And I answered her with all reverence that I was called **Poliphile**. "It pleases me well," she said, "if the result matches the name. But what is your beloved's name?" "**Polia**, my lady," I said then; to which she promptly replied: "Indeed, I thought your name meant 'much loved' <note>The name Poliphilo is a Greek pun: it can mean "lover of Polia" or "lover of many things."</note>, but from what I can understand, it means 'the lover of Polia.' By your faith, if she were here, what service would you do for her?" "That, my lady," I replied, "which belongs to her modest chastity, and which would be suitable and worthy to be done in your divine presence." Then she said to me: "Tell me more, I pray you, Poliphile: do you bear her great love?" "Alas, my lady," I replied, "yes, more than my own life," and sighing, I added, "Truly more than all the delights, riches, and precious treasures of the world." "Where then have you left," she said, "a thing so dear and so loved?" "I truly do not know," I answered, "in what place I am even now." Then she said, smiling: "What would you give to the person who would make you recover her? Do not worry: be of good cheer and rejoice in your heart, for you shall find her very soon." In such and similar talk, the beautiful **Nymphs** bathed themselves, and I also with them.

Within the thickness of this hedge, the branches and trunks were so neatly joined that one could easily walk atop them to go to the windows or stroll around. Around the pillar were four Harpies of fine gold, having their claws extended upon the Ophite plinth, their backs turned toward this pillar, and opposite one another. The tips of their wings extended up under the Amethyst basin, as if to hold it in the air. Their faces looked like those of maidens, but their tails were of serpents, twisted and ending in ancient foliage <note>original: "fueillage antique" — likely acanthus leaves or classical scrolling patterns.</note>, which joined at the very top of the pillar directly under the bottom of this basin, so that they served as a superb and magnificent ornament. 

In the very middle of the large basin on the inside, and plumb with the pillar, emerged a somewhat elongated vase, intentionally turned upside down upon its mouth, and decorated with beautiful foliage made of the same stone as the basin, protruding outward as much as the basin was deep; and it supported a round base, upon which were placed the three naked Charities or Graces <note>The Graces—Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia—represented beauty, charm, and joy.</note>, life-sized, made of fine gold, joined back to back, spurting water from their breasts like delicate thin threads, which looked like rods of fine silver. Each of them held a cornucopia <note>original: "corne d'abondance"</note>, which all joined into one a little above their heads. Among the fruits and leaves that sprang from the horns, the water came out through six small pipes and gushed upward to the level of the hedge or wall of greenery. The craftsman, to preserve modesty <note>original: "l’honneſteté"</note>, had made it so that each of the three ladies held her left hand over the part that should be covered. 

Upon the edges of the large basin, exceeding the aforementioned Ophite plinth by one foot in width all around its circumference, were six golden Dragons, standing on their feet at equal distances, in such a way and with such skill that the water coming from the breasts of the three ladies fell directly into their heads, which were hollowed and carved out; then the water came back out through their maws and fell between the Ophite plinth and the Porphyry basin, in which there was a channel one and a half feet wide and two deep. The rest of the dragons' bodies lay upon the hollow of the basin, until they joined their tails, which turned into ancient foliage, of which the vase supporting the three ladies was made and composed, without the basin being in any way deformed or obstructed within. 

But the reflection of the greenery from the orange trees, the luster of the stone, and the clarity of the water caused those looking on to see a diversity of colors, such as one sees in a rainbow. From the belly of the basin on the outside, between two Dragons, came Lion heads, emptying through certain small pipes the water that distilled from the Cornucopias; which, after having risen very high, fell back into this basin in the places where these Lion heads were, making a resonance sweet and graceful beyond measure.

The work was so excellent that I do not believe the hands of men had made it; for it is impossible to describe it well, and for human understanding to comprehend it. Nevertheless, I can say this: that never in all our time, nor before (so far as is known), was work so perfect seen; so far was anything else from approaching it. The entire area around the fountain was paved with square marble tiles of diverse colors and shapes. In the middle of each square was set a round piece of Jasper of a different color. The corners and angles of the squares outside the circles were decorated with foliage. Between the tiles and around the entire pavement were bands or borders to serve as separation, made of fine mosaic. It was a very green foliage, accompanied by many flowers—yellow, blue-gray <note>original: "perses," a color term used in the Renaissance for a deep, dark blue or bluish-gray</note>, red, and violet—composed of small cubic stones, so artfully joined that it seemed a flat painting. I found myself quite surprised by these things, for I was not accustomed to seeing such excellent works; and I would have willingly stopped to contemplate it more at leisure, but it was then necessary for me to follow the damsels, my guides and companions.

The appearance and look of this Palace seemed properly to smile at people: therefore, the more I approached it, the more I found it worthy of contemplation, for the richness of the walls, the excellence of the painting, the arrangement of the columns, and the distribution of the parts, such as halls, chambers, galleries, and offices. There were the feats of the magnanimous and powerful <term>Hercules</term> <note>The Greek hero known for his strength and twelve labors, frequently used in Renaissance art to symbolize virtue and power</note>, carved in <term>half-relief</term> <note>original: "demy bosse," also known as mezzo-rilievo, where the sculpted figures stand out halfway from the flat background</note>, and so properly defined that the figures seemed separated from the background; and they were surrounded by spoils, titles, and trophies of a matchless and admirable artifice. But what an entry! what a portico! what a stairway! Certainly I have nothing to compare it to: for everything was so singular that even a perfect understanding would be too small and weak to describe it. The <term>spiral and ascent</term> <note>original: "La viz & montée," referring to a winding or screw-shaped staircase, a marvel of architectural geometry at the time</note> was quite exquisite, considering that the art of Architecture had employed all its knowledge there. The arch of the gate’s vault was recessed from below between two moldings, with round and square panels, and inside strewn with roses and foliage in half-carving, highlighted with gold, and the background laid in azure. Before this gate was hung a curtain woven of gold thread and silk; and upon it were depicted two beautiful images, one with all the instruments suitable for labor, and the other contemplating the heavens. When we arrived before this curtain, the Nymphs took me by the hand to lead me inside, saying: "Poliphilo, this is the order that must be observed, and by which one must come into the presence of the Queen our mistress. It is not permitted nor lawful for anyone to enter this first curtain unless they are received by a vigilant damsel gatekeeper, named Cinofie (mutable, or moving) who heard us immediately, and came to us, opening the curtain slightly, so that we soon entered within." There was a small space, and after that another curtain, prettier than the first, diversified with all sorts of colors, and with all manners of beasts, plants, herbs, and flowers, of sovereign tapestry. There came to us another gatekeeper named Indalmene (sanctifying) who seemed marvelously curious; nevertheless she received us kindly and opened the second curtain, putting us inside. Arrived as I was at the first chamber, she looked at me as if completely astonished; and after I had greeted her, as was fitting, I was received by her with all sweetness, and likewise by her ladies. Then when I had passed the three curtains, I found a great portico, in the form of a low and open gallery, which contained in length as much as the entire body of the palace.
