The matron gatekeeper of the last curtain admonished and warned me that I should be steady and constant, without fearing anything in this world, and that I should persevere in following and putting into execution these good admonitions and wise counsel of Queen Eleutherilide, their mistress: for the end could only be good and honorable. ...the same stones and craftsmanship. Along the walls surrounding the space were seats of red and yellow <term>sandalwood<note>original: "bois de Sandal"; a fragrant, exotic wood highly valued in the Renaissance</note></term>, covered in green velvet, and square cushions filled with a soft material, like down or cotton. The velvet was attached to the edges of the frame with small nails of fine gold, over a border of hammered silver, fashioned in the manner of a ribbon. The walls of the palace were clad in sheets of gold and adorned with sculptures corresponding to such precious material, divided into seven squares by pillars and moldings of delicate proportion. 

In the middle of each of these squares, there was a roundel or triumphal wreath, composed of all kinds of fruits and foliage, imitated after nature from fine precious stones, according to the necessary colors, qualities, and resemblances. Inside the hollow of these roundels, the seven <term>Planets<note>original: "sept Planetes"; in the 16th century, these were the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note></term> were carved and chiseled in half-relief, along with their properties and nature. The remainder of the square outside the circle was enriched with foliage of fine silver, filed and applied over the gold leaf. Such was the wall of the first front. 

The wall on the left side was entirely similar, with the squares and wreaths of greenery, just like the preceding ones in number, ornament, and fashion; except that in these seven roundels were the seven triumphs of those who are ruled by the seven planets and inclined toward their constellation, made of the same workmanship and material. On the right side, I saw within the roundels the seven harmonies or concordances of these seven Planets, and the entry of the soul into the body, with the reception of the qualities infused by the celestial degrees. 

The fourth wall was like the others, except that the door occupied the middle space, and the other six spaces were of the same measure, proportion, and correspondence. These roundels contained the influences and operations proceeding from the inclination of the Planets, expressed by beautiful Nymphs, with the inscriptions, titles, and signs of their effects. The seventh roundel was situated in the middle of the frontispiece <note>The main decorative face or facade</note> of the portal, directly opposite the Planet of the Sun, which was higher than the six others on the opposite wall, because of the Queen’s throne, which was more elevated than the others. Thus all the corresponding parts were equal or similar to one another in number, position, and material. 

Each section of the wall was twenty-eight paces in length, such that the court was square, covered by a marvelous artifice. It was a <term>trellis of gold<note>original: "treille d’or"</note></term>, so industriously carved that it is impossible to properly describe it. From one pillar to the other, which formed the squares of the wall, there was a distance of four paces in seven divisions, which is the number most agreeable to nature. These pillars were of <term>oriental azure stone<note>original: "pierre d’azur orientale"; Lapis lazuli, a deep blue semi-precious stone</note></term>, of vivid color, and scattered with small gold flecks: the fronts or faces of which, between two moldings, were carved with candelabras, <term>grotesques<note>A style of decorative art characterized by fanciful human and animal forms interwoven with foliage</note></term>, foliage, <term>arabesques<note>Intricate, flowing patterns of floral or geometric lines</note></term>, horns of plenty, vases, masks, Satyrs, monsters, balusters, and other beautiful inventions and devices of a sculpture so rounded that it seemed to be entirely in the round.

For the leaves were of emeralds, the flowers of sapphires, rubies, diamonds, topazes, and other precious stones, daintily ordered and arranged according to their colors. Across this foliage there were likewise grapes counterfeited from amethysts and other exquisite stones, of a color matching their natural state. The expense of this building was infinite, for the whole trellis shone with a marvelous light, not only because of the material, which was incomparable, but also for the unparalleled craftsmanship; for I could never comprehend by what art or invention this work had been erected, nor certainly determine if it was nailed, soldered, or <term>set<note>original: "enchassée"; a jeweler's term for securing a stone in a metal frame</note></term>, which are the three ways of assembling used in <term>goldsmithing<note>original: "orfauerie"</note></term>. Her footwear was of green silk; the straps of her slippers were of gold, adorned with precious stones. She rested her feet on a cushion of crimson velvet, bordered with pearls, with four buttons of precious stones, with tassels or fringes of gold thread and crimson silk. To the right and to the left of her throne were seated the ladies of her court, in moderate and benign gravity, dressed in cloth of gold in a fashion so beautiful and becoming that I do not believe anything like it was ever seen in all the world. The Queen was in their midst in great pomp and magnificence, dressed in a garment bordered with precious stones in such great abundance that one would have said that nature had showered her superfluously with all the precious stones of her treasures.

When I arrived before her majesty, I humbly knelt and made such reverence to her as I knew how; and immediately all the ladies rose, moved (as I believe) by the novelty of seeing me. I was (without any doubt) in marvelous admiration, thinking of past things and considering the present ones, all filled with astonishment and confused by a bashful fear.

Then the ladies sat down again, and desiring to know news of me, they signaled to my companions and asked them softly in their ears who I was and how I had come there; whereby the eyes of all the assembly were turned upon me, occupied with looking at me.

Being thus on both knees before such high majesty, I found myself astonished and ashamed. Then the Queen questioned my companions about the manner of my arrival, and how I had entered within <note>original: "leans"; an archaic French contraction for "là-dedans," meaning inside or within these walls</note>. To which they recounted the whole affair to her, and let her know my name. Hearing this, she said to me graciously: "Poliphile, be of good cheer. I have well heard the account of your misfortune <note>original: "desconvenue"; referring to his previous trials and mishaps</note>: but I desire to hear how you escaped from the Dragon, and in what manner you found the exit from the dark caverns: for I am greatly amazed within myself, because no one, or few people, can arrive here by that way. And since your good fortune has led you here in safety, it seems reasonable to me to receive you into my grace, and to use toward you my customary liberality and benevolence."

I thanked her for this gracious reception, with the most humble and honorable words that were then in my power: and afterwards I recited to her succinctly, and point by point, how I fled the fury of the Dragon, and with what pain and difficulty I had reached that place; at which she marveled beyond measure, and likewise all the ladies. Then, continuing my speech, I told them how the five young ladies <note>original: "damoyselles"; these are the personifications of the senses who first discovered Poliphile</note> had found me wandering and trembling with fear. At which she began to smile, and said to me: "It sometimes happens that a bad beginning takes a happy and prosperous end. Now it had happened by chance, and without thinking, that I had sat upon the circle of Mercury: and I saw, turning around, how his kindness, his good aspect and influence, are diminished and depraved when he finds himself in the tail of the Scorpion <note>an astrological reference; Mercury's influence was thought to be weakened or turned "sour" when positioned in certain parts of the Zodiac</note>. Having looked at it, I straightened myself back toward the ladies and began to think how vile and poor my clothing was, since among so many rich ornaments I could be compared and called similar to the vile and deformed Scorpion among the noble signs of the Zodiac.

The rest of the ladies were seated on the other benches around the place, all richly adorned with varied and diverse garments, such as women know how to devise, their hair tied, braided, interlaced, and adorned in many beautiful and pleasant ways. Others had it curled and fluttering over their temples on both sides of the forehead. There were some with hair blacker than fine jet, tied with strings of large pearls; and around their necks were necklaces <note>original: "carcans"; heavy, ornamental collars or chokers</note> of inestimable price and value. All were so well-bred and well-taught that when the serving damsels bent their knees or bowed to show reverence to the tables, they also rose from their seats and did the same. The Queen's seat was directly opposite the third and last curtain, where there was a beautiful and large door, not of marble but of oriental Jasper <note>a precious variety of chalcedony, highly prized in the Renaissance for its deep colors</note>, made in the antique style, of a workmanship more than divine. The young girls brought a perpetual fountain <note>original: "fontaine sans fin"</note>, artificially constructed so that as the water fell into a golden basin, it rose again through hidden pipes to the very place from which it had issued. This circulation was achieved (at least as I conjectured) by two pipes, one more slender than the other, and a separation within the vessel which was pierced in the middle; whereby the air enclosed in this vacuum attracted the water like a sponge, then by constraint and force made it climb upward. It was first presented upon the Queen’s golden table by the two girls, who bowed their heads and bent their knees until they were nearly an inch from the ground. The other serving young ladies performed a similar reverence at the same instant—the same was done when setting down and removing the dishes, and consequently for every part of the service.

The two girls were followed by three young ladies. The first held a golden ewer <term>ewer: a large decorative pitcher used for carrying water for washing</term>, the second a basin of the same material, and the third a towel of white silk, exquisitely fine and delicate. The Queen washed in this fountain; the young lady carrying the basin received the water so that it would not return into the mechanism, but the one with the ewer replaced it with an equal amount of scented water. Then the third lady offered the towel to dry her hands. The base of this fountain was set upon four small wheels, by which it was rolled across all the tables to serve everyone. The center was embossed and slightly raised, crafted with elegant gadroons <term>gadroons: a decorative pattern of rounded moldings or fluting, common in Renaissance metalwork</term>; the rim was enriched with precious stones and beautiful sculptures.

The pillar was composed of two vases placed one atop the other, differing in shape, joined and assembled by two handles. The water, according to the judgment of my nose, was made of roses, lemon peel, ambergris <note>a rare, waxy substance used in perfumery, historically highly prized</note>, and benzoin <note>original: "benjouyn," a fragrant balsamic resin</note>, duly proportioned and yielding a most sweet odor.

Between the three **Angels**, right at the center of the base, was fixed a pillar made like an antique candelabra <note>original: "candelabre antique"</note>. At its peak was a cup similar to the others and of the same size, which filled the void left by the six in their midst. The serving maidens had placed glowing coals covered with ash within, and there boiled a golden vial <term>ampoule: a small flask or vessel</term> in each cup, full of water or some other liquor, which they (in my judgment) renewed every day. It seemed to me they were all different waters, such as **Rose**, **Myrtle**, **Elderberry** <note>original: "Suzeau," likely an archaic spelling for "sureau" (elderberry/elderflower)</note>, **Mint**, **Orange blossoms**, and other well-known varieties, mixed with many fragrant materials that breathed forth a scent so sweet that the likes of it was never before smelled.

Three very beautiful and graceful young ladies served the Queen, dressed in cloth woven with gold thread and silk. However, they changed their clothing whenever the tablecloths were changed, which occurred at every course. They came in the form of **Nymphs**, dressed in cloth of the same color as the tablecloth they brought, tucked up above the waist with a pleasant fold of their attire, swirling over their shoulders and drawn across the chest to reveal the beautiful valley that separated their small breasts, so round and perfectly white that the eyes of the onlookers were too sparingly satisfied, even though they contemplated them without ceasing. Their footwear was open over the top of the foot in the shape of a moon, fastened with gold buckles and straps. Their blonde and abundant hair hung down to their knees, but it was bound around the forehead with a garland of large, precious pearls, all of equal roundness. 

These three stood before the Queen, humble in demeanor and countenance, expert in their duties, prompt and ready to serve, although they served only for one table and one course. For when the next course came, they remained standing with arms folded; then the three newcomers served in their turn, and so on in order for each course of meat. Inside this chariot were the necessary supplies for the changing of the tables: namely, tablecloths, napkins, cups, plates, vessels, forks, meat, sauce, and the beverage, distributed by the young ladies of the chariot to the others who served the tables, who then placed all the remains of the cleared course back inside. And as they ceased, the singers began a harmony that would have lulled the **Sirens** to sleep. Because of this, two sounds and chords like celestial harmonies were continually heard: a delectable melody heard, a most sweet scent smelled, and an unparalleled delicacy tasted; for all things there were suited to dignity, grace, and delight. For the first course, all the vessels were of fine gold, like the Queen's table, and we were served a **cordial confection** <term>confiture cordiale: a medicinal preserve intended to invigorate the heart</term> made (as far as I could understand) from shavings <term>razure: scrapings or filings</term> of **Unicorn** <note>In the Renaissance, "unicorn horn"—often actually narwhal tusk—was prized as a universal antidote to poison</note>, of the two types of sandalwood, with pearls cooked and extinguished in **aqua vitae** <note>original: "eau de vie," high-proof distilled alcohol</note> until dissolved, manna, pine nuts, musk, and gold ground in rose water, preciously composed and assembled into a mass with sugar and starch. Each of us was given two pieces of it without drink: this is a food used to protect against all poison, deliver one from fever or melancholy humor, and preserve health and youth. I believe (truly) that the gods had harvested the wine we were given to drink from the **Elysian Fields** <note>In Greek mythology, the final resting place of the heroic and the virtuous; Poliphile suggests the wine is of divine quality</note>: for it is not possible that the habitable earth could produce such a precious liquor. The fifth tablecloth was of crimson-red silk, and such was the dress of the serving-maidens; the flowers were yellow, white, and violet **wallflowers**. The Queen’s tableware and table were of **Oriental Emerald**. This service being removed, another tablecloth of violet silk was laid, matching the clothing of the serving-maidens, covered with **Jasmine** flowers. Our food consisted of **Peacock** <note>original: "Pan," a common Renaissance spelling for "paon"</note> breast in green sauce, made of ground pistachios, sugar, starch, musk, thyme, wild thyme, marjoram, sorrel, and **solomon’s seal** <note>original: "falemonde," likely referring to the medicinal herb Solomon's Seal</note>. At the seventh and final change, they brought before the Queen a sumptuous ivory table, upon which was set another of **Aloeswood** <note>A highly fragrant wood used in perfumery and incense</note>, entirely engraved with foliage, flowers, vases, small monsters, and little birds; the hollowed-out spaces were filled with a fine paste of musk and amber. It was a magnificent masterpiece, fragrant and exquisite to behold. The tablecloths and napkins were made of **Carystian linen** <note>original: "lin de Carysto," referring to asbestos, which was famously woven into fireproof fabric in antiquity</note>; and likewise the robes and garments of the young ladies. The flowers were all sorts of sweet-smelling pinks and gillyflowers. But who could comprehend such great sweetness of so many different scents, renewed so often? The meat consisted of dates and pistachios ground in rosewater, with musk and sugar disguised with fine gold, so that the morsels appeared to be solid gold; and three were given to each of us. The tableware was of **Hyacinth** <note>A reddish-orange gemstone (zircon), not the flower</note>, certainly fitting for such great pomp and the excellence of this triumphant and divine banquet. When these cloths were lifted, a beautiful large golden basin full of glowing coals was brought in, onto which the napkins and tablecloths were thrown; they remained there so long that they were entirely engulfed in fire. Then they were pulled out; and when they had cooled, they returned to their original nature, clean and whole, as white as if someone had just taken them from a chest.

After the washing <note>This refers to the ritual hand-washing with scented water common at the end of a formal Renaissance banquet.</note>—which seemed a very new and marvelous thing, at least to me, who was not accustomed to seeing such mysteries—the more deeply I considered them, the more ignorant and astonished I found myself. # BOOK ONE OF POLIPHILE

...from behind, trailing down to half a foot from the ground. In this manner, all the vessels for both drinking and eating were served and carried. I truly believe that the gods had harvested the wine we were given to drink from the **Elysian Fields** <note>In Greek mythology, the final resting place of the heroic and the virtuous; a paradise.</note>; for it is not possible that the habitable earth could produce such a precious liquor. We drank of it at our pleasure. 

Then, the tablecloths being removed, others of grey silk were immediately brought in, the serving damsels being dressed in similar finery. They scattered **Damask roses**—white, bright red, and flesh-colored—over the table, bringing each of us six slices of fat **capon** <note>A castrated rooster, prized for its tender meat.</note> preserved in a sauce made of its own fat, saffron-colored rosewater, a little orange juice, and six slices of white bread. Then they set before us another sauce of lemon juice sweetened with sugar, the capon's liver pounded with pine nuts and diluted in rosewater, musk, and cinnamon. The Queen’s table and the vessels were of **Topaz** during this third service.

When the table was cleared, the fourth was immediately prepared, covered with a beautiful yellow satin, in which the serving damsels were dressed in a lovely fashion. Upon their arrival, they scattered flowers of **Lily of the Valley**. Then each of us was served seven breasts of **Partridge** and as many slices of bread, whiter than milk; the sauce was of pounded almonds, sugar, starch, yellow sandalwood, musk, and well-distilled rosewater. The Queen's table and vessels were then of **Chrysolite** <note>A yellowish-green gemstone, often associated with the sun in Renaissance lapidaries.</note>. We were given a second serving of the first drink.

The fifth tablecloth was of crimson silk, as were the clothes of the serving damsels; the flowers were yellow, white, and violet **gillyflowers**. We were each given eight pieces of **Pheasant** wing and as many slices of bread. The sauce was made of fresh egg yolks, pine nuts, orange water, pomegranate juice, sugar, and cinnamon. The Queen’s vessels and table were of **Oriental Emerald**.

Once this service was removed, another tablecloth of violet silk was laid, matching the clothing of the serving damsels, and covered with **Jasmine** flowers. Our meal consisted of **Peacock** <note>original: "Pan"; an archaic French term for peacock (paon).</note> breast in a green sauce made of pounded pistachios, sugar, starch, musk, thyme, wild thyme, marjoram, sorrel, and *salemonde* <note>A savory herb-based seasoning or preparation.</note>.

At the seventh and final change, they brought before the Queen a sumptuous ivory table, upon which was inlaid another of **Aloe wood**, all engraved with foliage, flowers, vases, little monsters, and small birds; the empty spaces were filled with a fine paste of musk and ambergris. It was a magnificent masterpiece, fragrant and exquisite to behold. The tablecloths and napkins were made of <term>lin de Carysto</term> <note>original: "lin de Carysto"; also known as "asbestos" or "mineral linen." In antiquity and the Renaissance, it was a marvel because it was cleaned by fire rather than water.</note>; the robes and garments of the damsels were likewise. The flowers were all sorts of sweet-smelling carnations and cloves. 

But who could comprehend such great sweetness of so many diverse scents, so frequently renewed? The food was made of **Dates** and **Pistachios** crushed in rosewater, with musk and sugar disguised with fine gold, so that the morsels appeared to be solid gold; and three were given to each of us. The vessels were of **Jacinth**, certainly suitable for such great pomp and the excellence of this triumphant and divine banquet. 

When these cloths were removed, they brought a beautiful, large golden basin full of glowing coals, upon which the napkins and tablecloths were thrown. They remained there so long that they were entirely engulfed in fire; then they were pulled out. When they had cooled, they returned to their original state, clean and whole, and as white as if they had just been taken from a chest.

...berries as large as **sorb-apples** <note>original: "Cormes"; the fruit of the service tree, which looks like a small pear or medlar and was eaten when overripe.</note>, all of their natural color, hanging by a thread of gold as if they had grown there. The young lady who carried it had one knee on the ground and supported the vessel on the other, which she held raised. This rich shrub, which stood among the roses, was shown to be decorated along its branches with large pearls, fixed to the tips of the shoots.

The second young lady held the drinking vessel, filled with a liquor far more precious than that which Queen Cleopatra once gave to the **Roman Captain** <note>Mark Antony; a reference to the famous story where Cleopatra dissolved a priceless pearl in vinegar to win a wager regarding the cost of a meal.</note>. The other three performed their duties as described above, and picked the five apples with a fork: then they presented them to us to eat. I do not think (in my judgment) that any man ever smelled or tasted food so excellent. It was (as I believe) the **Ambrosia** <note>The food of the Greek gods, said to grant immortality and exquisite pleasure.</note> upon which the gods feed. Then we returned the golden apples full of scents, which we had held in our hands during the dinner.

Afterward, they brought before us a miraculous work, namely an endless fountain of rare and novel invention, nonetheless producing the same effect as the first, but in another, more strange fashion. It was a square plinth made entirely of solid gold, measuring three feet in length, two in width, and four good inches in thickness. At each of the corners was a **Harpy** <note>A mythological monster with the head of a woman and the body of a bird.</note> extending her wings against the belly of a vase that was placed in the middle upon the center of the plinth, which was decorated with moldings. The front face and the back face were slightly curved in a half-round, like the fourth part of a circle: and were divided into three with suitable moldings. This plinth sat upon two wheels. The middle part of the front face contained a triumph of **Satyrs** and **Nymphs** <note>Spirits of the wild; Satyrs are goat-men associated with wine and revelry, while Nymphs are beautiful female nature deities.</note>, made in **bas-relief** <note>original: "demyboffe"; sculpture where the figures project slightly from a flat background.</note>: and on the back there was a sacrifice upon an ancient altar, along with several figures and personages. The other two-thirds, both on the front and back sides toward the corners, were covered and draped with the tails of these same Harpies, which were doubled and ended in foliage, expertly shaped and applied in **low relief** <note>original: "demy taille".</note>. The size of the vase in the middle did not exceed the width of the plinth at all, but rather appeared complete with all required and necessary proportion and ornament, so much so that it was perfect in everything belonging to an antique vase. Its mouth and opening rested on a **gadrooned** <note>original: "goderonné"; a decorative border made of repeated convex curves or fluting.</note> basin, wider by four fingers all around its circumference and roundness than the diameter of the vase.

In the middle of the basin there was also another vase, smaller by a fourth part than the one below, gadrooned toward the bottom for a third of its height: and where the gadroons ended, a belt was made in the form of a flat band, all set with **gemstones** <note>original: "pierrerie".</note>: and above, the head of a monster on each side of the mouth, from which came foliage embracing the body of the vase, and meeting with the foliage of another similar head carved on the other side: and in place of handles it had two round buckles in the form of rings, from which hung festoons of greenery, composed of flowers, fruits, leaves, and small branches, of many different kinds. Between these two buckles, directly in the middle of each side, was carved the face of an old man, whose chin also turned into foliage, and yielded water through the mouth, falling into the basin.

# POLIPHILE.

The opening of this last vessel surrounded a rich mountain, or a heap of precious stones, all without cut or polishing, gathered together in a single pile and pressed one against the other—roughly, without art, and without order. Because of this, the mountain appeared rugged and difficult to climb, yet it cast a brilliance of various strange colors. At the peak and summit of this mountain grew a pomegranate tree, whose trunk and branches were of gold, the leaves of emeralds, and the fruit of a natural size. The rind of the fruit was of unpolished gold, and the seeds were oriental **Rubies** <note>In the Renaissance, "oriental" referred to gemstones of the highest quality and hardness coming from the East, primarily India and Sri Lanka.</note>, each the size of a bean. The membrane or skin that separates the seeds was of appropriately fashioned silver.

The noble craftsman of this masterpiece had adorned it in certain places with split and half-opened pomegranates, the seeds of which appeared not yet to have reached maturity; he had composed these of large oriental pearls. A certainly superb invention, and one that almost put nature to shame.

Furthermore, he had placed there **balusters** <note>original: "baluſtres"; likely referring to the bell-shaped blossoms of the pomegranate tree.</note> or pomegranate flowers carved from crimson coral. Their openings were in the form of a calyx, serrated, and full of small threads of drawn gold. Then, he had passed a small pillar above the tree, fixed like a pivot into the axle of the chariot, passing through the empty hole within.

This pillar turned incessantly and supported a vessel of **Topaz**, wide at the bottom and encircled around the middle by two gold bands. These bands were fashioned into moldings of four small children’s heads, each having two wings and spitting water from its mouth.

The neck of the vessel was twice as long as the rest of the body, tapering and rising to a point, covered at the top with reversed foliage, upon which was placed another almost round vessel, also covered with beautiful foliage.

At the base of this last vessel, the tails of **Dolphins** <note>Dolphins were a common motif in Renaissance decorative arts, often symbolizing speed or appearing in watery contexts like fountains.</note> touched each side, joining the slender part of the vessel's neck. Their heads, which were covered in foliage, descended down to the gold bands or belts, between which were the heads of the small children. These were bent almost into the shape of handles with a beautiful grace, because the dolphins' heads were curved and vaulted, and the tails were low and held tight against the vessel. This was made with such artifice that when the chariot moved, the vessel and the pillar that supported it turned incessantly (as has been said), throwing water over the pomegranate tree. I thought that this resulted from a wheel of the chariot which caused another to turn—one that lay flat and was pegged—striking the bottom of the pillar, where a **lantern gear** <term>A "lantern gear" (or trundle) is an early type of gear consisting of two disks connected by cylindrical rods or "pins," used to transmit motion at a right angle.</term> had been made.

The wheels of the chariot were half-covered, up to the hub, in the form of two extended wings of fine gold, engraved with small monsters such as **Scyllas** <note>A legendary sea monster from Greek mythology, usually depicted as a woman with a girdle of barking dogs' heads.</note>, masks, and foliage. Thus was this fountain led past all the tables, and there we washed our hands and our faces with a water so very strongly scented that no man ever smelled a greater sweetness. Then the young ladies

Such and so great were the splendors, riches, triumphs, treasures, and delights of the Palace of this noble Queen, and her retinue so sumptuous, that one should not wonder if I have been unable nor known how to describe it distinctly and perfectly: for I do not think there is in the world a spirit so fine nor a tongue so eloquent, prompt, and well-spoken, that could do it justice. I am far from being sufficient for the task, especially considering that my heart was occupied with nothing else but thinking of my lady Polia; besides, I hold for certain that any human understanding (no matter how excellent one might choose) would have been troubled and confused among so many wonders, which are impossible to believe and even more difficult to recount. And even if there had been no other thought or imagination in my fantasy than that of her, it would have been enough to overwhelm and cloud all my senses. But who is he who could—I do not say recite, but only remember—all the rich finery and perfect beauties of the young ladies? The great prudence, the beautiful and wise speech, along with the intelligence, knowledge, and liberality of the Queen? The exquisite arrangement of the Architecture, the fitting proportion of the building, the excellence of the paintings and tapestries of silk and gold thread, the richness of the plate, the unparalleled workmanship of the sculptures, and the infinite multitude of precious stones? Certainly, it seemed to me that all those of the world were assembled there. The ornaments of the chambers, halls, galleries, cabinets, wardrobes, kitchens, baths, steam-rooms <term>estues: From the French "étuve," referring to heated rooms or vapor baths used for relaxation and health</term>, and courtyards were so sumptuous and well-appointed, that in all the kingdom of Fairyland <note>original: "Faerie"</note> none similar were ever seen. The invention and design of this manor was an incredible thing: for it was so harmonious and consistent in all its parts, that there was nothing to find fault with. But among the most excellent works, there was a ceiling made of Compartments—round, square, oval, triangular, hexagonal, and other shapes all of one size—separated by a band or border edged with two moldings or spacers like strings of rosebuds, the corners of the Compartments embraced by Acanthus leaves, otherwise called Bear's-breech <note>original: "Branque vrsine," the Acanthus plant, a classic motif in Corinthian architecture</note>: the inside filled with Arabesque foliage in half-relief <term>demybosse: A sculptural technique where the carving projects halfway from the flat background</term>. The relief was gilded, and the background was of Acre azure, so beautiful that it could be called singular and peerless.

### THE FIRST BOOK OF

I leave you to imagine the beautiful orchards, gardens, meadows, willow groves, fountains, and streams, enclosed and flowing between banks of white marble, bordered with flowers that are always green, nourished by sweet winds in serene weather, under a temperate sky, in a pleasant and healthy country, ringing with the song of birds, abundant in all earthly goods, and the hillsides covered with trees so neatly arranged that it seemed they had been planted by a line, and put there expressly to give pleasure to those who look upon them. As for the opulence, the great household, and the pompous service of the Queen, the incomprehensible multitude of youth who were there in the flower of their age, and the noble and gracious maidens—I can say nothing other than that I found myself marveled, so much so that I no longer thought I was myself, having lost the knowledge of the place where I had arrived. Truly I felt a very great pleasure, but I could not satisfy my desire to look, and I thought incessantly how and by what adventure I had entered therein. Nevertheless, seeing myself in a place of felicity and bliss, among all the glories of the world, amidst so many sweet creatures full of beauty more than human, and assured by the courteous words of the Queen—who had so humanely received me and promised her help and favor in the enjoyment of my loves—I resolved to give thanks to my good fortune, which had directed me so well, always remembering everything that had happened to me up until that hour. 

The lavish banquet having finished, the Queen wished (as a greater display of her status) to show how much she exceeded the entire world in height and magnificence. Therefore, while everyone was still seated in their places, she ordered a pastime not only worthy of being seen, but renowned forevermore. This was a ball or a dance in the following manner: 

Through the curtained door entered thirty-two damsels, sixteen of whom were dressed in cloth of gold—specifically, eight in one style: one in the habit of a king, another of a queen, two captains of strongholds <note>these represent the Rooks</note>, two knights, and two fools <note>original: "folz"; these represent the Bishops</note>, and the rest as women of war <note>these represent the Pawns</note>. Then entered another sixteen dressed in fine cloth of silver, however, dressed in the same fashion as the first ones. These were separated into two bands and placed themselves according to their qualities and offices upon the squares of the court, which was made in the form of a chessboard (as has been said). The sixteen in gold were on one side in two rows, and those in silver were opposite them in the same order. 

This being done, three musical damsels began to play three instruments of strange fashion, tuned in sweet harmony. To the measures and cadences of these instruments, the damsels of the ball moved just as their king commanded; and in doing him reverence, and the Queen likewise, they marched onto another square with inestimable bravery. When these instruments had begun to sound, the silver king commanded the damsel who was before the Queen, his companion, to place herself before the golden damsel who had advanced. Then, doing reverence to her king, she marched against her adversary. And thus they all changed places, or remained on a square, always dancing to the sound of the instruments, until they were captured and put out of the game in the presence of their King. And if the harmonious sound held a musical beat, the eight identical ones dressed in one style took just as long to move from one square to another; and they were not permitted to retreat unless they had an open passage to jump onto the part where...

This festival lasted, with its assaults and rescues, for a good hour or so, through turns, bows, and pauses so very well-measured that not a single note or cadence was lost. The gate and the windows of her house are at all times closed, and she does not consent in any way that men should know her. Nor is it lawful or permitted for bodily eyes to look upon a thing so sovereign. This is why the success of her effects is at all times uncertain. She shifts and transforms herself into many very strange forms; then she comes to manifest herself when one does not desire her at all, and when one thinks of it the least. At the opening of each of the three gates she will come to present herself before you; however, you will not be able to know her, except by conjecture, which foresees and considers her immediately, even though she changes her face and dress at every turn to make knowledge of her doubtful. This doubt and uncertainty often causes a man to remain without improvement, being deceived by hope. These two young ladies of mine, therefore, to whom I consign, recommend, and give you in charge, will teach you at which of the gates you ought to stop, and you will be able, by virtue of the ring I give you, to govern yourself by whichever of the two seems good to you. Having said this, she made a sign for them to approach me. Then, by gestures and by acts (it not being in my power, boldness, nor knowledge to speak), I thanked her most humbly for all her graces and benefits. Then my two companions took me familiarly, each by a hand; then, with the Queen’s leave, and likewise that of all the ladies, we went out through the same gate by which I had entered. I turned back at every step, like one who could not satisfy himself with seeing this triumphant dwelling, so sumptuous that it is impossible to believe that it was a building made by human hands, but rather that nature had made it for ostentation and as a display of an excellent masterpiece of her artifice—filled with beauty, grace, wealth, security, bliss, happiness, and perpetual duration. For this reason, I would have willingly stayed a little longer, but it was necessary for me to follow my guides. ...and they have come to the first turret, where they find a great number of maidens who ask to see their <term>melles</term> <note>Symbolic tokens or medals representing a person's character, disposition, or soul</note>, for they are experts at knowing their qualities. After having seen them, they receive and accept as a guest the one who has a token that matches and suits their nature. They embrace, follow, and accompany him through the other revolutions in various occupations and exercises, according to their inclination. Thus they go as far as the second turret, and then begin to gaze upon this beautiful place; then they navigate toward the third, wishing to understand it well because they take pleasure in it. 

In this place, whoever wishes to persevere with his first companion will find that she never abandons him; but because many more beautiful ones are found there, several repudiate the first ones and leave them to become acquainted with these new ones. And it should be known that from the second turret to the third, they find the water somewhat contrary, so much so that it is necessary to row. From the third to the fourth, it is even stronger and more difficult, although while passing they see various changing and inconstant pleasures. 

When they arrive at the fourth tower, they are received <gloss>by</gloss> other young ladies, skilled in wrestling and trained in the craft of war, who test and examine their tokens, and draw to their occupation or exercise those whom they recognize as suitable, letting the others pass who have no conformity with their temperament. In this passage, the water is rough and greatly resistant to the boats; therefore they are forced to row with all their might. 

The fifth turret, when they have reached it, seems very restorative to them; for there they contemplate the beauty of their own kind; and in this joyous and desired pastime, they walk full of fantasies and laborious occupations. There is practiced the Proverb which says: *The blessed have held the middle path* <note>original Latin: "Medium tenuere beati"</note>. That is to say, the fortunate have kept to the middle way. In this passage, the middle of our course is judged, to which happiness, wealth, or knowledge is married and conjoined; which, if a man does not have with him then, the less will he be able to acquire them in the future. 

Upon leaving this turret, the water—because of the slope of the place—begins to descend and take its course toward the final center; therefore, easily and with hardly any rowing, one is carried as far as the sixth turret, in which dwell certain beautiful matrons like widow women, of chaste and honest look and bearing, attending to divine service. Their devout countenance causes their guests to be inflamed with their love, so much so that they blame those who came before, making a firm and perpetual alliance with these last for the rest of the passage. 

Then, these six turrets having been passed, one navigates <gloss>by</gloss> the others in thick, dark air with many discomforts, and one finds the path very flowing and brief, because the closer the ways approach the center, the less length they have, and they are shorter and sooner passed. Therefore, they no longer have any need to row; for the water carries them along enough by itself, and they are as if plunged through sliding valleys into the abyss and whirlpool of the center, not without great affliction of spirit for the memory and recollection of the beautiful pastimes and gracious companies they left in the places they passed. And the more they realize that it is no longer possible for them to turn back, nor to turn the bow of their little boat—because the paths are narrow, and the bows of those who follow navigating after them touch their stern without ceasing—the more their pain doubles within them, seeing the writing

Then, considering this ungracious title, they are grieved beyond measure, and have a marvelous regret for having entered this bewildering orchard, subject to so many inevitable and unhappy necessities, even though it seems full of delights. At this point, Logic <note>Logistique: Personification of Reason or Rationality.</note> said to me again: "Know, Poliphile, that in the depths of this great abyss sits a harsh auditress, who judges those who enter, and scrupulously weighs and examines with a just balance all their actions, for which they must receive evil or good according to their merit. And because it would take too long to explain the whole matter to you, you shall be satisfied for this time with what I have told you. Let us now descend to our companion, Will." <note>Thelemie: Personification of Will or Desire.</note> When we had found her again, she asked us the cause of our delay, and Logic replied: "It was not enough for our Poliphile only to see what I have shown him, but it was necessary that I give him to understand that which, by the nature of the place, he could not personally conceive, so that through my interpretation—since otherwise it was not possible for him—he might somewhat know the true character of this place." At these words, Will changed the subject and said: "Let us go to sport in the other garden, which is no less delectable than the one you have shown him." This garden was on the other side of the palace, made of the same size and fashion as the glass one, and similar in the arrangement of the flowerbeds, except that the flowers, trees, and herbs of this one were made of silk, with colors matching their natural appearance. It was constructed entirely of gathered pearls of equal size and value, over which was stretched a stem of ivy whose leaves were of silk, the branches and the small creeping tendrils of fine gold, and the clusters <note>original: "corymbes"</note> of its fruit made of precious stones. All around, at equal distances, there were square pillars in the wall with their capitals, architrave, frieze, and cornice made of the same metal, placed there solely for ornament. The panels that served as walls were made of embroidery in gold and silk thread using flat stitch, <note>A needlework technique where the thread lies flat against the fabric to create a smooth, paint-like surface.</note> decorated with scenes of love and hunting so curiously depicted that a brush could not have done better. The floor <note>original: "parterre"</note> was covered in green velvet resembling a beautiful meadow at the beginning of the month of April. In the middle of the space, there was an arbor, <note>original: "berceau"</note> or round turret, in the shape of a trellis, whose poles and wicker-work were well-furnished with gold on top; all around it were bent branches of flowering rose bushes, covered in green leaves and mingled with white and red roses, all made of silk. These were so close to nature that one would have judged the imitations more beautiful than the real ones. Beneath this trellis were continuous seats following the circle, made of a fine red jasper; the floor below was paved with a single round piece of yellow jasper, mixed with several colors, but all blending into one, so clear and polished that one could see the whole garden in it as if in a large mirror. We entered beneath this trellis and sat upon the beautiful seats to rest there. Then Will <note>original: "Thelemie," representing human desire and will.</note> took her lyre, and tuning it to her voice, began to sing of the origin of these delights, the sovereign empire of their queen, and the honor that one could receive from accompanying Reason, <note>original: "Logistique," representing the rational soul.</note> so melodiously that I marvel Apollo <note>The Greek god of music and poetry.</note> did not run there to listen to her, for at that time I valued nothing else, however dear or desired it might have been to me.

Once the song had ended, Logistique <note>Logistique is the personification of Logic or Reason, guiding Poliphile’s intellect.</note> took me by the hand and led me out of this place, saying: "Poliphile, I wish to show you things more delightful to the understanding than they are to the sight, although both will find contentment there." During this talk, we entered another garden nearby, enclosed by vaults supported on pillars. These vaults were five paces in height from the floor to the keystone, and three paces wide from one pillar to the next. The whole structure was made of brick covered in natural ivy, so thick that one could not see a single brick; and there were one hundred vaults arranged in a circle, forming the enclosure of the precinct. At each vault stood an altar of porphyry, <term>Porphyry: a very hard, dark-red or purple stone, highly prized in antiquity and associated with imperial status.</term> and upon each altar a golden Nymph, all different in dress and posture, each with her face turned toward the middle of the garden. In that center was founded a square pedestal of chalcedony stone, <term>Chalcedony: a translucent, milky variety of quartz.</term> upon which sat a round plinth of vermilion jasper, two feet in height and a good pace and a half in width. This plinth supported a triangle of the same width, made of a stone as black as can be; the corners or ridges of this triangle did not extend beyond the circumference of the round plinth. On each of the three faces was fixed a divine image, having its feet placed upon the round plinth. In the empty space between the two corners of the triangle—which was one pace in height—the images extended their arms toward the slightly blunt or rounded corners, holding three cornucopias <note>Also known as "horns of plenty," these are symbols of abundance and nourishment.</note> positioned directly against the middle of the three angles. These horns were two feet and four inches in length, and were tied with fluttering ribbons over the surface and hollows of the black stone. These images, shaped like Nymphs of fine gold, as were the cornucopias and their bindings—

On the round plinth, at the place of the feet of each of the three images, there were hieroglyphs: <note>In the Renaissance, "hieroglyphs" referred to symbolic images believed to contain hidden divine wisdom, rather than the literal Egyptian writing system.</note> namely, beneath the first was a sun; beneath the second, a tiller or ship's rudder; and beneath the third, a shallow vessel filled with flames of fire. Upon the projection of each of the corners of the triangle, higher than the images, was an Egyptian monster made of gold in the form of a Sphinx, lying upon its four feet. One of these had a fully human face, the second was half-human and half-beast, and the third was entirely beast-like. All three had a band around their forehead, with another covering their ears in the manner of the hanging ribbons of a mitre, <term>Mitre: a liturgical headdress; here referring to the "infulae" or lappets that hang down the back.</term> descending along the neck down to the chest. They had the bodies of lionesses and were lying on their bellies. Upon their backs rested a solid gold pyramid, triangular in shape, having a height of five diameters of its base and rising to a point. On each of these faces a circle was carved, and above it a Greek letter: on the first an O, on the second an Ω, and on the third an N. <note>Together, these letters O Ω N (Ho On) mean "The Being" or "He Who Is" in Greek, a traditional name for God.</note> Logistique <note>Logistique represents the faculty of Reason.</note> turned toward me and said: "By these three figures—the square, the round, and the triangular—consists the celestial harmony. Be advised, Poliphile, that these are ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs which have a perpetual affinity and conjunction together, signifying and saying: 'To the divine and infinite Trinity, in a single essence.'

The square figure is dedicated to the divinity because it is produced from unity, and in all its parts it is unique and similar. The round figure is without end and without beginning, and such is God. Around the circumference and roundness are contained these three hieroglyphs, the properties of which are attributed to the divine nature. The sun, by its beautiful created light, preserves and illuminates all things. The tiller or rudder signifies the wise government of the universe by infinite wisdom. The third, which is a vessel full of fire, gives us to understand a participation in love and charity which is communicated to us by divine goodness. And although the three images are separate, they are yet one and the same indivisible thing, eternally comprised as one and inseparably joined, which distributes and communicates its graces and goods to us benignly, as you can understand by the horns of abundance <note>Cornucopias.</note> placed on the corners of the triangle, which is firm on all its sides. By this, it signifies to us that God is immutable and invariable, never receiving alteration nor change.

Look at this Greek word written beneath the figure of the sun: INDESCRIBABLE. <note>original: ΑΔΙΗΓΗΤΟΣ (Adiegetos)</note> Beneath that of the rudder: INSEPARABLE. <note>original: ΑΔΙΑΧΩΡΙΣΤΟΣ (Adiachoristos)</note> Beneath that of the fire: INSCRUTABLE. <note>original: ΑΔΙΑΡΕΥΝΕΣ (Adiareunetos)</note> For these three effects, the three animals were placed beneath the golden obelisk <note>The author here uses "obelisk" and "pyramid" interchangeably to describe the triangular structure.</note> which is set upon their backs, figuring the aforementioned things. For just as the human form exceeds and surpasses all others, faith and true opinion conceive and understand all things that seem incredible to us. In the pyramid there are three faces, on each of which is carved a circle or roundel, signifying the three times: past, present, and to come. And you must know that no other figure can perfectly contain the said three circles but the triangle. You should also note that it is not possible to see both sides of the triangular pyramid entirely at once and with the same view, but only one, and that is the one before you, by which the 'present' is understood. Therefore, not without cause were these letters O Ω N carved there. To my mind, it may seem to you that I am too wordy and superfluous in this discourse, but certainly, I am rather brief and succinct."

Know that the first stone is only known to itself: and although it is diaphanous or transparent, it is not totally clear to us. Nevertheless, he who has a better spirit mounts higher and ingeniously considers the color of the round figure: then he searches further and passes even to the third figure, which is of a dark color: and finally comes to contemplate another figure with three faces. From there forward, the sight and knowledge always go on diminishing and failing like a pyramid: for notwithstanding that man may be learned and expert, he can learn nothing else of it except that it is; but what it is or how, that cannot enter into his brain. <note>This passage reflects Neoplatonic philosophy: the closer one gets to the "First Principle" or God (the point of the pyramid), the more human reason fails, as the divine is ultimately unknowable in its essence.</note>

From these holy reminders that Logistique made to me, taken from the secrets of divine nature, I had more pleasure in my heart than from all I had seen before: and indeed I took to contemplating the Obelisk of such great mystery, upright, firm and equal, composed of incorruptible matter, eternally persevering, situated in the middle of this meadow, among several fruit trees of sweet taste and salutary effect, planted in order and properly placed, in grace, beauty, delight, pleasure, and marvelous utility, truly incessantly sustained by the sun, which never ends. After we had stayed there some time, my two companions took me again by the hands and led me out of this enclosure. Then Thelemie <note>Thelemie represents "Will" or "Desire."</note> said to me: "It is time to go to the three gates that we seek." To which consenting, we set ourselves to the way through this beautiful country, where the air was clear and the sky as serene as possible: but this was not without passing time in familiar and delectable talk, so much so that I, desiring to know and understand particularly the great riches and inestimable treasures of their Queen Eleutherilide, made them this honest request. "I pray you, O happy maidens, if my inquiry is not troublesome to you, tell me what history is carved inside the diamond which hangs at the necklace <note>original: "carquan"</note> of the Queen your mistress? For among all the precious stones that I have seen in her palace, that one seems so rich to me that I repute it beyond all esteem: and I think it is impossible to assign it a suitable price, seeing that it is such that the Jasper of the Emperor Nero where his figure was engraved, the Topaz of Queen Arsinoe of Arabia, and likewise the stone for which the Senator Nonius was sent into exile, were never worthy of being compared to it." <note>Poliphile refers to famous gems of antiquity: Nero's jasper; a massive topaz given to Arsinoe II (Queen of Egypt); and the famous opal of Nonius, who chose exile rather than surrender the gem to Mark Antony.</note> It is true that because it was a little far from me, and by reason

Then Logistique replied: "I know very well what you seek. That marvelous machine was not made without cause. And to understand the intention of the craftsman, remember that upon the forehead of the beast hung a copper ornament sown with writing, which in our language says: **L A B O R  A N D  I N D U S T R Y**. <note>original: "LABEVR ET INDVSTRIE"</note> That is to say: He who intends to acquire wealth must abandon idleness—signified by that heavy bulk of the body—and take the head, which is that inscription; for by working with industry you will find the desired treasure." By these words I found myself sufficiently instructed in that meaning, for which I thanked her with a very good heart. And seeing that they used such familiar intimacy toward me, I continued with even greater audacity to question them, saying: "Most wise Nymphs, upon leaving the great cavern I found a beautiful stone bridge; on the handrails of both sides there were hieroglyphs in two panels, one of <term>porphyry</term> <note>A hard, purple-red igneous rock, highly prized in antiquity for imperial monuments.</note> and the other of <term>ophite</term> <note>A green, mottled stone also known as serpentine, named for its resemblance to snakeskin.</note>: which (so it seems to me) I interpreted according to their meaning, except for the branches attached to the horns of an ox's head: for I could never recognize nor know from what trees they come: and also I desire to understand why the hieroglyphs were not all carved in the same stone." To which they answered me: "One of the branches is of **Fir**, and the other is of **Larch**. The nature of these two woods is that Larch cannot burn, and Fir never bends when it is put to use: wanting to signify by this that **patience** is to be praised, which is not inflamed by anger, and does not bend in adversity. The Porphyry stone is not without mystery, but rather has such a property that if it is put into a furnace to make lime, not only can it not be cooked, but it protects the other stones near it from softening in the fire; Ophite also is always cold, and can in no way be heated. In truth, Poliphile, I prize you greatly for what you desire to know, and for the care you take to inquire into things so worthy and commendable." Thus conversing, we arrived at a beautiful and pleasant river, bordered by all species of trees that are accustomed to grow along the waters: and over it was well-built a stone bridge with three vaults <note>Three arches.</note>, the piers of which projected in points to be firmer, and in order to better resist the course of the water.

The beauty of this one is feigned, false, and painted; and if you had seen the back of her shoulders, you would be compelled to vomit. You would recognize the treason and smell a carrion stench beyond measure. You would see her as so abominable that you would have great horror of her. Certainly, these damsels will not remain with you long, but will abandon you immediately, and you will be utterly stunned when you see them vanish from your presence. Pleasure passes, and shame remains, accompanied by **repentance**. Believe me, these are but vain hopes and most certain harm: a very short joy and perpetual regret, mixed with sighs that trouble the rest of a miserable life. It is a counterfeit sweetness consisting of dangerous bitterness: the birdlime <note>original: "gluz," a sticky substance used by hunters to trap birds</note> where the wretched are caught, and the end that consumes all good." Nevertheless, Thelemie <note>Will or Desire</note>, who took little account of such remonstrances, did not care in the slightest; rather, smiling at me, she signaled that I should not stop for the preachings of this meddler. The latter, recognizing my evil and perverse inclination, sighing with spite, turned her back on me and fled away at a run.

In this manner I found myself all alone, weary, troubled, and in such a state that I could not rightly judge whether I was sleeping or not. Desire singularly praised her beautiful breast: with which the eyes somewhat agreed, provided they could see it more fully; then, attracted by her beautiful countenance, they esteemed it more than all the rest. Appetite contradicted this, prizing above all things her golden hair—broad, thick, arranged in beautiful waves, and twisted into the shape of ringlets. My eyes stopped at their likenesses, and compared them to two stars shining in the morning, near the middle of a clear sky. Alas, the rays of her beautiful eyes passed through my heart like two darts shot by Cupid when he falls into a rage. I knew well within myself that this dissension could not cease without losing the pleasure of looking at the beautiful Nymph: which was impossible for me: wherefore I was like a man pressed by hunger finding himself among a great abundance of foods <note>Original: "viandes." In 16th-century French, this referred to food in general, not just meat.</note> which he desires all together, but he is satisfied by none that is presented.

-># POLIPHILE.<-

Had Zeuxis <note>A celebrated Greek painter (c. 5th century BCE) known for his realism.</note> seen her when he created the image of Venus, in my judgment he would have taken her as his model above all the maidens of Agrigento <note>Original: "Agrigente." Referring to the legend where Zeuxis selected the five most beautiful women of this Sicilian city to create a composite of ideal beauty for a painting of Helen of Troy.</note>, indeed, above all the girls in the entire world, judging her accomplished in every perfection of beauty. In contemplating her, I lost my senses, my spirit, my understanding, and all total knowledge; I knew not what else to do but to present her my heart, wide open. Of this heart, she has since made her own heritage, disposing of it at her pleasure and choosing it as her perpetual dwelling; and since then, it has become a quiver for Cupid’s <note>The Roman god of desire and erotic love.</note> arrows, and the workshop where he forges and tempers his sharp darts. I felt my heart beating incessantly within my chest like a muffled drum. Now, notwithstanding that through her gracious gaze she seemed to me to be the Polia I so greatly desired, yet the strange dress she wore and the place which was unknown to me kept me for a long time in doubt. She carried her left hand resting upon her breast and held a burning torch <note>Original: "flambeau."</note> reaching a little higher than her head. When she was near me, she extended her right arm, whiter than a lily, in which the veins appeared like little lines of vermilion drawn on white paper; and taking my left hand in her right, she said to me: "Poliphile, my peer, come now with me, and make no difficulty of it." At this word, I felt all my spirits troubled, and I was almost turned to stone, marveling how she could know my name. I was, in good faith, all ablaze with an amorous heat <note>Original: "ardeur amoureuse."</note>; and my voice, held back by fear and shame, did not permit me to answer her. Thus, I did not well know how to honor her; therefore, without another word, I reached out my hand to her, unworthy (so it seemed to me) to touch hers.

In taking it, I perceived (and it was true) that I touched something other than human; at which I felt a great fear, for I knew nothing beyond the common natural world, and I did not yet know what would happen to me because of it. I found myself in disarray, poorly dressed, and of a clumsy appearance—so different in form, status, and quality from such an excellent creature. Therefore, I considered myself unworthy of such company, knowing well that it is not permitted for the mortal inhabitants of the earth to enjoy the delights of heaven. I was flushed with great shame and filled with amazement, complaining within myself of my low condition. Nevertheless, I set myself to follow her, not having yet fully recovered my senses, but believing nonetheless that the outcome could only be most blessed, considering that I was being led to such a beautiful place by so singular a guide; for her sweet, amorous gaze could have rescued condemned and lost souls from the hands of Rhadamanthus <note>One of the three judges of the Underworld in Greek mythology, known for his inflexible justice.</note>; indeed (what is more), it could restore to their original nature bodies consumed and turned to ash.

Thus I went after her, my heart always beating, and trembling more than a lamb between the teeth of a wolf, marvelously inflamed with sweet amorous passion. "Oh," said I then, "most blessed of all lovers is he who would be, if not entirely, at least in some part, a sharer in the grace of this so exquisite damsel <term>damoyiselle</term> <note>A young noblewoman or lady-in-waiting.</note>." Then, all of a sudden, I blamed my foolish desires, saying: "Alas, I could hardly believe that such a nymph <term>Nymphe</term> <note>A minor female nature deity in Greek and Roman mythology, often used here to describe a woman of supernatural beauty.</note> would deign to involve herself with things as lowly as mortal men, who have nothing similar to her. Certainly, she deserves to be loved by the highest celestial gods, and to make Jupiter <note>The king of the gods, who frequently visited Earth in various disguises to woo mortals.</note> descend, disguised from his own form."

On the other hand, I consoled myself by offering her my heart and my soul, having nothing else more worthy to present to her, believing that this is what the gods find most agreeable. Thus I found myself troubled and confused by a diversity of thoughts, so much so that my heart was variably moved by applying itself too willingly to such hidden imaginings, ready and prepared to serve as a brand or a log within the powerful fire of love <term>feu d'amour</term>, in which I suffered with such sweet pleasure that torment was my recreation. The gaze of this Nymph did to me as the lightning does to oaks and other trees that it splits, breaks, and scatters, so much so that I no longer dared to raise my sight to contemplate her eyes; for when her light met mine, for a long time afterward all things seemed double to me, and I was dazzled, like those who have looked steadily and directly with their eye at the sphere of the sun.

In this manner I was taken, bound, and conquered; quite ready to cry out to her: "Madam, I surrender myself to you." This I had already for a good while concluded, confirmed, and resolved within myself, and had given my heart as a hostage; which soon recognized the accustomed flame, which was only covered and dormant; whereby it was promptly rekindled, like a brand which has been in the hearth and felt the fire. That love entered my heart like the wooden horse into Troy <note>Referring to the Trojan Horse, the hollow wooden statue used by the Greeks to infiltrate and burn the city of Troy.</note>, that is to say, full and stuffed with hidden enemies, who have entirely burned it and turned it to ash, wounding me with incurable wounds from which I never hope to recover, if not by means of this Nymph. Towards her, I thought to embolden myself to declare the pain that I could no longer suffer, almost lost by a blinded desire; and I was on the verge of making her hear, in a full voice, this speech <term>harengue</term> <note>A formal or lengthy address.</note>: "O divine Nymph, whoever you may be, moderate a little the ardor with which, without any misdeed on my part, you consume my..."

Then all in a moment I came back to myself and said: "If the gods knew that with evil intention I desired rare things, defended and forbidden to humans, could it not happen to me as it does to a profane person, and as it has happened to many others who have rashly and presumptuously offended their goodness? Peradventure this Nymph is reserved for some Demigod, who could with good cause be indignant against me if I attempted to commit such sacrilege." Finally, I presupposed that those who lightly embolden themselves, lightly also perish; and for such people, it is easy to fail and be deceived: for it is commonly said that fortune is not always propitious to the overly bold—especially since it is not easy to know the heart of another. Therefore, just as **Callisto** <note>A nymph of Diana who was cast out after being impregnated by Zeus/Jupiter.</note>, ashamed to see her belly grow, absented herself from the company of the chaste **Diana**: so I withdrew in shame, distancing myself from this importunate desire, yet always having my eye open to contemplate the beautiful Nymph and disposing myself to love her forever.

Feigning to give me liberty, Cupid put me into extreme servitude: and having accepted him as my lord, he behaved toward me like a cruel tyrant, considering that I was tightly bound by the chains of love, submitted and subjected to the privilege of his harsh laws (however pleasant they may seem), full of uncertain joy, and utterly overwhelmed by sighs. Seeing this, the beautiful Nymph, to reassure me, cast a sweet glance my way, and smiling, said to me: "Poliphile, I want you to know that true love has no regard for external things: and therefore let your clothing not diminish in any way your courage, which (perhaps) is noble, magnanimous, and worthy of seeing these sacred places <note>original: "lieux fainctz" — This likely refers to the "feigned" or "imagined" divine spaces of the dream-world.</note>. Remove all such fantasies from your mind, to the end that you may freely consider the great, inexplicable riches prepared for those whom the goddess **Venus** has chosen to be crowned, and who manfully labor, persevering in her service, in order to acquire her good grace." After she had said this, we walked at a fairly brisk pace, and as we went I said to myself: "O valiant **Perseus**, you would have fought the horrible monster for this woman more boldly than for the beautiful **Andromeda** <note>In Greek myth, Perseus rescued Andromeda from a sea monster; Poliphile suggests the Nymph is even more worthy of such a feat.</note>. I walked step by step with her, and sometimes lowered my eyes to see her feet, shod in a sole of red leather, tied above the foot with ribbons of gold thread and silk, adorned with oriental pearls: and sometimes it happened that the wind, stirring her garment, uncovered her legs, which seemed composed of scarlet, milk, and musk, all mixed together <note>A classic Renaissance poetic description of beauty: the red of health, the white of purity, and the scent of luxury.</note>. Reasonably, everyone can estimate that nothing is difficult for the gods, and that all things are easy for them; for which reason, they are called almighty with good and just cause. The chariot was made entirely of gold, composed of two squares measuring six feet long, three wide, and as many high, including its cornices and moldings. Above there was a platform one and a half feet high, two and a half wide, and five and a half long, descending in a slope toward the moldings of the first level. This slope was carved in a scale pattern <note>original: "taillée à escailles"; a decorative motif resembling fish scales or shingles.</note> using precious stones of various colors. At each of the four corners stood a horn of plenty <term>cornucopia</term> (a horn overflowing with produce, symbolizing abundance), full of leaves, flowers, and fruits made of gems, with the opening turned down over the edge of the corner of the first square's cornice. The rest of the decoration ran along the edges of the corners, which were rounded and fluted, covered in poppy leaves until the slender end curled into a snail-shell shape <note>original: "lymanon"; a volute or spiral scroll.</note>. Beneath the molding of the final level, at the corners of the plinth <note>the heavy square base of a column or pedestal</note> or square, aligned with the lower molding, was fashioned the foot of a harpy <note>a mythological creature with the face of a woman and the body of a bird of prey</note>. These feet were somewhat curved and raised in a half-circle, ending in parsley-like foliage that embraced the corner on both sides. The chariot had no shafts <note>original: "lymons"; the wooden poles between which a horse is hitched.</note>, but in their place, two scrolls in the shape of hooks emerged from beneath the harpy feet, where the harnesses were attached. Half of the wheels, up to the hub, were covered in foliage that split in two and emerged from a rose, through the center of which passed the end of the axle-tree. <image-desc>A detailed woodcut illustration of a triumphal procession. This chariot was drawn by six elephants, harnessed in pairs, more beautiful than those seen in the triumphs of Scipio Africanus <note>A Roman general famous for defeating Hannibal.</note>, the Great Pompey, or Bacchus after he had conquered the Indies. The traces <note>The ropes or straps used to pull the vehicle.</note> were made of twisted blue silk with gold and silver thread, woven into a four-edged cord resembling an ear of wheat. The breastplates <note>Harness straps across the elephants' chests.</note> of the elephants were of fine gold, enriched with precious stones, and featured buckles through which the traces passed. And upon each elephant sat a maiden, just as in the first triumph, carrying other musical instruments, all different from the previous ones but tuned to the same pitch. Two of them were dressed in red, two in yellow, and two in violet. The housing <note>original: "housse"; a decorative covering or caparison for an animal.</note> or covering of the elephants was of cloth of gold, with embroidery scattered with pearls and collars of large precious stones strung together. From their foreheads hung a globe <note>original: "pomme"; literally "apple," here referring to a round, spherical ornament.</note> of oriental pearls <note>High-quality pearls harvested from the Gulf or Indian Ocean, prized for their luster.</note>, the tassel of which was of silk of many colors, mingled with gold thread.

# POLIPHILE.

The following chariot was drawn by six **Tigers** spotted with reddish markings, harnessed with **Vine** branches laden with clusters of **Grapes**, which served as offensive weapons; and they walked at a slow, steady pace. In the middle of the top surface there was a golden base, one foot and four fingers in diameter, and three palms in height: specifically, one palm for the round plinth or **torus** <note>A large, convex, semi-circular molding at the base of a column or pedestal.</note>, half a palm for the **echinus** <note>A rounded molding, often found below the abacus of a capital.</note> and its little square fillet, and the remainder for the **trochilus** <note>A concave molding, also known as a scotia.</note> or cavetto, with an inverted **cyma** <note>original: "gueule rēuersee"; a wave-like architectural molding.</note> and the upper torus, enriched with their small square fillets. The surface of this base was slightly lowered and hollowed to make room for four eagle tails that rested upon the edge, made of dark **Aetites stone** <note>original: "pierre Aetite psane"; also known as eaglestone, a hollow geode traditionally believed to be found in eagle nests and possessed of magical properties.</note>. They had their backs turned toward one another and joined their wings at the tips to support an antique vase of **Ethiopian Hyacinth** <note>A reddish-orange gemstone, likely a variety of zircon or garnet, highly prized in antiquity.</note>, variegated with veins of **Emerald** and several other precious stones. Its height was two and a half feet, and its diameter was one and a half feet at its widest point. Its circumference was three times the diameter and a little more <note>Poliphile is noting a rough approximation of Pi (π).</note>. The foot of the vase rose four inches above the wings of those **Eagles**. At the widest part of its body, it was encircled by a frieze one palm wide; from this frieze to the beginning of another vessel, a **spout-jar** <note>original: "Gargoule"; here referring to a smaller secondary vessel or neck-piece attached to the main vase.</note> joined to the first, there was another palm. This latter vessel was one foot in height and began to widen at the top by about one and a half good palms; this half-palm was used for a small frieze decorated with flowers and foliage in **half-relief** <note>original: "demy bosse"; sculptures that project halfway from the background.</note>, pierced through and almost standing out from their background, carved from the same stone. The diameter of the vase at its widest was two and a half palms, and it was **gadrooned** <note>original: "goderoné"; a decorative pattern of repeating convex ridges or fluting.</note> below the frieze, with narrow gadroons toward the bottom and wide ones at the top. The neck was two and a half palms in length from the frieze to the mouth, making the total height of the foot of the vase—along with the one and a half palms below the frieze—decorated with gadroons turning in the fashion of **lilies**. The rim of the mouth was flat, furnished with moldings, cymas, ogees, echini, and others; as were the borders of the friezes. In that of the spout-jar, on the lower molding, half-rings were soldered across each side, which two **Lizards** were biting, made from the emerald vein of the stone. Their four feet rested upon the cover of the large vase that supported the spout-jar; it was joined to the frieze in the form of an ogee or inverted cyma, carved with **scales**, made of the same Hyacinth stone, and was one palm high, as I have said. The tails of the Lizards, which lay on their bellies along this cover, were twisted to form rings upon the molding of the frieze, with another below, which served as **handles**. The base finished in foliage that entered half a foot into the frieze on each side and was almost entirely in full relief, so that one could easily see the Hyacinth background. Thus, this foliage occupied two feet of the vase's circumference. It remains now to speak of the space that was left on the frieze. Between the two sets of foliage, measuring one and a half feet long on each side, were the sculptures that I shall describe hereafter; but first I will speak of the belly of this vase, which was covered with a **vine**, whose stumps, shoots, and tendrils were carved from a vein of **Topaz** suited for this purpose, the leaves of **Emerald**, and the grapes of **Amethyst**, set upon a background of Hyacinth so round and so polished that one would have judged it had been turned on a lathe; for it seemed that the leaves were separated from it...
