The following chariot was drawn by six Tigers speckled with reddish spots, harnessed with vine branches adorned with clusters of grapes, which served as offensive weapons; they moved along at a slow, steady pace. In the middle of the upper platform, there was a golden base one foot and four fingers in diameter, and three palms in height—specifically, one palm for the round plinth or **torus** <note>A large, convex molding at the base of a column.</note>, half a palm for the **echinus** <note>A rounded molding, often shaped like a sea urchin or an egg-and-dart pattern.</note> and its small square member, and the remainder divided between the **trochilus** <note>Also known as a scotia; a concave molding that casts a deep shadow.</note> (or "little boat"), the **cyma reversa** <note>A molding with a wave-like profile, curving outward at the top and inward at the bottom.</note>, and the upper torus, all enriched with their small square fillets. The surface of this base was slightly lowered and hollowed out to make room for four eagle tails that rested upon the edge, made of polished **Aetite stone** <note>original: "pierre Aetite pſane"; also known as eagle-stone, these were geodes believed to have magical properties and to be found in eagles' nests.</note>. They had their backs turned toward one another and joined their wings at a point to support an antique vase of Ethiopian Hyacinth <note>A reddish-orange gemstone, likely a variety of zircon or garnet.</note>, variegated with veins of Emerald and several other precious stones. Its height was two and a half feet, and its diameter was one and a half feet at its widest part. Its circumference was three times its diameter, and a little more. The foot of the vase stood four inches above the wings of these eagles. At the widest part of its body, it was encircled by a frieze one palm wide; from this frieze to the beginning of another "Gargoyle" vase <note>A secondary, smaller vessel used for pouring, joined to the main one.</note> attached to the first, there was another palm's distance. This latter vase was one foot high and began to widen at the top by about a good palm and a half; this half-palm was used for a small frieze made of flowers and foliage in **half-relief** <note>original: "demyboſſe"; sculpture that projects halfway from the background.</note>, pierced through with openwork, and appearing almost detached from their background, which was carved from the same stone. The diameter of the vase at its widest point was two and a half palms, and it was **gadrooned** <note>Decorated with a series of convex curves or ridges.</note> below the frieze, with narrow gadroons toward the bottom and wide ones at the top. The neck, from the frieze to the mouth, was two and a half palms long, making the total height of the foot of the vase equal to the palm and a half located beneath the frieze, which was decorated with gadroons turning in the shape of lilies. The rim of the mouth was flat, furnished with moldings, ogees, beads, echinuses, and others; the edges of the friezes were similarly adorned. On the "Gargoyle" vase, in the lower molding, half-rings were soldered across each side, which two Lizards were biting; these were made from a vein of Emerald. Their four feet rested on the cover of the great vase that supported the Gargoyle; it was joined to the frieze in the form of a cyma reversa (or "upturned throat") carved with scales, made of the same Hyacinth stone, and was one palm high, as I have said. The tails of the Lizards, which lay on their bellies along this cover, were twisted to form rings upon the molding of the frieze, with another below, serving as handles. The bottom finished in foliage that entered half a foot into the frieze on each side and was almost entirely in **full relief** <note>original: "boſſe"; three-dimensional sculpture.</note>, so that one could easily see the Hyacinth background. Thus, this foliage occupied two feet of the vase's circumference. It remains now to speak of the space left in the frieze. Between the two pieces of foliage, spanning a length of one and a half feet on each side, were the sculptures that I shall describe hereafter; but first I will speak of the belly of this vase, which was covered with a vine whose trunks, shoots, and branches were carved from a vein of Topaz suited for this purpose, the leaves from Emerald, and the grapes from Amethyst, all set upon a background of Hyacinth so round and so polished that one would have judged it had been made on a lathe; for it seemed that the leaves were separated from it by

Now, let us return to the band or **frieze** <note>A decorative horizontal band often found on pottery or architecture.</note> that encircled the said vase. In the empty space left between two sets of foliage, measuring one and a half feet on each side, were carved two beautiful histories. On the front side, there was Jupiter standing upright upon an altar of **Sapphire**, holding in his right hand a sharp sword of **Chrysolite** <note>A yellowish-green gemstone, today known as peridot.</note> shining like gold; and in the other hand, a sparkling thunderbolt made of wonderfully flaming **Rubies**. Before him was a dance of seven Nymphs dressed in white in the manner of religious women, singing (as it seemed) with a devout and holy joy; then they were converted into green trees, adorned with azure flowers, and they bowed most humbly before this great God. They were not all entirely transformed, but some more and others less; however, the last one was already entirely a tree, except for her face. The second had her **transmutation** <note>A change from one form into another; a metamorphosis.</note> only from the waist down, and so on for the others. Nevertheless, all showed some sign of transformation in the head.

On the other side was carved a plump young god, with a face resembling a girl, crowned with two **Serpents** <note>original: "Coleuures"</note>, one white and the other black, so well-crafted that one would have taken them for natural. He sat beneath an arbor covered by a vine stock, where little children climbed to harvest the grapes, and then brought their baskets full of grapes before this young god, who received them laughing. Some trod the vintage, others remained doing nothing except beating a tambourine and singing out of tune. Several lay on the ground, stretched out on their backs, asleep from having filled themselves with wine and drunk from the **Sibyl of the winepress** <note>original: "Sibille du preſſoir"; here referring to a large collection vat or a specific type of drinking vessel used during the harvest.</note>. And although the figures were very small, they were made to their proportion and measure so perfectly that there was nothing to criticize; and the craftsman had applied the precious stones according to their colors with marvelous dexterity joined with industry and great intelligence.

From the vessel issued a golden Vine, most abundant in leaves, laden with grapes made of **Oriental Amethyst**, and the leaves of **Persian Selenite** <note>Also known as moonstone; in antiquity, it was believed to wax and wane with the phases of the moon.</note>, which is not subject to the file <note>Meaning the stone is so hard or uniquely textured that a metal file cannot mar it.</note>, and pleases **Cupid**, for it maintains the health of whoever carries it upon them. It served as both a trellis and shade for the entire chariot, which had at each corner a candelabra sitting upon three feet of **Coral**, which is uniquely profitable to laborers because it drives away thunder, lightning, tempests, whirlwinds, and other foul winds. The pillar of the first was of **Portuguese Ceraunite** <note>A "thunderstone" (from the Greek *keraunos*), believed to fall from the heavens during a storm.</note>, of a celestial color, a friend to tempests, and much loved by the goddess **Diana**. It was shaped into balusters, assembled with small spheres and other ornaments of fine gold in filigree work. 

The second was of black **Onyx** stone, spotted with vermilion <note>Bright red.</note> drops, which has the scent of incense when it is rubbed. The third was of **Medea** <note>A legendary stone named after the sorceress Medea; ancient texts describe it as having gold-colored veins.</note>, of a dark gold color. Some were girded and crowned with branches of pine, cypress, and other similar trees: and they leaped and danced in no other way than at the Trieteric games <note>original: "ieux Trieteriques." These were festivals in honor of Bacchus (Dionysus) celebrated every three years.</note>. After them came the aged Silenus <note>The tutor and companion of Bacchus, often depicted as a jovial, drunken old man.</note>, mounted upon his donkey, and a goat with bristling hair, which was led in procession to be sacrificed. Then, among the last, appeared a woman walking furiously <note>In the sense of divine or ritual frenzy (*fureur*).</note>, who carried upon her head a winnowing fan <note>original: "Van à vanner." A shallow basket used to separate grain from chaff, which was also a sacred object in Bacchic mysteries, sometimes called the "Vannus Iacchi."</note> to winnow the laughter, the cries, and the songs (or rather howls) of that company: which were such that one could not hear another.

Hardly could one find eloquence so ready and so fluent that it would be sufficient to distinctly specify all these divine secrets and mysteries, to give an understanding of what providence conducts them, nor likewise to express the glory, felicity, and overflowing bliss in these four triumphs, accompanied by handsome young men and gracious nymphs, more cautious and prudent in all things than their young age might suggest. These beauties passed the time joyfully with their friends while in the flower of their first youth: so much so that some were still without beards, others showed only the small, soft downy hair resembling fine cotton. Many of the Nymphs had their torches lit, which was a marvelously fine sight to behold. There were a great number dressed in copes, chasubles, and religious ornaments <note>The author uses the terminology of Catholic vestments (*chappes, chasubles*) to describe the ritual clothing of these pagan figures.</note>. Some others carried lances from which hung certain trophies or ancient spoils: and they walked all together in a crowd, just as each one found themselves. The noise, the cries, the voices of the people, and the sound of the instruments—oboes, horns, trumpets, buccinas <note>term: buccines (buccinas). Ancient Roman wind instruments, usually curved, used for signals in war or ceremonies.</note>, and shawms <note>term: chalemies (shawms). Medieval and Renaissance reed instruments, the ancestors of the modern oboe.</note>—were so great that it seemed the very air must split. In this place of felicity, the blessed lived in every comfort and pleasure, glorifying the gods and following the triumphs through the beautiful fields dappled with greenery and flowers of all the colors, scents, and charms that it is possible to imagine, more fragrant than all the kinds of spices that nature could produce—indeed, certainly more beautiful than any painting—and without ever being withered by the Sun. For it is always spring there without change, the day without ever turning to night, and the season tranquil and temperate. Also, everything grows there without labor, and is brought forth by the goodness of the earth through the kindness of the air; and the fruits, herbs, and flowers remain incessantly in their perfection of goodness, beauty, scent, and greenery without wilting or drying in any manner. Never is there pain nor sickness, mourning, worry, melancholy, annoyance, nor displeasure. It is the habitation of perfect bliss, designated for those who serve the gods to their satisfaction. There was the beautiful Callisto of Arcadia, daughter of Lycaon <note>Callisto was a nymph of Artemis who was transformed into a bear and later the constellation Ursa Major.</note>. Antiope, daughter of Nycteus, wife of Lycus, and mother of Amphion the musician. Asteria, daughter of Coeus the Titan, Alcmene with her two husbands—one true, and the other supposed <note>Alcmene’s "true" husband was Amphitryon; Zeus took his form to be her "supposed" husband and father Hercules.</note>. Then the beautiful Erigone, who had her lap full of grapes. Helle was there as well, still mounted upon the ram with the golden fleece. One could see there Eurydice, whom the serpent bit on the heel. Philyra, daughter of old Ocean and wife of Chiron the Centaur, held...

And when they went upstream against the current of this brook, the water rose against their legs, making a little murmur as if it were angry to meet them. Some ran after the swans and threw water at each other with their hands. Others were sitting on the bank and making bouquets of little flowers, which they gave to their friends, with the usual accompaniments and attachments, which are gracious kisses; these were not spared there, but liberally and prodigally granted, more joined and more tightly closed than are the shells of oysters <note>A vivid Renaissance metaphor for a lingering, firm kiss.</note>. This notwithstanding, and however softly they were given and received, one could still see after the parting the impression and mark of their teeth on the neck, the cheeks, the lips, or the chin, without violence or any pain. Certain others were stretched out at the feet of the willows and alders in the shade, against whose roots the water came to strike murmuring; and there they rested in all pleasure, seeing the breasts of their lovers uncovered to give to the eyes a more agreeable and desired pasture than Cupid <note>original: "Cupido" — the Roman god of desire and erotic love.</note> finds in the tears of his good servants. Some sang love songs, with weak and trembling voices, broken by little sighs, and filled with sweet accents strong enough to soften and half-open a heart of stone. Some others were lying in the laps of their beautiful nymphs, to whom they told the most pleasant stories they could think of; and they in reward put wreaths, or tied bouquets in their hair. Alas, who then would have a heart so cold, and so frozen, that it would not ignite impetuously seeing such delectable effects of equal love? Mine (certainly) received a sweetness so great merely from contemplating them, that my heart participating in these delights, was on the point of leaving me to go into that beatitude <note>The state of supreme blessedness.</note> to seek its share of these benefits of Love. Sometimes I thought it was an enchantment, or that I had arrived in some land of Faerie. Then I remembered the ointments of <term>Circé: Circe, the Greek enchantress who turned men into animals</term>, the herbs of <term>Medée: Medea, a powerful sorceress of Greek myth known for her potions</term>, the magical song of <term>Byrrenne: Byrrhena, a character from Apuleius's 'The Golden Ass' associated with magic</term>, and the infernal murmuring of <term>Pamphile: Pamphila, another witch from 'The Golden Ass'</term>; for I well knew that corporeal eyes can see nothing beyond humanity, and that a mortal body made of earth—heavy, vile, burdensome, and dark—could not be in the place where the immortals rest. These things I thought within myself; however, after leaving all these daydreams and coming to remember the marvelous things I had clearly seen and perceived up to that hour, I recognized that they were not illusions, nor magical deceptions, but true things, imperfectly understood by my senses.

This made me return to contemplating the beauty of my guide and applying all the power of my spirit to it. My spirit suffered too grievous a pain from not daring to ask if she was my <term>Polia: The lady whose name means 'Many things' or 'Grey-haired (wisdom),' the object of Poliphile's obsessive love</term> or not, considering that she had recently given me some sign of it, though a doubtful one. Now I feared to offend her for a small thing, because I was inferior to her in all parts and qualities, and indeed almost unworthy of her speaking to me. Nevertheless, the words had several times come to the tip of my tongue, and I had always suppressed them, being perplexed and uncertain beyond measure of what I had to do then. Because of this, I found myself more astonished than <term>Sosia: A character in Plautus's play 'Amphitryon' who is driven to an identity crisis when he meets the god Mercury disguised as his double</term> when he met the god <term>Mercure: Mercury, the messenger god</term>, who had taken his own form, so much so that he could not judge if he was himself or another.

This is how I was assaulted by thoughts, and I said to myself: To have a place in this earthly paradise, I would be content to venture into all undertakings, however high and difficult they might be. No labor would seem troublesome to me. I would put my life to all hazards. I would fear no peril of sea or land. I would be content to enter the cave of the cruel <term>Polyphemus: The one-eyed Cyclops from Homer's 'Odyssey'</term>, to lodge in the house of <term>Calypso: The nymph who detained Odysseus on her island for seven years</term>, to serve longer than <term>Iacob: Jacob, the biblical patriarch who worked fourteen years for Laban to win the hand of Rachel</term>, to offer myself to the adventure of <term>Hippomanes: The suitor who raced the swift Atalanta, winning by dropping golden apples</term> against <term>Atalanta</term>, and to endure all pains, labors, and extreme dangers, feared and fled by everyone; for where Love dominates, fear and pain have no place. I would do all things willingly to acquire such a high good and to remain in this place of felicity, abundant and filled with all perfect delights, and principally to achieve the grace of this Nymph, who is beyond comparison more beautiful than <term>Helene la Greque: Helen of Troy, legendary for her beauty which launched a thousand ships</term>, indeed (certainly) than all others renowned for great beauty.

Alas, my life and my death are entirely in her power. But if it seems to the gods that I am unworthy of her friendship, I request at the very least that it be permitted for me to contemplate and serve her forever. Then I redoubled my thoughts: "O Poliphile, if the great labor turns you away, the reward summons and invites you; even if the perils frighten you, good hope should embolden you." ...insoluble, or else set me at liberty: for I can no longer hide the torment I endure, nor cover the brazier that consumes me. I find great pleasure in my sadness, and am in pain without struggling. The flame that diminishes me also nourishes me, and living makes me die. In living I do not taste life, and in dying I do not feel death; rather, I am like a block of ice placed in the middle of a burning furnace. Alas, this love is a heavier burden to me than the island of <term>Inarime: An ancient name for the volcanic island of Ischia, under which the giant Typhon was said to be buried</term> is to the giant <term>Typhoeus: A monstrous giant of Greek mythology, also known as Typhon, who challenged Zeus</term>. I find myself more lost here than inside a great <term>Labyrinth: The famous maze of Crete built to house the Minotaur</term>; indeed (to speak truly) more hard-pressed than ever was <term>Actaeon: A hunter in myth who was transformed into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds after seeing the goddess Diana bathing</term> by his dogs, so much so that I cannot tell in what part of the world I am, except that I am before the eyes of this lady who holds me. I cannot protect myself by fleeing, nor by resisting. Alas, if only she could take some pleasure in the pain I endure for her; without any doubt, that would be a kind of relief for me. While uttering such words, tears fell from my eyes, and I called upon death, very softly, for fear that I might be heard; several times I resolved to cry out with a great lament: "O noble Nymph, my only hope, have pity on me from now on, for I am at the point of death." Then, all at once, I blamed this plan as reckless and useless, saying: "Why do you waver, O inconstant and unsteady man? Dying for love will be more honorable to you than life." Then, changing my tune: "Perhaps," I said, "this is some goddess to whom you should not address yourself. Certainly <term>Syrinx: A nymph of Arcadia who, while fleeing the god Pan, was transformed into reeds at the River Ladon</term> of Arcadia would never have been transformed into a reed on the banks of the river <term>Ladon: A river in Greece associated with various myths of transformation</term> if she had refrained from speaking indiscreetly in the presence of goddesses. Similarly, <term>Echo: A nymph who was punished so she could only repeat the words of others</term> would not have been converted into the mere tail-end of voices if she had reported her business honorably. For this reason, although the gods are by their very nature all inclined toward mercy, such contempt and rash boldness could provoke them to a cruel vengeance. To see the truth of this: the companions of the wise <term>Ulysses: The Roman name for the Greek hero Odysseus</term> would not have perished at sea if they had not, like sacrilegious men, stolen the <note>original: "bestail d'Apollo"</note> cattle of <term>Apollo: The god of the sun; his sacred cattle were eaten by Ulysses' men, leading to their destruction</term>. <term>Orion: A giant hunter who was placed among the stars</term> would have avoided the ire of the gods if he had not intruded to do violence to the chaste <term>Diana: The Roman goddess of the hunt and chastity</term>. And <term>Phaethon: The son of the sun god who died when he lost control of his father's solar chariot</term>, son of <term>Phoebus: Another name for the sun god, Apollo</term>, was by his presumption cast down from the heavens. Thus, if by imprudence I committed some indecent act toward this so exquisite nymph, the same might happen to me, and (perhaps) worse." This discourse made me forget all my foolish enterprises, so that I found myself in great peace, and returned to contemplating the beautiful bearing, the good grace, and the excellent face of the lady, which greatly consoled me. In this way, I moved past all these troublesome thoughts and tried to stop my sighing, leaving aside that flattering hope which is the ordinary pasture upon which lovers live—though often mixed with a beverage of tears—and I mirrored myself in that divine beauty, content and satisfied to have the mere enjoyment of her by sight alone.

The last face contained another figure in the form of a King, severe and robust, holding a scepter in his right hand, looking toward the Sky in such a way that he made the air murky and dark. With his other hand he touched the clouds, black and rainy, full of hail and snow. His garment was of a shaggy skin, the fur turned toward his bare flesh, and he wore shoes in the antique style: and underneath was written:

->SACRED TO AEOLIAN WINTER<-
<note>original Latin: "HYEMI ÆOLIÆ S." Aeolia was the mythical home of the winds.</note>

Beyond the excellence of the art expressed by the craftsman of this altar, he had chosen the marble aptly: for amidst the whiteness were found some veins of a brownish hue, which served to show the darkness of clouds mingled with rain, snow, hail, and whirlwinds. Upon the top of the altar was placed the rough and rustic guardian of the gardens <note>The god Priapus</note>, marked with his emblem <note>The phallus, a symbol of fertility</note>, shaded by a trellis of greenery made into a vault and supported by four poles covered in leaves and flowers—the whole thing was heavily sketched out, or rather (to speak plainly) without much fine workmanship. In each space between two poles hung a burning lamp, attached to the middle of the vaulted arch by very delicate little copper chains; these, being moved by the wind, struck one another and gave off a sound like little cymbals. All around was this rural throng—Ox-drivers, Shepherds, and Laborers—who broke many glass vials against the image of their god, full of the blood of a Donkey they had sacrificed, mixed with wine and milk; and they threw bouquets and branches there at their pleasure.

In this procession, they led the old man Janus <note>The two-faced god of beginnings and transitions</note>, bound and tied with branches, flowers, and leaves. They went along shouting certain rustic and festive songs, calling upon Thalassius and Hymen <note>Thalassius and Hymen were Roman deities invoked during wedding processions</note>, dancing, leaping, and laughing with great joy. This triumph gave me more wonder than pleasure, and did not seem to me nearly so divine as the preceding ones.

# BOOK ONE OF

When we had passed further on, I saw through the forest certain nymphs—Oreads, Napaeae, and Dryads <note>Oreads are mountain nymphs, Napaeae are valley nymphs, and Dryads are tree nymphs</note>—along with the Nereids <note>Sea nymphs</note>, dressed in sealskins <note>original: "peaux de Veau marin"</note>, and others in flowers and leaves, dancing with Fauns and Satyrs, who were crowned with reeds and rushes. Likewise, the god Pan and Sylvanus <note>A Roman deity of the woods</note> were there; then Zephyrus <note>The West Wind</note> with his beloved Chloris, and all the other gods and goddesses of the woods, mountains, valleys, and fountains; together with several musical shepherds, playing old instruments made of straws and reeds, bagpipes of raw hide, bark pipes, and others of such strange resonance, with which they celebrated the sacred floral festivals. I leave it to those who can imagine it to consider the pleasure I had in seeing such novel things.

We had not traveled far, my guide and I, when I noticed through the treetops a high pinnacle like a round turret, which did not seem very far from that seashore where my guide was heading, and toward which all the streams we had crossed were flowing. When I had come a little closer, I saw more clearly something like a round semi-dome <note>original: "voulte ronde à cul de four"</note>, covered in lead (as it seemed to me) and enriched with a lantern with eight pillars; and above it another similar dome, supporting another lantern also with eight square pillars, in which was fixed a rod and a very shiny sphere.

I suddenly desired to see this beautiful building, which always seemed all the more exquisite the closer I approached it. Judging it from afar, I deemed it to be an ancient structure; therefore, I deliberated whether to pray my guide that she might be willing to lead me there, although we were still traveling toward the place where it stood. But I repressed my will, saying to myself: "Alas, I dare not ask for the thing I most desire <note>A reference to his ultimate quest for his beloved, Polia</note>, which would make me the most content of all men in this world if I could obtain it; how then shall I ask for this thing, which is neither necessary nor urgent for me?"

Thus I went walking along, my imagination always filled with such amorous variations, until we arrived at the seashore in a very pleasant place, where a sumptuous temple had been built <margin>Physizoe: the life of nature <note>From the Greek 'Physis' (nature) and 'Zoe' (life)</note>.</margin> consecrated to **Venus Physizoe**. Its shape was round, and it was as high as the diameter of its circle. To guide its construction, the Architect had first drawn a circle on the ground, and within it a square; then he had divided the diameter of the circle into five parts, from the circumference to the side of this square, and had added a sixth part at the center. Upon this, he had drawn another circle, and upon that erected this beautiful edifice as to its principal parts; indeed, he found all its measurements there, both the thickness of the walls and pilasters, and the space between the wall forming the enclosure of the temple and the columns supporting the central vault. Afterward, he had drawn ten lines equally from the center to the circumference, distant from one another like rays or semi-diameters; upon which he had made ten arches or vaults seated upon ten pillars of **Serpentine stone** <note>A dark green stone with mottled patterns like a serpent's skin</note>. Inside the work, against each of the pillars (which were two feet wide at their face and supported the arches of the vaults) was placed a **Corinthian column** of **Porphyry** <note>A hard, reddish-purple rock highly prized in antiquity</note>, of **Ionic height** <note>A technical architectural detail: though the style is Corinthian, the proportions follow the Ionic order</note>, which is to say nine diameters tall, without the capitals, which were of gilded copper, as were the bases on which were set the architrave, the frieze, and the cornice, which had...

This chapel will be described later at length and in detail. The exterior pillars projected as much as the wall was thick. The width of the pillar was derived from the space between two lines starting from the center and touching the circumference, dividing such a space into three, and the third part into two: one for the width of the pillar, the other also divided in two, to place one on each side of the pillars, upon which the arches of the vaults were curved. Besides the projection of the pillar divided into three, these two side-pieces had one along with the vaulting, and the pillar had the other two. These measurements were observed in former times by skillful architects, so as not to give the wall so much thickness that the windows would be darkened by it. ...golden mosaic, containing in its painting the properties of the twelve months of the year, and their arrangements according to the course of the Sun through the Zodiac, and likewise of the Moon, together with their conjunctions, oppositions, quadratures, eclipses, and other aspects; and why she appears horned, then half, and shortly after round. One could also see there the revolutions of that same Sun through the equinoxes, solstices, and tropics. Then, how night and day are made, with the division of the four annual seasons, namely Winter, Spring, Summer, and Autumn. Furthermore, the nature of the planets and fixed stars, with their influences and effects; which makes me presume that such a painting was the invention of the great astrologer Petosiris <note>original: "Petorisís"; a legendary Egyptian priest and astrologer</note> or of the mathematician Nechepso <note>original: "Necepsus"; an Egyptian Pharaoh-astrologer often cited in Hellenistic texts</note>. Without any doubt, it drew the beholder to a high and admirable contemplation, joined with singular pleasure; for the invention was ingenious, the figures excellent, the distribution and order proper, the painting rich, the proportion equal, the shading natural, and the whole expressed by a representation so lifelike that it gave contentment not only to the eyes, but revived the spirits: for (in truth) it was a work as worthy of being seen as any other that ever was. In one of the spaces was written in ancient letters the entire meaning of the things declared above, and all the other spaces between the half-pillars were enclosed by excellent moldings.

The walls of the temple were of marble enriched with all the ornaments that the industrious architect could and knew how to imagine. Above the frieze and cornice, upon the projections they made directly above the Porphyry columns, against the square pillars, was placed on one Apollo playing his lyre: and on the others, the nine muses, all in relief, or full roundness <note>Sculpted "in the round" rather than flat against the wall</note>, made of Parian stone <note>original: "pierre pilates"; likely referring to marble from the island of Paros</note>. The great dome or round vault was a divine work rather than an earthly one; and if it were made by human hands, it was not without challenging the over-presumptuous undertaking of the mortal mind: for in looking at this excessive mass, cast from a single piece of metal, I judged it to be almost impossible. 

All this roundness was enclosed by a vine of ten stocks, each coming out of a vase placed on the last cornice, directly above the muses and the columns, of the same cast of gilded copper. The vine filled the entire concavity of the vault, with beautiful interlacings and twists of its branches, leaves, and grapes; among which were made small children as if to gather them, and birds flying around, with lizards and snakes molded from life: all of it pierced through <note>Done in openwork or fretwork to let light pass</note>, and glazed with sheets of Crystal of various colors, resembling precious stones. The craftsmanship was so well conducted that to those who looked at it from below, the leaves, the grapes, and the little creatures appeared of natural size.

...because they <note>referring to the water spouts or the falling water itself</note> are dangerous as they fall: therefore, such an inconvenience must be avoided. Furthermore, the gutter wears away the ground around it; and if the water falls upon the stone, it splashes back and rots the base of the wall. Indeed (what is more), the water falling from these gutters, being blown by the wind against the wall, blackens it, covers it with earth, deforms it, and ruins the moldings: it even engenders many weeds, mosses, or shrubs, which loosen and cause the stones to fall. The height of the exterior wall did not exceed that of the keystones of the arches, except for the cornice above, which was hollowed out at the top in the form of a channel. Into this channel flowed the slope of the roof, extending from the central dome to the wall; it was made of gilded copper plates, fashioned like scales. This slope began on the outside exactly opposite the last line made on the inside, above the cornice of the frieze and <term>architrave</term> <note>the main beam resting on the tops of the pillars</note>: and it declined toward this gutter which received the rainwater, discharging it into the pipes of the pillars through which it was conducted into the cistern. This was furnished with another secret conduit to discharge it when it was too full and the water overflowed, retaining only what was necessary for the sacrifice. The faces of the pillars were crafted in <term>half-relief</term> <note>original: "demytaille"; also known as mezzo-rilievo, where the carving stands out from the background but is not fully detached</note>, with antique candelabras, birds, foliage, and small beasts, continuing up to the height of the cornice placed on the outside, opposite the interior one located above the figures of the Muses, upon which the great round vault began. From this cornice to the top of the pillar, there was as much slope as the roof below carried, which was of copper scales, as I have said. At the exterior cornice, upon which sat the <term>semi-dome</term> <note>original: "voulte à cul de four"; a vault shaped like a quarter-sphere or bread oven</note>, began a <term>flying buttress</term> <note>original: "arboutant"; a structural support that transmits the weight of a vault to a heavy outer pillar</note> decorated with the same moldings as the architrave, corresponding to the height of the pillar: its ends rested upon two square half-pillars, protruding by a third of their width—one from the wall, and the other from behind the top of the pillar. In these, niches had been made above the capital to house ten statues in <term>full-relief</term> <note>original: "boffe entiere"; sculpture in the round</note>, all in diverse poses. On both sides, the pillar was carved with sculpture just as on its face. The slope then began at the belt beneath the vault and descended to the top of the pillar with moldings similar to those of the enclosure, which was a denticulated and hemmed cornice, the underside recessed with rosettes. The flat part of the cornice where it joined the vault was hollowed all around to serve as a gutter and receive all the water that descended from it. This water then flowed through the flying buttresses and from there into the pillars, like that of the other roof, then cast itself into the cistern. These flying buttresses were covered with a <term>cartouche</term> or scroll (which some call a vault) in the form of a paper rolled at both ends, one opposite the other: that is to say, the one touching the wall toward the bottom, and the one against the pillar toward the top. From their folds emerged pods of beans, peas, and carobs, half-open so that one could discern their fruit for ornament. The top surface was divided by a flat ridge, carved with scales on both sides, and above it a well-wrought artichoke leaf, slightly turned back at the tip: such vaults are easily made by this practice. Into this channel flowed the slope of the roof, extending from the central dome to the wall; this roof was made of gilded copper sheets, fashioned like scales. The slope began on the outside exactly opposite the last line drawn on the inside, above the cornice of the <term>frieze</term> and <term>architrave</term> <note>The architrave is the main beam resting on the columns, and the frieze is the decorative band above it</note>. It declined toward this gutter which received the rainwater and emptied it into the pipes within the pillars, through which it was conducted into the <term>cistern</term>. This was equipped with another secret conduit to discharge the water when it was too full and overflowing, retaining only what was necessary for the sacrifice. 

The faces of the pillars were crafted in <term>half-relief</term> <note>original: "demytaille"; also known as bas-relief</note>, with antique candelabra, birds, foliage, and <term>grotesque beasts</term> <note>original: "beſtions"; small, stylized animal figures</note>, continuing up to the height of the exterior cornice positioned opposite the interior one located above the figures of the Muses, where the great round vault began. From this cornice to the top of the pillar, there was as much slope as the roof below carried, which was of copper scales, as I have said. 

On the exterior cornice, upon which the <term>semi-dome</term> <note>original: "voulte à cul de four"; a vault shaped like a quarter-sphere or an old oven</note> rested, began a <term>flying buttress</term> <note>original: "arboutant"</note> furnished with the same moldings as the architrave, corresponding to the height of the pillar. Its corners rested on two square half-pillars, projecting by a third of their width—one from the wall, and the other from behind the top of the pillar. On the outside of the pillar, niches were made above the <term>capital</term> <note>The top part of a column</note> to house ten full-relief statues, all in diverse poses. On both sides, the pillar was carved with sculpture just as on its face. The slope, then, began at the belt beneath the vault and descended to the top of the pillar with moldings identical to those of the enclosure, which was a denticulated and bordered cornice, with the underside recessed and decorated with rosettes. 

The flat surface of the cornice at the point where it joined the vault was hollowed out all around to serve as a gutter and receive all the water descending from it. This water then flowed through the flying buttresses and from there into the pillars, like the water from the other roof, and then emptied into the cistern. These flying buttresses were covered with a <term>cartouche</term> or scroll (which some call a vault) in the form of a paper rolled at both ends in opposite directions: specifically, the end touching the wall at the bottom, and the end against the pillar at the top. From their folds emerged pods of beans, peas, and carobs, half-opened so that one could discern their fruit as ornament. The top surface was divided by a flat ridge, carved with scales on both sides, and topped with a well-wrought artichoke leaf, slightly turned back at the tip. Such vaults are easily made by this practice: Turn a half-circle with a <term>compass</term>, and then place one of its feet on the corner of the half-circle, then open it as far as it...

At the top of each of the pillars was a chandelier of gilded bronze, made in the shape of antique vases with a wide opening and two handles. They were provided with a substance that could neither be consumed nor extinguished by wind, rain, or any other accident; for they burned endlessly and without diminishing <note>This refers to the "perpetual lamp," a common legend in Renaissance architecture where ancient tombs were said to contain lamps that burned for centuries without oxygen or fuel</note>. Between the handles of one to the next were attached curved festoons, which were much thicker at their center than at their extremities. These festoons were made of all sorts of leaves and flowers, filed and pierced with openwork <note>original: "percées à iour"; a metalworking technique where the material is cut through to create a decorative pattern of holes</note>, of the same material as their candelabras. The craftsman had bound them by the middle, and upon the binding was perched an eagle with its wings extended, looking upward toward the vault of the aisle—that is to say, the space between the row of columns and the outer wall, which on the inside was made of mosaic, depicting beautiful stories. I have said before that the height of a round temple is determined by the line of its <term>diameter</term>; and to find this height up to the final <term>cornice</term> <note>the decorative molding at the top of a wall</note>, one must divide that same diameter into six parts. In doing so, four of these divisions will give the height of the columns, <term>architrave</term>, <term>frieze</term>, and cornice, up to the beginning of the vault. The diameter of the large circle makes the total height, and that of the small circle the remainder of the height, which is the round vault.

### POLIPHILE.

All the measurements and proportions of this sumptuous edifice had been so well ordered and arranged that the interior and exterior harmonized and corresponded to one another in their pillars, columns, and moldings. O unhappy times! O our unfortunate century, in which such beautiful and worthy invention is so clumsily ignored. Certainly, we must not think we could have understood what an architrave, frieze, cornice, base, capital, column, pillar, pavement, entablature, proportion, partition, and measurement were, if the ancient architects had not taught us through drawing and writing. In the middle of this temple was raised the mouth of a faceted cistern, around which was shown, carved in half-relief <note>original: "demyboſſe" — a technique between low and high relief</note>, a dance of Nymphs who lacked nothing but speech, so well were they fashioned with their gracefully fluttering garments. At the keystone of the vault, in the middle of the circular foliage, was depicted in the same casting and material the head of Medusa, open as if she had wanted to cry out in great rage. From the depths of her throat came a hook, from which hung a knotted chain, hanging perfectly plumb <note>original: "reſpondante à plōb" — vertically aligned with a plumb line</note> with the opening of the cistern. This chain was of fine gold, at the end of which was a ring joined to another, soldered onto the bottom of an inverted plate—that is to say, with the hollow facing down and the back facing up—ending in a point, decorated with moldings, and having a diameter of one cubit. On its circumference were soldered four half-buckles, and to these four hooks, holding four other chains, where there was attached

All around there was a band of **Porphyry** <note>A hard, reddish-purple stone highly prized in antiquity and associated with imperial power</note>, as wide as the projection of the pillars within the work; and joining this one, another of **Serpentine** <note>A dark green stone with patterns resembling a serpent's skin</note>. Beneath the central pillars and the columns, there was a band of Porphyry, the width of the squares that supported the pillars; and on each side of it, another similar band of Serpentine, as wide as the pedestal of the columns. Around the cistern <note>A central basin or fountain</note> there were two, namely one of Porphyry and the other of Serpentine. The remainder of the pavement, between the cistern and the columns, was made of compartments in ten rounds and squares of varying colors: first, two of crimson **Jasper** <term>Jasper</term><note>An opaque variety of silica, often red or green</note> spotted with several veins; two of azure stone sown with flakes of gold <note>original: "pierre d'azur semé de paillettes d'or" — This is Lapis Lazuli</note>; two of green Jasper mixed with red and yellow drops; two of **Agate** <term>Agate</term><note>A translucent stone with wavy bands of color</note> marbled with white veins; and the last two of **Chalcedony**. These bands or rounds always decreased in size toward the cistern, following the shortening of the lines. Between the columns and the wall around the temple, the pavement was of **mosaic** <note>original: "musaique"</note> made of small square stones of all colors, composed into foliage, fruits, flowers, and little beasts of every kind, which you would have judged to be true and natural, not painted or counterfeit: the whole so polished, so level, and so beautifully adorned, that never did **Zenodorus** <note>A famous sculptor and architect of the 1st century AD</note> make the like in **Pergamon**. The *lithostrotos* <term>lithostrotos</term><note>A Greek term for a decorative stone mosaic floor</note> or pavement of the **Temple of Fortune at Praeneste** <note>A famous ancient Roman sanctuary known for its massive, intricate Nile Mosaic</note> was in no way equal to this one. 

Above the great round vault, in the middle of it, was a lantern of eight fluted and hollow columns, made of the same gilded copper, joined to one another by vaulting, bowers, and arches; then above the capitals were the architrave, the frieze, and the cornice, having a height of a third part of the columns. Upon the projections directly above each column, there was a figure of a **Wind**, carved according to their natures and conditions, their wings open, placed upon pivots, so that by them one could know which wind reigned, considering that the figure which bore the name of the one blowing turned its face directly toward it. 

Above there was a small rotunda <note>original: "retube" — likely a variation of "rotonde" or "cupola"</note> made with scales, in which were placed eight pilasters, of the height of two perfect squares taken from the space of the opening, covered by a reversed baluster-base, ribbed like a **Melon**, from which emerged a round rod, decreasing in thickness little by little, until it rose as high as half the vase; and there was fixed a large hollow ball of gilded copper, open at the top and pierced at the bottom in four places. This had been done (as I presumed) to the end that water or earth entering through the top opening should not hinder its function, nor weigh it down more than was appropriate. Through this mouth came the rod, planted straight in the middle, and it passed as far upward into a point as the ball had height. Upon the point was fixed a **Crescent Moon**, which appeared as if eight days old, its horns turned toward the sky. Inside this crescent was perched a **Sea-eagle**, having its wings extended.

Beneath hung from four buckles as many chains of the same material, cast with the whole of the machine, to show the excellence of the workman, who found the means to make a chain of one single piece, without applying any solder; and this by a mold divided into four parts, furnished in the middle with a hole where he cast the first ring, then added all the parts formed into one, by which one could make it as long as one desired. These cymbals, shaken by the wind, struck the belly of the large sphere, such that their resonance, mixed with the deep echoing of the sphere, composed a graceful and lofty harmony, quite different from the chains and vases hanging at the top of the temple in Jerusalem <note>original: "Hierufalem" — likely referring to the gold spikes or ornaments mentioned by Josephus as being atop the Temple to prevent birds from landing</note>, intended to drive away the birds. To conclude the summary of this temple, I will place its measurements here to satisfy the craftsmen. The wall where the eight windows were was one and a half feet thick, and the vaulting had the same; likewise, the projection of the pillars that supported the square structure showed this same thickness on all sides—namely, three feet in diameter. The door was **Doric** <note>The simplest of the classical orders of architecture, characterized here by its sturdy proportions</note>, carved from fine oriental **Jasper**, above which, on the flat surface of the frieze, this word was written in letters of gold, filed and set together: **KYLOPE** <note>original: "ΚΥΛΟΠΗ" — a transliteration of the Greek for 'Cylope', likely connected to the name of the place mentioned in the margin</note>. But when they had come and heard from the Nymph the reason for our arrival, they immediately received us with a kind countenance. Then they had us climb seven steps of **Porphyry** <note>A hard, purple-red stone associated with royalty and imperial power</note>, placed from the level of the pavement up to the door, where we found a beautiful resting place made of a single black stone, so polished that there is none like it (I believe) to be found at Mount Briance. It was crafted with mother-of-pearl inlay. There the maidens stopped, and we did as well. Then the Prioress began to say some prayers; whereat the Nymph, my guide, bowed in all reverence, and for my part, I did the same. However, I could never understand what she was saying because, in lowering my head, I cast my gaze upon the feet of my guide, who had part of her right leg uncovered because, in moving, her garment had pulled back a little. After the venerable Prioress had finished her orisons addressed to the gods **Foriculus**, **Limentinus**, and to the goddess **Cardea** <note>A triad of Roman deities who protected the entrance of a house: Foriculus for the door-leaves, Limentinus for the threshold, and Cardea for the hinges</note>, the Nymph and I stood up. Then the bolt was unlocked by the Prioress, and the doors opened without any noise, except for a sweet and pleasant sound. Wanting to see what caused this, I perceived beneath the door, on each side of its jambs, a metal tube, round and hollow, turning upon a polished vessel; this, rubbing upon a **Serpentine** <note>A dark green stone with patterns like a serpent’s skin</note> stone, smooth as ice, caused the door to open more easily than it otherwise would have, and from this came that graceful echoing. But one of the things that astonished me most was that the door, on both sides, without being pushed or pulled by anyone, opened as if by itself. Therefore, having entered within, I stopped on purpose to see if it was pulled by a counterweight or some other engine, and I saw that in the rebate where one door closed upon the other, there was a small steel plate, quite narrow, soldered onto the metal; then, in the wall and the back of the door on each side, was inset a tablet of **Loadstone** <term>Loadstone</term><note>original: "Ayemant" — a naturally magnetic mineral. inside the temple, always by the side of the <term>High Priestess</term> <note>original: "Prieuse." Before them all went a small nun carrying a torch of virgin white wax, which had not yet been lit. Each had a wreath of flowers on her head. These maidens were well-schooled in what was proper for divine service, expert in sacrifices, scrupulous in ceremonies, and singularly well-instructed in ancient institutions and mysteries. In this order they presented themselves reverently to the High Priestess: who, before any other work, took with marvelous devotion one of the caps and placed it on her head, then the rich Mitre, and after that one of the almuces. When they had thus gathered around the edge of the cistern, the <term>High Priestess</term> <note>original: "Prieuse."</note> beckoned me to approach. Then, by means of a golden key, she opened the lid with great devotion and unparalleled ceremony. Thereupon the young <term>nun</term> <note>original: "religieuse."</note> handed the candle she was holding to the one who had brought the Mitre, and took the book, which she opened with all reverence to hold it before the High Priestess, who began to read softly in the <term>Etruscan language</term> <note>original: "langue Hetrurienne." The author frequently references the Etruscans as a source of ancient, mysterious wisdom.</note>. Shortly after, she took the <term>holy brine</term> <note>original: "saincte saulmoire." A ritual mixture of salt and water used for purification.</note>, over which she performed several priestly blessings, and then poured it into the cistern. 

This done, she commanded that the candle or torch of the <term>Nymph</term> <note>Poliphile's guide through the temple.</note>, my companion, be lit; and she had the flame turned downward toward the middle of the cistern, questioning the Nymph in this manner: "My daughter, what do you ask for?" "Madam," she said, "I ask for grace for this man (pointing to me), and I desire that we might go together to the blessed kingdom of the great divine mother, to drink from her holy fountain." 

Upon hearing this, the High Priestess turned toward me and said: "And you, my son, what do you ask for?" To which I answered very humbly: "Madam, I ask for nothing more than to have the grace of the sovereign mother, but especially that this lady—whom I believe to be my most desired <term>Polia</term> <note>The object of Poliphile's quest and affection.</note>, though I am not yet certain—no longer keeps me in doubt nor in this amorous torment."

I am (without any doubt) that **Polia** whom you love so heartfully; and I confess that it is more than reasonable that such a great and steadfast love be rewarded with mutual goodwill."

"Therefore, I am here prepared to put an end to your sorrowful sighs, to remedy your grievous languors, to comply with and participate in your amorous thoughts, desiring to extinguish with my tears the burning of your afflicted heart, and even to die for you if it be necessary; as a pledge of which, and as a hostage of my love, I give you this kiss." Saying these words, she embraced and kissed me most closely, with a sweetness so natural that small round tears in the shape of pearls fell from her eyes. Her speech was then so courtly, and the kiss so savory, that I felt myself burn from head to foot, and almost entirely melt into tears; even the hearts of the High Priestess and her <term>religious maidens</term> <note>original: "religieuses." In the context of the Temple of Venus, these are the consecrated attendants or priestesses.</note> were so softened by it that they could not contain themselves from weeping.

It is certainly impossible for a man of no learning, and one so poorly spoken as I am, to declare sufficiently and in worthy terms what my heart was doing in the midst of the great fire that had then seized it; for if my soul had at that instant departed from my body, it would have left me greatly satisfied. But to come to the point, the High Priestess said to Polia: "Let us proceed, my daughter, to accomplish the inner sacrifices that we have so happily begun." 

<margin>phengite: clear, shining.</margin> Then they took their way toward the rich chapel or round sacristy joined to the temple, as has been said, which was opposite the entrance. ## How Polia offered the two turtledoves, and
### OF A LITTLE ANGEL WHO ARRIVED

*there: whereby the Prioress made her prayer to the goddess Venus: then the roses were scattered, and two swans sacrificed: upon the ashes of which miraculously grew a rosebush full of flowers and fruit, from which Poliphile and Polia ate. And how after the sacrifice they took leave of the Prioress: then came to another ruined temple: the custom of which Polia explains to Poliphile, and persuades him to go see several epitaphs and tombs that were there: which he did, and returned quite terrified.*

I cannot believe that Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of the city's religious institutions.</note> ever invented such beautiful and devout manners of sacrifice, nor the great Jew <note>Likely referring to Moses or the High Priest of Israel, comparing the pagan ceremony to the rituals of the Temple in Jerusalem.</note> likewise: for (in truth) such are not used at Caere in Tuscany <note>original: "Cerite en Thuscane." An ancient Etruscan city famous for its religious traditions.</note>, nor in all the land of Etruria: also the priests of Memphis <note>An ancient capital of Egypt, center of the cult of the bull-god Apis.</note> never performed them in such humble reverence to their god Apis when they threw the golden cup into the Nile. I even dare to assure that the image of the goddess Fortune was not honored with similar solemnity within the city of Rhamnus <note>A site in Attica, Greece, famous for its sanctuary of Nemesis/Fortune.</note>, nor certainly was the sovereign Jupiter in Anxur <note>The ancient name for Terracina, Italy, site of a famous temple to Jupiter Anxurus.</note>: and that those who celebrated the feast of Feronia <note>An ancient Italian goddess; her priests were said to be able to walk over hot coals.</note>, walking upon glowing coals without injury, did not come close to these women here.

Polia, then, having understood the sign the Prioress made to her, promptly stood up on her feet, while all the others remained on their knees: and was led by the good mother straight to a hyacinth <note>Likely referring to a vessel carved from a precious stone, such as blue sapphire or zircon.</note> pitcher, placed at one side of the chapel. I took careful note of all their acts: and when she turned her face toward me, it seemed to me that I saw the Sun when it shines upon fair Aurora <note>The Roman goddess of the dawn.</note> at daybreak. I saw her put her hands into that pitcher and draw out a sweetly fragrant liquid, with which she washed her face, which was purified by this means. 

Before the step of the altar was a great golden candelabrum, of rare and singular workmanship, adorned with gemstones: atop which was a round plate, slightly hollowed, about an ell <note>An old unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips.</note> in circumference, in which were placed Amber, Musk, Camphor, Labdanum, Thymiama <note>A generic term for incense or an aromatic blend.</note>, Myrrh, Mastic, Benzoin, Aloeswood, Blactebisantis <note>original: "Blactebiſantis." Likely referring to *Blatta Byzantina*, the operculum of a seashell used in ancient perfumery.</note>, and other scents that Arabia Felix <note>original: "Arabie heureuse." The fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula, famed for its spices and resins.</note> produces, duly composed by weight and measure: to which Polia, being admonished to do so, brought the burning candle, and after having lit these scents, extinguished it immediately, then set it aside, and moreover threw into the flame of these scents a branch of dry myrtle: and when it had caught fire, she carried it back onto the altar of sacrifice, to light all the other branches that were there. When the sacrifice was on the fire, the woman who performed the office of the Songstress began the service, and the others responded to her.

Before the prioress went two young nuns, sounding <term>Lydian shawms<note>original: "chalemyes Lydiennes." Ancient reed instruments played here in the Lydian mode, which in classical music theory was often associated with softness, sweetness, and the erotic.</note></term>, in the natural Lydian tone.

After the prioress was Polia, then all the others in order, each carrying a branch of Myrtle <note>A plant sacred to Venus, symbolizing love and fertility.</note>, singing in harmony with the shawms, and dancing with a step and cadence equal to them around the altar, saying these verses in rhythm.

->O fire of holy scent<-
->Thaw every cold heart,<-
->Join Love and Venus,<-
->So that it loses its chill,<-
->And receives the heat,<-
->For which we have come.<-

Thus these nuns surrounded the sacred altar, singing and dancing in time while the sacrifice was consumed, and they continued until the flame was extinguished, leaving only the smoke. I think those sweet scents and perfumes were placed there to cover the bad smell of the burning flesh. Immediately after, they all prostrated themselves on the pavement, except for the prioress: and it was not long before I clearly saw a small spirit emerge from the smoke, beautiful in every excellence, who had on his shoulders two wings so shining that my eyes could not look upon him properly. I felt my heart fail and was dazzled by the rays of his brightness, like a lightning bolt created from water, fire, cloud, and wind. But the prioress, noticing me, made a sign that I should not be afraid, and that I should only keep silent. This beautiful child held in one of his hands a crown of Myrtle, and in the other an arrow, sparkling with burning fire. His head was covered with small curls of gold, and crowned with a headband of Diamonds. He fluttered three times around the altar, then at the third time he vanished and turned into smoke, so that I lost sight of him, and I remained trembling and deeply thoughtful, seeing these miraculous things and such an admirable vision, which had (for certain) filled me with a devotional horror <note>The word "horror" here refers to a classical "shuddering awe" or religious trembling rather than fear.</note>.

Shortly after, the prioress made them all rise, and began to read from the book which was held open before her by the little Novice. The holy lady carried a golden rod in her hand, with which she then commanded Polia to gather the ash remaining from the sacrifice and place it in a golden sieve, prepared for this purpose: which she did, and sifted it onto the first step of the altar, so neatly and with such discretion that she seemed to have been born to this office. When that ash was sifted, the Prioress had her write and draw within it, using the first finger of her right hand, certain characters in the form of those that were in the book: then she made her kneel again, and similarly all the others.

During this, the doors and windows clashed one against the other with such impetuosity that the noise represented a great thunder, caused by wind enclosed within a cave without an exit.

If I was frightened on my part, it is no wonder. Upon this fruit-tree appeared three doves and certain other flying birds, which flitted from branch to branch, sweetly warbling their song; wherefore I presumed that the goddess showed herself to us in this figure, and as if by a divine vision. Then the Prioress rose from the ground and helped Polia to her feet: who seemed to me, beyond all comparison, more beautiful than she had ever appeared before. Both called me and had me enter the chapel, where I went to kneel before the rich altar, between the two of them. Then the Prioress plucked three of these miraculous fruits, ate the first, gave me the second, and the third was for Polia.

around which, in the time when it was still standing, fairs and markets were held, where every year innumerable multitudes of people from all nations came; and there were celebrated many kinds of games and pastimes, so much so that for the excellence of its structure, and for the abundance of sacrifices, it was greatly renowned and devoutly visited. But because its magnificence has declined, you see it now deserted and lying in ruin. <margin>Polyandrion: a sepulcher for many.</margin> It was anciently called the **Polyandrion**, <note>From the Greek *polyandrion*, literally "place of many men," a term for a communal cemetery or a site for those fallen in battle.</note> consecrated to **Pluto**, god of the shades: and therefore there are a great number of various tombs where those are buried who, through the importunity of unhappy love, have miserably ended their days. Each year, on the day of the **Ides of May** (which is the fifteenth of the month), all those who served love, or were under its protection—both men and women, from various regions both far and near—assembled in this temple to celebrate the solemnities of the funerals and annual obsequies of their friends who had thus deceased. They sacrificed to this **three-bodied Pluto**, to the end that they themselves might not fall into the misfortune of being the cause of their own deaths, and so hasten their appointed days. For this reason, they reverently made funeral offerings of **black ewes** that had not yet borne lambs, and they burned them upon an altar of copper, presenting the males to the god, and the females to the goddess **Proserpine** his wife, ordering the **lectisternia** <note>original: "lectisternes"; an ancient Roman ritual where images of gods were placed on couches and offered a banquet.</note> for three nights; then they extinguished the flame of the sacrifice with roses and the ashes of the fire. But the priests could give them out in exchange. After having thus scattered it, they also threw the reed into the sea, and spat there three times, saying at each stroke, "fu, fu, fu." Then they returned, scattering roses throughout the temple, especially upon the sepulchers, singing in a piteous and funereal tone, accompanied by complaints, tears, groans, and the sound of certain **milvine pipes**, <note>original: "chalemyes miluiennes"; pipes or shawms with a high, shrill tone resembling the cry of a kite (a bird of prey).</note> suitable for such a sacrifice. And after having taken their meal, they called upon the souls and left the remains of the food around the sepulchers for them. the excellence of its structure, and for the abundance of sacrifices, it was greatly
renowned, and devoutly visited. But because its magnificence has fallen away,
you see it at this hour deserted, and lying in ruin. It was anciently called Po-
<margin>Polyandrion, a tomb for many.</margin>
lyandrion, <note>original: "Polyandrion"; from the Greek for "many men," referring to a mass grave or cemetery.</note> consecrated to Pluto, god of the shadows: and therefore there are a great number of
tombs where those are buried who, through the importunity of unhappy love, have
miserably finished their days. Each year, on the day of the Ides of May (which is the
fifteenth of the month) all those who served love, or were under his
allegiance, both men and women, from various regions both far and
near, assembled in this temple to celebrate the solemnities of the funerals
and annual obsequies of their friends who had thus deceased: and they sacrificed to this
three-bodied Pluto <note>original: "Pluto tricorporel"; a reference to the god of the underworld, sometimes depicted with multiple forms or associated with the three-headed Cerberus.</note>, to the end that they themselves might not fall into the misfortune
of being the cause of their own death, and hastening their appointed days: and for this they
reverently made funeral offerings of black sheep, which had not
yet carried a lamb, and burned them upon an altar of copper, presenting the males
to the god, and the females to the goddess Proserpine his wife, ordaining the banquet-couches <note>original: "lectisternes"; the Roman ritual of Lectisternium, where images of gods were placed on couches and offered a meal.</note>
for three nights; then they extinguished the flame of the sacrifice with roses and ritual water <note>original: "arserie"; likely referring to a purifying liquid or wine used to douse sacrificial fires.</note>.
That this is so, you still see there a great rosebush, from which if anyone had then gath-
ered a rose, he was held as sacrilegious, having committed a marvelous offense against this god.
But the priests could give some in exchange. The sacrifice completed, the high
priest dressed in pontifical robes, and having before his breast a rich brooch made of a
precious stone called Synochite <note>original: "Synochite"; a legendary stone mentioned by Pliny, said to have the power to summon spirits.</note>, gave to each a little ash which he
carried in a golden Simpulum <note>original: "Simpule"; a small ladle-like vessel used in Roman sacrifices.</note>, and it was received with great devotion. Then the peo-
ple put it into a tube of reed or something else, and went out in
crowds to the seashore, where they blew this ash, observing a superstitious ce-
remony, casting out confused loud voices, mixed with howls and feminine
cries, saying: "Thus may they perish like this ash, who shall be the guilty cause
of the death of their lover." After having thus scattered it, they also threw the
reed into the sea, and spat there three times, saying at each stroke, "fu, fu, fu": and re-
turned back, strewing roses through the temple, especially upon the
tombs, singing in a piteous and funereal tone, accompanied by complaints, tears,
groans, and the sound of certain milvine pipes <note>original: "chalemyes miluiennes"; pipes producing a shrill, kite-like (milvine) crying sound.</note>, suitable for such a
sacrifice. This done, they assembled by nations separately, and sat in a circle
upon the pavement, where each put what they had brought to eat, and made of it
a banquet, which was the Silicernium <note>original: "Silicerne"; a Roman funeral feast eaten at the grave.</note>, where the guests kept silent while eating. And
after having taken their meal, they called upon the souls, and left for them around
the tombs the remainder of the meat. Besides these anniversaries, secular
games were held, which being finished they left the temple, and each bought
a Pancarpia <note>original: "Pancarpe"; a garland or wreath woven from many different flowers and fruits.</note>, that is to say a crown of flowers, which they put upon their
head, and took in their hand a branch of Cypress, used for funerals. Then the
priests, dressed in stoles and capes, sang, and carried the divine
images: even the Sicinnist dancers <note>original: "dãseurs Sicinistes"; dancers of the 'sicinnis,' a fast, satirical dance associated with satyr plays.</note> were mixed among the women, where they made

# 84

#### ->POLIPHILE.<-

There we sat upon the fresh and flowery grass. Then my eyes turned to contemplate the great perfection and excellence of beauty with which my companion was adorned, so much so that they found neither pleasure nor contentment in anything else. Therefore my heart, refreshed by a secret joy, left behind all base thoughts and simple fantasies, and my understanding rose to consider her admirable virtues. Nevertheless, it happened at times that I returned to consider the situation of this place, which was certainly beautiful and delectable. The air was serene and favorable, the greenery pleasant, the little hills shaded by groves, bedewed by fountains and streams flowing through the beautiful valley, bordered by all manner of fruit trees. The winds made themselves graceful, the earth was abundant and fertile, resonating with the song of birds; so much so that I would have almost thought these were the famed **Elysian Fields** <note>In Greek mythology, the Elysian Fields were the final resting place for the souls of the heroic and the virtuous, a paradise of eternal spring.</note>: for the beautiful fields and river of **Thessaly** <note>Original: "Theffalie." Likely referring to the Vale of Tempe in Thessaly, celebrated by ancient poets as a favorite haunt of Apollo and the Muses.</note> are in no way to be compared to it. Notwithstanding this, my eyes were always fixed upon my companion, without being able to look elsewhere, considering that my brain was occupied by nothing else; and I knew not on which part to rest my sight, for each was more beautiful and delectable than the last. Yet I looked most willingly at a little valley situated in the middle of her breast, between two breasts rounder than apples and whiter than flakes of snow, indeed (in truth) more sumptuous than the **Tomb of King Mausolus** <note>Original: "fepulture du Roy Maufolus." One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus was built for the Persian satrap Mausolus. Poliphile suggests her beauty surpasses this legendary monument.</note>: at least so it seemed to me, because there dwelt the tomb of my soul. Sometimes she cast her gaze upon me, and I felt it run through my whole body, like a flash of lightning, so much so that I shivered for an hour afterward. This having passed, I began again as before, urged by an insatiable desire by a sharp and importunate love, saying, without moving my lips, many words of piteous prayers, founded on plausible reasons, by which I asked for that which would have made me the most contented person in the world, which I obtained in my imagination; and I found myself in the midst of the treasures of the goddess **Venus** (just as **Mercury** <note>A reference to the mythological union of Hermes (Mercury) and Aphrodite (Venus).</note> did), the jewels of abundant nature.

But (alas) I found myself too deeply afflicted by that contagious disease <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for being "lovesick."</note>, besieged by the divine mother, and assailed by her son the great **firebrand** <note>Original: "boutefeu." Referring to Cupid, the bringer of the "fire" of passion.</note>, indissolubly bound and stuck fast under the bait of two beautiful eyes, marvelously sparkling: against which it served for nothing to make an effort to withdraw; for that was to enter further in, and it was no longer in my power to resist these diverse thoughts, seeing that my patience was almost vanquished.

So I deliberated (in whatever way it might be) to extinguish this unbearable heat, and putting all wise counsel aside, to tempt my Polia with a furious audacity, wishing nevertheless to say to her beforehand in a humble voice: "Madame, I would esteem dying for you as an eternal praise, and death would be (in my opinion) tolerable, sweet, and glorious. I say this because my soul is oppressed by a heat too violent, which increases incessantly, and strengthens within my heart so much that I cannot have a single hour of peace nor of rest."

I thought indeed by this way to give an end to my grievous martyrdom, but suddenly another counsel came to me, which said:

"What will you do, Poliphile? Think a little what end came to the violence done to **Deianira**, to the Roman **Lucretia**, and many other such renowned ladies <note>Deianira was the wife of Hercules, whose story involves themes of jealousy and unintended tragedy; Lucretia was a legendary Roman matron whose rape led to the fall of the Roman monarchy. The "counsel" warns Poliphile against forced affection.</note>. Consider that the Gods have often been refused by their earthly loves. What should a poor, simple person like you do then in this situation?"

Bring back, bring back to your memory that every long stretch of time comes to a certain end, at least for one who can endure it: indeed, even lions and other savage beasts are tamed through persistence; even the little **ant** <note>Original: "Formy," an archaic French term for *fourmi* (ant).</note> hardens the path by passing over it many times. For this reason, all the more so, a celestial spirit hidden within a human body might well feel some small spark of love. In this manner, then, both approving and blaming my own opinions, I withdrew from these troubling fantasies, hoping to reach the fruit of my long quest and, in the end, triumph in the victory acquired through my patience. I also remembered the holy prayers and sacrifices of Polia, where she had made special mention of me and extinguished her burning torch to show favor to her Poliphile. I thought it better and more certain to wait, enduring a happy (though late) reward and obtaining the perfection of my desire, than by perilous importunity to increase my pain and lose all hope for the future. Polia perceived that I was changing color too often; she saw me agitated, troubled, and almost out of breath, sighing blow after blow from the depths of my chest. To remedy this, she cast a sweet glance toward me, which chased away all these impetuous thoughts, so much so that from then on my soul remained in more tranquil hope amidst the flames of love, like the **Phoenix** <note>A mythical bird that, after living for centuries, consumes itself in fire only to be reborn from its own ashes; a common Renaissance metaphor for the transformative power of passion.</note> who burns itself in order to be renewed.

The place at first glance seemed dark to me, but as soon as my eyes were a little accustomed to it, I began to see a large round cave, vaulted and supported by six <term>embedded columns</term> <note>original: "colonnes nayues." These are columns that appear to be part of the living rock or are unadorned and "natural" in their setting.</note>, positioned directly beneath the six columns standing above, all made of <term>dark marble</term> <note>original: "marbre biz." A brownish-grey or dark-colored stone.</note>, as was the vault: whose blocks were so very well joined that the vault and the columns seemed properly to be of one piece. It is true that the cave was completely full of <term>saltpetre</term> <note>original: "Aphronitre ou baurach." In the middle of these six embedded columns was an altar of copper, composed of two perfect squares which made six feet in length and three in height, including the ordinary moldings. It was hollow in the manner of a tomb, but in the opening at the top, two good inches deep, there was a <term>grille</term> <note>original: "treilliz."</note> of the same casting, and on one of the sides a window, made (as I could understand) to put the fire beneath the sacrifice, and to draw out the extinguished ash. What made me presume this was that the said grille, with the surface of the altar, were all blackened by smoke, which (in my judgment) exited through the round opening above, and then through the small pipe that was in the vault set upon the six columns made in the Egyptian fashion. On the final face of the altar was written in well-carved Roman letters:
