They were rough and smoky, facing one another, with a bridge crossing the abyss, divided diagonally. One of the halves appeared as hot, glowing iron as if coming out of a furnace, and the other of ice, cold in every extremity. Between these two rocks, beneath the bridge, and around this pit on one side, everything seemed to be full of fire, casting flying and noisy sparks into the air, then falling back as extinguished ash, so often and so thickly that one could not have seen a foot's distance. Through the rock were several <term>fire-vents</term> <note>original: "souspiraux." Small openings or flues to allow smoke or heat to escape.</note>, like the small mouths of furnaces: and on the other side a dark and troubled lake, frozen in all rigor, adjoining the burning rock, with only the bridge between the two. And because two such contrary substances were found so close to each other, and could not naturally mix, as it was expressed by the painting, it seemed that a marvelous thunder was generated there.

Every man of good judgment can well imagine that where two lakes <note>original: "lącz" — a variant of "lacs" (lakes), referring to the pits of fire and ice</note> of contrary natures meet, a marvelous thunder must be generated there, by reason of the contrariety and perpetual discord of their differing qualities: for where they join, they both lose themselves in a deep abyss, fearful beyond measure. To tell the truth, the depth of this **Hell** was so ingeniously represented that it seemed a lifelike opening for the wicked: so well and artistically had the craftsman (to show his intention) known how to vary his colors and execute the lines of <term>Perspective|The art of representing three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface to give the right impression of their height, width, depth, and position</term> by precise measure.

Whoever looked carefully at this portrait could without difficulty recognize that it held much <term>verisimilitude|The appearance of being true or real</term>: for the noble master had depicted the souls in bodily form: among which, some stopped their ears for fear of hearing the terrifying noise.

Others covered their eyes with both hands, not daring to look at the abysses so hideously sunken and filled with abominable monsters.

The majority were pale and discolored, clutching their arms against their chests as if frozen with cold.

Some, to express the burning heat they suffered, vomited a thick smoke from their mouths.

Many had their hands locked one inside the other, or indeed their fingers interlaced like the teeth of a comb, as a sign of their sadness, accompanied by a pain too vehement to bear.

These souls met upon the bridge already described, and there came to confront and rudely strike one against the other, without any means of retreating because of the press of those following behind; nor (what is more) of going forward, because of the resistance of the others coming against them from the opposite side. And then this bridge would split in two (as has been said) to overturn each one into its specific torment, then it would rejoin itself, and in an instant was reloaded with new souls, without ceasing or delay. For this reason, the poor desperate souls wished for their own annihilation, which would have been less grievous to them than these insupportable **Furies** <note>In Greek and Roman mythology, the Furies (Erinyes) were deities of vengeance who punished spirits in the Underworld</note>. This excessive torment and this unlucky hell were so well represented in painting that those who paused to contemplate it fell into a marvelous horror.

# THE FIRST BOOK OF POLIPHILE

...and here I am snatched away by death. What do you want me to do about it? Go tell through the city and the world that the Roman lady Naevia died miserably for the love of the cruel Proculus. That will suffice. Farewell.

I then entered another alcove <note>original: "Tribune," referring to a semi-circular architectural niche or apse</note>, where there were the remains of a painting made in mosaic like the previous one, though for the most part broken and ruined as much as the alcove itself. It depicted a lady falling into a great fire, who had pierced her body through with a sword <note>A classic depiction of the suicide of Dido, Queen of Carthage</note>. Around her, one could see several feet of women, some bare with part of the leg showing, others covered by their garments; everything else was erased and knocked down by age or the length of time, due to the winds, rains, and the heat of the sun. Likewise, the pavement was demolished. There was no writing there, except for half of a broken epitaph, overturned on the ground, where there were these few letters, very difficult to understand.

Near this fragment lay on the ground an ancient vase of Alabaster, of the height of a good pace and a half <note>About four and a half feet</note>, still having one of its handles, but the other was broken along with part of its belly. It was set upon a quadrangle <note>A square pedestal or base</note>, where some ancient capital letters remained, part of them whole, and part destroyed.

I left these ruined tombs to go into another alcove <note>original: "tribune," referring to a semi-circular architectural niche</note>, where there appeared a fragment of a mosaic painting, almost entirely erased; nonetheless, one could still see a shipwreck, and a young man saving himself by swimming, carrying a beautiful girl on his back; and as they arrived on land in a desert place, there was still part of the figure of a Lion. In another spot they were in a small boat upon the sea; all the rest was demolished: therefore I could not well understand the story. But on the wall, which was of marble, there was a copper tablet, engraved with Greek capital letters, containing an Epigram in the same language: reading which, I was forced to weep for the miserable accident, and curse the inconstancy of Fortune. After having read and re-read it several times, I translated it into Latin <note>In keeping with the narrator's process, though the text will be presented in English for the reader</note>, in this manner.

# BOOK ONE OF

<image-desc>The printed text is enclosed within a large, elaborate ornamental border in a Renaissance or Baroque architectural style. The frame features complex C-scrolls, floral motifs, and stylized strapwork. At the top, two decorative scrolls meet in a central crest. Ho there, traveler! Rest your hands for a moment, I implore you: come forward and read these mournful <note>original: "polyſtonos," a Greek term meaning "much-sighing" or "full of grief"</note> words engraved in metal, and give them a kiss, adding: "Alas! A cruel monument of Fortune! They ought to have lived." *Leontia, a young maiden of high status, was driven by an overwhelming passion for the noble youth Lollius. Suffering under her father's cruelty, she fled. Lollius followed her; but while they were embracing, they were captured by pirates and sold to a certain merchant. Both were taken as captives onto a ship. When, during the night, Lollius suspected that Leontia was being taken away from him, he seized a sword and slew all the sailors. But the sea grew violent, and the ship, driven against the rocks near the shore, was wrecked and sank. We climbed onto a rock, driven by the impulse of hunger <note>The Latin "famis impulsu" suggests they were forced to seek land due to lack of food, or perhaps it is a transcription error for "flaminis," the force of the wind</note>. I took Leontia upon my shoulders. Be favorable and present, Father Neptune; I commit ourselves and our fortune to you. Then, with dolphin-like effort, I cut through the waves with my arms. But Leontia spoke to me while I was swimming: "Am I a burden to you, my life?" "Lighter than a water-gnat <note>original: "tipula," a small, light insect that skims the water</note>, Leontia, my little heart <note>original: "corculum," a Roman term of endearment</note>," I replied. And she asked again and again: "Do you have strength, my hope, my little soul?" I said, "Yes." Then, embracing my neck, she kissed her bearer as sweetly as sugar; she comforted me, encouraged me, and gave life to me as I dove through the water. I rejoiced that we would finally reach the shore in safety. But unexpectedly, a roaring lion attacked us. We embraced one another. The lion spared us as we lay there dying <note>This refers to the ancient belief that lions do not harm those who prostrate themselves or appear near death</note>. Terrified by this turn of events, we fugitives both climbed into a small boat that had been cast onto the shore along with a small oar. Rowing alternately, we sang as we wandered for a day and a third night; only the sky was visible everywhere around us. We were tortured by lethal hunger, and wasting away from long fasting, we fell into each other's embrace. Leontia, saying, "I love you, even as you perish of hunger." "It is enough to be with you, Lollius," I prayed; but she, sighing, said: "My Lollius, you are failing." "Not at all in love," I said, "but only in body." With trembling sunbeams and joined tongues we fed sweetly upon one another, and with mouths pressed close and open, injecting sweet kisses, we embraced like ivy. We both died of wasting away <note>original: "atrophia"</note>. Without the tides <note>original: "Plennyriis," from the Greek for "flood-tide"</note> raging, a breeze carried us here, and in this profitable place <note>original: "aere quaestuario," possibly implying a place where they are honored or "paid" their due in memory</note> we miserable ones were placed among the spirits of the underworld <note>original: "manes inter Plotonicos," referring to Pluto, god of the dead</note>, still joined in that same embrace. Those whom the greed of pirates did not keep, nor the lion's gluttony devour, nor the vastness of the sea refuse to take, the narrowness of this little urn now holds together. I wanted you to know of this misfortune.*

->Farewell.<-

### POLIPHILE

->Whose explanation is as follows:<-

*Alas, passer-by, I adjure you by the Gods of the underworld to read this a little: then, sighing, kiss this metal, saying: "Alas, the cruel misfortune and example of Fortune! They should have lived longer." Leontia, a young maiden captivated in her early years by the love of a noble youth named Lollius, afflicted by the ill-treatment of her father, fled, and Lollius followed her. Thus, when they had found and embraced one another, they were captured by pirates and sold to a merchant, both led captive and put upon a ship. But during the night, Lollius, thinking someone wished to take his Leontia from him, took a knife with which he killed all the sea-robbers <note>original: "escumeurs de mer," a colorful period term for pirates</note>. Then there arose a storm so violent that the ship was driven sideways against a rock near the shore, onto which they climbed, pressed by great hunger. I took Leontia and loaded her upon my shoulders, saying: "Be favorable to me, Father Neptune; I commend us and our adversity to you." Then I began to slice through the water with my two arms like a dolphin with its fins; and as I swam, my Leontia said to me: "I weigh upon you too much, O my life." And I answered her: "To me, you seem lighter than a drop of water <note>original: "coulandre d'eau," an archaic term here implying something weightless or a mere trickle</note>, Leontia, my heart." Often she asked me: "Are you not weary, my soul and my hope?" "No," I would say, "you give me strength." Then she would lean down to kiss and embrace her bearer, consoling and encouraging me, which made me joyful beyond measure. Finally we arrived at land, where (unexpectedly) we were attacked by a lion; wherefore we embraced as if to die, and that cruel animal spared us. Terrified by this event, we entered into a small boat equipped with a tiny oar, which we found upon the shore; and singing one after the other, we rowed for three days and three nights without seeing anything but water and sky. Thus tormented by mortal hunger and failing through too long a fast, we embraced one another, me saying: "Alas, Leontia, you are dying of hunger." "Lollius," she replied, "I have eaten enough just by being with you." Then, sighing, she said to me: "Lollius, my friend, you can do no more; your heart fails you." "Not in love," I replied, "but only in this body of mine." Alas, we lived no longer save on kisses; thus we died, tightly embraced, solely for lack of food. Afterward, these waves being calmed, a gentle wind brought us here, where we were buried all embraced, and by money collected from a quest, placed among the Plutonic souls <note>referring to the spirits in the realm of Pluto, god of the underworld</note>. Those, then, whom the greed of pirates could not hold, nor the hungry rage of lions devour, nor the deep abysses of the sea swallow, a small, narrow jar now contains them both within its belly.*

*I wished only to inform you of this misfortune, and so, farewell.*

# FIRST BOOK OF

<image-desc>The following text is enclosed within a large, ornate rectangular cartouche or decorative border. *Hark, traveler, stay your hands a moment, I adjure you: come forward and read these mournful <note>original: "polystonos," from the Greek for much-sighing or sorrowful</note> words and give kisses to the metal, adding: "Ah, cruel monument of Fortune! They should have lived." Leontia, a maiden, when she was overwhelmed by the storm of her first love for the noble youth Lollius, fled, having been afflicted by her father's torments. Lollius followed her; but while they were embracing, they were captured by pirates and sold to a certain merchant; both were taken captive onto a ship. When, at night, Lollius suspected Leontia was being taken from him, he seized a sword and slaughtered all the sailors. The ship, amidst the rising savagery of the sea, was dashed against rocks near the shore and sank. We climbed a rock, driven by hunger. Taking Leontia, I placed her on my shoulders, saying: "Be favorable, be present, Father Neptune; I commit ourselves and our fortune to you." Then, with a dolphin-like effort, I cut through the waves with my arms. But as we swam, Leontia spoke: "Am I a burden to you, my life?" "Lighter than a water-spider <note>original: "tipula," used here to suggest weightlessness</note>, Leontia, my little heart," I replied; and she asked quite often: "Do you have strength, my hope, my little soul?" I said: "You stir it up!" Soon, embracing my neck, she kissed her bearer sweetly <note>original: "sachariter," literally "sugarly"</note>, consoled me, encouraged me, and gave life to the swimmer <note>original: "urinante"</note>. I rejoiced; we finally reached the shore safe and sound. Suddenly, a roaring lion attacked; we embraced each other. The lion spared us, as we were like those about to die. Terrified by the event, we fugitives both climbed into a small boat cast upon the shore along with a small oar-blade. We rowed, singing in turns, wandering for three days and nights; only the sky was visible in every direction. We were tortured by lethal hunger, and wasting away from long fasting <note>original: "inedia"</note>, we fell into each other's arms. "Leontia," I said, "my love, you are dying of hunger." "It is enough to be with you, Lollius; I am fed by it." But she, sighing, said: "My Lollius, you are failing." "Not at all," I said, "in love, but only in body." We fed sweetly on the vibrating sun and on each other's tongues, and more tightly, with mouths open, we embraced like ivy, sweet kisses exchanged. We both died of wasting away. While the tides <note>original: "Plennyriis"</note> were not raging, a breeze carried us here; and on this mournful altar, wretched and bound in those very embraces, we are placed here as spirits among the Plutonic <note>original: "Plotonicos," referring to the underworld of Pluto</note> shades. Those whom pirate greed did not keep, nor the lion's throat devour, nor the immense sea take, the narrowness of this little urn now holds both. I wanted you to know this misfortune.*

->*Farewell.*<-

->Of which the explanation is as follows:<-

*Alas, passer-by, I adjure you by the gods of the underworld <note>original: "dieux infernaux," referring to the deities of the Greco-Roman subterranean realm, such as Pluto and Proserpina</note>, that you read this for a moment: then, sighing, kiss this metal, saying: "Ah, the cruel misfortune and example of Fortune! They ought to have lived longer." Leontia, a young maiden, smitten in her early years with the love of a noble youth named Lollius, afflicted by the ill-treatment of her father, fled, and Lollius followed her. Thus, when they had found and embraced one another, they were taken by pirates and sold to a merchant; both were led captive and placed upon a ship. But during the night, Lollius, thinking that someone wished to take his Leontia from him, took a knife with which he killed all the sea-scoundrels <note>original: "escumeurs de mer," literally sea-foamers, a period term for pirates</note>. Then there arose a tempest so violent that the ship was driven sideways against a rock near the shore, upon which they climbed, pressed by great hunger. I took Leontia and hoisted her onto my shoulders, saying: "Be favorable to me, Father Neptune <note>The Roman god of the sea</note>; I commend us and our adversity to you." Then I began to cut through the water with my two arms like a dolphin with its fins. And as I swam, my Leontia said to me: "I weigh upon you too much, O my life." And I answered her: "You seem lighter to me than a water-spider <note>original: "coulandre d'eau," a term likely derived from the Latin "tipula," referring to a water-strider or insect that skims the surface</note>, Leontia, my heart." Often she would ask me: "Are you not weary, my soul and my hope?" "No," said I, "you give me strength." Then she would stoop to kiss and embrace her bearer, comforting and encouraging me, for which I was joyful beyond measure. Finally, we arrived at land, where (without expecting it) we were attacked by a lion; therefore we embraced as if to die, and this cruel animal spared us <note>A common literary trope where the purity of lovers or the nobility of their plight tames wild beasts</note>. Terrified by this event, we climbed back into a small boat equipped with a tiny oar, which we found upon the shore; and singing one after the other, we rowed for three days and three nights without seeing anything but the water and the sky. Thus tormented by mortal hunger, and failing from too long a fast, we embraced one another, me saying: "Alas, Leontia, you are dying of hunger." "Lollius," she replied, "I eat enough just by being with you." Then, sighing, she said to me: "Lollius, my friend, you can do no more; your heart is failing." "Not in love," I replied, "but in this body of mine alone." Alas, we lived no longer except on kisses; thus we died closely embraced, solely for lack of food. Afterward, these waves having calmed, a gentle wind brought us here, where we have been buried all entwined, and by money gathered from a collection, placed among the Plutonic souls <note>original: "ames Plutoniques," the souls of the dead residing in Pluto's kingdom</note>. Those, therefore, whom the avarice of pirates could not hold, nor the hungry rage of lions devour, nor the profound abysses of the sea swallow up, a small, narrow urn now contains them both in its belly.*

*I wished only to warn you of this misfortune, and Farewell.*

# BOOK ONE OF

->O Reader<-

<image-desc>The English translation of the text is presented within a large, ornate woodcut illustration of a funerary monument. The monument features a classical architectural design with a triangular pediment supported by a rectangular frame. At the corners of the pediment are circular rosettes. The central portion of the monument consists of a large, unfurled piece of parchment or a hanging cloth scroll with curved, weighted edges, upon which the story is inscribed.</image-desc>

O Reader, this unhappy monument calls to you; stand here a moment, and thereafter it asks, as you read, to what end human pleasure falls. Here lies the ash of two lovers who, while they burned strangely with mutual and itching love, driven by the unrestrained impulse of wicked pleasure, met in a deserted place among ruined rocks. There, while both were urged to pay the desired gifts to Venus <note>original: "Veneri"; Venus was the goddess of love, here representing sexual passion.</note>, and I, Lopidia, lying on my back, saw a snake hanging above, threatening to fall from on high. 

"Alas! Stop what you have begun," I say, "my Chrysanthes: rise, flee! Behold, a serpent is about to devour us; I see it about to strike from the wall." 

Immediately he, terrified and looking up, said: "O my Lopidia, I pray you, go, flee for your life; leave me to attack this deadly Dragon <note>original: "Draconem"; in this period, "dragon" was often used interchangeably with a large, monstrous serpent.</note>." 

I had scarcely risen. Alas, wretched and miserable me! I saw my Chrysanthes, my very life, ensnared to his destruction. Tightly encircled by the serpentine coil, I saw him already gasping for breath; and suddenly, the throat of my Chrysanthes was wounded by its biting teeth. Then I saw my Chrysanthes being suffocated. 

"Alas, alas! I have perished, unhappy woman; I feel my Chrysanthes dying!" 

Immediately, in a fury, I rushed at the serpent. Having seized a club, I hastened to strike it, but the serpent twisted its fighting neck, and I could not drive it away from its tight embrace. At last, missing my stroke through carelessness, I killed my Chrysanthes—I, the most unhappy of women! 

Alas, I have died. What have I done? What shall I do? Shall such a wretched woman survive? Or the serpent and I? By no means! But with Herculean <note>original: "Herculeo"; a reference to the legendary strength and bravery of the hero Hercules.</note> daring—indeed, with a snarling fury of the underworld—with that same club turned with force, I struck and killed that coiled beast upon the fallen corpse. 

What was I to do then, a girl lost and dead? I carried my Chrysanthes and the beast, the witnesses of my crime, cast over my shoulders into the city. And so that I might not escape blame, repeatedly watering the ground with sighs, heartache, and tears, I ascended a certain platform in the public forum, and sighing, I made the matter known openly. A crowd of citizens rushed in throngs to the cruel and hated spectacle of the struggle; they marveled pityingly at the fall, they blamed fortune, and they condemned Venus. 

I bore witness to my crime; I invoked the powers of the underworld. "Come then," I said, "receive me, who will pay the penalty along with my Chrysanthes; now I will transfer all the guilt to myself." Then, in despair and in the public sight of everyone, I seized a sword and pierced my breast, and gave myself, most wretched, to be buried eternally in this tomb with his corpse. Farewell.

O Reader, come here, I pray you. This wretched monument calls to you, and further requires that you read to what end human pleasure falls. Here is the ash of two lovers, who formerly, inflamed beyond measure with love for one another, at the persistent persuasion of immoderate pleasure, found themselves in a deserted place among the ruins of an old destroyed temple, ardently desiring to fulfill their vows to the goddess Venus <note>In this context, fulfilling vows to Venus refers to the physical consummation of their love.</note>. I, Lopidia, lying with my face turned upward, saw a serpent upon a demolished wall, which was about to spring at us. "Stop now, alas, my friend Chrysanthes: get up and flee! For there is a horrible serpent that wishes to throw itself down from the wall to devour us both." Then he looked up, quite terrified, and cried out to me: "Oh Lopidia, save yourself, let me die with this beast!" I had no sooner risen (alas, miserable me) than I saw my friend and my life, Chrysanthes, mortally enveloped and bound very tightly by the coils of this serpent, so much so that he could no longer breathe, for it held him by the throat. Alas, I saw my dear Chrysanthes suffocated in my presence. Alas, unhappy woman, I am lost; my Chrysanthes is dead. Then, all of a sudden, I took up a staff like a woman possessed, and ran at the serpent. As I hurried to strike it down, it turned its head, gnashing its teeth, and I could not drive it away; therefore, wanting to redouble my effort with another blow, I missed my mark <note>original: "ie faulx"; from the verb "faillir," meaning to fail or miss.</note> and killed my friend Chrysanthes. Alas, alas, ill-fated woman, I am dead! But what have I done? What shall I do? Who shall remain, the serpent or I? Having said this, with a Herculean boldness <note>A reference to the Greek hero Hercules, famed for his strength and monster-slaying.</note>, or rather through an infernal rage, I took up that staff again and struck again at the cruel beast surrounding the body that lay dead on the ground, and likewise I laid it dead. What could a simple, distraught girl then think or do? I placed my Chrysanthes and the beast I had slain upon my shoulders, as witnesses to my crime; then I carried them into the city, bathing my friend with tears and accompanying him with the anguished sighs of my heart. Afterward, I climbed to a high place in the public square, where, weeping, I recounted the event. All the people ran to this hideous spectacle, and the folk looked at me with pity, blaming Fortune and cursing Venus. I confessed my crime and said, invoking the lower gods: "Come then, receive me with my friend Chrysanthes, to suffer condign <note>meaning "fitting" or "deserved."</note> pain and to be punished as is my duty, for I alone am guilty of everything." Then, being driven to despair, in the presence of the entire common multitude, I struck myself with a knife in the breast <note>original: "estomach"; often used in early modern French to refer to the general chest or heart area.</note>, and miserably gave my life as a prey, to be buried with this other body. Farewell.

Whoever you are who comes here to read me, beware if you love: and if you do not love, think (miserable one) that without love there is nothing sweet. But in seeking this sweetness, I have inconsiderately lost myself. Love also was the cause. I was on a horse, and desired with all my heart to please Dyruionia, a young maiden of perfect beauty: so I fell by misfortune, my foot remaining in the stirrup: whereby I was dragged and put to death.

Below the throne, on a plinth, were four gilded copper lion's paws that supported an antique chest, serving as a bench, and it seemed to be covered with a cloth of figured gold. ->THE INESTIMABLE MAUSOLEUM.<-
<note>original Greek: "ΜΑΙΣΟΛΑΙΟΝ ΑΤΙΜΙΤΟΝ" — While the French text translates this as "The Mausoleum without honor," the Greek word "atimiton" more accurately means "priceless" or "beyond value," referring to the magnificent tomb she built for her husband, which became one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note>
->That is to say:<-
->*The Mausoleum without honor.*<-

In her right hand, she held a cup, as if she wished to drink; and in the other, she carried a scepter, her hair hanging upon her neck and crowned with a closed, double crown, around which a portion of her hair was gathered and intertwined. In the corner of the vault of her throne, there was an oval shape within which was carved a crowned head, with a grave face, a long beard, and curled hair. This led me to guess that it was the true likeness of her husband, portrayed from life, held by two small flying children <note>Often called "putti" in Italian art, representing spirits or cupids</note> stationed upon the final molding of the vault. With their other two hands, they held a cord of gilded copper hanging below the head. On this cord were strung several small cylinders of the same material, like prayer beads. On the level of the final cornice supported by the square pillars, there was a plinth wider at the bottom than the top, adorned with its moldings; and above it was a round of gilded copper, where a black and shining stone <note>Likely obsidian or touchstone, often used in ancient monuments for its reflective quality</note> was set, decorated with such characters.

### BOOK ONE OF THE MIRROR OF LOVE. <note>original: "EROTOS KATOPTRON"</note>

->That is to say, Mirror of Love.<-

The golden circle was four fingers wide, made with small compartments and foliage in half-carving <note>original: "demy taille," referring to low-relief or bas-relief</note>. Higher than this circle, there was a man similarly made of gilded copper, standing upright in the middle of this <term>plinth</term> <note>the heavy square base supporting a statue or column</note>. He held in his right hand a spear, and in the left <note>original: "fenestre," likely a printer's error for "senestre," meaning left</note> an antique <term>targe</term> <note>a small, ornate shield</note>, engraved with beautiful sculpture. On the surface of the plinth were seated two small flying children <note>often called "putti" or cupids in Renaissance art</note>, completely naked, leaning their shoulders against the circle, and each holding a lit torch. Lower down there were two more similar children, also placing one hand on a ball, and with the other, holding the handle of an antique candlestick of gilded copper, shaped like vases.

The handles were two curved Dolphins, biting a knob of the candelabra: and their tails ended in a point on the swelling body or "belly" of the vase, which gradually decreased in size until the point where the mouth and opening were. Upon this opening were five points, namely four in a circle and one in the middle, higher than the others. The foot of the candlestick was positioned between the two legs of the child. All this sculpture was placed on a square of <term>serpentine stone</term> <note>a dark green stone with mottled patterns resembling snakeskin, highly valued for decorative masonry</note>, raised from the pavement without any moldings, except that I saw in the middle a trophy of maritime ensigns; and then I realized that it was in remembrance of the naval victory that this Queen <note>Artemisia II of Caria</note> obtained over the Rhodians. 

It consisted of the beak <note>or "ram"</note> of a galley, with part of the prow upon which was set a tree trunk, clothed in an antique <term>cuirass</term> <note>a piece of armor covering the torso</note>, with branches passing through the arm-holes. On one of these branches hung a small shield, and on the other, the handle of a pump for emptying the bilge-water. Beneath the cuirass were an anchor and a rudder crossed over one another. On the tip of the trunk that rose through the collar of the cuirass was a crested <term>cabasset</term> <note>a light, open-faced helmet shaped like a pear or almond</note>. All these figures were made with extreme perfection and beauty, worthy of being seen and celebrated in perpetual memory. I also believe they were carved by some of the same craftsmen who were employed at the <term>Mausoleum</term> <note>The Tomb of Mausolus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, built by Artemisia for her husband</note>.

->Whose meaning is as follows.<-

*Behold, passer-by, the likeness of me, Quintus Sertullius, and of my dear wife, Caia Rancilia, whom I took as a maiden; and then read what the fickleness of Fortune may do. In the flower of our age, when love has its greatest strength, we loved one another deeply. At last, with the consent of my father and her mother, we were both joined in marriage. But (O unhappy adventure!) on the first night, when we were about to extinguish—according to the law—the torches of insistent pleasure and offer our vows to the great goddess Venus: alas, in that very instant, the nuptial house collapsed upon our heads, and killed us even as we were embraced. Do not think, however, that the <term>Fatal Sisters</term><note>original: "sœurs fatales." A reference to the Moirai or Parcae, the three goddesses of destiny who spin and cut the thread of life.</note> have done anything new in this deed, for the hour of our destiny was no longer. Dearest parents, do not weep for our piteous death, so that by your mourning you do not make it more miserable; instead, may you live your years longer than ours. And you, reader, spend yours in joy.*

As I was reading of this piteous misfortune, I could not help but sigh. Turning my gaze, I saw another monument of white marble, placed between two columns carved from the stone in <term>half-relief</term><note>original: "demybosse." Beneath the vault sat a chest <insert>sarcophagus</insert> projecting outward; on its face were two doors. Into one entered several naked people, and from the other came small children, also completely unclothed. Between these two groups was a scroll which informed me that the chest signified this world, and its two doors represented the entrance through birth and the exit through death—though always accompanied by complaints, tears, and similar miseries. LIVRE PREMIER DE

### How this must be interpreted.

> *This is the monument of Trebia, daughter of Lucius Sextius Trebius: and as a memorial to her love and kindness, it was placed for her by Aulus Fibustius her husband, with whom she lived in great pleasure for only one month and three days.*

> *This dearest wife of mine has left to me, her sad husband, tears and perpetual mourning; for, driven mad by extreme jealousy and suspecting that I had been involved with another woman, she turned her sweet love into fury, such that she struck herself with a sword through her body. Alas, my dear love, why? My dear friend, you should have removed not only the act of jealousy from her who loved you, but at the same time the causes of suspicion. Now remain healthy and content; for my part, I am at my rest, quit and delivered from this life that is all too uncertain and unhappy.*

I then turned toward another semi-ruined gallery <note>original: "tribune." In this architectural context, it refers to a raised platform or a semicircular recessed area like an apse.</note> in which there still remained a small remnant of mosaic painting, though there was no tomb there. Among the figures I perceived Proserpina gathering flowers near Mount Etna—now called Mount Gibel <note>original: "mont Gibel." Derived from the Arabic *Jabal*, this was a common medieval and Renaissance name for Mount Etna in Sicily.</note>—with the nymph Cyane and the Sirens, her companions. Then I saw Pluto emerging from the top of the mountain through a great, burning maw, and how he ravished her, pulling her through the flames. Cyane watched her while weeping and was unable to help her; there the story ended, for even the figure of Cyane was not entirely whole. The wall was cracked and split open in several places, even pierced by ivy and the thick roots of wild fig trees. Nevertheless, I contemplated there with a steady eye a small river, which still had some slight appearance of human form, being only half-transformed <note>This refers to the nymph Cyane, who, in Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, dissolved into a fountain out of grief for Proserpina.</note>. And just as my mind was occupied in such pleasant contemplation, I felt something fall behind me, which frightened me somewhat, as I found myself alone in such a deserted place. Then, turning my head, I saw that it was a small lizard running on the wall, which had knocked down a stone. It was (certainly) a great displeasure to me that I could not see all that painting in its entirety at my ease, as most of it was ruined and faded because it had remained exposed to the open air for too long.

Musing, then, in this manner upon the abduction of Proserpina, I felt myself struck by a sad thought, which made me say to myself: "O poor, imprudent, and ill-advised man, full of useless curiosity, which is to amuse yourself with vain and past things. Why do you go seeking old, broken, and rotten stones? To what are you letting yourself be carried away? Now, if by misfortune your dear Polia were presently snatched from you, and if by your nonchalance you lost the treasure that you prize more than all the riches of the world, what would you do?" Saying this, I was seized by a fear accompanied by a terrible fever and pain, with a shiver so harsh that I could not hold myself upon my feet. <header>POLIPHILE.</header>

...as Aeneas had lost his Creusa while fleeing the great fire of Troy. And just the same, I had left my Polia far from me in a desert place by the sea. Alas, how I experienced in that hour the grievous anguish found in the condition of lovers. In truth, I was not so terrified even when I saw myself ready to be devoured by the dragon <note>Poliphilus refers here to an earlier episode in the story where he fled from a terrifying dragon in a dark forest.</note>; therefore my stay was not long, but I immediately abandoned that enterprise and began to run through the ruins and heaps of stones, among the briars and thorns, without regard for my napped robe <note>original: "robe pellée." Likely a robe with a fuzzy or velvet-like texture that easily snagged on thorns.</note>, from which shreds remained at every turn on the hooks of the bushes. For I had imprinted in my fantasy that I had come to my final misfortune, to my ultimate fear, and to the loss of all my hope. 

Thus running with all my strength, I happened to fall near Polia’s lap, out of breath, drowned in tears, half alive, and so lacking in courage and limbs that with great difficulty could I reach her. She was (certainly) a little moved to see me so greatly terrified, and she lifted me in her arms, wiping with a cloth my face all wet with tears, tarnished with sweat, and filthy with dust. Then she amorously asked me the cause of this accident, in words so sweet and so amiable that she could have raised the dead. Hearing this gracious request, I suddenly came back to myself and found myself in her lap, out of all doubt and unease. Then I told her my mishap point by point, at which she began to smile and kissed me softly, saying that soon Cupid <note>original: "Cupido." The god of love.</note>, our master, would come, and that meanwhile I should remain patient, considering that suffering is often the cause of great good. 

I found myself greatly consoled by these gracious words and such human remonstrances; therefore my Boxwood color <note>original: "couleur de Buys." Boxwood is known for its pale yellowish-white color, a common literary metaphor for extreme pallor caused by fear or sickness.</note> returned to its natural luster, and my excessive fear changed into firmness of heart, so much so that my eyes returned to their accustomed duty to live on their ordinary pasture <note>A poetic way of saying his eyes returned to their favorite activity: gazing at Polia.</note>. I had (certainly) stayed almost no time in this spot when Polia rose from where she was sitting, and inclining herself honorably, made a very gracious, humble, and honest reverence. Then she knelt down; at which I was completely astonished, for I did not know what moved her, and I looked at nothing else but her great and matchless beauty, with which my eyes were so occupied that it was impossible for me to turn them away. Nevertheless, I did for my part just as I saw her do, without knowing why or to whom, and I knelt down beside her. 

Then suddenly I perceived Cupid, quite naked, who was coming in a boat, and approaching the shore, turned the stern toward the ruined pier. My eyes could never endure the sparks of his divine brightness, but I was constrained to put my hand between them. Anyone can judge that I no longer thought myself among men, but in the company of the gods, seeing a celestial spirit in a visible body, which happens but rarely. I caught a glimpse of his head adorned with small curled hair, resembling little threads of gold, and two eyes decorating two small rounded cheeks of the color of a vermilion rose; and all the other parts so excellent in beauty that I would deem him very happy who would only have the power to think of it, let alone to describe it. He had (as a fleeting god) two wings of crimson color mixed with gold and azure, in the manner of a peacock's neck <note>original: "col d'vn Pã." The iridescent, shimmering colors of a peacock.</note>. Seeing this, Polia and I did not rise from our knees until he...

...began to speak: and I perceived that he marveled at the singular beauty of my lady, as well as her good grace and extreme sweetness. This led me to conjecture that in his heart <note>original: "courage." In this period, courage often referred to the heart or inner spirit as the seat of emotions.</note> he preferred her to his beloved Psyche <note>A reference to the myth of Cupid and Psyche; Cupid's love for Psyche was legendary for its trials and ultimate divine recognition.</note>, and esteemed her more beautiful and far more gracious beyond comparison. Then, with a divine voice (which can reunite and reassemble all things divided, strike down tempests, and appease the wrath of the sea), this little god began to say: "Nymph Polia, and you Poliphilus, true observers of the amorous laws of the goddess our mother, and who but recently have made profession in her holy temple, I let you know that your devout prayers and sacrifices have come before her deity, and have been pleasing to her, such that by your orations and voluntary service, you have obtained from her a happy end and fulfillment of your amorous desires. Now, therefore, put yourselves under my protection and enter into my boat, without which no one could pass to the kingdom of my mother, and without me leading them there myself, who am the true pilot and mariner of this voyage." At these words, Polia rose promptly and took me by the hand without saying a word; then she entered the bark and went to sit in the stern, where I likewise placed myself next to her. As soon as we were embarked, the Nymphs pushed off from the shore and began to row. The bark had six oars, not coated with tallow or any other grease, but with a precious mixture composed of Musk, Ambergris, Civet, Benzoin, Labdanum, and Storax <note>These are all highly prized aromatic resins and animal fixatives used in luxury perfumes and incense during the Renaissance.</note>, incorporated in suitable proportion with wood of white and yellow Cedar. The ribs <note>original: "Corbans." Referring to the structural timbers or frames of the ship's hull.</note> were of Aloeswood; for which reason a more aromatic scent was never smelled. The nails were made of fine gold, and in their heads were inlaid many precious stones. The benches appeared to be of red Sandalwood, and the oars of ivory, the thole pin <term>scalme</term><note>The peg or pivot on the gunwale of a boat that holds the oar in place.</note> of gold, and the oar-straps <term>tropes</term><note>Ropes or leather thongs used to fasten the oar to the thole pin.</note> of silk. There rowed six beautiful damsels in the flower of their youth, dressed in a delicate, light linen, fluttering in the air, and of such a kind that when the wind made it cling to the body, one could see all the muscles and lineaments of their persons and their gracious movements. Some had blonde and golden hair, arranged in braids around their heads; others wore it blacker than Ebony growing in the Indies; for which reason it was a singularly refreshing thing to see the two opposites placed across from one another to be compared. Their flesh appeared whiter than snow, but especially in the face, the neck, the shoulders, and the chest. Their heads were surrounded by hair puffed out with beautiful cords and tresses made in the fashion of lace tied with tissues of silver thread, and fastened behind with a string of large oriental pearls, so much so that there was nothing in the world more exquisite. There were some adorned with wreaths of roses and other flowers, beneath which their hair flew about their foreheads, and they had throats smoother than fine Alabaster; but even so, they were decorated with a sumptuous necklace of precious stones. Their persons were cinched beneath the breasts to make the garment join the body, which the teats pushed outward, like rebels unwilling to be pressed. When we were far from the shore, the Nymphs ceased their rowing <note>original: "enfrenerent leurs auirons," literally 'bridled their oars.'</note> and turned their faces toward their master, who was at the prow, making to him the most humble reverence they could devise; then they sat with their backs to us. It was enough to make even **Diana** <note>The goddess of the hunt, famous for her eternal virginity.</note> fall in love, to convert the chaste **Hippolytus** <note>A mythological figure who rejected all romantic advances in favor of a pure life.</note>, and to force the hand of prudent **Pallas** <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom, who is usually represented as being above romantic passion.</note>, who is always armed. Consider, then, how it must have felt for mortals, who were so near to it, and so apt and disposed to burn.

I was, then, like the little fish born in warm water, which, when put into another to cook, can no longer heat up nor boil <note>Poliphilus uses this metaphor to suggest he is already so saturated with the "heat" of love that he has reached a state beyond which he cannot be further affected.</note>.

I contemplated the wings of this divine spirit, in which there were some downy feathers, trembling in the wind, and resembling the plumage of a sea-egret not yet left from the nest.

O, how beautiful and shining they were, of a gold color verging on red, and in other places on azure or violet! There were some tending toward emerald, the colors so well matched that it is impossible for painting to imitate them so naturally.

It seemed, to tell the truth, that all the jewels of nature had been brought from her treasury to sparkle in this place; for they shone like plates of fine burnished gold, hanging in the wind and swaying against the Sun, so that the water seemed to be painted with their colors, which were suddenly erased by the inconstancy of the waves spreading out in great circles.

...shrubs and bushes of Myrtle and Mastic shaded the clear and smooth water, within which they could be seen as if in the glass of a mirror, depicted in such a way that they seemed to be the natural plants themselves. Continuing thus our sweet voyage, commanded by the sovereign monarch Love—who acted as our captain, and who is found to be bitter in extreme sweetness, yet singularly sweet in grievous bitterness, and by whom he who is even slightly in his grace may call himself happy—I saw the marine gods coming to pay him due reverence. First came old Neptune with his indigo-blue <note>original: "barbe inde," referring to a deep, violet-blue color like indigo dye.</note>, scattered beard, holding his fierce three-pointed fork, and mounted in a chariot pulled by two great whales. Around him were the Tritons blowing into sea-snail shells, twisted in a thousand strange fashions. They had made trumpets and horns of them, with which they made such a tremendous noise that they caused the air to resound on every side. These Tritons were accompanied by an almost infinite multitude of Nereid Nymphs, mounted on beautiful Dolphins, who naturally follow the Greek wind <note>The "vent Grec" or Gregale is the northeast wind of the Mediterranean; ancient lore suggested dolphins enjoyed swimming with it.</note> and love the name of Simon <note>A reference to the classical belief that dolphins were attracted to the name "Simô," meaning snub-nosed.</note>. There was Nereus with his lady Chloris, then Ino and Melicerta in chariots formed from turtle shells. The old father Ocean arrived accompanied by his spouse, the ancient Amphitrite, and all their beautiful daughters. Following them were the river gods Eridanus, Cephisus, Sperchius, and Tiber riding upon a round globe. There also was the sorrowful Aesacus, dressed in mourning and lamenting in a plaintive voice for his dear beloved whom the serpent had bitten. Alcyone hurried there, complaining of the long absence of her friend Ceyx. The changeable Proteus <insert>us</insert> was drawn by sea-horses. The fisherman Glaucus was there with his wife Scylla, and several monsters: Hippopsares and Anthropsares <note>Literally "horse-fish" and "man-fish" from the Greek *hippos* (horse), *anthropos* (man), and *opsarion* (fish).</note>, half-horse, half-fish, or half-man and half-fish, went swimming, diving, and leaping upon the sea, which whitened with foam and roared around them as it splashed upward, so high that one lost sight of them. All of this was done to honor our great captain, whom all things obey. Besides this, a great number of Swans arrived, some moving upon the water and others flying around our boat, singing with great melody to give praise to our master and to salute or revere him as best they could. Certainly, although I was among all the delights one could imagine, I was quite astonished to see so many marine gods, goddesses, Nymphs, and aquatic monsters of whom I had no knowledge. And yet, it seemed to me that I triumphed like a victorious Emperor beside my dear lady Polia; I even felt perfumed with an inestimable scent and enriched by all the delicious treasures of the world. Therefore, I said in my heart: "This is what I have so long desired; here is my help, so long awaited. Now I consider well-spent all the labors, pains, and martyrdoms I have suffered in this pursuit. Blessed be the steps I have walked in this quest of love. All that, I believe, is less than nothing in comparison to the smallest part of the ease I feel at this hour." Never did Cynthia <note>A name for the Moon goddess, Diana.</note> have such pleasure with her friend Endymion, for whom she left the heavens, contenting herself to rest in a fisherman's boat; for my lady could put all the gods at her command. Thus I was between my two lords and masters, looking now at one, then the other, with an inconstant and unsure eye, because I could not have known how to make it stay still.

I often strove to look at our master <note>original: "patron," referring to Cupid as the ship's captain or pilot</note> with a steady eye, but it was in no way possible for me, for my eyes could not endure the sparking of his rays. ...singing as if through a crystal, many divine accents throughout their throats, which seemed like alabaster washed with crimson; and I have no doubt they could have lulled to sleep the cruel Cerberus <note>The three-headed dog who guards the gates of the Underworld</note>, or moved to pity the spiteful Tisiphone <note>One of the Furies, the goddesses of vengeance</note> along with her sisters, the infernal Furies. Afterward, I said quite softly: 

"O sovereign Cupid, my natural lord, you were once wounded by your own arrows through your love for the beautiful Psyche <note>A mortal woman whose beauty rivaled Venus and who became the bride of Cupid</note>, whom you loved as affectionately as any simple mortal man could. You were greatly displeased by the fraudulent counsel her perverse sisters gave her, for which reason you placed yourself upon the cypress tree in the dark cloud and took pity on her laborious anguishes. Use now toward me that same praiseworthy pity, seeing as you know by experience the fragile condition of lovers. Moderate a little your great assaults, unstring your bow, and put away your firebrands; for I am already quite consumed by love. Nevertheless, I can reasonably infer that if you have been cruel toward yourself, I should have no hope of obtaining mercy, nor expect any pity." 

Thus I forged in my understanding a thousand cries and a thousand feigned prayers; and yet I persevered like gold in the cement <note>A reference to "cementation," an ancient process used to purify gold by heating it with additives to remove silver and other metals</note>, through all the trials of love. I thought that although a good that is long-awaited is more savory than a pleasure quickly acquired and without pain, it is still true that every strong love seeks to reach its certain desired end. Shorten then, my lord, this waiting; anticipate this tiresome hope; for help arrives far too slowly for anyone who has need of it. Then I accused most-just Nature; for notwithstanding that she has wisely composed everything, yet I said she had forgotten or failed to assemble the *will* and the *power*. 

Meanwhile, we still made our way forward, and the Nymphs sang without ceasing, moving from the Phrygian to the Lydian mode <note>Ancient Greek musical scales; the Phrygian was considered exciting and emotional, while the Lydian was soft and mournful</note>, without any discord. But Polia sang a song of thanks for the graces she had received from them, and sometimes she asked me what I thought of that company. Then she told me all the names of these Nymphs, affirming that perseverance alone carries away the crown as a reward. At such a height of all solace, we arrived at the island of Cythera <note>The sacred island of Venus/Aphrodite, the destination of their voyage</note>.

Sailing then in this manner, not by the mainsail or the mizzen-sail <note>original: *borde ou artimõ*</note>, but with the wings of Cupid, which he had extended to the wind, as has been said. Polia and I, united in our desires, both longing to reach the place destined for our bliss with the greatest ease that human sense could ever feel or tongue could say, sighing with sweetness through love's fire: and heated like a boiling pot over too great a fire, which overflows its brim, we arrived at the port of the holy island of Cythera <note>The sacred island of Venus, goddess of love</note>, in the boat of Cupid, which was neither stowed nor burdened with ballast, but rocking lightly upon the waves, and fashioned as follows.

Of the four parts, two were used for the stern and the prow, and the other two for the midship <note>original: *mizane*</note>, where it was wider by a third part. The gunwales <note>original: *postices*</note> stood two feet high above the deck, and the benches stood one foot and a half. The hull and the sides were covered with plates of gold: which extended over the prow and the stern, raised in the shape of a crozier <note>A hooked staff, similar to a shepherd's crook</note>, and curving back in the manner of a scroll, in the center of which was a rich ornament of pearls. The thickness of these scrolls formed the width of the <term>Palsecalme</term> <note>A horizontal support frame for the oars</note>, made of the same metal, engraved with a frieze four fingers wide and adorned with precious stones, while the thole-pins <note>original: *scalmes*; the pegs that hold oars in place</note> were of ebony. The entire body of the ship was so well made that one could not see a single joint; rather, it seemed to be of a single piece, without any caulking visible on the surface, except for the composition I have previously described. This was the mixture with which it was pitched or coated <note>original: *espalmé*</note>, and the painting upon it consisted of <term>Arabesques</term> of ground gold.

This place was so beautiful, so pleasant and delectable, that eloquence itself would find itself too poor in terms, figures, and rhetorical colors, if it wished to amuse itself by describing it; any comparison would be misplaced, for there was nothing suitable to compare it to among the places I had seen before. Indeed, it was the true retreat of solace <note>original: *soulaz*—a term for joy or delightful relaxation</note> and blessed delights, fashioned into gardens, orchards, and small groves, arranged as the ultimate goal and finishing touch of all pleasure. There were no rocks, mountains, nor anything that could bring annoyance to the sight, the body, or the mind; rather, it lay as flat as a palm all the way to the steps of the theater, entirely planted as a garden with fertile and fragrant trees, watered by fountains and streams, along which there were "trips," traps, and little surprises to provide laughter for the people <note>These "surprises" refer to *jeux d'eau* or water-tricks, common in Renaissance gardens, where hidden nozzles would spray guests when they stepped on a certain stone.</note>. There were no dark shadows there, nor gloomy turns without light, because the climate was in no way subject to the inconstancy and change of the weather, nor to the danger of foul winds, heat, frosts, or mists; instead, it was always flourishing and healthful, dedicated to eternity, and producing all the goods that nature can make grow. Therefore, I deem it too high and difficult an undertaking to try to define it in our common terms <note>original: *termes vulgaires*—meaning the everyday vernacular as opposed to a divine or scholarly tongue</note>. Nevertheless, hoping that my memory will serve me with what it was able to retain, I shall try to describe it in a few words.

This region is dedicated to merciful Nature, as the habitation and dwelling of the gods and beatified spirits. It measures in circumference (as I was able to conjecture) about three thousand paces. Its situation is in the middle of the sea, which encloses it with clear water, without rocks, mud, or pebbles; rather, the bottom is sown with a mineral material as shining as crystal, mixed—in place of pebbles and other useless things—with precious stones of every kind that one could imagine. <image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a formal row of seven topiary trees trimmed into various ornamental shapes, including conical, spherical, and tiered forms. They are planted behind a thick, low-cut rectangular hedge that stretches across the foreground.</image-desc>

From this enclosure to the Theater, which is in the middle and at the center of the circular island, there is a good third of a mile. Then, from the center to this Myrtle enclosure, twenty lines are drawn at equal distances; at their widest point, these divisions measure one <term>stade</term> <note>A classical unit of distance; a Greek stade was roughly 600 feet.</note> and a fifth part. In each division is arranged a small grove of trees suited to the nature of the location and the disposition of the part of the heavens toward which they are turned. This division of twenty can easily be made upon a circle of ten angles <note>A decagon.</note> in this manner: Divide the circle into four by its two <term>diameters</term>, then divide the <term>radius</term> <note>original: "demy diametre"</note> in two, and at the midpoint make a point. Over this point, draw a crossing line that touches the other diameter at the point where it joins the circumference. Then, the space found between the radius and the point or end of the crossing line will be the tenth part of the circle; divide this in two, and you will have twenty.

These twenty divisions were separated by enclosures of **porphyry** <note>A hard, purple-red igneous rock highly prized in antiquity for imperial monuments.</note>, like latticework open to the light, fashioned into foliage and interlaced patterns two inches wide. These were supported by **white marble** pilasters six inches in diameter, projecting two inches on each side. Above these ran the architrave, frieze, and cornice, made of the same marble, except for the said frieze, which was made of porphyry. All along the pilasters climbed <term>Jasmine</term> <note>original: "Gensemiz"</note>, <term>Privet</term> <note>original: "Lysset," likely referring to a species of Ligustrum or similar hedge-plant.</note>, **Hops**, **Honeysuckle**, **Common Privet**, **Wild Vine**, and other herbs suitable for covering a trellis or arbor. In the middle of each of these partitions, there is a gate seven feet wide and nine feet high, all built to the same level.

In these twenty divisions are found certain groves of different trees planted in rows, as follows: In the first are **Oaks** of every species. In the second, **Firs** and **Larches**. In the third, **Boxwood** clipped into figures representing the **Labors of Hercules** <note>The practice of topiary—shaping living trees into statues—was a hallmark of Renaissance garden design.</note>. In the fourth, **Pines**. In the fifth, **Laurels** mixed with several small shrubs. In the sixth, **Apple** and **Pear** trees of all kinds. In the seventh, **Cherries**, **Wild Cherries**, and **Morello Cherries**. In the eighth, **Plum** trees. In the ninth, **Peach** and **Apricot** trees. In the tenth, **Mulberry** trees. In the eleventh, **Fig** and **Pomegranate** trees. In the twelfth, **Chestnut** trees. In the thirteenth, **Palm** trees. In the fourteenth, **Cypress** trees. In the fifteenth, **Walnut**, **Hazelnut**, **Almond**, and **Pistachio** trees. In the sixteenth, **Jujube**, **Service-berry**, **Medlar**, **Dogwood**, and **Whitebeam** trees. In the seventeenth, **Cassia** and **Carob** trees. In the eighteenth, **Cedars**. In the nineteenth, **Ebony**. Then, in the twentieth and last, **Aloes**.

Their length, extending toward the center, measures half of a third of a mile <note>Approximately one-sixth of a mile.</note>. There, all manner of beasts that nature could create wander about, except only for the venomous ones and those ugly to behold. And despite the fact that some are naturally enemies of others, they are nonetheless tamed and live in harmony together: namely, **Satyrs** with goats' feet, horned **Fauns**, **Lions**, **Panthers**, **Lynx-cats**, **Giraffes**, **Elephants**, **Griffins**, **Unicorns**, **Stags**, **Wolves**, **Does**, **Gazelles**, **Bulls**, **Horses**, and infinite others, which never do harm or damage.

And because the entire circumference of any circular or round figure is of the same measure as three of its diameters—specifically if the said circumference is divided into eleven parts, and one subtracts one of the diameters, the remainder makes two portions <note>This is a Renaissance method for approximating the value of Pi as 22/7. The author suggests the ratio of circumference to diameter is 3 and 1/7 (or 3 and 2/11 in this specific geometric division).</note>—the diameter of this voluptuous island measures one mile and two-elevenths in length.

Next is another circular enclosure, reigning all around the center, made of **Orange** and **Lemon trees**, which is a good eight paces high and one foot in width. It is so thick with leaves that one cannot see through it, because its branches are so tightly joined that it truly resembles a painting laden with fruit and flowers. In truth, it is a work all the more excellent because it rarely happens that men see the like.

Beyond that enclosure, one finds an orchard so sumptuous that the best mind in the world would not know how to order it, I dare not even say, but even less to imagine it; so far is it from being able to declare by what artifice it was conducted—a thing that makes it known that none other than Nature made it for her own pastime.

This delicious garden extends towards the center for a length of one hundred and sixty-six paces, half of which is divided into beautiful meadows; this division is arranged by alleys tending straight toward the center, and others traversing circularly, which are five paces wide. The first meadows in the first line of its square tending toward the partition can contain fifty paces. But the fourth line towards the center goes always diminishing, and upon it, the first of the second meadow takes its dimension or measure. By the same means, the third is squared, because the force of the lines tending to the center is the cause of the curvature, as well as the narrowing of the said meadows and the passages to go around them. Thus the squaring is formed, while the traversing lines remain totally whole.

These ways are covered with trellises or vaulted arbors. At each crossroads there is a **turret** <note>original: "tournelle"</note> seated upon four **Ionic columns** of white marble. On either side of the paths is a low wall having projections in the form of a pedestal or <term>stylopode</term> <note>The base or platform upon which a row of columns is set.</note>, fabricated from the same marble. Upon these rest the columns, distant from one another by three diameters of their base. Within the low wall, which is hollow in the middle, are planted **rosebushes** which fill and populate the space between the columns with beautiful greenery. Above these columns rest the **architrave**, the **frieze**, and the **cornice**, made of **Porphyry** as red as **Coral**. Then inside the square, at the position of the columns from behind, grows another rose plant which climbs above the architrave and entirely covers the trellis, which rises five feet in height, made with round vaults like hats. The straight ways or alleys are covered with white roses, and the round or traversing ones with red ones, smelling as sweet as possible. Between the first square and the enclosure of orange trees, a circular path is led; and at the level of each of these, moving toward the center, one finds in the enclosure a window corresponding at the top to the level of the low wall, which is only three feet or so high, and serves as a seat for the aforementioned columns.

These meadows are bounded by the river, which is enclosed within its banks, constructed from the water's floor to three feet above with masonry of beautiful <term>green marble</term><note>Likely *verde antico*, a dark green stone mottled with white, highly prized in the Renaissance for its resemblance to lush vegetation.</note> and of <term>Doric structure</term><note>The oldest and simplest of the classical Greek architectural orders, signifying strength and stability.</note>. It is restrained between these two walls, just as the <term>Tiber</term> in Rome once was by the will of the Emperor <term>Tiberius</term><note>The Emperor Tiberius (reigned 14–37 AD) was known for his extensive public works, including flood management of the Tiber river.</note>. The river is ordinarily clear, pure, and clean, without canes, rushes, reeds, or other weeds or shrubs, but is entirely surrounded by flowers. It issues from a living spring and flows with hardly any turns; it is then conducted through certain pipes made specifically to bring it into the <term>precinct</term><note>original: "pourpris"; refers to an enclosed area or the grounds of a manor.</note>, to water the entire place, and from there to flow out into the sea through small streams all around the island. For this reason, the river can never overflow, but remains always in one state, without rising or falling, because as much water as the springs disgorge, just as much leaves through the pipes. It is twelve paces wide and four feet deep. The water is so clear and so subtle that it causes no <term>distortion</term><note>The author is marveling at the lack of optical refraction, which usually makes objects underwater look bent or displaced.</note> or hindrance between the sight and its object; for all things are seen there even to the bottom in their proper form and nature, no larger, nor longer, nor curved, nor slanted, nor in any way distorted. The sand at the bottom is mixed with flakes of gold, and in place of pebbles, it is set with precious stones. Along the banks grow <term>Irises</term><note>original: "Glaieulz"; while literally "gladioli," in this period the term often referred to various iris species.</note> of all colors, namely blue, white, red, and yellow. Swans fly there in great flocks. On both sides are planted Orange and Lemon trees, at a distance of three paces from one another; but at one pace from the ground they begin to put forth their branches, which join with one another, forming a vault of foliage three paces high. The other higher branches are bent over the river, forming another vault in the fashion of an <term>arbor</term><note>original: "berceau"; a "cradle" or arched trellis of greenery.</note> for shade, which rises seven paces high from the water. The foliage is so thick and so even that one leaf does not protrude beyond the other, except when they sway in the wind, which gives them a singular grace. In short, everything there is covered with fruit and flowers: it is also a true home for Nightingales, who hide themselves within and hold there their most delightful and pleasant choir.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a narrow river or canal lined with trees on both sides. The branches of these trees have been trained to form a series of leafy, arched tunnels (berceaux) that span across the water. Several birds, resembling swans, are shown swimming in the water within this shaded architectural greenery. Upon the water run <term>Skiffs</term><note>original: "Nasselles"</note>, Small Boats, <term>Frigates</term>, <term>Brigantins</term>, and little <term>Galleys</term><note>original: "Fustés"; small, fast, light-oared vessels.</note> of gold, guided by young damsels who pull the oar and sail at their pleasure, crowned with wreaths of flowers and greenery, dressed in

saffron-colored gauzes, bordered with gold-thread lace, so delicate that one could entirely see through them their flesh, as white as <term>Alabaster</term><note>A translucent white stone often used in sculpture to represent perfect, pale skin in Renaissance literature.</note>. These beauties are belted beneath the breast, which is uncovered to the half-roundness of the nipples, resembling little apples; and the neckline of their gowns is of the same gold-thread lace, enriched with fine precious stones.

When I saw them, they were engaged in a mock battle for pleasure against several handsome young men who were rowing in similar vessels; this represented a kind of graceful maritime battle, for they grappled with and provoked one another as is usually done in such affairs. There, the young ladies showed themselves to be very stubborn, so that the boats of the men and the ladies often overturned; but above all things, the young ladies were intent on the <term>booty</term><note>original: "butin"; here referring to the playful spoils or trophies taken during their game.</note>, and immediately stripped all those who surrendered to them as prisoners, then ran to others, and sank the barks and vessels where they could enter victorious, crying and laughing so very loudly that it seemed the air would split and burst. The river is always full of all species of fish with golden scales and blue eyes leaning toward green, which are neither wild nor fearful, but so tame that it is a marvel. Some among them were so large that they carried the young ladies in this combat, where they tamed, pushed, and turned them about in the manner of agile horses; and this was done by means of the <term>fins</term><note>original: "aëllerons"; literally small wings or fins, used here as handles or reins to steer the fish.</note> which they had grasped. This troupe passed through a great number of <term>Otters</term>, <term>Badgers</term>, and other aquatic beasts, gentle and in no way harmful, such that it was an incomprehensible pleasure to see and consider. Seeing these beautiful pastimes, these great crowds and delightful diversions, it seemed to me impossible that the happiness of these people could ever be in any way troubled by disaster or misfortune; which made me desire with all my heart permission for my lady and for myself to perpetually remain in that company; for I did not think that in all the rest of the world there was more contentment, even though through the woods, orchards, and gardens of the island, I had seen an infinite multitude of other young men and ladies passing the time in singing, dancing, conversing, reading stories and books of love, others telling tales, or playing musical instruments; several also embracing one another and gathering flowers by the handful, and especially such couples who arranged each other's clothing to make themselves more agreeable to those who were the object of their thoughts. In short, this joyful assembly amused itself in all the manners of pastime that it is possible to imagine. Therefore I shall leave them there, to say that beyond the bank of the river there was a meadow of as great an extent as the preceding one, furnished with its enclosure of columns or <term>peristyles</term><note>A continuous porch formed by a row of columns surrounding a perimeter or courtyard.</note>, ending at the water's edge, which one crossed over beautiful bridges made level with the paths or alleys that led to the center of the island. In each alley there was one bridge, either of <term>Ophite</term><note>A green mottled stone, sometimes called green porphyry or serpentinite, prized for its decorative qualities.</note> or else of <term>Porphyry</term><note>A very hard igneous rock, typically purple or deep red, historically associated with imperial and royal prestige.</note>, and so on sequentially. But each of them kept its alignment according to the width of the path to which it corresponded, and was covered with the same greenery of <term>Orange Trees</term> of which I have made mention above. The shirt puffed out through the slits and cutouts. In short, it was a thing of inestimable value, and almost beyond belief; for desire and the desired, knowledge and possession, will and power, had joined together so perfectly that there was nothing to find fault with. Alas, my God, these offensive machines <note>A military metaphor: the narrator views Psyché’s beauty and attire as siege engines designed to conquer the heart</note> could easily capture any heart rebellious or contrary to love; indeed, they could subjugate all strong resistance, overturn and strike down all free liberty, and (what is worse) stain all continence, however stubborn it might be. Therefore, I frankly confess that the great love I bear for **Polia** <note>The narrator’s own beloved, for whom he searches throughout the story</note> was violently shaken by this, and I felt it take a blow; which made me say softly, sighing: "O Polia, my dear lady, hold your ground now. This passage is dangerous. Here are marvelous ambushes. I do not doubt that these are manifest thieves, who against all reason acquire immortal renown through their amorous incursions and pillaging—indeed, they are highly praised and cherished by those very people who are miserably tormented by them, so that it seems such outrages are requested and sought by them at every instance."

She was flanked by two lascivious young ladies, of impudent and dissolute countenance; one named Asynecha, who incessantly shook and turned in every direction to show her flightiness. The other, Aschemosyne, entirely naked among the others who were clothed, made it well known that she was utterly shameless and held no regard for her honor. She carried in one hand a golden sphere, and with the other she held her long hair so that it would not cover her backside. She walked with a lewd and shameless bearing, with her green eyes looking here and there, giving them neither rest nor relief. In the fourth rank was Teleste, dressed in fine scarlet, her tresses hanging down, fastened above the ears with a beautiful fine garland.

Following us came our mistress **Psyche**, followed by her damsels, who had brought the gifts. She was dressed in a rich cloak, fastened on the right shoulder with a rich clasp of large **carbuncles** <note>Deep red gemstones, usually garnets, which in Renaissance lore were said to shine in the dark.</note>, and in the middle a **diamond table** <note>A diamond with a large, flat top surface.</note> the length of a finger and a half and a thumb’s width, such that it was of inestimable value and marvelous beauty. Within it could be seen an engraving of Cupid wounding himself, and Psyche handling (unwisely) the arrow of mortal sting. In her right hand (which she held free of her cloak), she carried the golden arrow; and in the other, an antique lamp of oriental **hyacinth** <note>A precious stone, likely a zircon or garnet, prized for its orange-red hue.</note>. She had cast her cloak over her shoulder, showing the lining of crimped cloth of gold, and beneath it her border of goldsmith’s work, interspersed with precious stones, all in perfection. She wore a robe of fine silk, entirely closed, woven with gold thread, and belted beneath her breasts. The chariot of Cupid was drawn by two tame serpents, walking on four feet and extending their necks, attached by traces of corded laurel with silk thread; their breast-collars were of gold, all chased with leaves of the same, enriched with fine gems. They walked step by step with the gravity of a **Triumph** <note>A formal, grand procession modeled after the victory parades of Ancient Rome.</note>, and according to the order described.

<margin>Pastophores carrying the shrine-canopy. Trophigeres carrying the trophies. Pyrgophores carrying the towers. Osmophores carrying fragrances.</margin>
First came the **Pastophores** <note>original: "Paſtophores"; Greek-derived term for priests who carried sacred shrines or images.</note>, then the **Trophigeres** <note>original: "Trophigeres"; those who carry the spoils or symbols of victory.</note>, **Pyrgophores** <note>original: "Pyrgophores"; those carrying ceremonial models of towers.</note>, and those who carried the **fasces** <note>original: "faiſſeaux de verges & cognées"; bundles of rods and axes, a Roman symbol of authority.</note> tied together. After them came others holding torches and candles lit with beautiful white wax; and the **Osmophores** <note>original: "Oſmophores"; scent-bearers.</note> as thurifers, carrying censers and other perfumes, from which emerged an incredible scent. There were others who carried gold vases with narrow necks, full of scented waters, which they sprinkled over the bystanders like a fine rain. Then came those who played instruments, namely lutes, viols, rebecs, flutes, harps, **hautboys** <note>Early ancestors of the oboe.</note>, cornets, trombones, lyres, **shawms** <note>original: "chalemyes"; loud, double-reed woodwind instruments.</note>, and others of all sorts, harmonizing with the voices of the female singers who accompanied them, crowned with wreaths of flowers and leaves of all colors mixed with pearls and other precious stones among beautiful gold foliage. This produced a harmony so melodious that **Apollo** never made the like for the **Muses** when he sang with his lyre; nor **Arion** when the dolphin carried him; nor the **Sirens** to deceive the sailors. These beauties did not walk all together in a crowd, but in order, three by three, each in her rank, in the places assigned to them; such that I would consider any tongue, no matter its eloquence, foolish and over-presumptuous to undertake to express the smallest part of this triumph—the divine bearing of the beautiful nymphs, their singular beauties, their sumptuous clothes, their gracious countenances, and the abundance of treasures, riches, great delights, and pleasures, which by the special grace of Cupid I was permitted to see in that instant.

->To the last<-
