At the very end, and ahead of the serpents that pulled the chariot, marched two **Aegipans** <note>A mythological creature similar to a Satyr, having the upper body of a man and the lower body and horns of a goat.</note> or **Satyrs**, with goat-beards and cloven feet, crowned with flowers of **Satyrion**, **Cynosorche**, and **Enula** <note>These are types of orchids and the Elecampane plant, traditionally associated with virility and aphrodisiac properties in Renaissance botany.</note>. In the middle of the square pedestal, at its widest part, was the **Ithyphallic symbol** <note>original: "Ithyphalle"; a representation of the male organ, used in antiquity as a symbol of fertility and to ward off the "evil eye."</note>, or virile member, as well-depicted as one could possibly say.

The footing, the **architrave** <term>the main horizontal beam resting on the columns</term>, the bases, the **stylopodes** <term>the base or pedestal of a column</term>, the frieze, and the bands encircling the building were of gilded copper; all the rest was of white **Alabaster**, naturally and industriously polished. On the exterior, it had two orders of columns and two levels of arches, one above the other. The third level consisted of square pillars, the arches made in a semicircle with the addition of a seventh part of their width. The columns, set against the wall, emerged only halfway from the masonry; they were fluted and **cabled** <term>originally 'rudentées,' a technique where the lower grooves of a column are filled with a rope-like molding</term> from the collar of their base up to their first third. The capitals, bases, and **stylobates** (otherwise called pedestals) were of gilded copper. At the corners of these pedestals, specifically beneath their moldings, were dried **ram’s heads** with their wrinkled and recurved horns, from which hung several beautiful festoons or bundles of greenery. These passed beneath a round medallion set in the middle of the recessed square, likewise enclosed by moldings, within which was carved in half-relief a **Satyric sacrifice**. In this scene, there was an altar, and upon it a tripod supporting a brass vessel boiling over a fire; on each side of the altar stood a naked **Nymph** blowing the fire with a small pipe.

There **Cupid** descended from his triumphant **Chariot** to enter the **Amphitheater**, which was arranged in the manner hereafter described. The foundation, the architrave, the bases, the stylopodes <term>the pedestals or blocks supporting a row of columns</term>, the frieze, and the moldings circling the building were of gilded copper, and all the rest of white **Alabaster**, naturally polished and further refined by industry. On the exterior, it had two orders of columns and two levels of vaulting, one above the other. The third level consisted of square pillars, with the vaults made in a semi-circle, with the addition of a seventh part of their width <note>This refers to a specific Renaissance architectural proportion for arches</note>. The columns, leaning against the wall, protruded only halfway from the solid mass; they were fluted and "rudented" <term>from the French 'rudentée,' referring to cabled fluting where the lower part of the grooves is filled with a convex molding like a rod</term> from the collar of their base up to the first third of their height. 

The capitals, bases, and stylobates (otherwise called pedestals) were of gilded copper. At the corners of these stylobates, specifically beneath their moldings, were the heads of dried rams with their wrinkled and recurved horns, from which hung several beautiful festoons or bundles of greenery. These passed beneath a round medallion set in the middle of a recessed square, likewise enclosed by moldings. Within this was carved in half-relief a **Satyric** sacrifice <note>A scene depicting followers of Pan or Bacchus performing a ritual</note>, featuring an altar, and upon it a tripod supporting a vessel of **Brass** boiling over a fire; at each side of the altar stood a naked **Nymph** blowing the fire through a small pipe. Above this frieze, accompanied by its cornice, there was another story <note>The original French "voulture" suggests a vaulted level or a specific architectural tier</note> entirely similar to the first. And although the art of architecture requires that columns placed in a building upon other columns should be smaller by a fourth part than the lower ones upon which they are set, and even that the third level seated upon the second should diminish by a fifth portion, nevertheless this was not observed in this sumptuous and well-proportioned edifice. Instead, they were all of one size and thickness, whether high, low, or middle.

But to tell the truth, those of the third level were square and **fluted pillars** <term>Cannelez: decorated with vertical parallel grooves, a hallmark of classical columns</term>, protruding from the wall by a third of their thickness. Between two of these pillars there was a window, not square like those of temples, but arched, as they are made for private houses. The **royal cornice** was without recession or projection <note>original: "sans faillie ne forget"</note>, but above it there was only a small wall a pace and a half in height. 

All this magnificent structure was built of fine **Indian Alabaster** <note>In the Renaissance, "Indian" often denoted exotic or high-quality materials from the East; alabaster was highly prized for its translucency</note>, transparent like glass, masonry without cement or any mortar; rather, the stones were so well squared, joined, and locked together that one need not fear its dissolution, but consider it durable for eternity. Its surface was not blackened by smoke, scorched by the sun, nor weathered by rain, but remained in its natural and original polish, without spot or blemish in any of its parts. The space contained within the work a length of thirty-two paces in diameter. The width of the enclosure and the walkways running around it was eight paces. This division or partitioning of the building's roundness and its columns was first made into four; each quarter was divided into eight, which made thirty-two divisions in total: and as many columns in a circle: for a column was placed upon each eighth part.

The enclosure was vaulted with double vaults, which formed two paths or walkways surrounding the building. The middle pillars were closer to each other than those of the outer front, and there was even less space between those of the interior; just as lines approach nearer to the center, the more they tend to narrow. The space from one pillar to the next decreased in width according to the proportion of the curvature, while the height always remained at an equal measure. 

The pavement of these beautiful walkways was of **mosaic** <term>Musaique: decorative art created by assembling small pieces of colored glass, stone, or other materials</term>, and likewise the ceiling <note>original: "fons des voultes", referring to the underside or soffit of the arches</note> of the vaults was finished in the same fashion, so that the work of one corresponded to the other. All was made in compartments enriched with **antique foliage** <term>Fueillages antiques: stylized leaf patterns, often acanthus or vines, characteristic of Roman architectural decoration</term>, so appropriately and with such good grace that the whole seemed to be of a single piece, not of joined stones. Inside these compartments were portrayed through beautiful stories all the effects and operations of **Love** <note>Referring to the mythological power of Cupid/Eros</note>.

In this marvelous building, one could easily recognize the fine spirit, the quick discourse, the excellent art, the ingenious design <term>Deseing: in the Renaissance, this term implied both the physical drawing and the intellectual concept behind a work</term>, the profound knowledge, the marvelous diligence, and the supernatural invention of the good craftsman <note>original: "ouurier", referring here to the architect or master builder</note> who had [made it]...

made: for in comparison to this work, the sumptuous temple of Ephesus, the Colosseum or Amphitheater of Rome, nor any other structure renowned in histories were nothing or very little. But to return to my subject, when we arrived at this great Royal gate, all the nymphs remained outside, and only **Cupid** entered with **Psyche** his beloved: then **Polia**, I, and the nymphs who held us bound, after having passed the two vaults, entered into the space of the theater, which was paved with a single stone of **jet** <term>Iayet: a gemstone-like organic material (lignite) known for its intense black color and mirror-like luster when polished</term> all of one piece, round and whole, so black and so polished, that when the Nymphs leading us had pulled me inside, no sooner had I set foot upon it than it seemed to me I was stumbling into an abyss, and was plunged into a great dark and terrifying pit. However, the walls surrounding it made me somewhat recognize where I was. Nevertheless, fear made my steps falter, and my foot twisted a little. In this stone, the color of the sky and the clouds could be clearly seen, along with the walls that formed its enclosure, just as one sees in the sea when it is calm <note>original: "bonasse", a term for a dead calm sea</note>. In the middle of the square, directly above its center, was the holy fountain of the divine mother of our master <note>Poliphile refers here to Venus, the mother of Cupid</note>, excellently beautiful and well-adorned. But before describing it, I wish to speak of the incredible structure and arrangement of the amphitheater, which exceeded not only the grasp of my mind, but all mortal thought: and then say that it was miraculously built. The steps built all around the square began at the level of the pavement, and were in three orders, in each of which were four steps, not solid but hollow, being six palms high and two and a half feet wide, filled with earth and sown with all manner of flowers, which rose no higher than half the height of the next step. At the fourth step there were no flowers, but it was made for a passage or walkway, covered by a **cradled trellis** <term>Treille en berceau: an arched garden structure or arbor over which vines are trained to grow</term>, measuring five feet in width and one and a half paces in height; this trellis did not obstruct the view from the fifth step, where the second row began, a little higher than the others, keeping suitable proportion: and so with the others, both of the third and fourth orders: for the same measure was observed in all. The armrests or supports of the first walkway were of black stone, shining like glass: the second of **Spartopolie** <note>original: "Spartopolie", likely referring to a grey-colored marble mentioned in ancient texts</note>: the third of **Hieratite** <note>original: "Hieratite", a "sacred stone" mentioned by Pliny, possibly a type of hematite</note>: and the fourth of **Cepronite** <note>original: "Cepronite", another obscure mineral from classical lapidaries</note>: so glittering that it would have seemed to you, looking through the trellises, that it was the sky presenting itself to your sight, and not a stone wall. Upon the edge of these armrests, the trellis began to turn into a vault: the whole so well-conducted by architecture, that all the squares of the steps corresponded to the level of a line drawn from the highest to the lowest, by an excellent artifice, divine invention, and almost incomprehensible. Higher than the fourth trellis, there was a wall a pace and a half high and as much in width, hollow, and then filled with earth, surrounded both inside and out with a molding made of **Alabaster** as was the rest of the building, except for the steps, which were of **oriental Jasper**, of several colors confused and mixed together: and they were bordered at the top by a molding of fine gold. This wall formed the cornice of the amphitheater, within which were planted **Cypress trees** two by two.

...rafters, or the ends of golden joists, beneath the architrave, as if to support it. Beneath these trellises danced many beautiful Nymphs, and when they found themselves at the openings between two columns, they would then turn toward the fountain located in the middle of the Amphitheater and make a very humble reverence, yet without losing their cadence or interrupting their measure. They moved in opposite directions to one another; that is to say, those of the high and low trellises moved toward the right hand, and those of the middle moved toward the left hand, such that it seemed some were moving toward the place from which the others were returning. The instruments providing the sound were two Trombones or golden **sackbuts** <term>Sackbut: a Renaissance brass instrument, the ancestor of the modern trombone</term>, and four oboes called **High-voice**, **Middle-voice**, **Counter-voice**, and **Low-voice** <note>original: "Epiphone, Mesophone, Antiphone, & Chamephone", Greek-derived terms for the different musical registers</note>, signifying the treble, tenor, bass-counter, and high-counter. Of these instruments, three were made of **Sandalwood** <term>Sendal: Sandalwood, prized for its fragrance and fine grain</term>—one red, another yellow, the third white—and the fourth was of Ebony, adorned with gold and precious stones, all tuned in excellent harmony accompanied by the angelic voices of these divine Nymphs, performing wonders with the difference and diversity of tones pronounced in equal proportion, yielding such a very sweet consonance that my soul was entirely ravished by it. The Nymphs of the middle trellis were naked and displayed their persons, which were more finely white than snow. The others preferred to be richly dressed in various habits and ornaments of silk, of all sorts and manners of colors, together with cloth and linen of gold or silver—striped, curled, figured, shifting, and of every design that one could imagine. In truth, these objects seemed to be doubled, and this was because of the wall, which was so black and so polished that it represented them just like a fine glass mirror. Opposite the great gate, and directly facing it, there was a flight of seven steps made of **Jasper** <term>Jasper: an opaque variety of quartz, usually red, yellow, or brown, used here for its luxury and color</term>, continuing up to the level of the first trellis; and beneath it, in the wall, was made a small golden postern gate through which one entered onto the first vaults, and from there to the highest ones. Then each subsequent trellis also had its golden door, of similar material and workmanship as the first. The first order of the seats was divided in two by the staircase beginning at the bottom of the portal or entrance. The first of the aforementioned seats was filled with earth, as I have said, and sown with **violets**; the second with **white flowers**; the third with **velvet-flowers** <term>Passeveloux: the Amaranth or "Cock’s-comb," known for its velvety purple or red texture</term>. In the first of the third and final order, there were **Pansies**; in the second, **Marigolds** <term>Solsy: likely "Souci," the common marigold, which follows the sun</term>; and in the last, **Columbines** <term>Ancolyes: Columbines, flowers often associated with folly or melancholy in the Renaissance</term>. All these flowers were more fragrant than the best perfumes of Arabia; and furthermore, they are in no way subject to the change of seasons, but rather remain unceasingly in their beauty, springtime, and natural vigor, without withering or drying, nor showing any appearance of doing so. I watched, as if entirely stunned, the grace and majesty of this place, its excellence, the ingenious distribution, and the arrangement of all its members, perfectly suited to one another, along with all the particularities specified above, so much so that I remained confused and almost outside of myself, like one who, while dreaming, thinks he is dreaming, and is uncertain whether he sleeps or wakes. All my senses were occupied and circumvented by an inexplicable pleasure, and my heart was set ablaze by an ardent flame of love, lit by the matchless beauty of my best-beloved **Polia**—so that I no longer knew who I was, nor in what place I had been transported.

The Nymphs of the middle trellis were naked, showing their persons more delicately white than snow. The others preferred to be richly dressed in various garments and ornaments of silk, of all sorts and manners of colors, together with cloth and fabric of gold or silver, striped, curled, figured, changing, and in every device that one could imagine. In truth, these objects seemed to be doubled, and this on account of the wall, which was so black and so polished that it reflected them just like a fine mirror. Opposite the great gate, and directly in front of it, there was a flight of seven steps of **Jasper**, continuing up to the level of the first trellis; and beneath, in the wall, was made a small golden postern gate through which one entered onto the first vaults, and from there to the highest. Then each subsequent trellis also had its golden door, of similar material and workmanship as the first. The first order of seats was divided in two by the staircase beginning at the bottom of the portal or entrance; and the first of the aforementioned seats was filled with earth, as I have said, and sown with violet-colored flowers; the second with white; the third with **velvet-flowers** <note>original: "Passeveloux", likely referring to the Amaranth or Cockscomb flower</note>. In the first of the third and final order, there were **Pansies**; in the second, **marigolds** <note>original: "Solsy", likely from the Latin solsequium</note>; and in the last, **Columbines**. All these flowers were more fragrant than the best perfumes of Arabia, and yet they are not in any way subject to the change of seasons, but remain ceaselessly in their beauty, springtime, and natural vigor, without withering or drying, nor showing any sign of it. I gazed, quite astonished, at the grace and majesty of this place, its excellence, the ingenious distribution, and the arrangement of all its parts, perfectly suited to one another, together with all the particulars specified above, so much so that I remained confused and almost outside of myself, like one who, while dreaming, thinks he is dreaming, and is uncertain whether he sleeps or wakes. All my senses were occupied and circumvented by an inexplicable pleasure, and my heart set ablaze with an ardent flame of love, kindled by the matchless beauty of my best-beloved **Polia**: so that I no longer knew who I was, nor to what place I had been transported.

...quite close to one another; but from two of these Cypresses to the <margin>next ones</margin> there was a distance of three paces. Nevertheless, they were all of one height and thickness, their tops leaning toward one another so that they formed certain small vaults in the manner of pyramids. That is to say, the top of the first was bent together with the top of the fourth, that of the second with the fifth, and so following four by four, all interlaced in such a way that if one passed over its neighbor, the other then curved beneath the following one.

In each space between four Cypresses (which contained three paces, as is said above) there was a plant of **Boxwood** with beautiful pommels or round balls, decreasing in size—namely, the second smaller than the first, and the third smaller than the second. But all were so round and so uniform that not a leaf exceeded the others, so that it seemed they had been sheared and thus delicately tended <note>original: "mignottées"</note> on purpose. Between two Cypresses there was a **Juniper** plant, tall and straight, to fill the void from one vault to the other, with a tuft of leaves upon the point.

The poles, osiers, and all the other timber for the trellises were of fine gold. The first was covered with flowering **Myrtle**, bent over a gold **architrave**, supported by a vault resting on columns of the same metal. These had for their **stylopode** <term>stylopode: a continuous base or pedestal supporting a row of columns</term> or pedestal the fourth step, the floor of which (making the path and way beneath the trellis) was paved with a paste or cement composed of **Musk**, **Amber**, **Benzoin**, **Labdanum**, and **Storax** <note>These are precious aromatic resins used to create a fragrant walkway</note>, of a blackish color. Amidst this were fixed oriental pearls, all of one size and thickness, arranged in antique foliage in the form of a mosaic, intermingled with little birds—a work (certainly) of such great singularity that no other can be compared to it. This pavement seemed made to be trodden upon only by divine feet.

The second trellis was covered with white and red roses, and the pavement made of **Coral** powder, cemented, still retaining its luster and natural color, decorated upon its surface with foliage and antique flowers, the leaves of **Emerald** and the flowers of **Sapphires**, all equal and polished to perfection.

The third was of **Jasmine** <note>original: "Gensemy"</note>, and the pavement of pulverized **Azure stone** <note>Lapis lazuli</note>, of a celestial color tending slightly toward green, worked with Moresque interlacings <term>Moresque: a style of ornament featuring complex, intertwined floral or geometric patterns, often called arabesque</term> made of precious stones of all colors and kinds that nature can produce, mixed with flakes of gold born within the stone itself; so much so that it is impossible to believe the admiration, pleasure, and contentment this gave to the beholders. I have no doubt that the celestial spirits would be satisfied by it, and what is more, marveled at it as well, for it surpasses all that was ever devised by men.

I gazed as if stunned at the grace and majesty of this place, its excellence, the ingenious distribution, and the arrangement of all its members, perfectly harmonized with one another, together with all the details specified above; I remained so confused and almost beside myself, like one who, while dreaming, thinks he is dreaming, and is uncertain whether he sleeps or wakes. All my senses were occupied and surrounded by an inexplicable pleasure, and my heart set ablaze by an ardent flame of love, kindled by the matchless beauty of my best beloved **Polia**, so that I no longer knew who I was, nor to what place I had been transported.

Courteously and in all reverence, Polia and I knelt before the holy fountain, where I felt myself assailed by a sweetness, the quality of which I could not well discern, being overcome with amazement and as if ravished in ecstasy seeing these Nymphs and listening to their harmonious songs, which exceeded without comparison all those I had been accustomed to hearing. Without any doubt, my body was consumed with extreme pleasure while contemplating their graceful manners and admirable countenances, even while gazing upon a structure of such high magnificence and thinking of its inestimable invention and arrangement, so that I was entirely steeped in these scents of exquisite and celestial perfumes, uncertain upon which of my senses I should then focus, and to which of the pleasures I should most apply or cling, because they were all distracted, each to its own object, which caused me all the greater pleasure as I saw my dear Polia participating with me in the fruit of this divine happiness; joined also that I found myself near a fountain so noble and so renowned, excellently constructed in the middle of this superb building, as I am about to describe it.

The fourth was of Ruby, the fifth of Topaz representing the color of gold, the sixth of Jasper, and the seventh of Beryl, tending toward the appearance of freshly made olive oil. This last one was hexagonal <note>original: "hexagone"</note>, that is to say, carved with six facets, corresponding directly to the middle of the entrance, between the first two columns: because in all angular figures that have an odd number of corners, one of them stands opposite the middle of the space between two of the other angles on the opposing side.

To form this seven-angled outline <note>A heptagon</note>, one must first draw a circle and divide it into four by a perpendicular line and a transverse line, which cross each other exactly at the center point. Then, with the compass, divide one of these quarters into seven equal portions; take four of these portions between the two legs of the compass, then step this measurement around the line of the circumference: and you will find it quite accurately divided into seven.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing the construction of a heptagon (seven-sided polygon) inscribed within a circle. Radial lines extend from the central point to each of the seven vertices of the polygon. At each vertex, a small circle is drawn centered on the corner. The entire construction is enclosed by a larger outer circle.</image-desc>

And, blinded by the affection and desire to see the goddess Venus, I broke the beautiful curtain; and in that instant, it seemed to me that I saw Polia change color and feel sorrow in her heart. Then, the majesty of the holy goddess was fully revealed to me, bathing in the fountain adorned with all the beauties that nature can imagine. As soon as I had cast my eyes upon this divine object, and at such an unexpected sight, Polia and I—moved by extreme sweetness and a long-awaited pleasure—remained as if ravished, losing consciousness and almost in ecstasy, filled with great fear and dread. I, in particular, was afraid because there came to my memory the piteous fortune of poor Actaeon <note>In Greek mythology, the hunter Actaeon was turned into a stag and torn apart by his own dogs after accidentally seeing the goddess Diana bathing.</note>, who, for having seen the goddess Diana bathing naked in the fountain in the valley of Gargaphia, was changed by her into a stag and immediately devoured by his dogs. For I feared that the same might happen to me. 

The goddess Venus was immersed up to her hips in the water of the fountain, which was so clear and so fine that the entire form of her body could be discerned in its natural perfection. This is contrary to the effect of all other waters, which represent all things plunged into their liquid as double, rendering them larger, curved, deformed, distorted, or diminished from their whole <note>Poliphile notes a lack of optical refraction; the water does not magnify or distort her body as normal water would.</note>. There sat that celestial body, resplendent as a Carbuncle <note>A legendary glowing red gemstone.</note> exposed to the rays of the sun. Her hair sparkled like small threads of gold and was twisted around her forehead, then hanging over her shoulders where it made a graceful fold, and from there descended to the water, upon which it floated all around the goddess. 

She wore upon her head a chaplet of small flowers mixed with precious stones; her eyes were loving and laughing, her cheeks rosy, her mouth small and delicate, her neck straight, round, and smooth, her chest high and polished like alabaster, and her breasts round with a great space between them. From her ears hung two large Oriental pearls, more beautiful and richer than those ever worn by Queen Cleopatra. To such beauty I could find nothing to compare among humans, for such a noble vision can be enjoyed only by the glorious and celestial gods.

Above all, it displeased me that among so many divine persons, I found myself a clumsy fool, poorly dressed and wrapped in an old, threadbare robe, impoverished beyond measure and of no value, different in every quality from this noble company. Then she called from the trellises **Adiachoriste**, with her three sisters, **Pistinie**, **Sophrosyne**, and **Aidosie**, whom she charged to accompany her, saying: “Never leave this woman for anything that may happen; and see that she be adorned with the firmest and most cordial love that ever was, so much so that it may be in perpetual memory. Give order also that she obey nature, without frustrating or defrauding it of its duty, but rather that she offer and present herself as an agreeable offering, in pure and sincere faith, to her true friend Poliphile, and be prompt to cordially desire and indissolubly love him.”

As soon as these Nymphs had heard the commandment of their sovereign lady, they came to us and each kissed the person who had been entrusted to her, feasting us with gracious words full of all sweetness and humanity; and consequently, they presented us their service with most affectionate courtesy.

When the goddess had finished her speech, her son <note>This refers to Cupid, the god of love and son of Venus.</note> notched an arrow and drew his bow with such force that with one hand he touched his breast and with the other the iron of the arrow; then he released it upon us with such power that it is not possible to recite it. Hardly had he let go of the string than I felt the <term>bolt<note>original: "vire", a type of heavy arrow used for crossbows.</note></term> pass right through my heart, and with the same stroke (the arrow still being all red and smoking with my blood) it struck into the breast of Polia, where it remained fixed, after having wounded me with a wound in which there was no longer any place for medicine, remedy, or any cure. This done, Cupid approached Polia and withdrew his arrow, which was halfway out. Then he washed it in the fountain to clean it of our blood with which it was soiled.

Alas, alas, I was at this stroke so seized by an excessive heat that spread all along my veins that I became clouded in my understanding. Nevertheless, I felt my heart open, and the figure of my most beloved Polia engraved there, adorned with her modest and praiseworthy virtues; and the trace was so deep that it is impossible to erase it; rather, it is a necessary thing that the imprint remain there all my life, and that my lady take such possession of it that no other may ever have a part in it, nor even pretend to enter. Upon me there was (certainly) no nerve nor artery that was not burned by this fire like dry straw in the middle of a great furnace, so that I almost no longer recognized myself, and thought I was changed into another form. Indeed, I wavered, unable to comprehend in what state my heart was. Yet it came back to my memory how the **Hermaphrodite** <note>Poliphile refers to the myth of Hermaphroditus and the nymph Salmacis, who merged into a single being with both male and female characteristics while in a fountain.</note> holding his beloved in his arms inside a fountain, felt and perceived two bodies becoming one. Wherefore my pulse was altered, and I breathed with great gasps, no more nor less than he who while sleeping...

Soon after, the goddess, joining her two hands in the shape of a hollow vessel, scooped up water from the fountain and threw it over us, so that our bodies were sprinkled with it, in order (as I believe) to wash and purify us from all other human affections. As soon as I was touched by this salty <note>original: "fallée," likely a variant of "salée" (salty), though it may refer to a ritual seal</note> liquid, my spirit awoke and returned me to my ordinary senses, so that all my internal parts, which were scorched and burned, were restored to their former state. It seemed as if I returned to myself, renewed and reformed into worthier conditions and qualities than before; or indeed, as if I were resurrected from death to life, just as the chaste Hippolytus <note>Hippolytus was a figure from Greek mythology who was restored to life by Aesculapius at the request of the goddess Diana.</note> was in times past at the prayer of the bright Diana. The Nymphs to whom I had been entrusted stripped me of my poor, worn-out robe and dressed me in a new one, all white, much better and more beautiful than my usual one.

Thus, after we were assured and certain of our love, refreshed, comforted, restored, and filled with joy, the Nymphs, our guardians, made us embrace and kiss one another; then they all kissed us, receiving us into their most holy college <note>A "college" here refers to a sacred society or organized group of attendants.</note>, into the work of secondary nature. Then the goddess, casting a gracious look upon us, spoke and amiably declared certain things which neither can nor should be repeated, and which it is not lawful to divulge to the common people, considering that they concerned the confirmation and strengthening of our love, to unite and join our hearts in a single will under the obedience of her fruitful laws, and to lead a long life of pure and perpetual friendship—even to make us firm, constant, and devoted in her service, promising her aid, favor, protection, and defense in all the accidents and adversities that might happen to us by fortune. This done, she also gave us her grace and holy blessing. 

Then, at that moment, from the golden door situated beneath the first trellis, there came forth a man-at-arms <note>original: "gendarme," here appearing as a divine warrior-figure</note> who descended the steps, coming toward the fountain, fierce in look and bold in countenance, but divine in majesty and of venerable dignity. He was large in body, with broad shoulders, a high chest, and thick, strong limbs. His head was covered by a light helmet with a crest, encircled by a wreath of flowers. He was dressed in a rich breastplate sumptuously crossed by a sash, from which hung a heavy <note>original: "psan," likely a printer's error for "pesant" (heavy)</note> scimitar adorned with gold and precious stones. He held in his right hand a flail and in his left a silver shield, with all the other ornaments and insignia belonging to a good soldier. After him came a wolf, all growling and snarling, following him step by step. 

When he arrived at the fountain, he suddenly began to disarm, and leaving his armor outside, he went in toward the goddess, who kissed and embraced him cordially upon his arrival. The greeting between the two was grand, and they shared a divine welcome. Seeing this, the Nymphs bowed humbly; then, showing their reverence, they took their leave, and we did the same, giving thanks to the holy goddess as best we could. Thus we departed from the place, leaving her to take her pleasure with her son <note>The "gendarme" is revealed to be the goddess's son, likely a representation of Cupid/Amor in a more mature, martial form.</note>, the man-at-arms, and others who resided continually around the fountain.

Now we departed from the theater in the manner described, changed into new qualities, and went out through the same gate by which we had first entered. There we found again all the Nymphs who had accompanied the triumph. For my part, I was completely inflamed with joy and affection, which was greatly increased in my heart, having forgotten all past pains, sorrows, and melancholies; I put behind me all anxieties, and steadied all my thoughts that were previously uncertain and doubtful, so much so that I no longer felt any difficulty in the love of Polia, whom I had resolved to serve and entirely obey as my singular lady and unique mistress: indeed, to love her more dearly than my own heart or my own life. All these gracious Nymphs placed themselves around her and me, surrounding us in a beautiful circle, and showing great pleasure that we had so well obtained our intention and fulfilled our wills, even that we had arrived at the true goal of our hope, the end of our desires and wishes. Then they led us, as if for sport, to see the beautiful places of the island, in marvelous pastime and recreation. 

Meanwhile, we passed along the paths divided within the gardens, covered in perpetual greenery and enclosed on both sides by a thick hedge of Boxwood <note>original: "Buys"</note>, three good paces in height, from which every ten paces grew a Juniper or a Myrtle, mixed together, each five paces high; truth be told, there were other passages enclosed with marble of similar height, but the thickness was only two and a half inches, entirely pierced through in the manner of a trellis, carved with antique flowers and foliage, mingled with Arabesque interlacings <note>Arabesque refers to an ornamental style of flowing, intertwined lines and floral motifs common in Renaissance decoration.</note>, through which several rose shoots passed, adorned with flowers, so neatly arranged that they did not in any way hinder the view of the workmanship. In this manner the Nymphs walked us along, always holding us by the hands: and after several topics were raised and decided on both sides, some of them said to Polia that since she and all those of the company had a crown of flowers on their heads, she ought to gather one for me, so that I might be of their livery <note>In this context, "livery" refers to a symbolic uniform or badge of service showing that Poliphile now belongs to the Nymphs' company.</note>. Then she placed and set it upon my head, and so we went off frolicking through the meadows and groves, along the streams and fountains, in the shade of alleys covered with Roses, Jasmine <note>original: "Gensemy"</note>, Periwinkle, Lemons, Rosemary, Myrtles, Honeysuckle, and every other kind of greenery, adorned with suitable flowers. These were arranged and placed in order, each apart and in separate bowers, for the contentment of the eye—indeed, for all the senses, which were (without any doubt) invited and provoked by the beauty of the place and the air, which was so sweet that one could desire nothing better.

Finally, we arrived at another beautiful and clear fountain, leaping out from a large spring and enclosed by large stones of white marble, naturally polished and shining without any paint or artifice. Its water created a small stream, murmuring across a flowery meadow and bordered along its banks by all the herbs and flowers that thrive in moisture. The entire surrounding ground was covered with Chamomile and Periwinkle, mingled with their white and azure flowers, so graciously united in perfect equality that from afar it resembled a carpet of greenery, four good paces wide.

Afterward, there was a grove of Orange and Lemon trees, flowering and laden with their fruit, measuring thirty-six paces in a circle. They were all of the same height and thickness, separated by equal distances, so that from the branches of one tree to those of its neighbor there was exactly one pace's measure. This was done to receive the rays of the sun and to ensure the view of the sky was not totally blocked by leaves for those walking beneath. Beyond that, there was yet another circuit of Cypress trees, and consequently of Palms with their fruit, separated from the first grove by a meadow sown with tiny Marjoram, four paces wide.

The fountain was in the center, built with six angles <note>hexagonal</note>, measuring twelve paces in circumference, where the semi-radius of the circle forms one of the six sides. The grove of Orange trees was enclosed on the inside by a trellis of red Sandalwood, a foot and a half high, pierced with openwork in the manner of a lattice, carved with foliage in a Moorish style <term>moresque: an intricate, interlacing floral or geometric design</term> of excellent invention. Through the openings of this trellis were interlaced plants of Roses and Jasmine, which did not cover or hinder the view of the rich workmanship. Among the trees were all manners of singing birds, such as Nightingales, Larks <note>original: "Calandres"</note>, Blue Rock Thrushes <note>original: "Passes solitaires"</note>, Linnets, Canaries, Finches, Goldfinches, and Siskins.

At the entrance adjoining the fountain was a trellis as wide as one of the six aforementioned sides, and just as high in its masonry. The rest was two paces in height: specifically, one pace for the upright supports <note>original: "plomb ou perpendicle"</note> and the other for the vaulting. Its length was twelve paces. The parts of the trellis that should have been made of wood were instead of fine gold. However, the roses covering it were natural, yet far more fragrant than common ones. The pavement below was made of mosaic, using precious stones of every imaginable color, depicting beautiful stories. Along the sides of the trellis were seats of Jasper, finished with moldings, seven inches high and six wide. Then, in the middle of the pavement under the trellis, there was a rich sepulcher <note>tomb</note>, before which the Nymphs bowed, making a great reverence, as did Polia and I. The Boar that had killed him in a frenzy lay struck down. The goddess Venus was shown there in a faint, supported by the arms of three Nymphs who wept with her, and Cupid wiped her eyes with a beautiful bouquet of roses. Between Venus and Adonis, there was a round medallion similar to the previous one in both material and workmanship; but the letters with which it was adorned contained nothing but this Greek word, **ΑΔΩΝΙΑ** <note>Original: "ΑΔΩΝΙΑ" (Adonia). In this context, the author interprets it as "pleasure," though it historically refers to the festivals held in honor of Adonis.</note>, which signifies pleasure. This pitiful event was represented so vividly in sculpture that, while looking at it, heavy tears were forced to fall from my eyes.

The upper side of the masonry was set perfectly level with the edge of the fountain, and in the middle, a small cavern was hollowed out between the stones, which appeared to be half-open. Inside was a large serpent of bronze or gilded copper, emerging from the depths of the cavern and gliding on its belly in a winding, wave-like motion. Its head was slightly outside the opening that released the water into the basin; the ingenious craftsman had specifically made it curved in this fashion to moderate and restrain the flow of the water, which was too forceful. Had the water found a straight conduit and pipe, it would have leapt beyond the edges of the basin. 

Upon the tomb stood a high-relief statue of the goddess Venus, life-sized, carved from a fine three-colored Sardonyx <note>A variety of onyx with parallel layers of sard (reddish-brown) and white.</note>. She was seated on an antique chair, in the posture of a woman recently recovered from childbirth. The body of the goddess was carved entirely naked from a white vein found in the onyx, and was only furnished with a small linen cloth—carved from a red vein occurring in the same stone—which covered her below the navel along with part of her thigh. Truly, it passed over her right breast, which seemed almost to push it back. Venus had cast it over her shoulder, so that it hung behind her over the fountain, and on the other side down to the base of her seat. Certainly, it was crafted and draped with such great skill that beneath it, one could easily see all the muscles, joints, and movements of the person. 

She held her son in her arms, who was nursing at her left breast while looking at his mother, and she at him, so graciously that everyone took great pleasure in it. The cheeks of the goddess and the child, together with the small teat, were slightly colored vermilion, thanks to a vein in the stone that had been found in just the right place. It was (believe me) an excellent work, and (to put it well) miraculous, for in these two bodies nothing was lacking but a soul. The hair of the goddess was parted by a straight line made in the middle of the forehead, curled along the temples in the form of small rings, then tied behind in a bundle, from there spreading downward to the seat, where the tresses were held and caught in small waves of openwork <note>Original: "percées à jour," referring to decorative perforations in the stone to mimic airy curls.</note>, all the hair being carved from a vein of onyx suited to its color. She had her left foot drawn back slightly toward her seat, and the other extended to the edge of the tomb. There, the Nymphs, kneeling, kissed this foot with great reverence and marvelous devotion. ...and we find the rosebushes all in bloom, laden with roses as before, but they are white in color. On the following eighth day, we return there once again, and then the goddess commands us to gather all the roses we had scattered upon the coffin, to throw them into the fountain, from which they drift away downstream, carried along by its course. This done, she enters her canal to bathe: then having emerged, she goes to embrace the sepulcher in commemoration of her lover **Adonis**, weeping and mourning his death. We all join her in her grief, remembering how on a similar day he had been beaten by the god **Mars**, and how the goddess, while rushing all naked from the fountain to try to help him in his need, pricked her thigh among the rosebushes—the foot of which we have kissed <note>This refers to the ritual kissing of the goddess's foot, specifically where she was wounded while running to the dying Adonis.</note>. That is why, every year on the day mentioned above, she has the tomb of the deceased opened to perform a beautiful procession around it, in which **Cupid** with great ceremony carries the shell containing his mother’s blood, while we all walk along singing. 

Then the goddess, performing the office of the lead mourner, takes the bouquet of roses with which her son wiped her eyes while she wept near the body of her lover, whom the Boar killed. But it must be noted that this bouquet is always in its full beauty, without ever withering or fading: and as soon as her precious blood is brought out of the sepulcher, all these white roses (as you see now) are stained a crimson color, and become red in a single moment. 

In this order of procession, we make three turns around the fountain; and no one but the goddess weeps, as she frequently presses to her beautiful eyes that tuft of roses previously mentioned. Once the procession is finished, the holy relics are returned to their repository, and the rest of the day is spent in dances, songs, and other pastimes. On this day, one can easily entreat her divine grace and obtain the fulfillment of whatever requests one wishes to make of her. 

Opposite the tomb, there are five small steps carved into the same stone, by which one descends to the bottom of the fountain, which is paved with **Mosaic**. The water leaves it through an underground conduit, leading outside the first **trellis** <term>treilliz: a decorative latticework structure, often covered in vines</term>. When these beautiful **Nymphs** had made us fully hear this solemn mystery and explained its ceremony, they began again to play their instruments and sing in sweet music the entire story of that history at great length, composed in verse, exactly as it had happened in ancient times. They danced in a round around the fountain for some time; then, having finished their harmony, they settled down to rest on their knees upon the fresh greenery. 

And I, without further consideration, using a great freedom to which I was not yet accustomed, threw myself into the lap of **Polia**. But it must be noted that this bouquet is always in beauty, without ever wilting or withering <note>original: "fœner," meaning to turn to hay or dry up</note>; and as soon as her precious blood is taken out of the tomb, all these white roses (as you see now) are stained a vermilion color, and become red in a moment. # BOOK ONE OF

When Polia had heard the Nymph Polyoremene, she immediately rose to her feet with a stately bearing, her cheeks slightly tinged with a virtuous modesty <note>original: "vergōgne honneste" — a typical Renaissance expression for a maiden's blush</note>. She was ready to obey and satisfy the petitioner's desire, though she wished to feign a certain degree of ignorance regarding what was being asked of her. Yet she could not pretend so well that a small, half-restrained sigh did not reveal how she had been moved. This sigh truly passed through the very center of my heart—or rather, through hers, because of the great harmony between our two souls, much like what happens with two flutes tuned to the same pitch and chord <note>An evocative Renaissance metaphor for "sympathetic resonance," where one instrument vibrates when another nearby plays the same note</note>. Then, she softly cast her beautiful eyes upon all the ladies and, with humble confidence and a low, resonant voice, she courteously greeted them. Then, having made a gracious curtsy, she sat down again upon the grass, where after a short pause she began to speak in this manner.

The little grace that you will find in my speech (noble and singular Nymphs) will make you lose a great part of the pleasure that could be found in the history that you ask to hear: for I am sure that my voice will seem, in this divine company, like the cry of a cormorant among the song of nightingales. Nevertheless, the desire I have to obey your gracious requests—which I hold as commands—will make me take up a humble boldness to speak in your presence without regard for my insufficiency: for certainly, you deserve to hear this discourse from a tongue more eloquent than mine to achieve the effect of your intention. However it may be, I shall be greatly content and satisfied in my spirit if by my speech (though it be heavy and ill-taught) I can give you any recreation; and I hope that my promptness in obeying you may well erase all the faults that might occur in me while doing so. Since it pleases you (then) to hear the origin of my ancestors, and my destiny in love—which, by means of my low condition, could not reach the height of your knowledge, because a small candle cannot give off a great light—I will acquit myself of it as briefly as possible, praying you that if it is not as proper as is required for your presences, it may please you to excuse the fragility <note>original: "imbecillité" — in the 16th century, this term referred to general human weakness or physical frailty rather than a lack of intelligence</note> of a mortal woman, little practiced in such affairs. my predecessors have found themselves among those who, by divine disposition, were transformed into such springs—as once happened to the wretched Dirce <note>In Greek mythology, Dirce was tied to a wild bull as punishment for her cruelty toward Antiope</note>, who was first tied to the tail of a wild bull by Zethus and Amphion to avenge their mother Antiope, whom King Lycus, their father, had cast aside for love of Dirce. Similarly, it happened to the beautiful Arethusa while fleeing the romantic pursuits of the river Alpheus, who had seen her bathing in his waters. So too with Byblis, daughter of Miletus, who, being rejected by her brother Caunus whom she loved beyond reason, dissolved entirely into tears; and several others whose tales I will leave aside for now. 

O lamentable transformation! O unhappy and pitiful accident! O immutable, infallible, and certain decree of the gods! Will I be able to recount this to you in firm and whole words, without the interruption of sighs? Will I be able to refrain from complaining and lamenting in this holy place of happiness, where all mourning and sadness are forbidden and defended, and where tedious melancholy is unknown to the inhabitants? Do not be astonished then, O blessed Nymphs, if my speech is sometimes broken <note>original: "syncopé" — Polia uses a term suggesting her voice might fail or skip like a musical rhythm due to her distress</note>, as much for the regret of the misfortunes that befell my ancestors as for the difficulty of my first loves, in which you will hear of a strange and more than bestial feminine cruelty, which nevertheless reached the happy end you now see: the greatest, most loyal, and most perfect love that ever existed between two creatures.

In the time when the Romans dominated all that can be known of the habitable earth, the noble house and family of Lelius was in great power and renown, established in the principal estates and high dignities of the Republic by means of their virtuous acts and several victories obtained against the enemies of the Roman name. Now, you know that in that imperial city, brave and magnanimous men were worthily rewarded. From this illustrious race and house came a man named Lelius Sylirus, who was sent by the Senate as Consul to the Trevisan region and March <note>The "March of Treviso" was a historical administrative region in Italy</note>, which was called at that time the "Great Mountain." There ruled a rich and powerful lord named Titus Butanichius, who had no children by his wife Roa Pia except for a single daughter—beautiful in every excellence and endowed with all the other gifts and perfections of nature—named Trivisia Calardia. This Titus gave her in marriage to the Consul Lelius Sylirus, along with the tenth part of the Venetian country, which is a land enclosed by mountains, dewed with fountains and streams, furnished with forests and very fertile lands, and possessing all the other conveniences required for the pleasure and utility of a person.

<margin>Zygos, a yoke.</margin>

The nuptials were solemnly and sumptuously celebrated, and the marriage was consummated while invoking the goddesses Zygia <note>original: "Zygie" — an epithet for the goddess Juno as the patroness of marriage, from the Greek word for "yoke"</note> and Lucina <note>The Roman goddess of childbirth</note>, who so favored them that there proceeded several children, both male and female. The eldest of these was named Lelius Maurus, so surnamed for his dark complexion. The second was Lelius Halcyoneus; the third, Lelius Tipula; the fourth, Lelius Narbonius; and the last, Lelius Musilistre. The daughters were so beautiful that one would have thought them born in heaven, for on earth no beauty comparable to theirs could be found. The first was named Morgane; the second, Quitie; the third, Septimie; the fourth, Alimbrica; the fifth, Astorge; and the sixth, Melmie. However, the parents, ungrateful for the benefits of the aforementioned goddess Lucina—who presides over childbirth—and becoming proud of their beautiful lineage, began to believe their children were procreated by their own virtue alone...

# POLIPHILE

...perverted, without recognizing the blessings of the gods. Alas, who could escape fatal destiny and the inconstancy of fortune? Or (to put it better) who is he that can exempt himself from the incomprehensible counsels and judgments of divinity? Certainly, this befell them because of their ingratitude, just as it did to the wretched Niobe <note>In Greek myth, Niobe's children were killed by Apollo and Artemis after she boasted she was superior to the goddess Leto</note>, or the sorrowful Atalanta and her husband Hippomanes <note>A couple transformed into lions by the gods for desecrating a temple</note>—and worse still, because they compared and preferred their children’s beauty to that of our mistress Venus: such was their presumptuous and reckless audacity. 

After this beautiful progeny had exceeded the years of childhood, the common people, who were coarse and unrefined by nature, presumed that Morgane <note>original: "Morgane la fée" — Morgan le Fay, here integrated into Polia's Romanized ancestry</note> was Venus herself. They built her a temple below the city where she resided; she did not show herself except on certain appointed days when she allowed herself to be seen by the multitude, which was only once each year, and even then she was entirely disguised in a habit other than her usual one. 

Because of this, there was always a great gathering and assembly of these superstitious people, who flocked there to honor her. As a result, from that time until today, the title and name of Morgan the Fairy has remained in this place. On account of these idolatries, sacrileges, and enormous crimes perpetrated by human ambition, the gods—who never leave offenses unpunished and do not permit such insolence to run its course—were irritated that mortal creatures would illicitly compare themselves to them by usurping the honors that belong to the gods. 

Even the most holy lady whom we serve <note>Venus</note>, indignant at their outrageous boldness, took such vengeance against them that the gods struck that temple of abomination with lightning, along with the Royal palace that was quite near to it. Everything was burned and scorched, reduced to ash and coals. In memory of this, the place still retains the name of the coals, and is called Casacarbona <note>Italian: "Casa" (House) and "Carbona" (Coal/Charcoal)</note>. 

<margin>Casacarbona</margin>
This Morgane was transformed into a fountain, as were her sisters Quintia and Septimia as they tried to flee; and Allimbrica was burned quite near the others. In this manner was the Royal house demolished, consumed, and overturned into a heap of coals, retaining this name in perpetuity. 

<margin>Allimbrica</margin>
And from there came the poor Allimbrica, changed into a small stream. With the same punishment were Astorgia and Melmia persecuted, in that they were converted into beautiful running waters, as if seeking refuge and safety with their father Lelius Sylirus. He was also transformed into liquid humor and matter; augmented and increased by his daughters, he forms a very beautiful river, still watering that region today, which is called Sily after a portion of his name <note>The Sile river, which flows through Treviso</note>. 

<margin>Sily</margin>
Similarly, his wife Trevisa Calardie, along with her father Titus Butanichius and her young brother Calian, weeping for the piteous adventure and misfortune of their lineage, were distilled into the sources of fountains, fleeing toward their son-in-law Sylirus or Sily. 

<margin>Titus Butanichius Calian</margin>
The male children were not exempt from this divine fury: for Musilistre, the youngest, became a small rivulet that passes along the city of Altino <note>An ancient Roman city on the Venetian lagoon</note>, and from there goes to join his father. The two others were still infants in the cradle, and were not treated so rigorously. The eldest, named Halcyon, was changed into a small bird bearing his name and dressed in Royal feathers <note>The Kingfisher</note>; the other into a small worm full of feet <note>Likely a centipede</note>. Both remain always around the waters and rivers, forever seeking their father.

Then, in memory and remembrance of his mother, he built a noble and magnificent city there, which he situated on the banks of his father Sily <note>The river Sile near Treviso, into which her father was previously said to have been transformed</note>, and populated it with the inhabitants of the Taurisano hill. In this city, he reigned for a long time in singular obedience, peace, and plenty of riches, in good friendship and alliance with his neighbors, living in all happiness and prosperity. There he died gloriously to the universal regret and sorrow of all his subjects, leaving the city to his heirs and successors, by whom it was ruled and governed for many years afterward. Following the changes of the seasons, all our region was assailed and infected by pestilence, so much so that many people were afflicted by it, and died in great numbers, of all ages and all conditions: but the cities especially found themselves surprised by this danger: whereby everyone strove to save themselves, abandoning them to retreat to the countryside. Among the others then surprised by this contagious sickness, I was one of the first, it being perhaps the will of the gods for my future good. Thus in this my grievous and painful affliction, I was abandoned by all my kin, except for my good nurse <note>original: "norrice" — traditionally a woman employed to suckle and take care of children, often staying with the family as a lifelong confidante.</note>, who wished to remain until the fatal decrees <note>A reference to the Fates of classical mythology who determined the moment of death.</note> had disposed of me at their pleasure. Now meanwhile, and most of the time as I found myself pressed by the heat of this illness, I lost consciousness and understanding, so that I said many things out of turn, mixed with excessive complaints. Then when I was able to return to myself, I called to my aid the goddess Diana, in whom I had at all times singular trust, and I served her purely and with good devotion from all my heart, supplicating her that it might please her to help me in that extreme necessity: and to move her to do this, I went on vowing and promising that if by her sweet clemence I escaped from this peril, I would serve her in chastity all the remainder of my life. Very soon after this vow and prayer, I began to come into convalescence, so that in very little time I found myself, by the grace of the goddess, entirely healthy, safe, and cured. To observe it perpetually. And for this purpose, I was received into the temple of the goddess <note>The goddess Diana, to whom Polia made her vow of chastity.</note> in the company of the other religious virgins, with whom I attended the divine offices, and I renounced the world entirely. It had already been more than a year since Poliphilo had seen me, and he could not know in what place I was. Furthermore, he was completely out of my remembrance, as something of which I had hardly thought, and for which I cared very little. Nevertheless, he was no less troubled by it, but rather persevered in his obstinacy of loving me. Now it happened (I know not if his vehement imagination caused such an effect, as they say can happen, or if fortune was thus favorable and propitious to him) that on the very day of my profession <note>The formal ceremony where a novice takes their final vows to enter a religious order.</note> he found himself in our temple among those who had come to see the ceremony. And seeing that I was the one for whom this solemnity was being held, he remained then utterly distraught, although he took a little hope for having found me again, persuading himself that there might be some remedy for his situation. Nevertheless, he did not rightly know what he ought to do, except to look at me, and contemplate my hair, from which were made the snares <note>original: "lacz" — a poetic metaphor common in Renaissance literature where a lady's hair is described as a net or snare that captures the lover's heart.</note> that held him thus captive.

After I had, of my own will, bound and constrained myself to the vows of religion, I no longer allowed myself (except very rarely) to be seen by men, and I kept myself as much as was possible from showing myself to profane persons. But Poliphilo, determined to die in his fantasy, had nothing else in his thoughts except to find the means to see me, blinded by love and importunate desire. At last, he searched so much and used such diligent care that he found me alone inside the temple, where I had gone to say my orisons <note>term: "orisons" — archaic word for prayers.</note>. When I saw him enter thus undone and as if half-dead, all my blood suddenly changed, and I began to shudder and tremble, feeling myself cold as ice, which caused in me a spite and a hatred toward him.

Then he began to look at me piteously, all pale, mournful, and colorless; and after a long while, when he was able to speak, he said to me in a low and trembling voice: "My lady, in your hand lie my life and my death; it is in you to give whichever of the two shall please you. Either one will be quite agreeable to me provided it proceeds from you; nevertheless, your beauty, more divine than human (under which cruelty could not lodge), makes me rather hope to have life. Notwithstanding, if you would rather that I die, it is much better today than tomorrow; it will be so much languishing gained for me. For this reason I pray you (if my life does not weary you) that it may please you to preserve it for me, and you will have one man more to serve and honor you, who will cost you nothing but a little of your goodwill, without in any way diminishing or worsening your exquisite virtues. But if I am born of an hour so ill-fortuned that I am not found worthy of such a grace as to be received by you as a servant, have (at least) the pleasure that I die; and this shall be sufficient reward for all the pains and labors I have suffered on your account. Alas, My Lady, if it does not please you to have pity on me, I may well call myself the most unhappy of all lovers, and with good reason curse the hour that I first saw you, and even detest my heart which was so light to believe the simple report of my eyes. For God's sake, My Lady, do not make them liars. Use toward me the goodness and sweetness that they promised me from you; join in me hope with desire, for in you is supported..."

When I heard this discourse (O Nymphs <note>Polia is addressing the group of Nymphs who are listening to her recount her life story.</note>), I was more irritated than before, and out of spite I rose from my place: from which I departed very angry, without deigning to look at him at all, so far was I from having any will to answer him, for I held his words to be foolish and took them with displeasure. 

The next day, when I no longer thought of him, as soon as I had arrived at the temple, I saw him return with a face as sad as the image of death, with which he began to trouble me in the same manner as the preceding day, saying in a humble and low voice: "Alas, sovereign Mistress of all beauties, have you not thought of putting an end to the hard pains that press me day and night and constrain me to come toward you? Soften somewhat the hardness of your heart: moderate the obstinacy of your imagination: for your noble nature does not show itself to be rebellious: do not stain your virtuous character with cruelty, which is the property of beasts: consider that my ill proceeds from you: and though you have no fault in it, it should still displease you that another suffers when you can remedy it. Do not return to me (my Lady) evil in place of the good that I wish for you. Do not lose your praiseworthy renown for a simple whim and stubborn persistence unbefitting your noble sex and condition. Alas, if you could feel the smallest part of my grief—and if feeling it is too painful for you, at least to comprehend it through imagination—it seems to me that I would be greatly relieved; and if you do not deign to think of it, at least may it please you to believe that my words fail from a heart mortally wounded: for which I curse my unhappy fortune, and bless the love that consumes me for the most beautiful Nymph in the world. On her account, I would have reached my end long ago, if a false contentment that I feign in my thoughts had not maintained me in strength, by being furnished with gracious responses such as I desire, and which are necessary for the salvation of my life. But that lasts hardly at all: for I find myself immediately frustrated, and know that these are nothing but dreams and frivolous fictions. In these mutations and diversities my days pass, and I live a harsh and languishing life, always seeking the means to discharge myself of this heavy burden, to deliver myself from this hard subjection and servitude, and to flee this bond that is too sweet: but as much as I seek to escape it, by so much more do I find myself more roughly entangled: and the more I think to tear myself away, the more I see myself ensnared <note>original: "engluant" — literally "limed," referring to the practice of using sticky "birdlime" on branches to catch birds; a common metaphor for being trapped by love.</note> and plunging into indissoluble errors. Why does he deceive with such lures those simple lovers of easy belief, and who loyally trust in him? O all-powerful gods, he presents honey, and gives them poison. He gives them a gracious welcome, and then leads them to the slaughterhouse <note>original: "l'escorcherie" — a place where animals are flayed or skinned; Poliphilo uses this graphic image to describe how Love leads victims to their destruction.</note>, so much so that all his art is but pretense and simulation: so different and contrary are his effects. And I, who did not guard myself against him, have fallen into his ambushes and traps, where I have been robbed and stripped by him of all good, pleasure, and joy: for which I know not where to seek help except from you.

But I see in your face no sign of pity, giving no indication that my suffering displeased you: which makes me believe that you are consenting to the outrage he does me, and that the sweetness that shows in you is a bitterness hidden to the detriment of my life, which will not remain much longer with me: and in this I comfort myself. Alas, I may well call myself unhappy, since she who ought to have sustained it is the cause that it takes so swift an end. Ha, Polia, help me: for without you I cannot help myself.

Then, in uttering these words, he let out a great sigh, and fell as if dead at my feet, having lost the use of all his senses, except for his tongue, which served him to make long, anguished lamentations, more piteously than I have known how to tell you: and notwithstanding that, there was never found in me any spark of sweetness, no, what is more, not a single sign that his distress displeased me: for I did not deign to answer him a word, nor lower my eye toward him, but remained obstinate, my ears closed to his prayers, and more deaf than the solid rock, persisting in my fierce <term>feuere: archaic French for "fierce" or "haughty"</term> will: for which (as I have told you) his heart broke with grief, and he died of it.

Moving her story forward to this point, Polia could never restrain herself from letting out a small sigh: and sometimes while speaking, tears flowed down her face: which moved all the listening Nymphs to compassion for that piteous adventure caused by too vehement a love: who, turning their eyes upon me, blamed Polia in their thoughts, on account of her excessive cruelty. But desiring to hear the end of this story, after having waited a little while, they urged her to pursue and finish her tale. Then, taking a fine linen cloth that hung over her shoulders, she gently wiped her face: then having steadied her voice, she continued her speech in this manner. You have heard (O most happy Nymphs) a cruelty so strange, that there is no heart, however gracious it may be, that could in any way bear it. And I marvel how the gods deigned to be so merciful as to tolerate my obstinate ingratitude, and that they did not on the spot punish the iniquity of my spirit. not a single drop of tears, nor could my heart express the beginning of even the slightest sigh, and I thought of nothing else except reaching my lodgings. There is no need to ask (O beautiful Nymphs) if I found myself quite astonished, and surrounded by every fear: for immediately I began to hear that which I myself wished to cry out, namely: "Alas, unhappy, unfortunate woman!" This cry proceeded from a loud female voice accompanied by mournful lamentations. Soon after, I saw coming two miserable young ladies, naked and with disheveled hair, so that it was a sight of great horror; they stumbled and tripped often, by striking against the roots or stumps of trees. These poor women were piteously enchained with chains of glowing iron, and were pulling a chariot all seized with fire, by which their tender and delicate flesh was cruelly burned and scorched. Their hands were tied behind their backs, which smoked and sizzled like a hot iron cast into water, while they gnashed their teeth and let fall great streams of tears upon the chains to which they were attached.

These poor suffering women having come to the place where I was, I saw arrive around the chariot several cruel beasts, such as Lions, Wolves, hungry Dogs, Eagles, Ravens, Kites <note>original: "Millans" — a species of bird of prey, typically the Red Kite.</note>, Vultures, and others, whom this executioner stopped there—executioner, I say, not a child, though he showed the appearance of one <note>This "child" is Cupid, depicted here not as a playful cherub but as a vengeful deity punishing those who reject love.</note>: and after descending from his chariot, he untied these two poor martyrs: then with a sharp sword he pierced their bodies right through the heart. To this carnage ran all the aforementioned predatory beasts ready for their meal, and the child cut the two young ladies each into two pieces, from which he pulled the hearts, and threw them to the birds of prey, and likewise all the entrails: then he dismembered and quartered the remainder of the bodies: then these hungry beasts ran immediately to devour that tender feminine flesh, and tear it with their claws and teeth. Alas, I watched these miserable limbs, which still trembled between their gums, and heard the breaking and crushing of bones, so that I felt the greatest pity in the world. Never was there a more cruel butchery, nor a more piteous spectacle. O, what a strange manner of burial! Certainly, the memory alone almost makes me die of fear. Imagine, I pray you, in what a state I must have been, hidden inside this bush, distraught with terror: and you will judge that I must have found myself more dead than alive.

Sometimes I said, trembling: "Alas, have I been brought here by the will of the gods to be slain as a sacrifice? Have I deserved such a cruel punishment? What country so wild can produce and nourish such furious and fearsome beasts? What inhumanity can be compared to this? Never was such a thing seen or heard. Oh, horrible vision! Oh, event <gloss>by</gloss> far too hideous, miserable to think upon, and pitiful to hear. Alas, where have I come now? This is my last day." In this manner I complained sorrowfully, and dissolved entirely into tears, waiting from one moment to the next for these beasts to come and devour me. However, I took as much care as I possibly could to avoid being seen by this murderous child <note>This refers to Cupid (Eros), who in this allegorical vision acts as a judge and executioner of those who reject love.</note>, and I lowered my eyes to my chest, which was all bathed in tears, saying softly in a weak voice and with broken words:

"Oh, unhappy day. Oh, cursed and detestable hour. Oh, poor unfortunate girl. To what calamity have you <gloss>arrived</gloss>? Who ever saw a destiny so perverse? Oh, holy Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt and chastity. Polia is a devotee of Diana, which is why she initially resists Poliphilo's romantic advances.</note>, to whom I am vowed, is this the moment that must end my life in the flower of my age? Was I then born to satisfy wild beasts?" Thus I grieved, weeping bitterly, tearing out my hair, and scratching my face; and what increased my pain even more was that I dared not complain, nor even sigh, or open my mouth even slightly to give air to my heart, which was suffocated with sadness. And what is worse, I saw no way to avoid this manifest peril. Finding myself then in this extreme despair, and like a lost thing, I know not how nor in what manner I was carried back to the place where I had been taken, safe and sound, and without any harm, except that I was weeping and all tarnished with tears. # POLIPHILO

In what way I could have strayed from my path and been transported to an unknown place; in the end, all of this led me to presume that it was a portent of some misfortune prepared for me in the future. This thought troubled me with various imaginings and fantasies, so much so that I spent the rest of that day in great melancholy and full of fear, without knowing why. I reached such a state that I did not dare to sleep alone, fearing that during the night I would be molested by some visions or phantoms, just as I had been the preceding day. For this reason, I called my <term>nurse</term> <note>In this context, a "norrice" (nurse) was a trusted older woman who had raised the noble child and remained as a confidante and servant.</note> to keep me company, for I trusted her greatly. Thus, we retired and entered my bed together, where my heart still trembled and could not find peace. Nevertheless, with some difficulty, I fell asleep and was frequently awakened by terrifying dreams, especially during my first slumber, in which my weary and labored body was seized by a deep sleep. 

It seemed to me that I heard the door of my chamber being broken down, and I saw two tall executioners <note>original: "bourreaux"</note> enter furiously. They were filthy and poorly dressed, rough, cruel, and unpleasant to behold. Their cheeks were swollen, their eyes squinting and sunken, their eyebrows thick and black, and their beards long, tangled, and full of grime. Their lips were hanging, thick, and swollen; their teeth long, sparse, yellow, rusted, and slimy. Their complexion was deathly, their voices hoarse, their gaze spiteful and deformed, and their skin rough like <term>tanned leather</term> <note>original: "bazanne," referring to sheepskin tanned with bark.</note>. Their hair was bristly, greasy, half-graying, and resembled the bark of an old elm tree. Their hands were large, gnarled, and bloody, their fingers curved, their nails red and uneven, and their noses snub and full of mucus. In short, they truly seemed like cursed, wicked, wretched, and infamous men. 

Their bodies were encircled by ropes worn like sashes, and other tools of their trade, to show what they knew how to use. These great villains, frowning and looking at me askance, began to bray or bark, for they had no human speech. They said to me (flinging their hands upon me as if to seize me): "Come, proud and wicked creature; come, rebel; come, enemy of the gods; come, mad and senseless maiden, who despises divine graces and blessings. Soon a cruel punishment shall be inflicted upon you, as upon the evil woman that you are, and such as you saw done yesterday to two other perverse and proud young ladies <gloss>similar</gloss> to yourself." 

I leave you to imagine, oh Nymphs, what a fright this was for me when I felt near me two such monsters, who uncovered my head and seized me by the hair, wanting to drag me I know not where. I defended myself according to my small power, thinking to resist their effort; but it was in vain, for they were too rough. Therefore I began to cry out in a loud voice, "Alas, for God's mercy!" asking for help. But they took no account of it and pulled me more outrageously to drag me out of my bed, with insults and outrageous threats. And as they forced themselves to do this, such a great stench came from their bodies and clothing that no heart could endure it, combined with the horror of their deformed and disfigured faces. I was long troubled and molested by this unpleasant altercation, during which I struggled and twisted myself too roughly in my bed, so much so that I woke my nurse who was fast asleep. Nevertheless, she felt, and perhaps heard, some poorly formed and imperfect words; therefore, seeing me tormented in this state, she squeezed me in her arms.

Then I promised her to follow her advice, provided that I could be delivered from the great troubles and marvelous dangers into which I feared falling.
