As I had then vowed and dedicated my virginity to the goddess Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon, who was famously a virgin and the patroness of those who took vows of chastity.</note>, and had by profession bound and obliged myself to serve her all my life, the service of **Venus** <note>The goddess of love, beauty, and desire; the opposite pole to Diana's chastity.</note> seemed to me grievous and intolerable, as something entirely different and contrary to my first institution, especially seeing that I had declared myself her enemy and adversary. And if I now wished to take her side, it was a necessity to erase and abolish all other oaths, vows, and promises already made, and to forget and cast out of my imagination all contrary wills and opinions. Knowing this, my good nurse—desiring above all my health and fearing (as she said) that worse might befall me—to remedy it to the best of her power, used this speech toward me:

“My daughter, it is a common saying, and one seen through experience, that he who takes counsel from others in his affairs cannot fail all alone. For this reason, I pray you, take heed of yourself, and consider that through any simplicity, lack of consideration, contempt, or rashness of heart, you may have offended the gods. Certainly, there is no doubt that those who deny their power, or disobey them, are in the end sharply punished; and the punishment is all the greater because it has been long delayed. Therefore one should not be astonished if their Majesties are angered against any of you young ladies, who very often through imprudence and lightheadedness, or through a foolish and superstitious opinion that you hold, run into an infinity of errors. This has caused many to come to a piteous and miserable end, as I could prove by various stories, which would be too long to recite. Furthermore, you must consider that <term>Love</term> <note>original: "Amour." Referring here to Cupid, the god of desire, depicted as a powerful and often capricious tyrant.</note> is a cruel tyrant, endowed with such power that he wounds, burns, and consumes without any regard or mercy, not only mortal men, but (what is more) the sovereign Gods—even the great **Jupiter** who makes the rain and the fair weather. For what difficulty has he found (my daughter) in all his amorous enterprises? There is nothing so true as that he could not exempt himself from this servile subjection, but rather, to achieve his intentions, was constrained to transfigure himself even into the form of a beast <note>A reference to the many myths where Jupiter changed his shape to pursue lovers, such as becoming a bull for Europa or a swan for Leda.</note>. Now let us leave the other deities and speak only of **Mars**, who is ceaselessly armed in every piece: he never had the power to resist love, let alone defend himself—much less would I say, to rebel; a thing which, if he ever intended to do it, he immediately found himself bruised and sliced with wounds. Believe me (my daughter) that his power is great. And if he can outrage the gods, what do you think he can do against humans, who are tender and fragile, especially those he finds suited to his service, who—even though they are powerless and weak—have the audacity and presumption to resist him? Without any doubt, they find him more furious and inhuman than others who obey him with humility; and that makes me say that it would not be wisely done of you to think you could exempt yourself: for he himself was burned by his own torch <note>original: "brandõ" (brandon). The flaming torch is a traditional attribute of Cupid, used to ignite the fires of passion.</note> for love of the beautiful **Psyche** <note>In the famous myth of Cupid and Psyche, the god of love himself falls in love with a mortal woman, proving that even Love cannot escape the power of desire.</note>. When she was in the flower of her age, she was many times sought in marriage by several young gentlemen, and especially by one among the others who was equal to her in age, lineage, wealth, beauty, and grace—as brave, wise, and virtuous as possible. 

Nevertheless, she never deigned to condescend to him in any way, despite whatever prayers or promises he could make to her. Instead, persevering in this foolish **overconfidence** <term>presumption or arrogance (original: oultrecuydance)</term>, she passed the best part of her time (which is marvelously brief and scarce) without considering, my daughter, that there is nothing in this world more agreeable than the correspondence of equal and reciprocal love. In this manner, the damsel remained hardened in her detestable and perverse obstinacy until she passed the age of twenty-eight. seeing the malice of this foolish young woman, <note>Cupid, referred to in the previous section, takes his revenge here.</note> went and shot her with such a blow from his golden arrow that it entered up to the feathers into her fierce heart. The wound was so grievous and so perilous that it was impossible to remedy it. Then she began to long in vain for the sweet prayers and requests that this young gentleman had wasted while wooing her; but it was no longer possible to obtain them. Finally, the poor damsel, pressed by an intolerable heat, fell into an extreme fever and into a languor that brought her near to death. But the physician who was called to visit her—wise and very expert in his practice—recognized by the movement of her pulse that her illness proceeded from nothing other than an immoderate heat. <note>In the medical theory of the time, "love-melancholy" or "erotomania" was thought to be caused by an overheating of the blood and spirits due to unfulfilled desire.</note> Therefore, he ordered that there was no other remedy to save her life than to marry her immediately. Having heard this, the parents lost no time in exerting themselves to this effect; they found a gentleman of good lineage and great wealth, but already old and nearly at his final age, much more decrepit than he appeared on the surface, for he was thin and withered.

He had sunken cheeks, hanging lips, and eyes that were red, raw, and weeping. His hands were trembling and, on the back, resembled a sheep’s rennet; <note>The "caillette de mouton" refers to the wrinkled, pale, and veined texture of a sheep's stomach lining.</note> his nose was snub, snotty, and full of discharge; his voice was hoarse, and his neck wrinkled like the face of a marmoset. His gums were swollen and pale, where there were only the roots of two hollow teeth above and as many below—long, wobbling things in the front, gnawed by canker sores that had given them a yellow color stained with black. He wore a cap on his head because he was scabby, resembling the spine of a mangy dog. His robe was all covered in drool over his chest; he was bent over as if searching for his grave, <note>Original: "courbé comme cherchant la fosse," a common metaphor for the extreme stoop of the elderly.</note> and his beard was as coarse as the hair on a donkey's ears. The rest of his body was rotted and turned to dung; and when he moved his clothes, there came forth a smell of stale urine such that no living man could approach him. Never did this old man think of anything other than his greed.

I believe that on the morning of his wedding, the crows sang the morning-songs <note>An "aubade" is typically a romantic morning serenade; here, the nurse suggests crows—birds of death—sang because the groom smelled like a corpse.</note> to him, so strongly did he smell of carrion. The triumph was great, and the nuptials were solemnized with all pomp and magnificence. Finally, that "holy" night came which the good damsel had so greatly desired, hoping that then her desires would be satisfied, not considering the quality of the groom; for she was blinded by her affections and thought of nothing else but gathering the fruit of this gracious assembly, being totally inclined and abandoned to her sensuality. She lay down in an evil hour between the arms of this old man, who was colder and more frozen than the month of January; but she could draw nothing from it except a face all soiled by the saliva and spit of the elderly husband, who slavered like a hunting dog, so that the next morning you would have said a snail had crawled all over her beautiful face. Now it happened in the course of time that this sluggish husband, doting and exhausted, became more **jealous than an old monkey**, so much so that all the pleasures she received from him were nothing but threats, scolding, and other such furies. Then she began to recognize her misfortune, feeling shame and disgrace for her past faults, and grieving heavily—not so much for the cowardly and withered old man, nor for the fruitless marriage, but for the time she had uselessly spent, which could never return. Therefore, when she came to think of the ease, solace, and contentment received by other young brides lying in the arms of those they had loved, receiving the **reward** <note>original: "guerdon"</note> of their sweet affections through the fulfillment of their wishes, it was to her a worsening of grief, which tormented her all the more because this imagination returned to her memory at every turn. Finally, weary of the annoying ways and unbearable temperaments of this **old porpoise**, <note>original: "vieil Marſouyn" (sea-hog), a derogatory term for a coarse, ugly, or gluttonous man.</note> she fell into a melancholy so terrible that she wept incessantly, without anyone being able to cheer her with any pastime her parents could show her; for she took no taste nor appetite in anything, except in cursing her life and calling upon death to help her. From this she came to conceive a furious rage and enmity against herself, so great that she became the mortal enemy of her own life. To put an end to it, she one day secretly took a knife and plunged it into her stomach, like a woman abandoned by hope and confidence, a murderer of the body she should have held most dear. Alas, my daughter, if at the age you are now, such a misfortune happened to your person (as it might happen for some similar offense, from which, nevertheless, the gods wish to preserve you), I would die of mourning before my time. Alas, is there any calamity or misfortune in this world that could trouble me so much as if my eyes had seen you fall to the piteous end of this miserable young lady? Therefore, my daughter, know and hold for certain that the **wrath of the gods** is inevitable, and that sooner or later those who despise them are infallibly punished. Of this, the beautiful **Medusa** <note>The nurse uses a version of the myth where Medusa's transformation into a Gorgon is a punishment for her "rigor"—her coldness or refusal to return the love of her suitors.</note> can give testimony; because she used such rigor toward those who loved her, her hair was changed into living snakes. Because of this, she was afterwards shunned by the heroic figures who had sought her, even though she then followed them and desired their acquaintance. Thus, young ladies in this beautiful age where you are now, take little account of celestial dispositions and well-ordered causes, which induce and incline young people to fall in love at the time determined for it; this is a species of rebellion and disobedience. For it seems they wish to presumptuously resist the holy laws and decrees of **Mother Nature**, bringing shame upon her; for which, very often, it turns out badly for them. Ah, my daughter, our years, which are so short and brief, should be held more dear than all the treasures and **riches**

...and riches of the world: for our life is much more fleeting than the winds, and vanishes sooner than the bubbles that form upon the water when it rains. For this reason, one must take care to employ it well, and to gather the fruit when the season for it has come; for it is too late to think of it once old age has surprised us—which it often does accompanied by regret and repentance for having ill-used our youth. And then we strive to seek it out again, painting our faces, stretching and smoothing our dry and wrinkled skin by every means possible to us, longing for time past and displeased with the present, in which we are rejected by all, banished and deprived of the sweet looks, good cheer, and gracious conversation of young men, who know our true state and perceive well enough that we are young only in **painting** <note>Meaning the use of heavy cosmetics or makeup to hide aging.</note> but truly old in nature.

Alas, my God, youth thinks not at all of the end, because it seems so distant; and when it approaches, then the desire to live only increases. Therefore, my daughter, I pray you above all else, as you love your life, to take heed of these signs that have been shown to you, lest they be omens of the **wrath of the gods** <note>original: "l’ire des dieux"</note> conceived against you for some foolish opinion you have too obstinately maintained in the past. Without any doubt, it is necessary to appease them by amending your perverse will—if you have had any—and resolving to obey them henceforth in all humility. And if you have carelessly used their graces, see to it, my dear, that hereafter they may be content with you and your service.

Now, to accomplish all these things, and in order to better understand how you ought to conduct yourself, I am of the mind that you should go immediately to the temple of the goddess **Venus**, where you will address yourself to the **Prioress** <term>Prieuse: a title used here for a high priestess or superior of a religious order dedicated to Venus</term>, to whom you shall declare and confess point by point the reasons why you believe the gods are indignant with you, and what might be the cause of such threats made in the visions that have befallen you. You must not fail, as I tell you, to recount the whole matter to her word for word, revealing moreover all the faults and errors you might have committed. By doing this, I hope she will give you good and salutary counsel, so that you may avoid the doubts and suspicions in which you find yourself, and prevent divine punishments, if through misdeed or negligence you have deserved any.

...one must be virtuous and resist this first assault. Think a little to whom you have given yourself: and to what service you have bound yourself of your own free will. Thus I remained confused and uncertain, thinking of a thousand difficulties that presented themselves to my mind, so that I was almost in deliberation to persevere in my first purpose. Nevertheless, I was in less than no time diverted from it by **Cupid**: who, seeing that my heart wavered, set it ablaze with a flame more ardent than the first, which spread throughout my whole body, just as the mortal venom did in the entrails of the valiant **Hercules** <note>Hercules died in agony after wearing a shirt soaked in the poisoned blood of the Centaur Nessus; Polia uses this to describe the burning intensity of her newfound passion.</note> by the shirt stained with the blood of the Centaur **Nessus**, when he approached the fire to make a sacrifice. All my senses were suborned and moved from their severe intention at the suggestion of **Love**, who drove from me all doubts and variable thoughts, drawing to himself my soul and all my affection.

Then my heart turned toward my **Poliphile**, and I began to desire him most ardently, greatly displeased by what had happened to him. Then after several doubts, fears, difficulties, and diverse fantasies, I ventured to go see if he was still where I had left him, in order to contemplate (at the very least) in death the one whom I had not deigned to look upon in life. Alas, it was a great regret to me to have borne a grudge against one who wished me so much good. I would have wished (certainly) to find him in his first state, that is to say, alive, healthy, and of good will. On the other hand, I feared being surprised alone with a dead man: for (perhaps) the blame would have been imputed to me, seeing especially that a wrongdoer is frightened by a little noise and cannot hide their misdeed, of which they easily accuse themselves.

I was for a long time in this troublesome perplexity: but **Love** conquered fear, and made me follow the importunity of my desire, so that I set out to run alone to the temple where my **Poliphile** had remained: and as soon as I had entered, I did not go to kneel before the altar as I was accustomed to do, but ran straight to the place where he had been dragged by me, where I found him still dead and tarnished, colder than marble, since he had thus remained all the past night. Seeing him so greatly changed, I turned quite pale with fear and pity, which moved me immediately to weep, and to wish that I could be a participant in death with him, to keep him company in this final passage. So long did I continue my sorrow, that strength abandoned me, and I fell upon this body in a faint: but after having returned to myself, I took to saying:

"Ah, **Death**, who finishes all goods and all evils, all joys and all sadness, come to me I pray you, to join me with this man whom my cruelty and harshness have delivered into your hands, only for having too much loved this wretched woman—truly more than his own soul—just as he has well shown. Alas, it is he who held me as his good and perfect contentment. Am I not then the most unhappy person in the world, not being able now to find the end of this life? Alas, why does it last so long? Is my soul so enclosed within my body that it cannot find the way out? Ah, my eyes, you make me see dead the one you did not deign to look upon in his life. Where are you, **Death**, who follows those who desire you, and takes those who think to flee you? Now I truly experience your cruel condition. Ah, the cursed day that I came into the world: I was (without any doubt) born at an ill hour. Who is he who could say which of us two is more unfortunate, either this my friend **Poliphile**, most [dear...]"

...so much more perfectly fashioned, because the conqueror of the gods <note>Love, or Cupid, who is frequently described in Renaissance literature as the power that subdues even the highest deities.</note> who was present there, guided my hand and directed my work. Then I made a cord of green silk, woven with some of my own hair as a sign of perfect friendship, and sent it to him, praying him to wear it around his neck in remembrance of me, wishing by this to signify that his heart and mine were entwined and joined inseparably by an indissoluble and firm knot forevermore, inasmuch as I had elected and chosen him above all others to be my sole lord, master, and possessor of my person in perpetual friendship, making myself a servant to sweet thoughts. I was resolved and determined to cast aside all harshness, to leave behind those troublesome manners I used to have, to soften my rough spirit, to abandon my foolish opinions, and to change my silly and wild customs into gracious and humane conduct; from fearful and ashamed, to become a joyful and bold lover; to transform my disdain into welcoming affection; and to make my will, which used to be inconstant, firm and unchanging; desiring that of which I yet had no experience: totally subjected to the laws of love, and full of contentment for having won my beloved Poliphile, from whom my soul could not be distracted or separated; thus did I enjoy in thought the blessing that was absent in person. 

That same day, while alone in my chamber, I saw emerging through the windows which were then open, a chariot of ice, drawn by two white stags attached with leaden chains, upon which sat a lady crowned with a wreath of willow <note>Willow was often associated with celibacy and mourning; here it represents the cold, sterile chastity of the goddess Diana.</note>, carrying an unstrung bow and a quiver entirely emptied of arrows, who seemed very angry and aggrieved, looking at me sideways as if I had offended her; at which I was terrified, so much did she show me a wicked face. 

But suddenly I perceived another chariot of fire following and chasing her, drawn by golden cords by two beautiful doves; upon it sat a powerful lady <note>Venus, the goddess of Love.</note>, wearing a beautiful hat of roses upon her head, and before her a young flying child <note>Cupid.</note>, who held a lit torch <term>brandõ</term> <note>From the Old French "brandon," meaning a torch or firebrand used to ignite passion.</note>, with which he pursued that cold and frozen lady so long that her chariot of ice melted in the heat of the fire; and in less than a moment, both vanished into the air. When this vision had passed, I found my lap and the entire floor of my room strewn with vermilion roses and branches of myrtle <note>Myrtle was sacred to Venus and served as a symbol of love and immortality.</note>; which made me cast away all fear and take a strong assurance that this lady of the doves and her child had defended my cause; by which I was led to the final point of determined love and totally resolved to pursue my undertaking.

Madam, if the humble and devoted servants of the goddess mother of Love deserve to be heard in their requests, I beseech you that it may please you to receive the one that I wish to make at present, insofar as it is founded upon a perfect confidence of obtaining what I justly and with good reason pursue for my benefit: which is to find in this temple a remedy for all the evils <note>original: "maulx", referring to his emotional sufferings or heartaches</note> that I have endured. Now you have been commissioned in this holy place as sovereign minister to give order <note>to provide aid or governance</note> to those who with sincerity of heart invoke the aid of the goddess; and I am assured that your power is such that (by means of her grace) all discordant wills are by you reconciled and reduced into perfect union. LIVRE SECOND DE

## How after Poliphile had finished his SPEECH, POLIA IN THE PRESENCE OF the Prioress declared to him that she was ardently seized by love for him, and was totally disposed to please him: as a token of which she gave him a kiss; and the words that the Prioress said to her.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter E, containing a scene of a figure sitting in a landscape with trees and mountains.</image-desc>

In all my life it would not be possible for me (Poliphile, my dear friend) to sufficiently acknowledge and reward what you have done for me, nor to repair the great ingratitude that I have committed against you, except through pure faith and perfect friendship. Alas, I recognize and know for certain that the harshness I have shown you is the cause of the pain you have suffered for so long: and if, through my own regret, I could make amends for it, be assured that you would have to consider yourself satisfied. Now I confess to having failed, being deceived by a wicked error which has held me, more than I would wish, in a life full of sorrow and bitterness. But now I have taken an example from the greatness of your noble courage, adorned with the excellent virtue of love, joined to the perfection of constancy: by which you shall attain that which you have so long awaited. Certainly your perseverance will make you joyful and content. I can no longer hide myself: wherefore I must tell you that I am entirely yours, and I submit myself and my will to the discretion of your good pleasure. Know, friend, that Cupid <note>The Roman god of desire; Polia describes her change of heart as a physical conquest by the deity.</note> has so pursued my heart that it is constrained to retreat to you as its refuge and sanctuary, determined to give you relief from all pains and sorrows. I know well that many young ladies, for having been rebellious to their lovers, have met a most miserable end. And if it had not been for that, the so renowned Daphne <note>A nymph who fled Apollo and was transformed into a laurel tree to escape him.</note> would not have been converted into a Laurel. Similarly, Arethusa would not have become a fountain, if she had not refused the embraces of the god Alpheus. But through such offenses several others have experienced what it is to anger Love, and to contradict or displease him. Without any doubt, his power is so great that no force can resist him. Before him, it is useless to flee, to hide oneself, or to wish to defend oneself. Nothing in the world resists him, not even furious weapons, even if they were enchanted. And there is no heart so hard, harsh, wild, rebellious, or obstinate, that his arrows do not pierce through and through: wherefore (not without good reason) I, who am weak and without defense, must fear his fury: for after the blow, groaning would serve me little, considering that I would not be heard, any more than Narcissus who despised his lover Echo: nor like Syrinx <note>original: "Syringue"</note> who was changed into a reed for having been harsh to the god Pan. For this reason (O friend Poliphile) I wish now to conde-

Reverend lady, I have always understood that one of the principal virtues with which a man can be adorned is to know how to contain and govern himself during great occurring adversities; and this by moderating his passions and restraining the ardor of his spirit <note>original: "courage"; in this context, it refers to the seat of emotions or the heart rather than just bravery</note>, without allowing himself to be carried away into weakness <term>imbecillité: from the Latin 'imbecillitas', meaning physical or spiritual frailty rather than a lack of intelligence</term> through thoughtlessness and a lack of patience, considering that every good comes from suffering under hope, persevering until the end. But that is truly a high and difficult thing, which happens to few people. Nevertheless, when some attain it, they acquire praise <note>original: "loz"; an archaic term for honor or renown</note> and the reputation of the wise; they are even called constant, virtuous, and temperate by everyone. 

Now it is so that to reach this honor, from the very beginning of my undertaking, I proposed to suffer and endure everything that Love might wish to do with me, judging it a great folly to enter a combat with fear and faint-heartedness; whereas, on the contrary, there is nothing more invincible than the firmness of a man, who, in whatever presents itself, must not lose heart nor abandon his hope. And from this comes the common saying, that he cannot be esteemed virtuous who has not been tested in some difficulty of importance; for the perfection of a thing is known by its opposite <note>Poliphile refers to the philosophical principle that qualities like "virtue" or "sweetness" are only understood when compared to "vice" or "bitterness."</note>. If I had then acquired the love of this damsel without pain or trouble, I could leave her without regret; but great rewards are reached through hardship, and he who overcomes his enemy without finding resistance in him, lessens and diminishes the honor of his victory. 

Thus labor gives the good, and perseverance brings it to perfection. Nevertheless, my desire grew all the more as I had less means to see her again; and then I knew by true experience that the regret one has at being deprived of the thing loved is, beyond comparison, greater than the pleasure of having it at one's wish, inasmuch as nature does not rejoice so strongly in the perception of delights as it feels sadness when it comes to lose them. I certainly esteemed it as nothing to suffer for such a beautiful damsel; and death would not have been grievous to me if I had thought she would have been grateful for it. 

Nonetheless, I had some hope which promised me that I would see her again one day, and that my pains would find some relief: but that served only to increase my strong passion, which made me say between my teeth: "Alas, she is greatly wronging me; she ought well to know what I endure for her love; and it seems to me that she flees from me. One often fails through negligence in many intentions; even the common proverb says that a cowardly lover never had a beautiful lady-love <note>A variation of the proverb: "Faint heart never won fair lady"</note>. And even if I had the opportunity, I was still uncertain of her will, because one always holds as less certain that which one most desires. Also, I saw clearly that refusal would be my death; and there was more likelihood that I should be rejected than that there would be acquiescence on her part, seeing that I was in no way equal to a damsel so excellent, accomplished with all the virtuous qualities required in a gentlewoman of an illustrious house. to your renown, would make me the most contented man in the world. It is that it might please you to accept me as a friend, or (if I am not worthy of that title) at the very least to hold me as your servant. In doing this, Madam, I shall consider myself more than compensated for the loss of my heart, which has left me to follow you: and I shall no longer count the labors <note>original: "trauaux"; implying the physical and emotional efforts of a courtly lover</note> that I have endured while adoring you; which, certainly, I would have long ago made known to you, if my fortune had permitted it, or given place, time, and means to do so. Wherefore, seeing that I could not set things in order, and that my pains were always worsening from bad to worse, I wished to write this present letter to you, not out of audacity or rash presumption, but by the great importunity of love, which I cannot resist: joined with the fact that I estimate you so prudent that you will excuse my error if I have committed any by loving too affectionately. In truth (Madam), I do not presume so much of myself as to think I deserve your good grace. Even so, I dare to say that if love is paid with reciprocal will, I deserve that you wish me well: something which you could not refuse without charging yourself with ingratitude—and it cannot enter my imagination <note>original: "fantasie"; referring to the internal mental faculty of forming images or thoughts</note> that a damsel so well-born, accomplished with perfect beauty, and of all laudable qualities, could be devoid of pity: for without that, all other virtues do not shine at all in a person. The grace I ask of you (Madam) is of such small importance that in refusing it to me, you would do wrong and injury to your goodness, considering that I intend nothing else but that you wish to hold me as yours, and believe that I shall be such a one in heart and pure affection for as long as my life lasts. Beseeching you furthermore to add faith to the contents of this letter, and to think that there is a hundred times more than I can either say or write to you.

I thought indeed that after having read this letter, my lady would be somewhat moved by it, and show some appearance of friendship: but I lost my time, my labor, and my writing, no more and no less than if I had addressed it to a stone: for just as much gratitude would I have received. Nevertheless, considering that one does not fell a tree with the first stroke of the axe, a few days later I sent her another, the tenor of which was almost similar.

If my torment (Madam) were less than your cruelty, I would advise my heart to have patience. But since your inhumanity exceeds my martyrdom, I am resolved to abandon my life to whatever may happen to it. Nevertheless, in the meantime, I beseech you to tell me: what use is it to love you, since you take no account of it and hold me in indifference? I know well that it is not in my power to break the bond by which I am held: and the more I might strive to escape the net <note>original: "filé"; a snare or hunting net, often used as a metaphor for being "caught" in love</note> in which I am entangled, the more I would put myself in great distress, and would be unable to find the way out, no more than the fish that has entered into a weir-basket <note>original: "Nasse"; a wicker trap used for fishing</note>. For this reason, Madam, I am constrained to bend and bow before you, in whom consists my liberty and my salvation. Do not deny me your favor then: for if for lack of it I should come to die, as might easily happen, my death would be imputed to you as a great crime. Take then (if it please you) a little compassion for him who loves you more than himself. Alas, Madam, I believe it is not possible that this great Architect of the world's machine <note>original: "ouurier de la machine du monde"; a Renaissance philosophical concept of God as the master craftsman of the universe</note>, who has...

# BOOK SECOND OF

one might well say, and with good reason, that your perfections are as poorly employed in you as a treasure hidden in the earth, which is useful to no living person. No man will ever know how to speak of you, considering that you will depart this world just as you entered it, and not otherwise. Would it not then be better, and more honorable toward posterity, that you should leave a flourishing renown to endure perpetually after you, just as several noble ladies have done whose histories are read in all places, and who are and shall be esteemed most happy by means of their friends <note>original: "amys"; in the tradition of courtly literature, this refers to the poets, historians, and lovers who immortalized these women in writing</note>, who make them live without fear of death? In truth, Madam, there would be no memory of them if they had not rendered themselves amiable and gracious to those who sought them. As for you, I dare well say that Heaven never made one more beautiful, nor more accomplished, if you had set aside this harshness and rebellious manner which you employ, more by fickle opinion than by the instinct of your nature, which is sweet and humane of itself. It is true that the fault is mine for having elevated you only to destroy my life: and the worst is, that in thinking of it I harden myself in loving you. Alas, I have too lightly believed the report of my eyes, which did not consider your heart so well as your beautiful person. O God, who would have ever thought that such beauty was thus armed with rigor? Alas, I have felt the harm that could come to me from it sooner than I foresaw it. Do not allow, however, Madam, that I perish by your fault, seeing that you can remedy it: for the gods, who punish cruelty <note>original: "cruaulté"; in this context, the "cruelty" of a lady is specifically her refusal to grant her suitor any romantic favor</note> more sharply than all other vices, might be angered against you as for a thing repugnant to nature, which is made to love its like. For this reason, Madam, and since my well-being and my woe lie under your judgment, take pity on my languor <note>original: "langueur"; the "sweet sickness" or physical wasting away caused by unrequited love</note> which none other than you could alleviate: and you will do a thing which shall be rewarded by the gods both in this world and in the other.

Such or similar was the third letter I sent her, which was as profitable as the first ones: for I could have no response, word, sign, nor demonstration upon which I might build any hope, no more than if my writing had fallen into the sea. Nevertheless, I resolved to pursue my undertaking and die as her most affectionate servant, because I could think of nothing else. Quite often I spoke to her in my imagination, feigning to myself that we were conversing familiarly together, and that among other things I said to her: "Alas, Madam, you have a very hardened heart. It is too different from your face, which is so sweet, benign, and gracious. You would perform an act of great charity if it pleased you to save my life, for you can gain nothing from my death. It is enough for me that my service pleases you, and I ask for no other **guerdon** <term>guerdon: a reward or payment, specifically the romantic favor a knight or lover hopes to receive from his lady</term>." Thus I made my complaint by heart, changing my words in a thousand ways, composing responses and promises in the air, based upon the appearance of her sweet demeanor. In this I found myself deceived, for her heart was not the same, but rather steeped in I know not what false opinions with which young girls are ordinarily accustomed to being instructed—things which are afterwards difficult to remove from their imagination. Thus I was caught in this trap, as if unawares and ill-advised, and consequently subjected to this tyranny or miserable servitude of love, to observe its oppressive <note>original: "torcionnieres," meaning extortionate or unjustly harsh</note> laws, loving without being loved, serving without thanks, nor any hope of receiving a reward—and all because of a desire caused by an attractive look, which made me estimate that in the empire of Cupid all wills were equal, and that just as I had liberally given myself to her service, I should in like case be well treated and received.

Upon this, Madam, I conducted a trial without a judge and without a party <note>Poliphile describes his internal monologue as a legal "process" where he is the only participant</note>, and I condemned Love alongside my Polia as consenting and guilty of my death, capital enemies of all good, and worthy of receiving punishment for it. Then, soon after, I revoked my sentence and begged them for mercy. Most often I composed within myself a feigned and deceptive solace, enjoying in my thought that which in reality was forbidden to me, and my desire too useless: thus consuming my life in regrets and lamentations, searching everywhere for that which, having been found, worsened my pain more and more. Finally, after many wasted steps, fortune was so prosperous for me that I found this lady at the temple of Diana <note>The temple of the goddess of chastity—a place where Polia feels safe from romantic pursuit</note> one day when she did not suspect me, for she was accustomed to going there in secret. In truth, Madam, there would be no memory of them if they had not made themselves lovable and gracious to those who sought them. As for you, I dare well say that Heaven never made one more beautiful, nor more accomplished, if you would only set aside this **harshness** <note>original: "rudeſſe"</note> and rebellious manner that you use—more by a frivolous whim than by the instinct of your own nature, which is sweet and humane of its own accord. It is true that the fault is mine for having exalted you only to destroy my own life; and the worst of it is, that in thinking of it, I only harden my resolve to love you. Alas, I have too lightly believed the report of my eyes, which did not consider your heart as well as your beautiful person. O God, who would have ever thought that such beauty was thus armed with **rigor** <note>original: "rigueur"; meaning emotional coldness or severity</note>? Alas, I felt the pain before I foresaw the harm that could come to me. Do not permit, however, Madam, that I perish by your fault, seeing that you can remedy it; for the gods, who punish **cruelty** <note>original: "cruaulté"</note> more sharply than all other vices, could be angered against you as something repugnant to nature—which is made to love its like. For this cause, Madam, and since my well-being and my suffering lie under your judgment, take pity on my **languor** <term>languor: a state of physical and emotional exhaustion caused by unrequited love, a standard "sickness" in romance literature</term> which no one other than you can alleviate. You will do a thing for which you will be rewarded by the gods, both in this world and in the next.

Such or similar was the third letter that I sent to her, which was as profitable as the first ones: for I could obtain no response, word, sign, nor demonstration from it upon which I might found any hope, no more than if my writing had **fallen into the sea**. Nevertheless, I was resolved to pursue my undertaking and die as her most affectionate servant, because I could think of nothing else, and quite often I spoke to her in my imagination, feigning to myself that we were conversing familiarly together, and that among other things I said to her: "Alas, Madam, you have a very hardened heart. It is too different from your face, which is so sweet, benign, and gracious. You would perform an act of great charity if it pleased you to save my life, for from my death you can gain nothing. It is enough for me that my service pleases you, and I ask for no other **reward** <note>original: "guerdon"; a term from the tradition of courtly love referring to the favor or prize a knight hopes to receive from his lady</note>." Thus did I make my complaint by heart, changing my words in a thousand ways, composing responses and promises in the air, based on the appearance of her sweet bearing—in which I found myself deceived, for her heart was not the same, but rather soaked in I know not what false opinions with which people are ordinarily accustomed to instruct young girls, things which are afterwards difficult to remove from their fantasy. Thus was I caught in this trap, unawares and ill-advised, and consequently subjected to this tyranny or miserable servitude of love, to observe its **oppressive laws** <note>original: "loix torcionnieres"; legalistic language suggesting the "torturous" or unjust demands of Love</note>, loving without being loved, serving without thanks, nor any hope of receiving recompense, and all through a desire caused by an attractive gaze, which made me believe that in the empire of **Cupid** <note>the Roman god of desire</note> all wills were equal, and that just as I had freely given myself to his service, I ought in a similar case to be well-treated and welcomed there.

Upon this (Madam), I conducted a **legal trial** <note>Poliphile uses the metaphor of a "process" or lawsuit to weigh the "crimes" of Love and Polia against him</note> without a judge and without a party, and condemned Love along with my Polia as consenting and guilty of my death, capital enemies of all that is good, and worthy of receiving punishment. Then, soon after, I revoked my sentence and begged them for mercy. Most often I composed within myself a holy and deceptive solace, enjoying in my thought that which was forbidden to me in effect, and whose desire was too useless: thus consuming my life in regrets and lamentations, searching everywhere for that which, having found it, only worsened my pain more and more. Finally, after several wasted steps, fortune was so prosperous to me that I found this lady at the **temple of Diana** <note>Diana, the goddess of the hunt, was also the protector of virgins; the temple represents a sanctuary of chastity</note>, one day when she did not suspect me: for she was accustomed to going there in secret, and the best part was that she was alone. At this, I was so overcome that, in approaching her person, I lost my senses, my composure, and my memory, so that my tongue forgot its office, and I knew not what to say; rather, I remained for a long space of time as if lost. Nevertheless, at the end, I regained a little courage and said to her, trembling:

Friend body, my very dear companion, it is now time to rejoice, banishing from yourself all melancholy: for never did an Emperor acquire a victory more glorious than that which we, you and I, have obtained against our adversaries. You may find strange (my lady) the discourse that I have made of our misfortunes, and (perhaps) it will seem an incredible thing to you. But suddenly they rose, knowing the discourse was finished: during which Polia had occupied herself while speaking by making me a garland of flowers, which was found perfect along with her tale: and being still on her knees, she placed it on my head, of which the Nymphs greatly prized the fashion: but above all they esteemed her beautiful speech, her gracious bearing, and her more than admirable beauty, taking singular pleasure in hearing the noble source of her race <note>original: "race"; referring here to her lineage or family ancestry.</note>, together with the prosperous success of her loves which she had recited with such good eloquence, that it was impossible to do more. Soon after, the desire took them to return to their ordinary pastimes: wherefore they began again to sound their instruments, and to dance around the fountain: to which they called us, showing a very great familiarity and cordial intimacy. Then the dances being finished, they took their leave, and kissed us all one after the other, very happy with our company. Now, these Nymphs having departed, and Polia and I finding ourselves alone in this place full of felicity, you can think that we had enough to say: for we had never had such good leisure to declare the affections of our hearts <note>original: "courages"; in the 16th century, this often referred to the seat of emotions and the inner spirit rather than just bravery.</note>. However, I began to say to her:

"My lady, you have (I believe) sufficiently known the love I bear you, and how I have chosen you as the mistress of my heart, as the one without equal in virtues and beauty of all those I ever saw in my life: and you know that to acquire your good grace, I have passed through all the miseries that a poor lover can endure: so much so that from the day I first saw you, I have not had an hour of rest: but now that the inspiration of the gods has rendered you more tractable, and that your heart which used to be filled with cruelty has been moved to sweet mercy, I thank sovereign goodness for it, and beseech you that, all doubts and suspicions removed, our love may be unvarying, and our wills entirely in conformity." To which she replied to me:

"Poliphile my lord and friend, I pray you never to wish to recall past things, and to hold for certain that you are the sole guardian of my..."

heart: which you can recognize by my deeds and actions, considering especially that in the presence of so many Nymphs I have, until my dying breath, allied and given myself to you: truly so strictly bound that no other shall have a part; and just as you are the first, so shall you be the last. Having said this, she threw her two arms around my neck, embracing and kissing me so lovingly that I thought I would faint with joy. And for my part, I did no less, being overcome by such extreme pleasure that I knew not if I were in heaven or on earth; so much so that I almost did not recognize myself or my Polia, to whose face, by the sheer force of love, a vermillion color had risen, mixed with her natural whiteness, which gave her such beautiful luster that it was enough to make a heart die that was not subject to death. Meanwhile, and all in an instant, tears issued from her eyes like crystal, or small round pearls, such that you would have said they were drops of dew upon the leaves of an unfolding red rose at sunrise in the season of the month of May. And as I was at this height of bliss, that worthy figure vanished, rising into the air like a little smoke of benzoin <note>original: "Beniouyn"; a balsamic resin used in incense and perfumes.</note>: and she left behind an odor so exquisite that all the scents of Arabia Felix <note>original: "Arabie heureuse"; the Latin name for the southern Arabian Peninsula, legendary in antiquity for its perfumes and spices.</note> could not compare to it; which was the cause of my awakening, and it seemed to me that I heard her say as she passed, "Farewell, farewell my friend Poliphile."

# ❧ How Poliphile brings his HYPNEROTO-
## MACHIA TO AN END, LAMENTING THE DREAM
### *which was so brief, and that the Sun rose so early to break his sleep, as if it were envious of his happiness.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'J' (replacing the 'T' to fit the English 'Just') featuring scrolling foliate patterns and floral motifs.</image-desc>

Just as soon as this angelic spirit had vanished from my imagination, I awoke, weary and broken by the tight embraces with which she had held me, in my view: and I remained full of bitterness, seeing her absent from me, she through whom I ought to live, who led and raised me to such high thoughts. Thus abandoned by all my supernatural felicities, except for memory, I knew not whom I should complain of, if not the Sun, who (perhaps) being envious of my well-being, shortened that blessed night, notwithstanding that it was in his power to delay a little longer, just as he once did for several others <note>A reference to the Greek myth where Zeus lengthened the night he spent with Alcmene.</note>. Oh, how much I would have been indebted to him who had sent me the sleep that the beautiful Psyche carried closed in her box <note>In the myth of Cupid and Psyche, Psyche is sent to the underworld to bring back a box of divine beauty, but upon opening it, she is overcome by an infernal sleep.</note>! But (alas) at the height of this wish, I heard the sweet—
